It commonly appears in questions about whether something has been done yet (e.g., "Avete già + past participle?"). For one person formally, you’d usually say "Ha già..." (Lei). Word order can change with pronouns: "L’avete già trovata?" = "Have you already found her/it?"
target_language_example: Avete già finito di mangiare?
native_language_example: Have you already finished eating?

meaning: "have you ever" / "have you ever (not)" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used in questions (and sometimes negative statements) with the present perfect to ask about life experience up to now. It refers to "you" as voi (plural) or as formal "you" (e.g., to one person in polite speech). With negation: "non avete mai..." = "you have never..." / "you never...".
target_language_example: Avete mai visitato Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Rome?

meaning: “Have you ever eaten…?” (asking about someone’s past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask one or more people (voi) if they have ever eaten/tried something at any point in their life. It uses the present perfect (avere + mangiato) and often introduces a food you’re curious about: Avete mai mangiato + [food]? You can answer with: Sì, l’ho mangiato / No, non l’ho mai mangiato.
target_language_example: Avete mai mangiato il sushi?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) or to be polite/formal with one person (Lei) if they have ever heard something or someone before. Often followed by an infinitive (sentito + suonare/cantare...) or by a noun (sentito questa parola).
target_language_example: Avete mai sentito parlare di questa città?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of this city?

meaning: "Have you ever seen...?" (asking if someone has ever seen something at any time).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd person plural (voi) of "avere" in the present tense, used for addressing multiple people or as a polite/formal "you". It’s typically followed by a person/thing + an infinitive ("Avete mai visto Tom ballare?") or a noun ("Avete mai visto un orso?"). Often used with "prima" to mean "before" ("... prima?").
target_language_example: Avete mai visto questo film?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie?

meaning: "Have you ever seen a …?" (to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group (or one person politely with "voi") if they have ever seen something. "mai" = "ever" and usually goes between the auxiliary and the past participle: "avete mai visto…?" Change the article as needed: "un" (masc. singular), "uno" (before s+consonant, z, gn, etc.), "una" (fem. singular). With one person informally: "Hai mai visto un/una…?".
target_language_example: Avete mai visto una lucertola così grande?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a lizard this big?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "mangiare" for "voi" (2nd-person plural). Use it when talking to more than one person: "Avete mangiato?" = "Have you eaten?" In a statement it means "You ate..." / "You have eaten...". (In some contexts "voi" can be used as a polite form, but the most common polite singular is "Lei ha mangiato".)
target_language_example: Avete mangiato qualcosa oggi?
native_language_example: Have you eaten anything today?

meaning: "have you spoken/talked with" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has talked with a person (con + name/pronoun). It’s the present perfect of parlare: avete parlato = “you have spoken / did you speak?”. Often followed by a topic: a riguardo (“about it”), di... (“about...”), or ne (“about it”) as in “Ne avete parlato con loro?”.
target_language_example: Avete parlato con il medico di questa cosa?
native_language_example: Have you spoken with the doctor about this?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "prendere" used with "avere": "voi" + "avete" + past participle "preso". Used for many meanings of "prendere": taking (medicine, an object), getting/buying something ("Dove avete preso...?" = Where did you get it?), and in set phrases like "prendere parte" (to take part/participate). Word order changes with questions: "Avete preso...?" = Have you taken...?.
target_language_example: Avete preso i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Did you get the tickets online?

meaning: "have you heard" / "did you hear" (you all / formal you).
additional_notes: Second-person plural of "sentire" (to hear). It can mean literally hearing a sound/words, or more generally "to hear about" news (often with "di": "Avete sentito di...?" = "Have you heard about ...?"). Used for speaking to a group, or as the polite/formal "you" in some regions/contexts.
target_language_example: Avete sentito che domani scioperano i treni?
native_language_example: Have you heard that the trains are on strike tomorrow?

additional_notes: Second-person plural of the passato prossimo of trovare (“to find”). Used when speaking to more than one person (voi) or as a polite/formal “you” (especially in some regions) to ask if someone has found something, like a job.
target_language_example: Avete trovato una soluzione?
native_language_example: Have you found a solution?

additional_notes: Past tense of vedere (to see). Used with voi (you all) or as the polite form for addressing one person (like English “you” but formal). Often used in questions to ask if someone has seen a person/thing, or has watched something (a show, a movie). The object can be a noun (Avete visto Tom?), a pronoun (Lo avete visto?), or a whole clause (È questo quello che avete visto?).
target_language_example: Avete visto il mio telefono da qualche parte?
native_language_example: Have you (all) seen my phone anywhere?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) if they have seen something, using the past tense (passato prossimo) of vedere: avete visto = “you have seen / did you see”. It’s often followed by a masculine singular noun with il (il film, il giardino). Before a vowel, il becomes l’: Avete visto l’aereo? In some regions/older usage, voi can also be a very formal singular “you,” but standard polite singular is Lei (Ha visto...?).
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto il mio zaino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my backpack?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) if they’ve seen something that belongs to you. Very common when you’ve lost an object or can’t find it. Agree the ending with the noun you’re looking for: il mio (masc. singular), la mia (fem. singular), i miei (masc. plural), le mie (fem. plural). In informal singular you’d say: Hai visto il mio ...?
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto il mio zaino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my backpack?

meaning: "Have you seen this?" (speaking to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people whether they have seen something/someone. It uses the plural "voi" form: "avete visto" = "have you seen". "Questo" means "this" (masculine singular) and can be followed by a noun (e.g., "questo documento") or used alone. For a single person you’d say: "Hai visto questo?" For feminine: "avete visto questa ...?"
target_language_example: Scusate, avete visto questo passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen this passport?

additional_notes: Form of "avere bisogno di" (to need). "Avete" is for "you" plural (you all) or formal "you" (e.g., speaking to customers). It’s followed by "di" + an infinitive (Avete bisogno di aggiornare…) or "di" + a noun with an article (Avete bisogno di un dizionario?). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it “Do you need…?”
target_language_example: Avete bisogno di aiuto con la prenotazione?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the booking?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has certain items or people (e.g., in a shop, hotel, restaurant, or talking to a family). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural (you all) and is also used as the polite/formal "you" in some regions. "Dei" is a partitive meaning "some/any" before a masculine plural noun; the feminine plural form is "delle" (Avete delle camere?), and for plural nouns starting with s+consonant, z, ps, gn, etc., it becomes "degli" (Avete degli asciugamani?). Often in English it translates as "any" in questions.
target_language_example: Scusi, avete dei biglietti per oggi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have any tickets for today?

meaning: “do you (plural/formal) intend to…?” / “are you planning to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s intention or plan. It’s the verb phrase "avere intenzione di" (to intend/plan to) conjugated for "voi" (you all) or formal "you" in some contexts, followed by an infinitive (e.g., cominciare, ritornare).
target_language_example: Avete intenzione di venire con noi domani?
native_language_example: Are you planning to come with us tomorrow?

meaning: 'are you afraid of' / 'are you scared to'.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("voi"), asking if they’re afraid of someone/something or afraid to do something. If it’s followed by a verb, use "di" + infinitive: "Avete paura di dirlo?" (= Are you afraid to say it?). If it’s followed by a noun/pronoun, it means "afraid of": "Avete paura di me?" (= Are you afraid of me?).
target_language_example: Avete paura di fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Are you afraid to ask a question?

meaning: “you have a …” / “do you have a …?” (to a group).
additional_notes: "Avete" is the 2nd-person plural of "avere" (to have), used when speaking to two or more people ("you all"). With rising intonation or a question mark, it’s a common way to ask if someone has something available: "Avete un…?" = “Do you have a…?”. "Un" is the masculine singular article (“a/an”); for feminine you use "una" (e.g., "Avete una penna?").
target_language_example: Scusi, avete un tavolo libero?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a free table?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or question whether the people you’re speaking to (voi) object to someone/something, or have an issue with it. Can refer to people (con lui/lei/loro/me) or things/ideas (con questo, con quello che...). In speech it can sound confrontational depending on tone; for one person you’d say “Hai un problema con…?” and more formal/plural “Ha/Avete un problema con…?”.
target_language_example: Avete un problema con questa soluzione?
native_language_example: Do you have a problem with this solution?

meaning: "do you have a…?" / "you have a…" (addressing you-plural or polite).
additional_notes: From the verb "avere" (to have). "Avete" is 2nd-person plural: used when speaking to more than one person (you all), and also commonly as a polite/formal way to address one person (e.g., a customer, receptionist, waiter). "Una" is "a" for feminine singular nouns, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., una prenotazione, una stanza).
target_language_example: Scusi, avete una penna?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a pen?

additional_notes: Imperfect past of “avere bisogno di” (to need). Used for an ongoing situation in the past, a repeated past need, or to set background (“he/she needed…”). Follow with a noun/pronoun (aveva bisogno di lei/noi) or an infinitive, often passive: “aveva bisogno di essere + past participle” (needed to be cleaned/done).
target_language_example: Quando ero bambino, avevo bisogno di più tempo per fare i compiti.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I needed more time to do homework.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere bisogno di" (to need): "aveva bisogno" = "he/she used to need" or "he/she needed" (ongoing situation in the past). "Di" + a noun tells what is needed: "di soldi" = "(some) money" (not specific bills/coins). Often used with a subject (lui/lei/Tom) or after "che" in reported speech: "mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di soldi".
target_language_example: Quando ha perso il lavoro, aveva bisogno di soldi.
native_language_example: When he lost his job, he needed money.

meaning: he/she needed space (time/room away from someone or something).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of "avere bisogno di" (to need): "aveva bisogno di" = "he/she needed" or "he/she was in need of". "Spazio" can mean physical room or, very often, emotional/personal space (especially in relationships). You can change the subject: "Lui/Lei aveva bisogno di spazio".
target_language_example: Dopo la discussione, mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di spazio.
native_language_example: After the argument, he/she told me that he/she needed space.

meaning: he/she needed a (used to need a).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of avere (“aveva”) to talk about a past need (often ongoing, repeated, or background information). It’s followed by di + an article + noun: aveva bisogno di un/uno/una… (“needed a/an…”). The subject can be implied from context (lui/lei).
target_language_example: Ieri sera aveva bisogno di un taxi per tornare a casa.
native_language_example: Last night he/she needed a taxi to get home.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **avere** (“to have”) with **fame** (“hunger”) to talk about being hungry. **Aveva** is the **imperfetto** (imperfect past) form of *avere* for **lui/lei** (“he/she”), often used for background situations or ongoing states in the past (e.g., *stamattina* = “this morning”).
target_language_example: Dopo la passeggiata, aveva fame e ha mangiato un panino.
native_language_example: After the walk, he was hungry and ate a sandwich.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (aveva) to describe an ongoing emotional state in the past. You can change the subject and tense: ho il cuore infranto (I’m heartbroken), aveva il cuore infranto (he/she was heartbroken). Common in serious or emotional contexts (breakups, loss, disappointment).
target_language_example: Dopo la rottura, aveva il cuore infranto e non voleva uscire.
native_language_example: After the breakup, he was heartbroken and didn’t want to go out.

meaning: he/she intended to; was planning to.
additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avere intenzione di" (“to intend/plan to”), used to talk about someone’s intention in the past (often a plan that was in progress, not yet completed, or later changed). Followed by an infinitive: "aveva intenzione di + verb".
target_language_example: Avevo intenzione di chiamarti ieri, ma poi mi sono dimenticato.
native_language_example: I was planning to call you yesterday, but then I forgot.

additional_notes: Uses the expression "avere nostalgia di" + a person/place/thing to say you miss it. "Casa" here means “home.” "Aveva" is the imperfect tense (“he/she used to have / was having”), often used for an ongoing feeling in the past.
target_language_example: Quando era all’estero, aveva nostalgia di casa.
native_language_example: When he was abroad, he was homesick.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "avere paura" (to be afraid). Used to describe an ongoing state in the past or background context. Often followed by "di" + noun/infinitive (e.g., "aveva paura di cadere") or "del/della" + noun (="di" + "il/la").
target_language_example: Da bambino aveva paura del buio.
native_language_example: As a child, he was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "avere paura di" (to be afraid of / to be afraid to do). Use "aveva paura di" to talk about a past, ongoing state of fear. It can be followed by an infinitive to mean “was afraid to (do something)” (e.g., "andare", "dire"), or by a noun/pronoun to mean “was afraid of (someone/something)" (e.g., "di Sami").
target_language_example: Da bambino, aveva paura di dormire da solo.
native_language_example: As a child, he was afraid to sleep alone.

additional_notes: From the expression **avere ragione** (“to be right”). **Aveva** is the imperfect tense of *avere* and often corresponds to “was”/“used to be” right in the past, depending on context. You can add **riguardo a / su** to say “about” someone/something: *aveva ragione su di lei* = “he was right about her.” Note: **avere ragione di + infinitive** means “to have reason to…”: *Non aveva ragione di essere arrabbiato* = “He had no reason to be angry.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, avevi ragione tu.
native_language_example: Sorry, you were right.

additional_notes: "Avere torto" means "to be wrong". "Aveva" is the imperfect past tense (used for an ongoing state in the past or background information), often translated as "was" or "used to be". You can also ask "Chi aveva torto?" = "Who was wrong?"
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse colpa mia, ma avevo torto.
native_language_example: I thought it was my fault, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere" + "un". Used to say someone/something had (or used to have) something in the past, often describing a state or ongoing situation/background: "Aveva un problema" (He/She had a problem), "Il latte aveva un cattivo sapore" (The milk had a bad taste). "Aveva" can mean he, she, or it depending on context; with feminine nouns it becomes "aveva una".
target_language_example: Da bambino aveva un cane.
native_language_example: As a child, he had a dog.

additional_notes: Used when talking about (usually criminal) investigations to say someone could prove they were elsewhere at the time. You can change the verb/person: ho un alibi (I have an alibi), hai un alibi? (Do you have an alibi?), aveva un alibi? (Did he/she have an alibi?). Often followed by a time expression: per quella notte / per ieri sera.
target_language_example: Non poteva essere lui: aveva un alibi per quella sera.
native_language_example: It couldn’t have been him: he had an alibi for that evening.

additional_notes: From avere (to have) in the imperfetto: aveva = “he/she had / used to have / was having.” It’s followed by a feminine singular noun with una (“a”). The subject is often understood from context (e.g., Tom aveva una… = “Tom had a…”).
target_language_example: Quando era piccolo, aveva una bicicletta rossa.
native_language_example: When he was little, he had a red bike.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of “avere bisogno di” = “to need.” Used for ongoing/repeated need in the past, or to describe a past situation/background. Structure: avere bisogno di + noun (avevano bisogno di aiuto/denaro) or + pronoun (avevano bisogno di voi).
target_language_example: Quando erano piccoli, avevano bisogno di molta attenzione.
native_language_example: When they were little, they needed a lot of attention.

meaning: "you were right" (informal singular), in the past.
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (tu) that they were correct about something, often after you realize it later. Common with prepositions: avevi ragione a + infinitive ("you were right to..."); avevi ragione riguardo a / su ("you were right about..."). In the plural/formal you’d say: avevate ragione (you all were right) / aveva ragione (he/she was right) / aveva ragione (Lei was right).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: avevi ragione su tutto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: you were right about everything.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of an earlier instruction or suggestion. Literally “I had said to…”, followed by an infinitive (e.g., fare, restare, prendere). The pronoun can change: ti/vi avevo detto di… = “I had told you (sing./plural) to…”. Often has a reproachful tone in context (“I told you to…”).
target_language_example: Ti avevo detto di non uscire senza chiavi.
native_language_example: I had told you not to go out without keys.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of "avere bisogno di" + noun/infinitive, used to say you needed something (often as background, ongoing, or not tied to one single moment). "Di" is required: avevo bisogno di cibo / di dormire. Common variants: "ho bisogno di" (I need), "avevi/aveva/avevamo... bisogno di".
target_language_example: Ieri avevo bisogno di dormire presto.
native_language_example: Yesterday I needed to go to sleep early.

meaning: "I was afraid of" / "I was afraid to".
additional_notes: Imperfetto of "avere paura" (to be afraid), used to describe an ongoing or habitual fear in the past. Use "di" + noun (avevo paura di mio padre = I was afraid of my father) or "di" + infinitive (avevo paura di prendere un raffreddore = I was afraid of catching a cold).
target_language_example: Da bambino avevo paura di parlare in classe.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid to speak in class.

meaning: “should have” / “ought to have” (past advice or criticism).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere (“to have to / must”). Used to say someone didn’t do something in the past but it would have been the right thing to do: Avrebbe dovuto + infinitive. Often implies regret, reproach, or a missed obligation (“he should have… but he didn’t”).
target_language_example: Avresti dovuto chiamarmi prima di partire.
native_language_example: You should have called me before leaving.

meaning: “could have / would have been able to” (conditional past of potere).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a possibility or ability in the past seen from a hypothetical/conditional point of view. Common in regrets/criticism (“He could have told me”) and in imagined outcomes (“She could have caught a cold”). Often followed by an infinitive: avrebbe potuto dire/fare/andare. Negative: non avrebbe potuto (“couldn’t have / wouldn’t have been able to”).
target_language_example: Avrei voluto chiamarti, ma non avrei potuto farlo.
native_language_example: I wanted to call you, but I couldn’t have done it.

meaning: "I should have" / "I would have had to" (past obligation, often with regret).
additional_notes: It’s the conditional past of dovere (avrei + dovuto) and is usually followed by an infinitive: avrei dovuto + fare/dire/andare… It expresses something you were supposed to do in the past but didn’t (often implying regret or criticism). In questions/negatives it works the same way: Non glielo avrei dovuto dire? = “Shouldn’t I have told him/her?”
target_language_example: Avrei dovuto studiare di più per l’esame.
native_language_example: I should have studied more for the exam.

additional_notes: Used with the conditional perfect (avrei dovuto + infinitive) to say you regret a past action or decision. It often appears with a negative: non avrei mai dovuto + infinitive = 'I should never have (done something)'.
target_language_example: Non avrei mai dovuto accettare quell'offerta.
native_language_example: I should never have accepted that offer.

meaning: “I could have” / “I would have been able to.”
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of potere (“can/to be able to”), used for past possibilities or abilities (often hypothetical or unreal). Common in “how could I have…?” questions (Come avrei potuto…?). Often appears in conditional sentences with se (“if”): Se + imperfect subjunctive …, avrei potuto + infinitive (“If…, I could have / would have been able to …”).
target_language_example: Avrei potuto aiutarti, ma non lo sapevo.
native_language_example: I could have helped you, but I didn’t know.

meaning: "you should have" / "you ought to have" (talking about something in the past).
additional_notes: This is the conditional perfect of "dovere" ("to have to / must"). It’s used to say what someone was expected to do in the past, often with a tone of advice, criticism, or regret. "Avreste" is 2nd person plural ("you all"), and it can also be used as a polite form in some contexts.
target_language_example: Avreste dovuto dirmelo prima.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: “you should have” / “you ought to have” (but you didn’t).
additional_notes: Conditional perfect of dovere: avresti (you would have) + dovuto (had to/should). Used to express regret, criticism, or advice about a past action not done. Usually followed by an infinitive: Avresti dovuto + verbo (es. dire, fare, rifiutare).
target_language_example: Avresti dovuto chiamarmi prima di uscire.
native_language_example: You should have called me before going out.

additional_notes: Future tense of avere successo (“to succeed”). Used after a subject (explicit or implied): Tom avrà successo = “Tom will succeed.” It can also refer to things (an idea, a plan, a business): Il progetto avrà successo = “The project will be a success.”
target_language_example: Sono sicuro che la tua idea avrà successo.
native_language_example: I’m sure your idea will succeed.

meaning: had some problems; had trouble (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) to say you experienced difficulties. Often followed by "a" + infinitive: "abbiamo avuto dei problemi a entrare" = "we had trouble getting in." The "dei" means "some" (not specific problems).
target_language_example: Ho avuto dei problemi a trovare parcheggio.
native_language_example: I had trouble finding parking.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ha avuto successo" (he/she/it was successful), "hanno avuto successo" (they were successful). Common with people, projects, plans, missions, etc.: "La missione ha avuto successo."
target_language_example: Il progetto ha avuto successo grazie al tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: The project was successful thanks to your help.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" to talk about having/experiencing something in the past (events/conditions like "un ictus", "un crollo nervoso", or situations like "un esame", "un test") or to say you possessed something (e.g., "avere un pianoforte"). You’ll also see it inside longer forms like "aver avuto" = "to have had" (e.g., "Vorrei aver avuto..." = "I wish I had had...").
target_language_example: Ho avuto un problema con la macchina ieri.
native_language_example: I had a problem with the car yesterday.

additional_notes: Used in the passato prossimo with the auxiliary avere: (io) ho avuto una…, (lei) ha avuto una…, (noi) abbiamo avuto una…. The past participle avuto doesn’t change with gender/number when used with avere. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (una cotta, una chiacchierata, una morosa, una esperienza, etc.).
target_language_example: Ho avuto una buona idea durante la riunione.
native_language_example: I had a good idea during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used in legal/courtroom contexts to indicate the place where a witness sits/stands to give testimony. Often used with "essere/salire/andare/ritornare sul banco dei testimoni" (to be/take the stand/return to the stand). Note: "banco" can look like English "bank," but here it means a bench/stand.
target_language_example: Il testimone è salito al banco dei testimoni per rispondere alle domande.
native_language_example: The witness took the stand to answer the questions.

additional_notes: Used for a small, packaged snack bar made with oats/granola (often with nuts, honey, or chocolate). In Italian you may also hear “barretta ai cereali” (cereal/grain bar).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo una barretta di granola e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have a granola bar and a coffee.

additional_notes: A simple time expression: "dopo la scuola" = "after school." Often used with "giocare a" (to play): "giocare a baseball dopo la scuola". You can swap in other activities: "calcio dopo la scuola", "studio dopo la scuola".
target_language_example: Di solito gioco a baseball dopo la scuola.
native_language_example: I usually play baseball after school.

additional_notes: "Bei" is the plural of "bel" (meaning "beautiful/nice") and is used before a plural noun (like "fiori"). It’s an adjective + noun phrase used to compliment flowers, often with "molti" (many) or in phrases like "grazie per...".
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei bei fiori per tua madre.
native_language_example: I bought some beautiful flowers for your mother.

additional_notes: Used after a verb (often "parlare") to say you do something well in French: "parlare bene il francese" = "to speak French well". You can also intensify it with "così" (so) or "davvero" (really): "parlare così/davvero bene il francese".
target_language_example: Parlo bene il francese, ma non lo scrivo molto bene.
native_language_example: I speak French well, but I don’t write it very well.

additional_notes: Used when offering someone a choice of drink. Often appears in questions with different levels of politeness: “Vuoi…?” (informal singular), “Vuole…?” (formal singular), “Volete…?” (plural), “Vorrebbe/Vorreste…?” (more polite: “would you like…?”).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo, preferisci bere tè o caffè?
native_language_example: After lunch, do you prefer to drink tea or coffee?

additional_notes: Common idiom used to describe someone who drinks a lot (usually alcohol). You can change the verb for different subjects/tense: "bevono come una spugna" (they drink like a sponge), "beveva come una spugna" (used to drink/was drinking heavily).
target_language_example: Non uscire con lui: beve come una spugna.
native_language_example: Don’t go out with him: he drinks like a fish.

additional_notes: Often used with forms of "stare" to make the present or past continuous: "sto/stai/sta... bevendo del latte" = "I am/you are/he is... drinking (some) milk"; "stavo..." = "I was...". "Del" is a partitive article meaning "some" (not necessarily all the milk). You can also say "bevendo latte" (more general) or "bevendo il latte" (the milk, specific).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare: sto bevendo del latte.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk: I’m drinking some milk.

additional_notes: "Bevuto" is the past participle of "bere" (to drink), used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno bevuto" = "I/you/he… drank / have drunk". "Del" is the partitive article (di + il), meaning "some" with masculine singular uncountable nouns (e.g., del vino, del succo). With other nouns you’ll see: "dello" (dello spumante), "dell’" (dell’acqua), "della" (della birra), "dei/degli/delle" for plural.
target_language_example: Ieri sera ho bevuto del vino a cena.
native_language_example: Last night I drank some wine with dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of bere (“to drink”): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno + bevuto. "Del" means “some” (an unspecified amount), so "ho bevuto del caffè" = “I drank some coffee / I had some coffee.” You can also say "ho bevuto caffè" (more general: “I drank coffee”).
target_language_example: Non ho bevuto del caffè oggi.
native_language_example: I didn’t drink any coffee today.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo of "bere" (to drink): ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno bevuto. "Del tè" means "some tea" (partitive "del" = di + il) and is often used when the exact amount isn’t specified. In questions, word order can stay the same ("Avete bevuto del tè?").
target_language_example: Ho bevuto del tè dopo cena.
native_language_example: I drank some tea after dinner.

meaning: “(a) glass of” (a drink) / “a glass made of” (a material).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) for drinks/amounts: "un bicchiere di acqua/vino/birra" = a glass of water/wine/beer; (2) for the material something is made of (often with a modifier): "un bicchiere di plastica/vetro" = a plastic/glass cup. With drinks you often use an article (un/uno/il): "Un altro bicchiere di..., per favore".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to beer served in a glass (not a bottle or a can). In bars/restaurants you can ask for it with: “Un bicchiere di birra, per favore.” “Bicchiere” = glass; “di birra” = of beer.
target_language_example: Scusi, mi porta un bicchiere di birra, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you bring me a glass of beer, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or talk about a serving of milk in a glass. Common with quantities like "un" (a) or "un altro" (another): "un bicchiere di latte", "un altro bicchiere di latte".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di latte, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of milk, please.

additional_notes: Used to order wine or refer to one serving of wine in a glass. Common patterns: “Potrei avere un bicchiere di vino?” (Could I have a glass of wine?) and “finire/riempire/mettere giù il bicchiere di vino” (finish/fill/put down the glass of wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Used when asking about availability or talking about buying tickets for a specific concert. You can also say "i biglietti del concerto" (the concert’s tickets), but "per il concerto" highlights what the tickets are for. Singular: "un biglietto per il concerto".
target_language_example: Ho comprato due biglietti per il concerto di stasera.
native_language_example: I bought two tickets for tonight’s concert.

additional_notes: Used to order beer politely in a bar/restaurant. Often said as a short order: “Una birra, per favore.” You can also use it after a fuller request (e.g., “Posso avere una birra, per favore?”). Note the polite forms with staff: “Mi dia…” (more formal) or “Dammi…” (informal).
target_language_example: Scusi, una birra, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, a beer, please.

additional_notes: Used to order beer politely in a bar or restaurant. Often shortened to "Una birra, per piacere." You can swap in quantities: "Due birre, per piacere" (two beers) or "Un'altra birra, per piacere" (another beer).
target_language_example: Scusi, una birra alla spina, per piacere.
native_language_example: Excuse me, a draft beer, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" (= "to need"). "Del" = "di + il" (“of the”), and "suo" agrees with the thing owned ("aiuto"), not with the person who owns it. In context, "suo" can mean “his” or “her”; Italian often relies on context to clarify. You can also say "ho bisogno del tuo aiuto" (“I need your help”).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del suo aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: I need his/her help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used with the expression "avere bisogno di" (to need). "del" = "di" + "il" and is used before a masculine singular noun (il computer, il denaro, il telefono, il diario, il libro). With other nouns you change the article: "dello" (lo), "dell'" (l'), "della" (la), "dei" (i), "degli" (gli), "delle" (le).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del passaporto per viaggiare.
native_language_example: I need the passport to travel.

additional_notes: Used with the structure "avere bisogno di" + noun/pronoun: "(avere) bisogno del mio aiuto" = "(to) need my help." "del" is the contraction of "di + il". You’ll often see it after "ha/hai/aveva/avete bisogno..." and in questions like "Perché hai bisogno del mio aiuto?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del mio aiuto, dimmelo.
native_language_example: If you need my help, tell me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di + [noun]" = "to need + [noun]". Here: "(avere) bisogno del nostro aiuto" = "(to) need our help". You can add "ancora" to mean "still": "Hai ancora bisogno del nostro aiuto?". With people: "ho bisogno del tuo/suo/nostro aiuto" = "I need your/his/her/our help".
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del nostro aiuto, chiamaci.
native_language_example: If you need our help, call us.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" (to need). "Suo" is the formal/polite possessive (also meaning "his" or "her" depending on context). In everyday speech, you may also hear "Ho bisogno del tuo aiuto" (I need your help) with "tuo" for someone you address with "tu".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del suo aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: I need your help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "avere" (to have): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I/you/he/she/we need your help." You can put it in the future with "avrò bisogno..." (I will need...), or make it negative: "non ho più bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "I don't need your help anymore."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho bisogno del tuo aiuto oggi.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I need your help today.

additional_notes: "Avere bisogno di" means “to need.” "Del" = "di" + "il" (“of the”), and "vostro" is the formal/plural way to say “your” (to one person politely, or to more than one person). Very common with different tenses: "ho/avrò/abbiamo bisogno del vostro aiuto".
target_language_example: Scusi, ho bisogno del vostro aiuto per compilare questo modulo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help to fill out this form.

additional_notes: Used with forms of avere (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) to express necessity: avere bisogno di + noun (need for something) or avere bisogno di + infinitive (need to do something). Often strengthened with adverbs like veramente (really) or urgentemente (urgently).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con te.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di aiuto" = "to need help." You can change the verb for tense/person: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno bisogno di aiuto" (present), "avevo/avevi/aveva... bisogno di aiuto" (past/imperfect). Often used to offer or ask for assistance: "Hai bisogno di aiuto?"
target_language_example: Scusa, ho bisogno di aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need help with this form.

meaning: need food / in need of food.
additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "(io) ho bisogno di cibo" = "I need food". You can intensify it with an adverb like "disperatamente" (desperately). Often appears in lists: "bisogno di cibo e acqua" (need food and water).
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, avevamo bisogno di cibo e acqua.
native_language_example: After the trip, we needed food and water.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di dormire" = "to need to sleep." Often refers to being tired and needing rest; you can add "di più" (more) to say you need more sleep.
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, ho bisogno di dormire un po'.
native_language_example: After the trip, I need to sleep a bit.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **avere bisogno di** (“to need”): *ho bisogno di lei* = “I need her.” **Lei** can mean “her,” and it can also be the polite/formal “you” depending on context; in these examples it means “her.”
target_language_example: Non posso farlo da solo: ho bisogno di lei.
native_language_example: I can’t do it alone: I need her.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like "avere bisogno di" (to need) or "c’è bisogno di" (there is a need for). With people, Italian uses "di" + stressed pronoun: "di me" (me), "di te" (you), "di lui/lei" (him/her), etc. Example: "Hai bisogno di me?" = "Do you need me?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno di me, chiamami subito.
native_language_example: If you need me, call me right away.

additional_notes: Used after avere bisogno di (“to need”): avere bisogno di più + noun = “to need more + noun.” Common with uncountable nouns (burro) and abstract nouns (pratica, potere). In speech you may also hear: Mi serve di più… (“I need more…”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: We need more time.

additional_notes: Built from "avere bisogno di" (to need) + "più soldi" (more money). You can change the subject and tense: "ho/avevo/avrò bisogno di più soldi". Often used in everyday contexts about finances.
target_language_example: Per finire il progetto, ho bisogno di più soldi.
native_language_example: To finish the project, I need more money.

meaning: need money / be in need of money.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di soldi" = "to need money". You can add a time word like "ora/adesso" (now) or a reason with "per" + infinitive: "Ho bisogno di soldi per...".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di soldi per pagare l'affitto.
native_language_example: I need money to pay the rent.

meaning: need space (room), or need personal space/time alone.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di + noun" = "to need + noun". "Spazio" can mean physical room (more space in a house, car, suitcase, etc.) or emotional/personal space (some time alone or distance in a relationship). Often heard as "Ho bisogno di spazio".
target_language_example: Dopo una giornata lunga, ho bisogno di spazio.
native_language_example: After a long day, I need some space.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di te" = "to need you." It can express practical need (help, support) or emotional need depending on context. The subject changes the verb form (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) but "di te" stays the same.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di te adesso.
native_language_example: I need you right now.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di un + noun" = "to need a + (masculine singular) noun". Use "di una" for feminine singular (e.g., "bisogno di una mano"), "di" + plural article for plural ("dei/degli/delle").
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un biglietto per domani.
native_language_example: I need a ticket for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere" (to have): "ho/hai/ha bisogno di un abbraccio" = "I/you/he/she need(s) a hug." Often appears with intensifiers like "solo/solamente/soltanto/semplicemente" (“just/simply”) to emphasize that a hug is all someone needs.
target_language_example: Dopo quella brutta giornata, ho bisogno di un abbraccio.
native_language_example: After that bad day, I need a hug.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere: avere bisogno di + noun/verb = “to need.” Often said in legal/travel situations. Pronouns may change (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno bisogno) and with “penso che…” you commonly see the subjunctive: “penso che tu/lei abbia bisogno…”.
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ho bisogno di un avvocato.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need a lawyer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" + noun to say you need something: "(Io) ho bisogno di..." (I need...), "(Tu) hai bisogno di..." (You need...), "(Lui/Lei) ha bisogno di..." (He/She needs...).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un martello per appendere questo quadro.
native_language_example: I need a hammer to hang this picture.

bisogno di un passaggio a casa

target_language_multi_word_term: bisogno di un passaggio a casa
additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere bisogno di" (to need) + "un passaggio" (a lift/ride, usually by car) + "a casa" (home). Common when offering or asking if someone still needs a ride home: "Hai/Ha/Avete ancora bisogno di un passaggio a casa?".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti do un passaggio: hai bisogno di un passaggio a casa?
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you a ride: do you need a ride home?

additional_notes: Used with forms of the verb "avere" (to have): "avere bisogno di" = "to need". "Una" agrees with a feminine singular noun that follows (e.g., una ricetta, una forchetta, una scorta). For a masculine noun use "bisogno di un" (e.g., un medico) or "bisogno di uno" (e.g., uno zaino). Common tenses: "ho bisogno di una..." (I need a...), "avrò bisogno di una..." (I will need a...), "avrai bisogno di una..." (you will need a...).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di una prenotazione per entrare?
native_language_example: Do I need a reservation to get in?

meaning: need a vacation / need a holiday.
additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere bisogno di" (to need) to express that someone really needs time off to rest. Often strengthened with words like "proprio" (really) or "davvero" (truly).
target_language_example: Dopo questa settimana stressante, ho bisogno di una vacanza.
native_language_example: After this stressful week, I need a vacation.

meaning: "a bottle of" (a bottle containing a drink or other liquid).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the container/quantity: bottiglia di + noun (e.g., bottiglia di vino, bottiglia di latte, bottiglia di profumo). You can add amounts like una mezza bottiglia di (half a bottle of).
target_language_example: Vorrei una bottiglia di acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one specific bottle of champagne. Very common in requests with "aprire" (to open): "Aprire una bottiglia di champagne" = "to open a bottle of champagne". You can swap in other drinks: "una bottiglia di vino" (a bottle of wine), "una bottiglia d’acqua" (a bottle of water).
target_language_example: Porto una bottiglia di champagne per festeggiare.
native_language_example: I’m bringing a bottle of champagne to celebrate.

additional_notes: Used when buying, recommending, or bringing wine. The partitive structure “di” indicates the contents: a bottle containing wine. You’ll often hear it with an adjective (e.g., “una buona/bella bottiglia di vino”) or in questions in shops/restaurants (“Quale bottiglia di vino consiglia?”).
target_language_example: Per la cena ho comprato una bottiglia di vino rosso.
native_language_example: For dinner I bought a bottle of red wine.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a quantity of beer measured in bottles, often with a number (e.g., due/tre/quattro bottiglie di birra). Singular: una bottiglia di birra.
target_language_example: Per la festa abbiamo comprato sei bottiglie di birra.
native_language_example: For the party we bought six bottles of beer.

meaning: good at playing tennis (said about a female).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has skill at an activity: essere bravo/brava a + infinitive. Here brava agrees with a female subject (lei/Yumi); for a male you’d say bravo. You can turn it into a question with intonation or a question mark.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è brava a giocare a tennis.
native_language_example: My sister is good at playing tennis.

meaning: a good/nice person (usually said about a woman).
additional_notes: "Brava" agrees with the person being described (brava = feminine; bravo = masculine). In this context, bravo/brava means "good/kind/decent" rather than "brave" (so it’s not about courage). Often used as a compliment: "Che brava persona!" = "What a nice person!"
target_language_example: Giulia è una brava persona: aiuta sempre gli altri.
native_language_example: Giulia is a good person: she always helps others.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is skilled at something. Common patterns: (1) "essere bravo/a a" + infinitive: "Sono bravo a cucinare" (I’m good at cooking). (2) "essere bravo/a a" + noun (often a sport/activity): "È bravo a calcio / a rugby" (He’s good at soccer/rugby). Agree "bravo" with the person: "bravo" (male), "brava" (female).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è molto brava a parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: My sister is very good at speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has ability/skill in the French language. "Bravo" changes to match the person: bravo (male), brava (female), bravi (mixed/plural), brave (female plural). Often used with other subjects too: "bravo in matematica" = good at math.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è brava in francese, ma io sono bravo in inglese.
native_language_example: My sister is good at French, but I’m good at English.

meaning: "good boy" / "good guy" (a nice, well-behaved young man).
additional_notes: Used to praise a boy/young man for being kind, well-mannered, or doing the right thing. Often used with "un" (un bravo ragazzo) to describe someone: "Tom era un bravo ragazzo." "Bravo" changes with gender/number (bravo ragazzo, brava ragazza, bravi ragazzi, brave ragazze).
target_language_example: È un bravo ragazzo: aiuta sempre i suoi amici.
native_language_example: He’s a good guy: he always helps his friends.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or talk about unpleasant information. Often said with verbs like avere/portare/dare (“to have/bring/give”) and with per to say who the news is for (e.g., brutte notizie per lui).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho brutte notizie per te.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I have bad news for you.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) smells pleasant. Often said as an exclamation: "Che buon odore!" = "That smells so good!". With people, it usually refers to perfume/soap ("Hai un buon odore" = "You smell nice").
target_language_example: Che buon odore in cucina!
native_language_example: It smells so good in the kitchen!

additional_notes: Used to say something is a good suggestion/plan (È una buona idea?) or to agree with someone’s proposal (Sì, buona idea.). Often used with the article: una buona idea (“a good idea”).
target_language_example: Andiamo in treno: è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Let’s go by train: it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is healthy or in good condition. Common with the verb essere: “essere in buona salute” (to be in good health), and also as an adjective phrase with di: “essere di buona salute” (to be in good health).
target_language_example: Sono in buona salute, grazie.
native_language_example: I'm in good health, thanks.

additional_notes: Plural feminine form. Use it when the friends are women/girls (or an all-female group): "Siamo buone amiche" = "We’re good friends." For a mixed group or male friends, use "buoni amici"; for two women, you can also say "due buone amiche".
target_language_example: Siamo buone amiche da tanti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: Common way to announce or introduce something positive. Often used after verbs like avere/portare (to have/bring): “Ho delle buone notizie (per te/voi)” = “I have good news (for you).” Can also stand alone as an announcement: “Buone notizie!” Note: “notizia” is singular; “notizie” is plural.
target_language_example: Ho buone notizie per te: domani non lavoriamo.
native_language_example: I have good news for you: we’re not working tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say two or more people have a friendly relationship. Often with "essere" (to be) or "diventare" (to become): "Siamo buoni amici" = "We’re good friends." You can add "dei" before it when it follows "sono" to mean "some"/"(they are) good friends of yours": "Sono dei tuoi buoni amici."
target_language_example: Siamo buoni amici da molti anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been good friends for many years.

additional_notes: Used to politely order a coffee (usually an espresso) in a bar/café or restaurant. You can add a quantity (Un caffè / Due caffè / Tre caffè) or address the waiter first (Cameriere, …).
target_language_example: Un caffè, per favore, e un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: A coffee, please, and a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to order coffee politely (at a bar/café or restaurant). Often preceded by a quantity: "Un caffè, per piacere" (one coffee), "Due caffè, per piacere" (two coffees). You can also use it for different types of coffee: "Un caffè lungo/cappuccino/decaffeinato, per piacere". In Italian, "un caffè" usually means an espresso.
target_language_example: Un caffè decaffeinato, per piacere.
native_language_example: A decaf coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or describing how you take your coffee. Often contrasted with “senza zucchero” (without sugar). You can also specify the amount: “poco zucchero” (a little sugar), “molto zucchero” (a lot of sugar).
target_language_example: Vorrei un caffè con lo zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: I'd like a coffee with sugar, thanks.

additional_notes: Used when stating a preference or ordering coffee without adding sugar. You can also hear it as a request: “Un caffè senza zucchero, per favore.”
target_language_example: Per me un caffè senza zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: An unsweetened coffee for me, please.

additional_notes: Used in the passive voice to say that someone received a kick from a horse. The agent is introduced by “da” (= by): “(Lei) è stata calciata da un cavallo” (she was kicked by a horse). You may also see past historic “fu” or “venne” instead of “è stata,” especially in writing.
target_language_example: Il contadino è stato calciato da un cavallo e ha chiamato l’ambulanza.
native_language_example: The farmer was kicked by a horse and called an ambulance.

additional_notes: Used when someone has to do something differently than originally intended. "Il suo" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context (e.g., Mary/Tom). In Italian you can also say "cambiare i suoi piani" for "change his/her plans" (plural). Note: "piano" here means "plan," not the musical instrument.
target_language_example: A causa della pioggia, Maria ha dovuto cambiare il suo piano.
native_language_example: Because of the rain, Maria had to change her plan.

additional_notes: Past participle used with avere in the common phrase cambiare idea (“to change one’s mind”): ho/hai/ha cambiato idea, etc. The “one’s” is understood from the subject, so you usually don’t add a possessive (not *la mia idea*). Often used to say you decided differently after thinking more.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho cambiato idea: vengo con te.
native_language_example: Sorry, I changed my mind: I’m coming with you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "cambiare" in the passato prossimo to say someone has had a big, positive (or sometimes negative) impact on your life. Very common pattern: "(Tu/Lui/Lei/Voi) mi hai/ha/avete cambiato la vita" = "You/He/She/You all changed my life." You can also change the pronoun: "ti/ci/gli/le" depending on who is affected.
target_language_example: Grazie di tutto: mi hai cambiato la vita.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything: you changed my life.

additional_notes: Used to specify a group of Canadians based on where they live. The verb "vivono" is 3rd person plural ("they live"), and it’s followed by a place (in + country/city): "che vivono in Australia" = "who live in Australia". "che" here means "who/that" and introduces a describing clause.
target_language_example: Ci sono molti canadesi che vivono in Italia.
native_language_example: There are many Canadians who live in Italy.

additional_notes: Used to say what a dog is like (e.g., size, condition) or to identify/describe it. Often appears with a possessive: “Il tuo cane è…?” (Is your dog…?), “Il vostro cane è…?” (Is your dog…?). Note: Italian “cane” = “dog” (not English “cane”).
target_language_example: Il mio cane è molto tranquillo.
native_language_example: My dog is very calm.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone can/knows how to sing a specific song. Often appears with verbs like "potere" (can/be able to) or "sapere" (know how to). You can swap in another song: "cantare quella canzone" (that song) or add a title: "cantare la canzone '…'".
target_language_example: Sai cantare questa canzone in italiano?
native_language_example: Do you know how to sing this song in Italian?

additional_notes: Used for the action of singing a (specific or unspecified) song. Very common with verbs like "lasciare" (let) and "potere" (can), and can be followed by "per" to mean singing for someone/audience: "cantare una canzone per tutti" = "sing a song for everyone."
target_language_example: Vuoi cantare una canzone con me?
native_language_example: Do you want to sing a song with me?

additional_notes: Used to check/confirm something the speaker believes is true. “Giusto?” works like an English tag question (“right?” / “isn’t that so?”). You can swap “il francese” with another language or subject (e.g., “capire l’italiano, giusto?”). Often said with “riuscire a” (“to manage to / be able to”): “Riesci a capire…?”
target_language_example: Riesci a capire il francese, giusto?
native_language_example: You can understand French, right?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/returning (andare/venire/tornare) to say you go home by walking: “andare/tornare a casa a piedi”. Word order is usually “a casa a piedi”.
target_language_example: Oggi torno a casa a piedi.
native_language_example: Today I'm walking home.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like andare/tornare (“to go back”) to mean “go home now” (a casa adesso). With essere/stare (“to be”), it means “at home right now” (in casa adesso). Note the difference: a casa = to/at home (direction/goal), in casa = inside the house.
target_language_example: Devo andare a casa adesso, ci sentiamo dopo.
native_language_example: I have to go home now; we’ll talk later.

additional_notes: Means "my house" or "my home" depending on context. Often used in friendly expressions like "Casa mia è casa tua" (“My home is your home”). You can also use it to talk about someone visiting your place or giving directions: "a casa mia" = "at my place/at my home."
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a casa mia dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place after dinner?

meaning: "home now" / "(to) go/come home now" (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: With verbs of movement like andare (to go) and venire (to come), Italian normally uses the preposition: andare/venire **a casa** (to go/come home). So you’ll usually see **a casa ora** = “home now / go home now.” Without a verb, **casa ora** can mean “(our) home now” in sentences like “Boston è la nostra casa ora.”
target_language_example: Devo andare a casa ora.
native_language_example: I have to go home now.

additional_notes: Usually said as **a casa presto** with verbs of movement like **andare** (to go) or **venire** (to come): *vado a casa presto* = “I’m going home early”, *vengo a casa presto* = “I’m coming home early”. **A casa** is used without an article (*a casa*, not *alla casa*) when you mean “(to) home”.
target_language_example: Oggi vado a casa presto perché sono stanco.
native_language_example: Today I’m going home early because I’m tired.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "sua" (= his/her/its) with "casa". In Italian, the possessive agrees with the thing owned (here: casa, feminine singular), not with the owner. Often used with a preposition like "a" or "vicino a": "a casa sua" = at his/her place; "vicino a casa sua" = near his/her home. The article is often omitted with "casa" in common expressions (e.g., "a casa sua").
target_language_example: Stasera ceniamo a casa sua.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re having dinner at his/her place.

additional_notes: Usually said as "a casa tutto il giorno" (or "in casa tutto il giorno"). "A casa" emphasizes being/staying at home; "in casa" emphasizes being inside the house. Very common with verbs like "stare", "essere", and "rimanere".
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa tutto il giorno perché non sto bene.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying home all day because I don’t feel well.

additional_notes: Common phrase for unpleasant or negative information. Often used with verbs like ricevere (to receive), dare (to give), avere (to have), or sentire (to hear): Ho una cattiva notizia / Ho delle cattive notizie. You can also say Brutte notizie with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho delle cattive notizie.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I have some bad news.

meaning: 'the cause of the' / 'the case (lawsuit) of the'.
additional_notes: Most commonly it means the reason for something: "la causa della morte" = "the cause of death". In legal contexts, "causa" can also mean a court case/lawsuit (e.g., "la causa della Corona" = "the Crown’s case"; often also seen as "causa contro [someone]" = "case against [someone]"). It’s the phrase "causa di" + the feminine singular article ("della" = "of the").
target_language_example: Non conosciamo ancora la causa della scomparsa.
native_language_example: We still don’t know the cause of the disappearance.

meaning: a set phrase with pronouns used in expressions like “ce la faccio” = “I can manage / I can do it.”
additional_notes: “Ce la” is a common pronoun combination (ce + la) that usually doesn’t translate word-for-word. You often see it in fixed expressions: “ce la faccio” (I can do it / I can manage), “ce l’ho fatta” (I made it / I managed). It refers to “it” in a general sense (a task, situation, goal) and is very frequent in everyday Italian.
target_language_example: Non ce la faccio oggi: sono troppo stanco.
native_language_example: I can’t manage today: I’m too tired.

meaning: part of verbs like “andarsene”: “(from here) away / off” → “to leave, go away”.
additional_notes: “Ce ne” is a fixed combination of pronouns (ce = ci, ne = “from there/of it”) that often appears with pronominal verbs like **andarsene** (“to leave/go away”) and its forms: **ce ne andiamo** (we’re leaving), **ce ne possiamo andare** (we can leave), **ce ne stiamo andando** (we’re in the process of leaving). In English you usually translate the whole verb (“leave/go away”), not the two pronouns separately.
target_language_example: È tardi: ce ne andiamo.
native_language_example: It’s late: we’re leaving.

additional_notes: From the verb "andarsene" = "to leave / go away". "Ce" and "ne" are pronoun particles that are part of the verb; you commonly see them with different people: "me ne vado" (I’m leaving), "te ne vai" (you’re leaving), "se ne va" (he/she leaves), "ce ne andiamo" (we’re leaving). Often used to announce departure or to say someone wants/asks you to leave ("vuole che ce ne andiamo?").
target_language_example: È tardi: ce ne andiamo adesso.
native_language_example: It’s late: we’re leaving now.

additional_notes:
Used with the verb essere (sono = 'are') to say that some quantity exists/is available. 
- ce = roughly 'there/here' (like ci)
- ne = 'of it/them' (often referring to a previously mentioned thing)
Common in questions and with quantities: "Ce ne sono molti?" (Are there many?), "Quanti ce ne sono?" (How many are there?), "se ce ne sono" (if there are any).
target_language_example: In frigo ce ne sono ancora due.
native_language_example: There are still two of them in the fridge.

additional_notes: "Centro commerciale" means "shopping mall" in everyday Italian. "Con" means "with" and introduces the person you go with: "al centro commerciale con Tom" = "to the mall with Tom". The phrase often appears after verbs of going (andare, venire) and can be preceded by "al" (= a + il, "to the").
target_language_example: Vado al centro commerciale con mia sorella.
native_language_example: I’m going to the shopping mall with my sister.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: cerca di + verb (e.g., cerca di capire = try to understand). It can be a suggestion/command (Cerca di… = Try to…).
target_language_example: Cerca di parlare più lentamente, per favore.
native_language_example: Try to speak more slowly, please.

meaning: "try not to" (used to tell someone to avoid doing something).
additional_notes: Common in advice and requests, often as an imperative: "Cerca di non..." + infinitive. The negation "non" goes right before the infinitive (e.g., "non fare", "non preoccuparti"). It can sound like a gentle instruction rather than a strict order.
target_language_example: Cerca di non dimenticare il passaporto.
native_language_example: Try not to forget your passport.

additional_notes: Formed from the verb "cercare" + "di" + infinitive: "cercando di + verb". It often implies an attempt/effort that may or may not succeed. Common with verbs like trovare, capire, aiutare, salvare, sopravvivere.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Italian.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary "avere" ("ho/hai/ha... cercato di") + an infinitive to say someone made an attempt to do something. Literally "cercare" means "to look for", but "cercare di + infinitive" means "to try to".
target_language_example: Ho cercato di chiamarti ieri, ma non avevi campo.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you had no signal.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "cercare di" + infinitive (e.g., "cerchi di ricordare" = "try to remember"). "Cerchi" is the formal (Lei) form, often used to give polite instructions or advice. In informal speech to a friend you’d more often say "cerca di...".
target_language_example: Cerchi di arrivare in orario, per favore.
native_language_example: Please try to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "cercare di" + infinitive, common in written stories and narration. In everyday speech, you’ll often hear the passato prossimo instead: "ha cercato di" = “(he/she) tried to”.
target_language_example: Cercò di aprire la porta, ma era bloccata.
native_language_example: He tried to open the door, but it was stuck.

additional_notes: Used before a noun for an emotion or feeling (e.g., ansia, confusione, preoccupazione, rabbia). "Cercò" is the passato remoto (common in narratives and in some regions); in everyday speech you often hear "ha cercato di nascondere la sua".
target_language_example: Cercò di nascondere la sua paura, ma tremava.
native_language_example: He/She tried to hide his/her fear, but was trembling.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or confirm something, often in reply to a question or doubt. It’s followed by a clause introduced by che (e.g., Certo che è vero). In speech it can be an emphatic standalone answer: Certo che sì! Neutral/common, not slang.
target_language_example: —Hai capito? —Certo che ho capito!
native_language_example: —Did you understand? —Of course I understood!

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask for additional information or alternatives. It can stand alone (Che altro?) or be followed by a verb (Che altro sapete...?), and it often implies “besides that” or “in addition”.
target_language_example: Che altro possiamo fare adesso?
native_language_example: What else can we do now?

additional_notes: An exclamation used to react with admiration or enthusiasm, often before a feminine singular noun: Che bella sorpresa! Che bella fotografia! With masculine nouns: che bello; plural: che belli/che belle. Often used with Guarda… / Senti… / Cavolo… for emphasis.
target_language_example: Che bella giornata oggi!
native_language_example: What a beautiful day today!

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or guidance. "Dovrei" is the conditional of "dovere" ("must/to have to") and often sounds polite or uncertain, like asking what the best course of action is. You can add details after it: "Che cosa dovrei fare riguardo a..." ("What should I do about...") or "Che cosa dovrei fare senza..." ("What would I do without...").
target_language_example: Non so che cosa dovrei fare adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do now.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone does in general (their job/role) or what they are doing at a specific time, depending on context (e.g., with "adesso" = right now). It agrees with the subject: "Che cosa fai?" (you), "Che cosa fanno?" (they). Often shortened in speech to "Che fa...?" or "Cosa fa...?".
target_language_example: Che cosa fa tuo padre di lavoro?
native_language_example: What does your father do for a living?

meaning: “what are you doing?” / “what do you do?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing (right now or at a certain time: Che cosa fai domenica?/ora?) or what they do in general (work/role), often with context (Che cosa fai in Giappone? = what are you doing there?). In the exclamation “Che cosa fai!”, it can sound like a reprimand or surprise (“What are you doing!?”). Also commonly said as “Cosa fai?” or “Che fai?” (more casual).
target_language_example: Che cosa fai stasera?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

meaning: 'What are you (plural) doing?' / 'What do you (plural) do?'.
additional_notes: Uses the plural 'voi' form: fate (from fare). It can ask about what someone is doing right now or what they plan to do, depending on context (e.g., with a time like questa estate). Often shortened in speech to 'Che fate?' or 'Cosa fate?'.
target_language_example: Che cosa fate dopo la lezione?
native_language_example: What are you (all) doing after the lesson?

meaning: "what ... to him?" / "what ... to him/them?" (in a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask a question where the action is directed to someone via the indirect object pronoun gli (“to him”; also often used colloquially for “to them”). It commonly appears before verbs like dire (to say/tell), comprare (to buy), succedere (to happen): Che cosa gli hai detto? = “What did you tell him?”
target_language_example: Che cosa gli vuoi dire?
native_language_example: What do you want to tell him?

additional_notes: Used to ask “what” while referring to someone with the indirect object pronoun **le** (“to you” in the polite **Lei** form, or “to her”). It often appears in questions like **Che cosa le piace…?** (“What do you like…?”), **Che cosa le hanno rubato?** (“What did they steal from her/you?”), or **Che cosa le devo?** (“What do I owe you?”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, che cosa le serve?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you need?

meaning: "what ... of it/them/him/her"; often in "Che cosa ne sarà di..." = "what will become of..."
additional_notes:
"Ne" is a pronoun meaning “of it/of them/about it,” referring to something already known from context. 
- With the future of "essere" (sarà/saranno) + "di" + person/thing: "Che cosa ne sarà di..." = “What will become of...?” (expresses worry/uncertainty).
- With "fare": "Che cosa ne hai fatto?" = “What did you do with it/them?”
The "di" part can refer to a person (di lui/lei/me/te/noi/voi) or a thing/place (del Giappone).
target_language_example: Che cosa ne sarà di noi senza questo lavoro?
native_language_example: What will become of us without this job?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. Very common in polite conversation, especially with Lei (e.g., Che cosa ne pensa? = What do you think?). The pronoun “ne” refers back to something already mentioned, often introduced with di/del/della/di quel…: Che cosa ne pensa di…? = What do you think about…?
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensa di questa proposta?
native_language_example: What do you think about this proposal?

meaning: "What do you think about…?" (asking for someone’s opinion about something).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion. It’s made of: che cosa (“what”) + ne (“about it/about that”) + pensi ("you think") + del (= di + il, “about the”). The noun that follows is usually introduced by di (del/dello/della/dei/degli/delle), depending on gender/number: e.g., del libro, della lezione, dei tuoi piani. You can also address someone directly: Tu che cosa ne pensi del…?
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensi del ristorante nuovo?
native_language_example: What do you think about the new restaurant?

additional_notes: A question in the present continuous using stare + gerund (sta facendo = is doing). Often used with context words like lì (there) or con... (with...) to ask what someone is doing in a place or with an object. You can change the person: che cosa stai facendo? (you), che cosa sto facendo? (I), che cosa stanno facendo? (they).
target_language_example: Che cosa stai facendo con il mio telefono?
native_language_example: What are you doing with my phone?

meaning: "what are you ... (doing)?" (introduces a question with the present continuous).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now, followed by the verb "stare" + a gerund: "Che cosa stai + verb-ando/-endo?" (e.g., aspettando, bevendo, leggendo). You can also hear "Cosa stai..." (more common and slightly more informal) or "Che cosa stai facendo?" = "What are you doing?".
target_language_example: Che cosa stai cercando?
native_language_example: What are you looking for?

meaning: "what are they" (starting a question in the present continuous).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now. It’s typically followed by a present participle (gerundio), e.g., "che cosa stanno facendo/ dicendo/ scrivendo?" You can also use "cosa stanno..." (more common in speech) or "che cosa state..." for "what are you (plural) ...".
target_language_example: Che cosa stanno facendo i bambini?
native_language_example: What are the kids doing?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening now or what will happen next. Often followed by a time word (adesso = now) or a situation (e.g., dopo la morte = after death). You can also say "Che succede?" (more casual) or "Cosa succede?".
target_language_example: Che cosa succede se perdiamo il treno?
native_language_example: What happens if we miss the train?

meaning: "what ... (to) you?" (used to start a question addressed to 'you').
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions. "Che cosa" means "what" and "ti" is the unstressed pronoun for "to you" (or sometimes "you" with certain verbs). It often appears with verbs like dire (Che cosa ti ha detto...? = What did he/she tell you?), rubare (Che cosa ti hanno rubato? = What did they steal from you?), venire in mente (Che cosa ti viene in mente? = What comes to mind for you?). In everyday speech you may also hear "Cosa ti..." instead of "Che cosa ti...".
target_language_example: Che cosa ti serve per la ricetta?
native_language_example: What do you need for the recipe?

additional_notes: "Che cosa" means "what" and "vi" is "you" in the sense of "to you" or "you all" (also used as a formal/polite "you"). It’s used to start questions like: "Che cosa vi motiva?" (What motivates you?), "Che cosa vi è successo?" (What happened to you?), or "Che cosa vi consiglio?" (What do I recommend to you?).
target_language_example: Che cosa vi serve per oggi?
native_language_example: What do you need for today?

meaning: “what do you want?” / “what do you mean?” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “what thing do you want.” Used to ask what someone wants, intends, or is asking for. With an infinitive it’s often about intention/meaning: “Che cosa vuoi dire?” = “What do you mean?” You can also hear “Che vuoi…?” (more blunt) or “Cosa vuoi…?” (very common).
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa vuoi fare stasera?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, symbol, or message. Often followed by the thing you’re asking about (e.g., Che cosa vuol dire questa parola?). You can add “esattamente” (exactly) for emphasis or “in + language” (e.g., in arabo). With formal “Lei,” it becomes “Che cosa vuol dire?” or “Sa che cosa vuol dire?” (= “Do you know what it means?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, che cosa vuol dire “scontrino”?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what does “receipt” mean?

meaning: 'what' (used to ask what something is or what someone is doing).
additional_notes: Used mainly in questions: Che cosa...? = “What...?” It’s slightly more explicit/formal than just "che". It can also introduce an embedded question after verbs like sapere/dire/capire: "Sapete che cosa vogliamo" = “You know what we want.” Often interchangeable with "cosa" (especially in speech).
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi fare stasera?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Direct question using "che cosa" (= what) + "vuoi" (you want). Often used to ask what someone wants in general (Che cosa vuoi?), what they want to do/buy (Che cosa vuoi comprare?), or what they want from someone (Che cosa vuoi da lui? = What do you want from him?). Can sound abrupt depending on tone; "Che cosa vuoi, per favore?" is softer.
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa vuoi da me?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you want from me?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants or is asking for. It can be a direct question (Che cosa vuole?) or followed by “da + person” to mean “What do you want from ...?” The verb “vuole” is the formal form (Lei) and also the 3rd-person singular (“he/she wants”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, che cosa vuole da me?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you want from me?

meaning: 'which search engine' (asking what search engine someone uses).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which search engine someone uses. Often followed by a verb like "usate" (do you use) or the more formal "utilizzate" (do you use). Adding "voi" can emphasize the subject (“you all/you”) or make the question sound a bit more direct.
target_language_example: Scusa, che motore di ricerca usi di solito?
native_language_example: Sorry, which search engine do you usually use?

additional_notes: Used in questions about the current time or a specific time. Common patterns: "Che ora è?" (What time is it?), "Che ora era?" (What time was it?), "Che ora sarebbe...?" (What time would it be...?), and "Da che ora a che ora...?" (From what time to what time...?) for opening hours or time ranges.
target_language_example: Scusa, che ora è adesso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it now?

meaning: "what kind/sort of" (often expressing criticism or surprise).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask or exclaim about the type of something: "Che razza di madre..." = "What kind of mother...". Frequently has a negative, judgmental tone in exclamations (similar to "what the hell kind of..."). In questions it can be more neutral, depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Che razza di posto è questo?
native_language_example: What kind of place is this?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask for a category, style, or specific variety of something. It’s usually followed by a noun (che tipo di + nome): Che tipo di macchina? / Che tipo di lavoro? In speech you may also hear the shorter form "Che tipo?" when the noun is clear from context.
target_language_example: Che tipo di musica ti piace?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like?

additional_notes: Used to ask about preferences or to identify food. Often followed by verbs like piacere (Che tipo di cibo ti piace?), volere (Che tipo di cibo vuole/volete?), or essere (Che tipo di cibo è questo?). In informal speech you might also hear Che cibo ti piace? ("What food do you like?") but che tipo di cibo focuses on the category/type (e.g., Italian, spicy, vegetarian).
target_language_example: Che tipo di cibo preferisci: italiano o giapponese?
native_language_example: What kind of food do you prefer: Italian or Japanese?

meaning: "what kind/type of music" (used to ask someone’s music preference).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask what genre or kind of music someone listens to or likes. Often followed by a verb like ascoltare (to listen to) or piacere (to like). You can make it more formal by using Lei (e.g., Lei che tipo di musica ascolta?).
target_language_example: Che tipo di musica ti piace di più?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like most?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which kind of bread someone likes, is eating, or wants to order (e.g., at a bakery/restaurant). You’ll often see it with polite forms like "Le piace...?" / "Vuole...?" and plural "Vi piace...?".
target_language_example: Scusi, che tipo di pane vuole con il panino?
