target_language_example: Se non hai niente di gentile da dire, chiudi il becco.
native_language_example: If you don’t have anything kind to say, shut up.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons or emphasis: "more/sooner than anyone else". It refers to all other people except the one being talked about. Often follows phrases like "più di" (more than) or "prima di" (before).
target_language_example: Preferisco parlare con te più che con chiunque altro.
native_language_example: I prefer talking to you more than to anyone else.

additional_notes: Used mainly for doors, rooms, cars, etc. It’s the feminine singular form (because it agrees with a feminine noun like porta, stanza, macchina). For masculine nouns you’ll often see chiuso a chiave (e.g., Il cancello è chiuso a chiave). Common with verbs like essere/restare/rimanere (“to be/stay/remain”) and with tenere (“to keep”).
target_language_example: Ho trovato la porta chiusa a chiave.
native_language_example: I found the door locked.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of the verb phrase “chiudere a chiave” = “to lock (a door/car/room) with a key.” It describes someone locking something (a car, doors) or locking someone inside (“chiudere a chiave qualcuno in una stanza” = to lock someone in a room). In everyday speech, Italians often use passato prossimo instead: “ha chiuso a chiave”.
target_language_example: Ho chiuso a chiave la porta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I locked the door before going out.

additional_notes: Simple past (passato remoto) of "chiudere" used especially in stories and written narration. The subject isn’t stated, so it can mean "he" or "she" (or a named person from context). "Gli occhi" literally means "the eyes" but in English you usually translate it as "his/her eyes" based on context.
target_language_example: Poi chiuse gli occhi e si addormentò.
native_language_example: Then he/she closed his/her eyes and fell asleep.

additional_notes: Used to say a door (or something like it) is locked using a key. Often said with "la porta" (the door): "Ho chiuso a chiave la porta" = "I locked the door." It can also be used reflexively to mean locking yourself in somewhere: "Si è chiuso a chiave in camera" = "He locked himself in his room."
target_language_example: Hai chiuso a chiave la macchina?
native_language_example: Did you lock the car?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb in the passato prossimo: (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) + chiuso + la porta. In questions, Italian often keeps the same word order and relies on intonation: “Hai chiuso la porta?” = “Did you close the door?”
target_language_example: Ho chiuso la porta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I closed the door before going out.

additional_notes: "Ci" is an object pronoun meaning "us" (also sometimes "to us" depending on the verb). "Aiuterà" is the future tense of "aiutare" (to help) and can refer to he/she/it or the formal "you" (Lei). You often use it when talking about plans or expectations: "Penso che ci aiuterà" = "I think he/she will help us."
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: Marco ci aiuterà con i bagagli.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: Marco will help us with the bags.

additional_notes: Used to report a request in the past: "chiedere a qualcuno di + infinitive". Here, "ci" = "to us" and "chiese" is the passato remoto of "chiedere" (common in narratives; in conversation you may also hear "ci ha chiesto di").
target_language_example: Il professore ci chiese di consegnare i compiti entro venerdì.
native_language_example: The teacher asked us to hand in the homework by Friday.

meaning: 'there was/were' or 'there would be' (in the subjunctive, used in dependent clauses).
additional_notes: From the verb "esserci" (to be there). "Ci fosse" is the imperfect subjunctive, commonly used after verbs like "pensare/credere" (to think/believe) and in sentences like "se..." (if...) to talk about what was/would be present: "Ho pensato che ci fosse..." = "I thought there was..."; "Se ci fosse tempo..." = "If there were time...". Often followed by "qualcosa" (something) or "nessuno" (no one).
target_language_example: Non credevo che ci fosse tanta gente alla festa.
native_language_example: I didn’t think there were so many people at the party.

meaning: "has" + "ci" (usually “us” or “about it/there”), used before a past participle.
additional_notes: “Ci” is a clitic pronoun that comes before the auxiliary “ha” (passato prossimo). Its meaning depends on the verb: with many verbs it means “us” (e.g., ci ha convinti = “(it) convinced us”), but with verbs like pensare it often means “about it/there” (ci ha pensato = “(he/she) thought about it”).
target_language_example: Quella notizia ci ha sorpresi.
native_language_example: That news surprised us.

additional_notes: Used when someone asks a group that includes the speaker (ci = “us”) to do something. Structure: [subject] ci ha chiesto di + infinitive (e.g., aiutare, aspettare, smettere). Past tense: ha chiesto = “asked” (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: L'insegnante ci ha chiesto di fare silenzio.
native_language_example: The teacher asked us to be quiet.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" (to give) in the passato prossimo: "ha dato". "Ci" is a pronoun meaning "to us" (or sometimes "us"). The subject (he/she/you formal/a name like Tom) is understood from context or stated separately (e.g., "Tom ci ha dato..."). Often followed by what was given: "ci ha dato il segnale", "ci ha dato delle uova", "ci ha dato molto da mangiare".
target_language_example: Il professore ci ha dato i compiti per domani.
native_language_example: The teacher gave us the homework for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when someone communicates information to a group including the speaker. Literally: ci = “to us”, ha detto = “has said/told” (past). It’s often followed by what was said (e.g., “una bugia”, “il perché”) or by del/di cui to mean “told us about …” (e.g., “Ci ha detto del suo viaggio”, “la macchina di cui ci ha detto Tom”).
target_language_example: L'insegnante ci ha detto che domani c'è un test.
native_language_example: The teacher told us that tomorrow there is a test.

meaning: 'you have' with ci = 'us/to us' (often 'you have [done something] to/for us').
additional_notes: "Ci" is an object pronoun meaning "us" (or sometimes "to us"); it comes before the verb. "Hai" is "you have" (tu + avere) and is often used with a past participle: "ci hai detto" (you told us), "ci hai portato" (you brought us), "ci hai pagato" (you paid us), "ci hai incontrati" (you met us). Agreement can appear in the past participle when "ci" refers to people: "ci hai incontrati" (met us, masc./mixed) / "ci hai incontrate" (fem.).
target_language_example: Perché non ci hai chiamati ieri?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you call us yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is trustworthy/reliable. It’s the verb "fidarsi di" = "to trust" + "di" before the person you trust: "ci possiamo fidare di lui/lei?". "Ci" here means “we/ourselves” (we can trust). You can also change the subject: "Mi posso fidare di...?" (Can I trust...?), "Ti puoi fidare di...?" (Can you trust...?).
target_language_example: Non lo conosco bene: ci possiamo fidare di lui?
native_language_example: I don’t know him well: can we trust him?

meaning: “he/she/you can help us” / “can you help us?”
additional_notes: "Ci" means “us” (or “to us”), and "può aiutare" means “can help.” Used to ask for help politely (often with Lei: "Ci può aiutare?"), or to say that someone is able/willing to help you. You can add more information with "a" + infinitive: "ci può aiutare a..." (“can help us to...”).
target_language_example: Scusi, ci può aiutare a trovare questa via?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help us find this street?

meaning: 'there will be' / 'there are going to be'.
additional_notes: Future tense of "esserci" ("to be there" / "there to be"). Used to say that something will happen/exist ("Ci saranno altre offerte") or that people will attend/be present ("Anche loro ci saranno?"). Often followed by a noun: "ci saranno degli esami / delle difficoltà".
target_language_example: Domani ci saranno molti turisti in centro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow there will be lots of tourists downtown.

meaning: “there will be” / “it will be there” (future of *esserci*).
additional_notes: Used to say that something will exist, happen, or be available in the future. *Ci* often means “there” (in that situation/place), and *sarà* is “will be.” It can also mean “(someone) will be there,” e.g. *Tom ci sarà* = “Tom will be there.” In questions: *Ci sarà una torta?* = “Will there be a cake?” Negative: *non ci sarà* = “there won’t be / won’t be there.”
target_language_example: Domani ci sarà molta gente alla festa.
native_language_example: Tomorrow there will be a lot of people at the party.

additional_notes: From "servire" (to be needed / to be useful). "Ci" means "to us" and "serve" is "is needed" (or "is useful"). Often used to say something is needed or required: "Ci serve un..." = "We need a...". In questions, it can mean "What do we need it for?" or "What’s it for us?": "A cosa ci serve?".
target_language_example: Ci serve una prenotazione per entrare?
native_language_example: Do we need a reservation to get in?

additional_notes: Impersonal structure: "si" = "one/you/people" in general. "Fidarsi" takes "di" + person/thing: "Ci si può fidare di Tom" = "Tom can be trusted." The "ci" is a pronoun often used with "si" in this construction; in practice you learn it as the fixed pattern "ci si può fidare (di...)". Negative: "Non ci si può fidare (di...)" = "You can't trust (them/it)."
target_language_example: Di quello che dice, non ci si può fidare.
native_language_example: You can’t trust what he says.

additional_notes: Common goodbye when you expect to meet again, often with a time or place: "Ci si vede domani" (see you tomorrow), "Ci si vede alla festa" (see you at the party). "Ci" can refer to the place you’re talking about (there), and "si" makes it impersonal (like “we’ll see each other”).
target_language_example: Va bene, ci si vede stasera alle otto.
native_language_example: Okay, see you tonight at eight.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like voglio che / spero che / è importante che to talk about what you want, hope, or need to exist or happen. It’s the present subjunctive of esserci (“to be there”), referring to the presence/existence of something.
target_language_example: Spero che ci sia abbastanza tempo.
native_language_example: I hope there is enough time.

meaning: "we" in reflexive/recriprocal forms (often in the past: "we ... ourselves" / "we ...").
additional_notes: Used with reflexive (and some reciprocal) verbs, especially in the passato prossimo: the pronoun **ci** = “ourselves / each other” (for **noi**), and **siamo** is the auxiliary **essere** (“we are / we have” depending on English). Examples: **ci siamo alzati/e** = “we got up”, **ci siamo persi/e** = “we got lost”, **ci siamo arresi/e** = “we gave up”, **ci siamo fatti una risata** = “we had a laugh.” The past participle often agrees with the subject: **alzate/perse** (all women), **alzati/persi** (all men or mixed group).
target_language_example: Ci siamo incontrati davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: We met (each other) in front of the station.

meaning: "We met" / "we got to know each other" (said by women).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "conoscersi" (to meet/get to know each other). "Ci" = each other; "siamo" is the auxiliary used with reflexive verbs. The ending "-ute" agrees with a group of females (speakers are women). For a mixed group or men, you usually say "ci siamo conosciuti".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciute in Italia durante un corso di cucina.
native_language_example: We met in Italy during a cooking class.

meaning: "we met" / "we got to know each other".
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb "conoscersi" (to meet/get to know each other). "Ci" here means "each other," and "siamo" is the auxiliary "essere." Used to talk about when/where two people first met: "ci siamo conosciuti + time/place".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti all'università nel 2019.
native_language_example: We met at university in 2019.

meaning: "we had fun" (said by a group of women).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb *divertirsi* (“to have fun”). It uses *essere* (*siamo*) and agrees with the group: *divertite* = feminine plural. For a mixed/masculine group you say *ci siamo divertiti*. *Ci* is the reflexive pronoun (“ourselves”) and you can add details like *molto*, *davvero*, *alla festa*, *con Tom*.
target_language_example: Non abbiamo vinto, ma ci siamo divertite tantissimo.
native_language_example: We didn’t win, but we had a lot of fun.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of divertirsi (“to have fun”). Used to say you (as a group) had a good time. The pronoun ci here means “ourselves” (reflexive), not “there.” You can add where/when: ci siamo divertiti alla festa (at the party), ieri (yesterday), così tanto (so much).
target_language_example: Ci siamo divertiti molto al concerto.
native_language_example: We had a lot of fun at the concert.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb "incontrarsi" (to meet each other). It uses "essere" in the passato prossimo: "siamo" + past participle. The past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject: "incontrate" = feminine plural (a group of women, or women speaking). Masculine/mixed group would be "ci siamo incontrati". "Ci" means "each other" here.
target_language_example: Ci siamo incontrate per la prima volta a scuola.
native_language_example: We met for the first time at school.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the reflexive verb "incontrarsi" (to meet each other). It uses "essere" as the auxiliary: (noi) siamo incontrati, with the reflexive pronoun "ci" = "each other". Often used for planned meetings ("We met on Sunday") or chance meetings ("We ran into each other on the way").
target_language_example: Ci siamo incontrati per caso al supermercato.
native_language_example: We ran into each other by chance at the supermarket.

meaning: “we got lost” / “we’re lost” (also: “did we miss something?” in questions).
additional_notes: From the verb *perdersi* (to get lost). Literally it’s the past tense (*passato prossimo*): *siamo persi* = “we got lost,” with *ci* meaning “ourselves” (reflexive). In questions like *Che ci siamo persi?* or *Ci siamo persi qualcosa?* it often means “What did we miss?” / “Did we miss something?”
target_language_example: Scusa, siamo arrivati tardi: ci siamo persi l’inizio del film?
native_language_example: Sorry, we arrived late: did we miss the beginning of the movie?

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present somewhere. Common with numbers and quantities: "Ci sono cinque persone" = "There are five people." Often followed by a place phrase: "ci sono ... sul tavolo / in città / in questa stanza". Singular form: "c'è" = "there is".
target_language_example: Ci sono molti ristoranti vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that some unspecified number of things exists/is present somewhere. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono alcuni libri...". In everyday speech, Italians often drop "alcuni" and just say "Ci sono libri..." (= There are books / There are some books).
target_language_example: Ci sono alcuni posti liberi vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: There are some free seats near the window.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "esserci" (there is/are) to say that additional items/people exist or are available. "Altre" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., case, opzioni). With masculine plural nouns, use "ci sono altri". In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it mean "are there...?"; in negatives: "non ci sono altre ..." = "there aren’t any other ...".
target_language_example: Ci sono altre domande?
native_language_example: Are there other questions?

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to say something continues to exist or remains unsolved/uncompleted. It’s the plural form of "c’è ancora" (there is still). "ci" is part of the expression "ci sono" = "there are"; "ancora" means "still/yet".
target_language_example: Ci sono ancora due posti liberi.
native_language_example: There are still two free seats.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (tante cose, tante persone, tante mosche) to say a large number exists. For masculine plural use: “ci sono così tanti …” (e.g., tanti problemi). Often followed by a noun, and sometimes by “che …” (“there are so many … that …”) or “da + infinitive” (“so many … to …”).
target_language_example: Ci sono così tante domande che non so da dove cominciare.
native_language_example: There are so many questions that I don’t know where to start.

additional_notes: Used to say that some people/things exist or are present. "Ci sono" = "there are" (plural). "degli" is an indefinite article meaning "some" before a masculine plural noun (e.g., degli orsi, degli aggiornamenti, degli elementi). In questions, it asks if some exist/are present: "Ci sono degli ...?"
target_language_example: Ci sono degli ristoranti aperti vicino a qui?
native_language_example: Are there some restaurants open near here?

additional_notes: Used to say that some things exist/are available/present. "Ci sono" = "there are"; "dei" is an indefinite plural article meaning "some" (often before a masculine plural noun, e.g., "dei film", "dei suggerimenti"). In questions, it often means "Are there any…?".
target_language_example: Ci sono dei ristoranti aperti vicino a qui?
native_language_example: Are there any restaurants open near here?

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to say that some things/people exist or are present. Often starts a statement or a question: "Ci sono delle…?" = "Are there any…?" (expecting a plural answer). "Delle" is an indefinite plural article (roughly “some”).
target_language_example: Scusa, ci sono delle sedie libere qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are there any free chairs here?

additional_notes: Used to say that two of something exist/are present. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is), using "sono" because the thing that exists is plural. Often followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono due finestre" (There are two windows).
target_language_example: In cucina ci sono due sedie.
native_language_example: There are two chairs in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say that things exist/are present in a place: "ci sono" = "there are" (plural of "c'è"), and "in" introduces the location (in/inside). Very common in questions with "quanti/quante" (how many): "Quante città ci sono in America?"
target_language_example: Quanti supermercati ci sono in questa città?
native_language_example: How many supermarkets are there in this city?

additional_notes: Used to say that many things exist/are present. It’s the plural of "c’è" and matches feminine plural nouns (molte frasi, molte stanze). With masculine plural nouns, use "ci sono molti" (molti libri). Often followed by a noun; you can add a place: "In Italia/Nella città ci sono molte...".
target_language_example: Qui ci sono molte opzioni vegetariane.
native_language_example: There are many vegetarian options here.

additional_notes: Uses "ci sono" (there are) to say that many people are present/exist in a place or situation. Often followed by a place (e.g., "in Europa") or used alone to mean a place is crowded.
target_language_example: In questa stanza ci sono molte persone, facciamo silenzio.
native_language_example: In this room there are many people, let’s be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to say that many people/things exist or are present. It’s the plural form of "c’è" (there is). Usually followed by a plural noun: "Ci sono molti modi" (There are many ways).
target_language_example: Ci sono molti ristoranti in questa zona.
native_language_example: There are many restaurants in this area.

additional_notes: Uses **ci sono** (“there are”) to state the existence/presence of something in a place. **Molti** agrees with the plural noun (**alberi**). Often followed by a location phrase (e.g., *nel parco*, *in questa foresta*) or a relative clause (*che crescono…*).
target_language_example: In questo quartiere ci sono molti alberi e l’aria è più fresca.
native_language_example: In this neighborhood there are many trees and the air is cooler.

additional_notes: Uses **ci sono** (plural of **c’è**) to say that something exists/is present somewhere. Often followed by extra details like adjectives (**alti**, **moderni**) and a place (**qui intorno**, **in quella città**).
target_language_example: In centro ci sono molti edifici storici.
native_language_example: Downtown there are many historic buildings.

additional_notes: Used to say that many books exist/are present in a place. "Ci sono" is the plural form of "c’è" (there is/there are) and is followed by a plural noun. You can add a location with "in" or "nella/nella mia" + place (e.g., "in questa biblioteca", "nella mia stanza").
target_language_example: Ci sono molti libri sul tavolo.
native_language_example: There are many books on the table.

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that an excessive number of something (plural) is present. It’s made of: "ci sono" = "there are" + "troppi" = "too many" (masculine plural). Change "troppi" to match what follows: feminine plural "troppe" (Ci sono troppe persone), singular "troppo/troppa" with an uncountable noun (C’è troppo rumore / C’è troppa gente).
target_language_example: Ci sono troppi autobus in centro oggi.
native_language_example: There are too many buses downtown today.

meaning: "there are lots of / a ton of".
additional_notes: Very common, fairly informal way to say there are many of something. It’s built from "ci sono" (there are) + "un sacco di" (a lot of). Usually followed by a plural noun ("Ci sono un sacco di persone"), but it can also be used with uncountable nouns ("Ci sono un sacco di traffico / di gente"). More neutral alternatives: "ci sono molti/e" or "ci sono tanti/e".
target_language_example: Ci sono un sacco di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: There are lots of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used mainly with time expressions, especially in questions like: "Quanto tempo pensa/pensi/pensate che ci voglia per andare da [place A] a [place B]?". "ci voglia" is the subjunctive form (from "ci vuole" = "it takes"), commonly triggered by verbs of opinion like "pensare" (pensa/pensi/pensate) and by indirect questions.
target_language_example: Quanto tempo pensi che ci voglia per andare da Roma a Firenze?
native_language_example: How long do you think it takes to go from Rome to Florence?

additional_notes: Impersonal expression used mainly (1) to say how much time/effort is required: "Quanto tempo ci vuole?" = "How long does it take?" and (2) to say something is necessary: "Ci vuole pazienza" = "You need patience." Often followed by a time/quantity (un attimo, due ore, molto) or by "per" + infinitive ("ci vuole un’ora per arrivare").
target_language_example: Per arrivare in centro ci vuole mezz’ora.
native_language_example: It takes half an hour to get downtown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Chinese cuisine in general, whether you’re eating it, cooking it, or ordering it. Often appears with verbs like mangiare (to eat), cucinare (to cook), and ordinare (to order). You may also hear/see "ristorante cinese" (Chinese restaurant).
target_language_example: Stasera ordiniamo cibo cinese.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re ordering Chinese food.

additional_notes: Used to talk about Japanese cuisine in general or to identify whether a dish/restaurant is Japanese. In questions, you’ll often hear it with "che tipo/i di" (what kind(s) of): "Che tipo di cibo giapponese...?"
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo cibo giapponese.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating Japanese food.

meaning: halal food (food prepared according to Islamic rules).
additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe food that meets halal dietary requirements. You might see it on menus or use it when ordering: "Avete cibo halal?" or "Servite cibo halal?".
target_language_example: Scusi, avete cibo halal?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have halal food?

additional_notes: Common in advice or warnings about unhealthy eating (often with verbs like mangiare “to eat”, smettere di “to stop”, or essere dipendente da “to be addicted to”). You can also say "junk food" as "cibo junk" in informal contexts, but "cibo spazzatura" is the standard Italian phrase.
target_language_example: Cerco di evitare il cibo spazzatura durante la settimana.
native_language_example: I try to avoid junk food during the week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the highest point of a mountain. Often appears with prepositions like “in cima alla montagna” (at the top of the mountain) and with verbs like “raggiungere” (to reach). “Cima” can also mean the top of other things (e.g., “la cima dell’albero” = the top of the tree).
target_language_example: Dopo tre ore di cammino, siamo arrivati in cima alla montagna.
native_language_example: After three hours of walking, we arrived at the top of the mountain.

meaning: five years (or: at five years old).
additional_notes: Used for duration ("per cinque anni" = for five years), age ("a cinque anni" / "quando avevo cinque anni" = at age five / when I was five), and in the pattern "Sono cinque anni che..." meaning "It’s been five years since...".
target_language_example: Sono cinque anni che vivo in Italia.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Italy for five years.

meaning: about his/her age; roughly the same age.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is approximately the same age as another person. "la sua" means "his" or "her" depending on who you’re talking about (e.g., "circa la mia età" = about my age; "circa la tua età" = about your age).
target_language_example: Cerco qualcuno circa la mia età.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone about my age.

meaning: about how many hours per day
additional_notes: Used to ask for an approximate amount of time spent on something each day. It often appears in questions, with the activity verb placed at the end (e.g., studiare, lavorare). You can use it with different subjects: tu/Lei/voi, etc.
target_language_example: Circa quante ore al giorno lavori?
native_language_example: About how many hours per day do you work?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an idea or thing, meaning “the thing that…”. Common in more formal or written Italian; in everyday speech people often use “quello che” instead. It’s followed by a verb clause: “Ciò che dici è vero” = “What you say is true.”
target_language_example: Non capisco ciò che hai detto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you said.

meaning: 'what he/she says' (the thing that he/she says).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of someone’s words. "Ciò che" means "what/that which" and "dice" is "says" (present tense of dire). Often followed by a person’s name (e.g., "ciò che dice Tom") or understood from context.
target_language_example: Non credere a tutto ciò che dice.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything he/she says.

additional_notes: Uses "ciò che" (= "what/that which") + past tense "ha detto" (has said/said). It refers back to a statement already made. The person who spoke is understood from context (he, she, you, a named person: "ciò che ha detto Mary"). Often followed by opinions or evaluations: "è sbagliato", "è contrario ai fatti", "ci ha convinti".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ha detto ieri.
native_language_example: I'm sorry about what you said yesterday.

meaning: what he/she did; what (someone) has done.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to an action already mentioned or understood from context. "Ciò che" = "what/that which"; "ha fatto" is the passato prossimo of "fare" and agrees with the subject (e.g., "ciò che hai fatto" = what you did/you’ve done; "ciò che hanno fatto" = what they did).
target_language_example: Non riesco a credere a ciò che ha fatto ieri.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what he did yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the pronoun phrase "ciò che" (= “what / that which”) + "hai detto" (past: “you said/you have said”). It can act as the subject or object of the sentence: "Ciò che hai detto mi ha convinto" (“What you said convinced me”).
target_language_example: Non ho capito ciò che hai detto.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

meaning: "what I want" / "the thing that I want".
additional_notes: Uses the relative expression "ciò che" (“what/that which”) + "voglio" (“I want”) to refer to a desired thing or action. Often followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "Questo è ciò che voglio fare") or by a noun phrase (e.g., "Ciò che voglio è un computer nuovo"). A common alternative is "quello che voglio" with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Dimmi ciò che vuoi davvero.
native_language_example: Tell me what you really want.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing (or things) that someone wanted. It’s built from "ciò che" (= "what/that which") + "voleva" (imperfect of "volere", "to want"). The subject is implied by context (he/she).
target_language_example: Ho trovato ciò che voleva Luca.
native_language_example: I found what Luca wanted.

additional_notes: Uses "ciò che" (= “what/that which”) to refer to an unspecified thing or action. "Vuole" can refer to he or she (Italian often relies on context for the subject). If you need to be explicit, you can say: "ciò che lui vuole" / "ciò che lei vuole".
target_language_example: Non posso darti ciò che vuole.
native_language_example: I can't give him/her what he/she wants.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to refer to “the thing(s) that are …”: ciò che è giusto (what is right), ciò che è richiesto (what is required), ciò che è tuo (what is yours). It’s fairly formal and close to “quello che è,” but “ciò” sounds more abstract/general. Often appears in set expressions like Riprendersi ciò che è suo (“to take back what is his”).
target_language_example: Ho imparato a riconoscere ciò che è davvero importante.
native_language_example: I learned to recognize what is really important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a thing (or things) needed, talked about, etc., where Italian requires "di" after the verb/adjective (e.g., avere bisogno di). Very common in sentences like "Ciò di cui ho bisogno è..." = "What I need is...". Often followed by a verb: "ciò di cui avevo bisogno".
target_language_example: Non ho ancora trovato ciò di cui ho bisogno.
native_language_example: I still haven’t found what I need.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the hobby/collection of postage stamps. Often used with possessives (la mia/ la sua collezione di francobolli) and verbs like avere (to have), mostrare (to show), essere fiero/orgoglioso di (to be proud of).
target_language_example: Da bambino, ho iniziato una collezione di francobolli con mio nonno.
native_language_example: As a child, I started a stamp collection with my grandfather.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of people defined by what follows in the relative clause (che + verb). It’s a more formal/plural way to say "those who"; for women only you can also hear "coloro che" used, but the explicitly feminine form is "coloro" is masculine plural/mixed, while "coloro" often covers mixed groups in Italian.
target_language_example: Coloro che parlano inglese possono aiutarmi?
native_language_example: Those who speak English, can you help me?

additional_notes: Used (often with the verb essere/venire/fu) to describe someone being hit by lightning. You may also see the plural: "colpito da un fulmine" (masc.), "colpita da un fulmine" (fem.), "colpiti/colpite da un fulmine" (plural).
target_language_example: Durante il temporale, un albero è stato colpito da un fulmine.
native_language_example: During the storm, a tree was struck by lightning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the normal, habitual way. It can go at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or after what it refers to: "Come al solito, era in ritardo" / "Era in ritardo come al solito." Often implies mild annoyance or irony depending on tone.
target_language_example: Come al solito, ha dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: As usual, he forgot his keys.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to yourself. With adjectives it often means “as + adjective + as me” (e.g., alto come me = as tall as me). With nouns/plurals it means “people like me / those like me” (quelli come me).
target_language_example: Nessuno capisce questa situazione come me.
native_language_example: No one understands this situation like I do.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is attending/acting in an official role on behalf of your company. It often follows verbs like partecipare (to take part), andare (to go), intervenire (to speak/attend), or essere presente (to be present).
target_language_example: Sono qui come nostro rappresentante aziendale per discutere il contratto.
native_language_example: I’m here as our company representative to discuss the contract.

meaning: like her mother; as her mother (did).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone to her mother, in looks, personality, skills, etc. It can mean (1) “like her mother” (similar to her), or (2) “as her mother (did/was)” when talking about a role or situation that repeats. Note: Italian come usually means “like/as,” not English “come.”
target_language_example: Parla piano, come sua madre.
native_language_example: She speaks softly, like her mother.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone to his father (similarity in job, behavior, etc.). With verbs like "chiamarsi" or "essere chiamato", it can mean "(to be) named like his father" (e.g., having the same name).
target_language_example: Luca parla inglese come suo padre.
native_language_example: Luca speaks English like his father.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re talking to. It often follows a noun (e.g., persone come te = people like you). Variants: come me (like me), come lui/lei (like him/her), come voi (like you, plural/formal), come loro (like them).
target_language_example: Non conosco nessuno come te.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like you.

meaning: "like a" / "as a" (to compare someone or something to something else).
additional_notes: Used to make comparisons and similes: verb + come un + noun (e.g., "corre come un razzo" = "runs like a rocket"). It can also express how you interpret something: "lo prendo come un complimento" (“I take it as a compliment”). Note: Italian "come" often means “like/as,” not English “come.”
target_language_example: Dorme come un bambino quando è stanco.
native_language_example: He sleeps like a baby when he’s tired.

meaning: like a child; like a little kid.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s behavior to a child’s, often to criticize them for being immature. It can also describe being treated in an overly protective or patronizing way ("He treats me like a child").
target_language_example: Non parlarmi così: non sono come un bambino!
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that: I’m not like a child!

meaning: "like a" / "as a" (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun in comparisons or to describe someone/something in terms of another thing (often in similes): "X è/era ... come una ...". With masculine nouns you use "come un" (or "come uno" before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.).
target_language_example: È testarda come una mula.
native_language_example: She’s as stubborn as a mule.

meaning: like a sponge; (especially) drinking a lot.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like "bere" to mean someone drinks heavily (often alcohol). It’s a colorful, colloquial comparison: they "absorb" drinks like a sponge.
target_language_example: Ieri sera ha bevuto come una spugna.
native_language_example: Last night he drank like a sponge.

additional_notes: Used with the plural/formal “voi” to compare or say someone is similar to the people you’re speaking to. With nouns/pronouns it often means “people like you” (persone come voi). With adjectives/adverbs it makes comparisons: “intelligente/alto/ricca come voi” = “as smart/tall/rich as you (all)”.
target_language_example: Non conosco molte persone come voi.
native_language_example: I don’t know many people like you (all).

meaning: "how did you" / "how have you" (you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone did something. "Avete" is the verb "avere" (you have) used as an auxiliary in the passato prossimo (e.g., "Come avete risolto...?" = "How did you solve...?"), or as the main verb "have" depending on context. It addresses more than one person (voi) or can be used as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Come avete trovato questo ristorante?
native_language_example: How did you find this restaurant?

meaning: “How does it feel?” / “What does it feel like?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s feelings or experience in a situation. It uses the impersonal “si” (= “one/you” in general), so it often corresponds to English “How does it feel to…?” or “What’s it like to…?”. Frequently followed by “a + infinitive”: “Come ci si sente a essere…?”
target_language_example: Come ci si sente a vivere da soli?
native_language_example: What does it feel like to live alone?

meaning: “How do you manage to…?” / “How can you…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is able to do something, often with surprise, disbelief, or curiosity. It’s built from come (how) + fai (you do/make) + a + infinitive: “Come fai a saperlo?” = “How do you know?” In everyday speech it can sound a bit challenging depending on tone.
target_language_example: Come fai a ricordarti tutti questi nomi?
native_language_example: How do you manage to remember all these names?

meaning: “how it works” / “how it works (how it functions).”
additional_notes: Used to ask for or explain the way something works. Often followed by a noun (e.g., come funziona la lavastoviglie) or by “questo/quella cosa” (“this/that”). It can also be used in questions (“Come funziona?”) or embedded in a longer sentence (“Spiegami come funziona”).
target_language_example: Puoi mostrarmi come funziona questa app?
native_language_example: Can you show me how this app works?

additional_notes: Used in indirect questions after verbs like sapere (to know), capire (to understand), or spiegare (to explain): “Sai come funziona il sistema?” = “Do you know how the system works?” Word order stays like a normal question (come funziona...), even though it’s inside a longer sentence.
target_language_example: Non capisco come funziona il sistema.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how the system works.

meaning: "How did you..." / "How have you..." (asking about method or way).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask how someone did something. It’s literally “how + you have,” using the auxiliary verb *avere* for many past tenses (e.g., *passato prossimo*): *Come hai fatto?* = “How did you do it?” In some contexts it can mean “What did you say?” when followed by *detto?* (*Come hai detto?*).
target_language_example: Come hai fatto a imparare l’italiano così in fretta?
native_language_example: How did you manage to learn Italian so quickly?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone does something or how someone knows something. "Come" means "how" and "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (a thing/idea) or "him" (a man). It commonly appears before verbs like conoscere (to know/meet), sapere (to know a fact), fare (to do/make): "Come lo conosci?" = "How do you know him?" / "How did you meet him?"
target_language_example: Come lo dici in italiano?
native_language_example: How do you say it in Italian?

meaning: "How did you know that...?" (spoken to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group how they found out some information. "lo" refers to the fact/information, "sapevate" is past tense (imperfect) of "sapere" for "voi" (you plural). Often followed by a full clause with "che". For one person you’d say: "Come lo sapevi che...?"
target_language_example: Come lo sapevate che oggi era il mio compleanno?
native_language_example: How did you (all) know that today was my birthday?

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or skepticism about someone’s reliability or honesty. It’s a question with the reflexive verb fidarsi di (“to trust”), followed by the person you’re talking about (di te/di lui/di lei/di loro/di voi). You can also use it with names or nouns: “Come mi posso fidare di Marco?” / “...di questa azienda?”
target_language_example: Hai mentito una volta: come mi posso fidare di te adesso?
native_language_example: You lied once: how can I trust you now?

meaning: "How can I...?" (asking for instructions or possibility).
additional_notes: Used to ask for help or advice on how to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive (come posso fare/andare/pagare...) or by a verb phrase like "fare per" + infinitive. In polite requests you can also use "Come posso..." at the start of a question.
target_language_example: Scusi, come posso arrivare alla stazione da qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how can I get to the station from here?

additional_notes: Used to ask how something is possible or how someone is able to do something. It often expresses surprise, disbelief, or criticism (depending on tone and context). You can change the subject by adding it after: “Come può Tom…?”; or use an object pronoun: “Come può aiutarti…?” (How can it help you?).
target_language_example: Come può essere vero tutto questo?
native_language_example: How can all of this be true?

additional_notes: Used with impersonal si to ask how something is done in general. Very common in the pattern “Come si fa (a) + infinitive...?” = “How do you/does one + verb...?” or simply “Come si fa?” = “How do you do it?/How is it done?”
target_language_example: Scusa, come si fa a comprare i biglietti online?
native_language_example: Sorry, how do you buy tickets online?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the name/word for something you’re pointing at. Literally “how is this called,” but the natural English meaning is “What is this called?” You can add a category or language: “Come si chiama questo in inglese?” (“What is this called in English?”). For feminine nouns, use “questa”: “Come si chiama questa pianta?”
target_language_example: Scusa, come si chiama questo in italiano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this called in Italian?

come si usa questa macchina fotografica

target_language_multi_word_term: come si usa questa macchina fotografica
additional_notes: A common question to ask for instructions. “Come si usa…?” = “How do you use…?” The “si” makes it impersonal/passive-like (literally “how is this used”). You can swap in another object: “Come si usa questa stampante?” (printer). In conversation, it’s often used after “Sai/Sa/Sapete…”: “Sai come si usa…?” = “Do you know how to use…?” (tu/Lei/voi).
target_language_example: Scusi, come si usa questa macchina fotografica?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how do you use this camera?

meaning: "How is it going?" / "How is it going so far?"
additional_notes: Used to ask how something is progressing (work, a party, a weekend, a situation). You can add a topic with "con" or by naming it directly: "Come sta andando con il progetto?" / "Come sta andando la festa?". With an adjective/adverb like "bene", "male", or "veloce", it asks about the way something is going: "Come sta andando (così) veloce il treno!" = "How fast the train is going!" (often an exclamation).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come sta andando il corso di italiano?
native_language_example: Hi! How is your Italian course going?

meaning: "How do you feel?" (asking about someone’s physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone about their well-being. Often followed by time words like "adesso" (now), "oggi" (today), "in questo momento" (at this moment). With "riguardo a..." it means "How do you feel about ...?" (your opinion/feelings about a person or situation). Informal because it uses "ti" (you, informal); the formal version is "Come si sente?"
target_language_example: Ciao, come ti senti oggi?
native_language_example: Hi, how do you feel today?

additional_notes: A common, general check-in asking about the situation in someone’s life or in a specific area. Often followed by a context: *al lavoro* (at work), *tra te e…* (between you and…), *a Washington* (in Washington). You can answer with *Bene*, *Così così* (so-so), *Non c’è male* (not bad), or *Male*.
target_language_example: Ciao! Come vanno le cose con il nuovo appartamento?
native_language_example: Hi! How are things going with the new apartment?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (or to speak formally to one person) for their opinion or feelings about someone or something. It uses the reflexive verb "sentirsi" (to feel) and is followed by "riguardo a" + a noun/pronoun (or sometimes an infinitive/idea). Singular informal is "Come ti senti riguardo a...?" and formal singular is also "Come si sente riguardo a...?".
target_language_example: Come vi sentite riguardo a questa decisione?
native_language_example: How do you feel about this decision?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the normal/typical way, as you expect. Often refers to habits (bedtime, being late) and can sound neutral or mildly ironic depending on tone (e.g., “in ritardo come al solito” = “late as usual”). You can add emphasis with “proprio come al solito” (“just as usual”).
target_language_example: Come al solito, ho dimenticato le chiavi a casa.
native_language_example: As usual, I forgot my keys at home.

meaning: how to get (there); directions on how to arrive.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire/dirmi (to tell me) or sapere (to know) to ask for or give directions. It’s often followed by a + place name (a Shinjuku) or by a + article for common places (alla banca, al municipio). You can also add da qui (“from here”).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare alla stazione da qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the station from here?

meaning: how to get to the station.
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions. Often follows polite phrases like “Mi può/potete dire…?” (Can you tell me…?) or “Mi potrebbe dire…?” (Could you tell me…?). “Alla stazione” is usually understood as the train station; you can also say “alla stazione ferroviaria” to be extra clear.
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare alla stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the station?

additional_notes: Used when asking for directions. Often comes after a verb like sapere (“to know”): *Sa/Sai/Sapete come arrivare allo zoo?* (“Do you know how to get to the zoo?”). *allo zoo* = *a + lo zoo* (“to the zoo”).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi può dire come arrivare allo zoo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the zoo?

come eliminare il mio account di

target_language_multi_word_term: come eliminare il mio account di
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions on deleting your account on a specific service/platform. It’s usually followed by the service name (e.g., Facebook, Instagram). In requests you may see polite forms like dimmi (informal, to one person), ditemi (informal, to multiple people), or mi dica (formal).
target_language_example: Scusi, può dirmi come eliminare il mio account di Instagram?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to delete my Instagram account?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like sapere (to know) to say someone knows the way/method to fix computers. It’s an infinitive phrase: come (how) + riparare (to repair) + i computer (computers). In Italian, computer is often invariable: i computer (plural) and il computer (singular).
target_language_example: Non so come riparare i computer, ma posso provarci.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to repair computers, but I can try.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the method/steps for solving something. It often follows verbs like capire (to understand), scoprire (to find out/discover), and dire (to tell): e.g., Capisco/Ho capito come risolvere il problema; Dimmi come risolvere il problema. You can swap il problema for another noun: come risolvere questo esercizio (how to solve this exercise).
target_language_example: Non so come risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: I don't know how to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used with "come se" + subjunctive (here, imperfect subjunctive "conoscesse") to describe a hypothetical or unreal situation. Often implies criticism, like someone is acting/speaking like a know-it-all. You can change the verb/person: "come se sapessi tutto" (as if you knew everything), "come se conoscessero tutto" (as if they knew everything).
target_language_example: Mi dà fastidio quando parla come se conoscesse tutto.
native_language_example: It annoys me when he talks as if he knew everything.

meaning: "as if it were" / "as though it were".
additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an imagined or unreal situation. It’s often followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., fosse, avesse, facesse) because it describes something hypothetical or contrary to fact. You can also use it for strong impressions: Mi sembra come se fosse... = “It feels/seems like...”
target_language_example: Parla con me come se fossi un bambino.
native_language_example: He talks to me as if I were a child.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone speaking or acting like a know-it-all. It’s built with "come se" (“as if”) + the imperfect subjunctive (here: "sapesse" from "sapere"). Change the verb ending to match the subject: "come se sapessi tutto" (as if I knew everything), "come se sapessero tutto" (as if they knew everything).
target_language_example: Mi ha corretto come se sapesse tutto.
native_language_example: He corrected me as if he knew everything.

meaning: "how one/people" (how something is done; how things are).
additional_notes: Used to introduce how something is done or how something happens, often with an impersonal verb: come si fa, come si dice, come si vive. It can also appear with verbs like aspettarsi: come si aspettava = “as (he/she) expected.”
target_language_example: Non so come si dice questo in italiano.
native_language_example: I don't know how you say this in Italian.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or talk about someone’s physical or emotional state. With "Lei" it’s the polite/formal way; with friends you’d often say "come ti senti?" (to one person) or "come vi sentite?" (to multiple people). The "si" here is reflexive and refers to the person who feels (e.g., "Lei sa come si sente?" = "Do you know how you feel?").
target_language_example: Dopo l'operazione, mi può dire come si sente?
native_language_example: After the operation, can you tell me how you feel?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or talk about someone’s feelings or emotional state. "Vi" can be plural "you all" or formal "you" (to one person, polite). Often follows verbs like dire (to say/tell), capire (to understand), sapere (to know): "Ditegli come vi sentite" = "Tell him/her how you feel."
target_language_example: Dimmi come vi sentite dopo la notizia.
native_language_example: Tell me how you feel after the news.

additional_notes: Past participle of "cominciare" used with "avere" (present perfect) to talk about the beginning of an action: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno cominciato a" + infinitive. Often interchangeable with "iniziato a".
target_language_example: Ho cominciato a lavorare qui a giugno.
native_language_example: I started working here in June.

additional_notes: "Cominciò" is the 3rd-person singular passato remoto of "cominciare" (he/she/it began). It’s common in written stories and historical narration, especially in Southern Italy; in everyday speech you often hear "ha cominciato a" instead. Use "a" + infinitive: "cominciò a parlare", "cominciò a piovere".
target_language_example: A un certo punto cominciò a piovere forte.
native_language_example: At a certain point it started to rain hard.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "commettere" (to commit) + "un errore" (a mistake). It’s often in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha commesso un errore" = "I/you/he/she made a mistake." You can also say more casually: "ho fatto un errore".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho commesso un errore.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, I made a mistake.

meaning: classmates (people in the same class at school).
additional_notes: Used for school or course contexts to refer to the other students who attend the same class as you. Singular: "compagno di classe" (male) / "compagna di classe" (female). Can also refer to classmates from the past (e.g., "i miei compagni di classe delle superiori").
target_language_example: Domani esco con alcuni compagni di classe dopo scuola.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going out with some classmates after school.

additional_notes: Used with "stare" + gerund ("mi/ti/si sta/stai/sto comportando") to describe someone’s behavior, usually followed by an adjective: "in maniera così stupida/strana/infantile". "In maniera" can often be replaced by "in modo" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Perché ti stai comportando in maniera così scortese?
native_language_example: Why are you behaving in such a rude way?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "(stare) comportarsi" (to behave) + "in modo così" + an adjective: "in modo così stupido/strano/infantile" = "so stupid/strange/childish". Very common in questions like "Perché ti stai comportando in modo così …?" (Why are you acting so …?).
target_language_example: Perché ti stai comportando in modo così scortese?
native_language_example: Why are you behaving so rudely?

additional_notes: "Comprai" is the simple past (passato remoto) of "comprare" and is common in storytelling, writing, and in some regions of Italy; in everyday speech many people use "ho comprato" instead. "Un paio di" means “a pair of” and is used for things that come in twos (shoes, gloves, glasses).
target_language_example: Comprai un paio di pantaloni nuovi.
native_language_example: I bought a pair of new pants.

additional_notes: Use this before a masculine singular noun: comprare un vaso, un cane, un hot dog. For feminine singular, use “comprare una …” (una casa). “Comprare” may look like English “compare,” but it means “to buy.”
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare un biglietto per Roma.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a ticket to Rome.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’re buying something new. It’s incomplete by itself in Italian: you normally add a noun after it (e.g., comprare un nuovo tappeto = to buy a new carpet). The adjective must agree with the noun: un nuovo (masc. sing.), una nuova (fem. sing.), dei nuovi / delle nuove (plural).
target_language_example: Devo comprare un nuovo telefono perché il mio non funziona più.
native_language_example: I have to buy a new phone because mine doesn’t work anymore.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object introduced by "per" to say who the gift is for: "per lui" (for him), "per lei" (for her), "per loro" (for them), or a name/noun ("per Maria", "per mio padre"). The verb "comprare" is a regular -are verb.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per mia sorella.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my sister.

additional_notes: "Comprare" means "to buy." "Una" is the feminine singular form of "a/an" and is used before a feminine noun: "comprare una macchina" (buy a car), "comprare una cuociriso" (buy a rice cooker), "comprare una fattoria" (buy a farm). For a masculine noun, use "comprare un/uno" (e.g., "comprare un libro").
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una bottiglia d'acqua.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "comprare" (to buy) + "una macchina" (a car). Very common when talking about purchasing a vehicle; you can add adjectives like "nuova" (new) or "usata" (used): "comprare una macchina nuova/usata".
target_language_example: Stiamo pensando di comprare una macchina usata.
native_language_example: We’re thinking about buying a used car.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase: "comprare" means "to buy". It’s often used after another verb (e.g., "ha intenzione di..." = "intends to..." / "stavo risparmiando per..." = "I was saving to..."). You can swap in other items after "comprare" (e.g., "comprare una macchina", "comprare un biglietto").
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una nuova bicicletta per andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a new bicycle to go to work.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense (passato prossimo): ho/ha/hai comprato. “Dei” is a partitive article meaning “some.” It often appears with an indirect object pronoun: “Le ho comprato dei fiori” = “I bought her some flowers”; “Ti ho comprato dei fiori” = “I bought you some flowers.”
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per mia madre.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for my mother.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (past tense): the past participle "comprato" with an auxiliary verb (usually "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno" + comprato). "Del" is the partitive article meaning "some" (bread is uncountable in this context). You can also ask it as a yes/no question: "Hai comprato del pane?"
target_language_example: Ho comprato del pane per la cena.
native_language_example: I bought some bread for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "comprare" (to buy) in the past: "ho/hai/ha... comprato qualcosa per...". "Per" introduces the recipient (a person) or the occasion/purpose (e.g., "per Natale" = for Christmas). You can add the person as an indirect object too: "Le hai comprato qualcosa..." (= Did you buy her something...?).
target_language_example: Ho comprato qualcosa per mia sorella.
native_language_example: I bought something for my sister.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle comprato with avere to talk about a completed purchase: ho comprato questo per... = “I bought/I’ve bought this for…”. The person is introduced with per + name/pronoun (per Tom, per mia madre). Word order is flexible; you can add io for emphasis: Io ho comprato questo per....
target_language_example: Ho comprato questo per te.
native_language_example: I bought this for you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "comprare" in the past (passato prossimo): "(ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) comprato un + [noun]". "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (use "uno" before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, etc.; and "una/un'" for feminine nouns). You may also hear it with a reflexive form: "si è comprato un..." = "he bought himself a...".
target_language_example: Ho comprato un biglietto per domani.
native_language_example: I bought a ticket for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle "comprato" (from "comprare", to buy). Often appears with the auxiliary "avere": "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno comprato un cane" = "I/you/he-she/we/you all/they bought a dog". With pronouns: "Gli/Le ho comprato un cane" = "I bought him/her a dog" (as a gift). "Mi sono comprato/a un cane" means "I bought myself a dog" (uses "essere" + reflexive pronoun; ending agrees: comprato = masculine, comprata = feminine).
target_language_example: L'anno scorso abbiamo comprato un cane per i bambini.
native_language_example: Last year we bought a dog for the kids.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *comprare* (“to buy”). It often appears with *avere* (e.g., *ho comprato...* = “I bought/I have bought...”). With an indirect object pronoun, it shows who you bought it for: *Gli ho comprato...* (“I bought him...”), *Le ho comprato...* (“I bought her...”). *Mi sono comprato...* means “I bought myself...”.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un computer nuovo per lavoro.
native_language_example: I bought a new computer for work.

additional_notes: Used with a noun right after it (e.g., “ho comprato un nuovo estintore” = “I bought a new fire extinguisher”). It’s built from the past participle of *comprare* (“comprato”) and “un nuovo” (“a new”, masculine). With *avere* it forms the common past tense: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno comprato…* If the noun is feminine, use *una nuova*: *Ho comprato una nuova borsa*.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un nuovo telefono.
native_language_example: I bought a new phone.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "comprare" in the past (passato prossimo): "ho comprato" = "I bought / I have bought". "una" is the indefinite article for feminine singular nouns (una rivista, una macchina, una pizza). Often you’ll see it as part of a longer sentence with the subject and auxiliary: "Ho comprato una..." / "Gli ho comprato una..." (= I bought him a...).
target_language_example: Ho comprato una pizza per cena.
native_language_example: I bought a pizza for dinner.

additional_notes: Past action: the past participle (comprato) is normally used with the auxiliary avere (e.g., ho/abbiamo comprato una casa = I/we bought a house / have bought a house). You can add details like nuova (new) or più piccola (smaller): ha comprato una casa nuova; vorrei aver comprato una casa più piccola.
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato una casa vicino al mare.
native_language_example: We bought a house near the sea.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with an auxiliary verb to form the past tense (passato prossimo): **ho/ha/hanno comprato** (with *avere*) = “(I/he/they) bought.” You may also see the reflexive form **si è comprato una macchina fotografica** = “he bought himself a camera.” *Macchina fotografica* is the common Italian word for “camera.”
target_language_example: Ho comprato una macchina fotografica nuova ieri.
native_language_example: I bought a new camera yesterday.

additional_notes: “Comprò” is the passato remoto (historic/simple past) of comprare (“to buy”), used often in stories, news reports, and in some regions to talk about the past. The subject is usually implied (“he/she”). “Un” is the masculine singular “a/an” (use “una” for feminine nouns).
target_language_example: Ieri comprò un biglietto e partì subito.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she bought a ticket and left right away.

additional_notes: "Comprò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "comprare" (to buy), used often in narratives, books, and (in many regions) for completed actions in the distant past. In everyday conversation many speakers prefer "ha comprato un dizionario" (has bought/bought a dictionary).
target_language_example: Ieri comprò un dizionario e lo regalò a sua sorella.
native_language_example: Yesterday he bought a dictionary and gave it to his sister as a gift.

additional_notes: "Comprò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "comprare" and means "bought" in completed, narrative past events (common in stories and in some regions; in everyday speech many people use "ha comprato"). "Per" means "for" and introduces the recipient of the gift (per lei, per il suo ragazzo, per sua figlia, etc.).
target_language_example: Ieri comprò un regalo per sua madre.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she bought a gift for his/her mother.

additional_notes: "Comprò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "comprare" (to buy), used especially in written stories and in some regions to talk about a completed past action. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun introduced by "una" (a/an). In everyday conversation you’ll often hear passato prossimo instead: "ha comprato una...". If the subject is explicit, you can add it: "Lui/Lei comprò una...".
target_language_example: Ieri comprò una maglietta rossa al mercato.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she bought a red T-shirt at the market.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of comprare, common in stories, books, and some regions; in everyday speech you’ll often hear the passato prossimo instead: ha comprato una macchina fotografica (“has bought/bought a camera”). With an indirect object, mi comprò = “he bought me” (i.e., bought it for me).
target_language_example: Ieri ha comprato una macchina fotografica nuova.
native_language_example: Yesterday he bought a new camera.

additional_notes: A noun + adjective phrase: computer (masculine) + nuovo (new). The adjective usually comes after the noun. You can change the possessive: il mio computer nuovo (my new computer), il tuo computer nuovo (your new computer), il suo computer nuovo (his/her new computer).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un computer nuovo ieri.
native_language_example: I bought a new computer yesterday.

additional_notes: Common way to say “laptop” in Italian. Often used with possessives: il mio/tuo/suo/vostro computer portatile. You’ll also hear just “portatile” (short for computer portatile) when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer portatile per lavorare in viaggio.
native_language_example: I need a laptop to work while traveling.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like guardare (to look), esaminare (to examine), ascoltare (to listen) to say you do something with care or close attention. It’s the opposite of doing something distrattamente (distractedly).
target_language_example: Leggi il contratto con attenzione prima di firmare.
native_language_example: Read the contract carefully before signing.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which person someone is with (going with, going out with, traveling with, etc.). Very common in spoken Italian; in English you’d often say “Who… with?” even though the literal word order is “with who?”. Can refer to a friend, company, or a romantic date depending on context (e.g., "Con chi esce?" can mean "Who is he/she going out with?").
target_language_example: Con chi vai al concerto stasera?
native_language_example: Who are you going to the concert with tonight?

meaning: 'with whom' / 'with which' (or 'to/with which' depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to a person or thing already mentioned. It often translates as “with whom” (people) or “with which” (things), and in some cases means “to buy/pay/etc. with” (the means or instrument): e.g., soldi con cui comprare = “money to buy (it) with.”
target_language_example: È il collega con cui lavoro ogni giorno.
native_language_example: He’s the colleague I work with every day.

meaning: to talk to (someone); with whom to talk.
additional_notes: Used after a noun/pronoun to mean “someone to talk to” or “with whom to talk.” It uses cui (= “whom/which”) after a preposition (con). Common with negatives like nessuno/alcun (e.g., “I don’t have anyone to talk to”).
target_language_example: Cerco qualcuno con cui parlare un po'.
native_language_example: I'm looking for someone to talk to for a bit.

meaning: “to play music with” / “to have someone to play music with.”
additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun **cui** after **con** to mean “with whom/with which.” It’s commonly used after words like **nessuno/qualcuno/amici**: *Non ho nessuno con cui suonare* (“I don’t have anyone to play with”). Here **suonare** means playing an instrument (music), not “playing” a game.
target_language_example: Cerco qualcuno con cui suonare la chitarra il sabato.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone to play guitar with on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without difficulty. It often comes after the verb (e.g., “risolvere con facilità”), and can describe how someone answers, finishes, or solves something.
target_language_example: Parla italiano con facilità.
native_language_example: He/She speaks Italian with ease.

additional_notes: Used before masculine plural nouns that take the article "gli" (typically words starting with a vowel, or with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, y). It’s the preposition "con" + the definite article "gli" (no contraction like *coi* here). Example patterns: con gli amici, con gli Stati Uniti, con gli stranieri.
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con gli amici stasera.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my friends tonight.

meaning: with the others; with other people.
additional_notes: Used to refer generally to other people in a group (not you/me). Often appears after verbs like interagire (to interact), parlare (to speak), lavorare (to work), and behaves like “with others / with other people.” In formal or instructional contexts it’s common with polite forms like “Parli…” and “Sia…”.
target_language_example: A scuola, devi collaborare con gli altri.
native_language_example: At school, you have to work together with others.

meaning: "with (his/her/their) eyes"; using your eyes to show something (a look).
additional_notes: Literally “with the eyes.” Used to describe eyes + an adjective (“con gli occhi verdi/luccicanti”), or to say someone communicates only through a look (“mi ringraziò con gli occhi” = thanked me with a look). You can change the article to match the person: con i miei occhi (with my eyes), con i tuoi occhi, con i suoi occhi, etc.
target_language_example: Mi ha salutato con gli occhi, senza dire una parola.
native_language_example: He/She greeted me with a look, without saying a word.

meaning: with your eyes blindfolded; (figuratively) very easily.
additional_notes: Literally means doing something while unable to see (e.g., wearing a blindfold). Very often used figuratively to say you can do something effortlessly or from memory: "Lo faccio con gli occhi bendati" = "I can do it with my eyes closed / I can do it in my sleep."
target_language_example: Questo esercizio lo faccio con gli occhi bendati.
native_language_example: I can do this exercise with my eyes closed.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun (i = “the” for masculine plural): con i cani = “with the dogs,” con i tuoi amici = “with your friends.” It can express being together/doing something with someone, sharing something (in comune con i…), or “be careful with” in warnings (attenzione con i coltelli).
target_language_example: Vado al parco con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I’m going to the park with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with children, spending time with them, or interacting/working with them. "Con" = "with"; "i" = "the" (plural masculine); "bambini" often means "children" in general (can include boys and girls).
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa con i bambini.
native_language_example: Today I'm staying home with the kids.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine plural noun: con i loro gatti = “with their cats.” It’s made of con (“with”) + i (“the,” masculine plural) + loro (“their,” agrees with what is owned, not with who owns it). For other forms: con il loro (masc. sing.), con la loro (fem. sing.), con le loro (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Sono usciti con i loro amici.
native_language_example: They went out with their friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanied by their parents. The preposition "con" + plural article "i" + possessive "loro" (their) + plural noun "genitori" (parents). "Loro" doesn’t change for gender/number; it stays "loro".
target_language_example: I bambini sono andati al museo con i loro genitori.
native_language_example: The children went to the museum with their parents.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean you are with/using/interacting with things or people that belong to you: con i miei bagagli (“with my bags/luggage”), con i miei clienti (“with my clients”). The preposition “con” is “with”, and “i miei” agrees with a masculine plural noun (i miei amici, i miei piedi). For feminine plural, you’d use “con le mie …”.
target_language_example: Non parlare con i miei amici di questo.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to my friends about this.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your friends (going somewhere with them, meeting them, or doing an activity together). It often comes after verbs like andare/venire (to go/come), uscire (to go out), pranzare (to have lunch), ecc. Note: if the speaker is female, you might say "con le mie amiche" (with my [female] friends).
target_language_example: Stasera vado al cinema con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to the cinema with my friends.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like aiutare (“to help”) to say you need help with your homework. In school contexts, compiti usually means “homework,” but it can also mean “assignments/tasks” depending on context. You can swap the possessive: con i tuoi compiti (with your homework), con i suoi compiti (with his/her homework).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: devo finire con i miei compiti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I have to finish my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your parents or that you live in the same home. Common after verbs like "vivere" (to live), "passare/trascorrere" (to spend), "andare" (to go), and "stare" (to stay).
target_language_example: Questo weekend resto a casa con i miei genitori.
native_language_example: This weekend I’m staying home with my parents.

meaning: "with his" / "with its" (referring to masculine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to indicate possession: con i suoi valori (with his values), con i suoi vicini (with its neighbors). It can also mean “with his family/relatives” when the noun is understood from context: Tom passava molto tempo con i suoi (…grandparents/parents/etc.). Changes with gender/number: con le sue (feminine plural), con il suo (masculine singular), con la sua (feminine singular).
target_language_example: È molto paziente con i suoi studenti.
native_language_example: He/She is very patient with his/her students.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing something together with their friends. "Suoi" usually means "his" but can also mean "her" depending on who you’re talking about; the gender comes from the context (e.g., "Mary uscì con i suoi amici" = "with her friends"). For a group of female friends, you can also say "con le sue amiche".
target_language_example: Stasera cena con i suoi amici.
native_language_example: Tonight he/she is having dinner with his/her friends.

meaning: with his/her homework; helping with his/her tasks.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere occupato (to be busy) or aiutare (to help) to say someone is busy doing their homework/tasks, or that someone helps them with it. "Suoi" agrees with the thing owned (compiti = masculine plural), not with the person; it can mean "his" or "her" from context. Often you’ll also hear "con i compiti" (with the homework) if "his/her" is not important.
target_language_example: Posso aiutarti con i tuoi compiti dopo cena.
native_language_example: I can help you with your homework after dinner.

additional_notes: Means someone is together with their own children. "Suoi" agrees with "figli" (masculine plural), and can refer to either a male or female parent depending on context (e.g., "Mary ... con i suoi figli" = “with her children”).
target_language_example: È andata al parco con i suoi figli.
native_language_example: She went to the park with her children.

additional_notes: Means someone is accompanied by, traveling with, or living together with his/her parents. Literally: “with the his/her parents.” Note: in Italian, "suoi" can refer to a male or female person (it agrees with "genitori," not with the person).
target_language_example: Stasera cena con i suoi genitori.
native_language_example: Tonight he/she is having dinner with his/her parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being together with your parents (having dinner, traveling, speaking with them) or living in the same home. "Con" = with, "i" = the (plural), "tuoi" = your (plural), "genitori" = parents. Often appears in questions like "Vivi/Stai vivendo con i tuoi genitori?" (Do you live/Are you still living with your parents?).
target_language_example: Domani pranzo con i tuoi genitori.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m having lunch with your parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something together with the listener’s parents (plural/formal “you” = voi/vostri). Common in questions about living, traveling, arguing, or speaking at home. Singular forms: con tuo padre (with your dad), con tua madre (with your mom), con i tuoi genitori (with your parents).
target_language_example: Andate spesso a cena con i vostri genitori?
native_language_example: Do you often go out to dinner with your parents?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun starting with most consonants (il). It can mean: (1) together/along with something (con il latte), (2) having a feature (la casa con il tetto rosso), (3) with/toward someone in a certain way (generosa con il suo denaro), or (4) in the sense of speaking/meeting with someone (parlare con il mio insegnante). For masculine singular nouns starting with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y, use "con lo"; before a vowel use "con l'".
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con il mio amico.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my friend.

additional_notes: Used to say a food is served/eaten together with ketchup, or that ketchup is added as a condiment. Common in orders and everyday talk about food. Literally “with the ketchup,” but in English you usually just say “with ketchup.”
target_language_example: Vorrei un hamburger con il ketchup, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hamburger with ketchup, please.

meaning: "with my" (with + the + my + masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun you possess: con il mio papà, con il mio amico, con il mio stipendio. If the noun is feminine singular, use "con la mia" (con la mia mamma). Plural: "con i miei" (masc.) / "con le mie" (fem.). In Italian, possession is usually expressed with article + possessive (il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie).
target_language_example: Stasera esco con il mio amico.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm going out with my friend.

meaning: as time goes by; over time.
additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually as time passes. Often followed by a change in opinion, situation, feelings, etc. Common with past tenses (passato prossimo/imperfetto/passato remoto) to describe how something evolved.
target_language_example: Con il passare del tempo, mi sono abituato alla nuova città.
native_language_example: Over time, I got used to the new city.

meaning: "with his/its" or "with your" (formal) + a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: con il suo libro (with his/your book). "Suo" agrees with the thing owned (here: masculine singular), not with the owner.
