Depending on context, "il suo ragazzo" can mean "her boyfriend" or "his boyfriend" (it means "her/his boyfriend"), and you often rely on the subject or context to know whose it is.
target_language_example: Sono venuta con il suo amico.
native_language_example: I came with his friend.

additional_notes: Used with "con" (with) + "il suo" (his/her/its) + "cane" (dog). "Suo" agrees with the thing owned (cane = masculine singular), not with the owner, so it can mean either "his dog" or "her dog" depending on context. Often used to say someone is accompanied by their dog (e.g., going for a walk).
target_language_example: Sono arrivati al parco con il suo cane.
native_language_example: They arrived at the park with his/her dog.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "con" (with) + a possessive: "il suo coltello". "Suo" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the thing owned: "coltello" is masculine singular). Italian often includes the article with possessives ("il suo"), where English usually doesn’t ("his/her"). Can also refer to formal "your" (Lei): "con il suo coltello" = "with your knife" (formal).
target_language_example: Ha aperto il pacco con il suo coltello.
native_language_example: He/She opened the package with his/her knife.

additional_notes: Used to say something is accompanied by/using something: con la carta (with the card), con la maionese (with the mayonnaise). It’s the preposition con + the feminine singular article la. Before a vowel, it becomes con l’ (con l’acqua). With masculine singular you usually say con il / col (col pane).
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con la salsa, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a sandwich with the sauce, please.

additional_notes: Literally “with the mouth open.” Used to describe someone sleeping, breathing, or eating with an open mouth. With "mangiare" it often implies bad manners (eating with your mouth open).
target_language_example: Non parlare con la bocca aperta.
native_language_example: Don’t talk with your mouth open.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an action using your left hand. It often contrasts with "con la mano destra" (with the right hand).
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la bottiglia con la mano sinistra?
native_language_example: Can you open the bottle with your left hand?

meaning: "with my" (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun you possess: con la mia fidanzata (with my girlfriend/fiancée), con la mia banda (with my band). Italian often uses the possessive + article (la mia) where English usually just says “my.” Sometimes the noun is implied and omitted in context: Sono uscito con la mia. (“I went out with my [girlfriend/partner].”)
target_language_example: Stasera esco con la mia sorella.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with my sister.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your family, or doing something in the company of your family (living with them, staying at home with them, going somewhere with them). Note: Italian "con" means "with" (not the English verb "to con").
target_language_example: Oggi ceno con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: Today I’m having dinner with my family.

meaning: 'with his/her/its' (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun that belongs to someone: con la sua mano (with his/her hand), con la sua musica (with her music). Italian possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: la sua = feminine singular; il suo = masculine singular; le sue = feminine plural; i suoi = masculine plural. Often followed directly by the noun.
target_language_example: È arrivata con la sua amica.
native_language_example: She arrived with her friend.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/spending time/living with their family. "Sua" agrees with the thing owned (famiglia), not the person, so it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Oggi pranza con la sua famiglia.
native_language_example: Today he/she is having lunch with his/her family.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/doing something with their (female) cat. Italian possessives agree with the noun: gatta (feminine singular) → sua. Depending on context, sua can mean “his,” “her,” or “your” (formal).
target_language_example: Ogni sera guarda un film con la sua gatta sul divano.
native_language_example: Every evening she watches a movie with her cat on the sofa.

additional_notes: “Con” means “with.” Use “con le” before feminine plural nouns: con le amiche (with the friends), con le mani (with the hands), con le bacchette (with chopsticks). It can express accompaniment (with someone) or means/instrument (with something). Often “con” + article combines: con + le → con le (not *colle*).
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con le mie sorelle.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with my sisters.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanied by their friends. "Amiche" is feminine plural, so it refers to female friends (or a group of friends treated as feminine). "Loro" means "their" (of them).
target_language_example: Maria è uscita con le loro amiche dopo cena.
native_language_example: Maria went out with their (female) friends after dinner.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to say you do something using your hands instead of tools or cutlery: *mangiare con le mani* (eat with your hands), *piantare con le mani* (plant by hand). It can also describe manual skill/handiness: *essere bravo con le mani* = be good with your hands (good at practical/manual work).
target_language_example: Preferisco farlo con le mani, non con la macchina.
native_language_example: I prefer to do it by hand, not with the machine.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with your friends, when the friends are all female or the group is referred to in the feminine plural. Often follows verbs like andare/uscire (go out), viaggiare (travel), passare il weekend (spend the weekend). If the group is mixed or all male, you typically say “con i miei amici.”
target_language_example: Stasera vado al cinema con le mie amiche.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to the cinema with my (female) friends.

meaning: with words; (fig.) good with words / wordplay.
additional_notes: Often used literally (“with words”), but very commonly in expressions like "giocare con le parole" (to play with words / to twist words) and "essere bravo con le parole" (to be good with words, speak well, be persuasive). Depending on context, it can be positive (clever, witty) or negative (avoiding the point, being slippery).
target_language_example: Non giocare con le parole: dimmi sì o no.
native_language_example: Don’t play with words: tell me yes or no.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun to mean “with her/his/its …”. The possessive agrees with the noun owned (sue = feminine plural), not with the owner. Often followed by a noun like: con le sue osservazioni (with her/his remarks), con le sue studentesse (with her students).
target_language_example: Mi interrompe sempre con le sue domande.
native_language_example: He/She always interrupts me with his/her questions.

additional_notes: Means someone is together/spending time with her (female) friends. It’s made of con (with) + le (the, plural feminine) + sue (her, plural) + amiche (female friends). For male friends: con i suoi amici. For mixed/unspecified groups you’ll often hear: con i suoi amici.
target_language_example: Stasera esce con le sue amiche.
native_language_example: Tonight she’s going out with her friends.

additional_notes: "Lei" can mean "her" (third person feminine) or formal "you" (used to be polite). With "con" it often means being together with someone (e.g., "andare/uscire con lei" = to go/go out with her). With some verbs it can translate as "to" + person in English, e.g., "scusarsi con lei" = to apologize to her, and "essere d'accordo con lei" = to agree with her.
target_language_example: Preferisco parlarne con lei domani.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk about it with her tomorrow.

con lo scopo di ottenere un nuovo

target_language_multi_word_term: con lo scopo di ottenere un nuovo
meaning: with the aim of getting a new …
additional_notes: Used to state a purpose/goal. It’s followed by what you want to obtain (often a noun), e.g. “un nuovo lavoro/impiego” (“a new job”). In everyday speech you can often use simpler alternatives like “per” (“to/in order to”) or “con l’obiettivo di” (“with the goal of”).
target_language_example: È venuto qui con lo scopo di ottenere un nuovo contratto.
native_language_example: He came here with the aim of getting a new contract.

additional_notes: Used to explain someone’s purpose or reason for doing something. It’s fairly formal and common in writing. You can swap in another verb after “di” (e.g., con lo scopo di lavorare = with the aim of working). Similar options: “con l’obiettivo di…”, “per…” (more common and less formal).
target_language_example: Sono qui con lo scopo di studiare italiano.
native_language_example: I’m here with the aim of studying Italian.

additional_notes: Used with recipes and food preparation to say an ingredient is combined with sugar (often after verbs like mescolare "to mix" or unire "to combine"). Literally "with the sugar" (con + lo), but in English you usually translate it simply as "with sugar".
target_language_example: Sbatti i tuorli con lo zucchero fino a ottenere una crema chiara.
native_language_example: Beat the egg yolks with sugar until you get a light cream.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "con" (with) + the stressed pronoun "loro" (them). "Loro" refers to a group of people (not objects); for objects you usually use "con essi/esse" (more formal/rare) or rephrase. Often answers “with whom?”: "Vieni con loro?" = “Are you going with them?”
target_language_example: Vuoi venire con loro stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with them tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **con** to mean being together/with someone (e.g., *essere/stare/rimanere con lui* = “to be/stay/remain with him”). After a preposition like **con**, Italian uses the stressed pronoun **lui** (not *lo*, which is a direct object pronoun). It can also mean “toward him” in expressions like *essere severo con lui* (“be strict with him”).
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con lui stasera.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with him tonight.

meaning: 'with me' (together with me / in my company).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanying you or doing something together with you: Ho una bambina con me. It can also mean “toward me” after some emotions/attitudes: Sei arrabbiato con me? It’s very common in invitations: Vuoi venire con me? / Vuoi fare una passeggiata con me?
target_language_example: Vieni al cinema con me?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the movies with me?

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/doing something alongside your sister (e.g., eating, playing, sharing a room). It can also show a relationship involving her: *si è sposato con mia sorella* = “he married my sister.” In phrases like *provarci con (qualcuno)*, *con* means “on (someone)” → *Smettila di provarci con mia sorella* = “Stop hitting on my sister.”
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con mia sorella stasera.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "con" to say you are together with your brother (doing an activity, going somewhere), or that something is in your brother’s possession/at his place (e.g., "Il mio computer è con mio fratello" = my computer is with my brother). It can also appear in set expressions like "andare d’accordo con" (to get along with) and "essere confuso con" (to be mistaken for).
target_language_example: Stasera ceno con mio fratello.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m having dinner with my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your uncle, often meaning you live/stay at his place or in his company. With singular family members in Italian, the possessive usually comes without the article: "mio zio" (not *il mio zio*).
target_language_example: Stasera ceno con mio zio.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm having dinner with my uncle.

con mio zio la scorsa settimana

target_language_multi_word_term: con mio zio la scorsa settimana
additional_notes: A time + company phrase often used with verbs like "stare", "restare", or "rimanere" to say you stayed with someone last week (e.g., "Sono rimasto/a con mio zio la scorsa settimana"). "Scorsa settimana" means "last week" (literally, "the past week").
target_language_example: Ho dormito con mio zio la scorsa settimana perché ero in visita.
native_language_example: I slept at my uncle’s place last week because I was visiting.

con mio zio la settimana scorsa

target_language_multi_word_term: con mio zio la settimana scorsa
additional_notes: Used to say you were with your uncle during the previous week. Common structure: **con + [person]** (“with…”) + a time expression like **la settimana scorsa** (“last week”). In the past, you’ll often see it with **essere**: **sono stato/a con…** or **sono rimasto/a con…** (stato/a, rimasto/a change for gender).
target_language_example: Sono stato con mio zio la settimana scorsa per aiutarlo in casa.
native_language_example: I was with my uncle last week to help him at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/along with you and your group. Common after verbs like venire (to come), stare/essere (to be), cantare (to sing), giocare (to play), studiare (to study), or in invitations and suggestions (e.g., Vieni con noi!).
target_language_example: Vuoi venire al cinema con noi stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to the movies with us tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their mother (doing something with her, staying with her, living with her, etc.). "Sua" agrees with the noun it refers to (madre is feminine), and it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context. Often you can omit the subject in Italian: "Vive ancora con sua madre" = "(He/She) still lives with his/her mother."
target_language_example: Oggi vado al cinema con sua madre.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to the movies with his/her mother.

meaning: with his wife / with her wife.
additional_notes: Means “with his/her wife.” In Italian, "sua" agrees with the thing possessed (moglie = feminine singular), not with the owner. Without context, "sua" can mean his, her, or even your (formal) — e.g., "con sua moglie" can also mean “with your wife” when speaking politely (Lei).
target_language_example: Viene con sua moglie stasera.
native_language_example: Is he coming with his wife tonight?

additional_notes: Means someone is together/doing something with their sister. Italian uses the possessive (suo/sua) to agree with the thing owned (sister = sorella, feminine singular → sua), not with the owner, so it can mean either “his sister” or “her sister”; context usually makes it clear. After many prepositions like con (“with”), the possessive is typically used without the article: con sua sorella (also possible: con la sua sorella, but less common and usually more specific/emphatic).
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con sua sorella.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with his/her sister.

meaning: with his brother / with her brother.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is accompanied by their brother. In Italian, "suo" can mean both "his" and "her" (it agrees with what is owned—"fratello"—not with the owner), so the context tells you whose brother it is. Also note that "con" can mean "with" in the sense of "together with" (and sometimes "against/with" after certain verbs like "arrabbiarsi con" = "to get angry with").
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con suo fratello.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with his/her brother.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is with their father (going somewhere together, living/staying together, etc.). Italian "suo" can mean both "his" and "her"—the gender comes from "padre" (father), not from the owner. You can swap in other possessives: "con mio padre" (with my father), "con tuo padre" (with your father), "con il padre di Mary" (with Mary’s father). It can also describe relationships: "una relazione difficile con suo padre" (a difficult relationship with her/his father).
target_language_example: Sono uscito con suo padre a comprare il pane.
native_language_example: I went out with his/her father to buy bread.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is staying/living together with their uncle (same home or in the uncle’s company). It commonly follows verbs like vivere/abitare (to live), rimanere (to stay), andare (to go).
target_language_example: Domani dormo con suo zio perché i miei genitori sono via.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m sleeping at his uncle’s place because my parents are away.

meaning: with him/her/them; with you (formal); on oneself (carrying).
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like avere/portare/tenere to say someone has something with them (they are carrying it). "Sé" is a reflexive pronoun referring back to the subject (lui/lei/loro). With the polite imperative "Lei", you can say: "La porti con sé" = "Take it with you."
target_language_example: Ho il passaporto con me.
native_language_example: I have my passport with me.

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular pronoun te (you). It can mean being together/along with someone (Vengo con te), having something in your possession (Portala con te = take it with you), or speaking directly to someone (essere onesto con te). For the formal singular, use con Lei; for plural, con voi.
target_language_example: Posso venire con te al supermercato?
native_language_example: Can I come with you to the supermarket?

meaning: with trepidation (anxiously), expecting to be contradicted/disproved.
additional_notes: Used to say you are waiting anxiously to see if what you said will be proven wrong or denied by facts or by someone else. The past participle must agree with who is being contradicted: smentito (masc. sg.), smentita (fem. sg.), smentiti (masc./mixed pl.), smentite (fem. pl.). Often follows verbs like aspettare/attendere (“to wait/await”).
target_language_example: Aspetto con trepidazione di essere smentito dai risultati.
native_language_example: I’m waiting anxiously to be proven wrong by the results.

meaning: with trepidation / anxiously, expecting to be proven wrong.
additional_notes: Used in formal or journalistic writing to express that you strongly suspect something is true, but you hope someone will contradict it (smentire = to deny/contradict; essere smentiti = to be contradicted / proven wrong). Often said with a touch of irony or skepticism: “We’ll wait anxiously to see if the facts prove us wrong.”
target_language_example: Diciamo che i prezzi saliranno ancora, ma aspettiamo con trepidazione di essere smentiti.
native_language_example: We’re saying prices will rise again, but we anxiously hope to be proven wrong.

additional_notes: A strong, emotional way to say you feel something very deeply. Common with verbs like "amare" (to love), and it can also be used with negative feelings for emphasis (e.g., "Ti odio con tutto il mio cuore" = "I hate you with all my heart"). You can change "mio" to match the subject: "con tutto il tuo cuore" (your), "con tutto il suo cuore" (his/her), "con tutto il nostro/vostro cuore" (our/your plural).
target_language_example: Grazie per l’aiuto: te ne sono grato con tutto il mio cuore.
native_language_example: Thanks for the help: I’m grateful to you with all my heart.

meaning: with a; having a (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant (un padre, un passato, un nocciolo, un leggero accento, un estraneo, un madrelingua, un fucile, un palanchino). It can mean (1) accompanied by/along with (“with a father…”), (2) describing a characteristic (“a man with a complicated past”), or (3) the instrument/means used (“killed with a crowbar”). For masculine nouns starting with s+consonant, z, ps, gn, etc., use “con uno” (e.g., con uno zaino).
target_language_example: Vado al parco con un amico.
native_language_example: I’m going to the park with a friend.

meaning: with a stick (using a stick as a tool/weapon).
additional_notes: Used to say you do something by using a stick (e.g., to hit someone or to write/draw). The preposition “con” means “with,” and “bastone” is “stick/cane.” In everyday speech you might also hear “con un palo” (with a pole) depending on the object.
target_language_example: Ha disegnato un cuore per terra con un bastone.
native_language_example: He/She drew a heart on the ground with a stick.

meaning: with a knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is done using a knife as the tool/weapon (con = “with”). Often answers “How?/With what?” In everyday contexts it can describe cutting food or getting hurt; in news/crime contexts it can describe stabbing.
target_language_example: Ho tagliato il pane con un coltello.
native_language_example: I cut the bread with a knife.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something in a friendly, warm way. Common with verbs like accogliere (to welcome), salutare (to greet), parlare (to speak), rispondere (to answer). It can also be used more generally to suggest a positive attitude.
target_language_example: Mi ha risposto con un sorriso.
native_language_example: He/She answered me with a smile.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: con una gita (a trip), con una pipa (a pipe), con una dentista (a dentist, feminine). Before a vowel it often becomes “con un’ ”: con un’amica (with a friend). For masculine nouns you use “con un”: con un amico (with a friend).
target_language_example: Vado al cinema con una mia amica stasera.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with a friend of mine tonight.

meaning: with a credit card; by credit card.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "pagare" (to pay) to say the payment method. In shops and restaurants you may also hear "con carta" or "con la carta" (with the card) when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Preferisco pagare con una carta di credito, grazie.
native_language_example: I prefer to pay with a credit card, thank you.

additional_notes: Used to say what tool you use to write or draw. Often in instructions (school/exams/forms) when you should write in pencil (so it can be erased). You can swap the tool: con una penna (with a pen), con una biro (with a ballpoint pen).
target_language_example: Compila questo modulo con una matita, per favore.
native_language_example: Fill out this form with a pencil, please.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like colpire (to hit) or attaccare (to attack) to say what object/weapon was used. Commonly follows the verb or comes at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: L'ha minacciato con una mazza da baseball.
native_language_example: She/he threatened him with a baseball bat.

additional_notes: Used to say the tool/instrument you use to write or sign. Often followed by an adjective specifying the pen, e.g. "con una penna blu" (with a blue pen). Common in instructions and polite requests: "Per favore, scrivi/scriva con una penna".
target_language_example: Puoi compilare questo modulo con una penna nera?
native_language_example: Can you fill out this form with a black pen?

meaning: with a girl; (in dating context) going out with a girl.
additional_notes: Literally means “with a girl.” In contexts with verbs like “uscire (con)” or “stare uscendo (con),” it commonly means “to go out with / date a girl.” The gender agreement changes as needed: con un ragazzo (with a boy).
target_language_example: Stasera esco con una ragazza che ho conosciuto online.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with a girl I met online.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/along with one person from their group of friends. "suo/suoi" agrees with the person (his/her), and "amico/amici" can be changed for gender/number (e.g., "con una delle sue amiche" = with one of her (female) friends).
target_language_example: Giulia è al bar con uno dei suoi amici.
native_language_example: Giulia is at the bar with one of her friends.

additional_notes: Uses "voi" to mean "you" when speaking to more than one person, or as a formal/polite "you" (less common than "Lei"). Often used to say you’re accompanying someone or staying together with them: "sono/siamo con voi" (I’m/we’re with you).
target_language_example: Scusate il ritardo: siamo con voi tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: Sorry we’re late: we’ll be with you in five minutes.

additional_notes: Condivise is passato remoto (a literary/storytelling past tense), especially common in books and narratives; in everyday speech you’ll often hear ha condiviso instead. Il suo pranzo means “his/her lunch” (suo can refer to either his or her depending on context). The person you share with comes after con (with): condivise il suo pranzo con me/lui/lei.
target_language_example: Condivise il suo pranzo con un amico.
native_language_example: He/She shared his/her lunch with a friend.

meaning: to confirm the price by email.
additional_notes: Polite, common in customer service/business contexts when you want written confirmation. You can use it with "potrebbe/potresti" (you, singular) or "potreste" (you, plural/formal). "Tramite" means "via/by means of" and is interchangeable with "via" in many situations.
target_language_example: Può confermare il prezzo tramite e-mail oggi stesso?
native_language_example: Can you confirm the price by email today?

meaning: “I had known (him/her/them) for a long time.”
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense (conoscevo) to describe an ongoing state in the past: knowing someone over a period of time. With a direct object pronoun it becomes: lo conoscevo da molto tempo (“I’d known him/it for a long time”), la conoscevo… (“her/it”), li conoscevo… (“them,” masculine/mixed), le conoscevo… (“them,” feminine).
target_language_example: La conoscevo da molto tempo, ma non sapevo dove abitava.
native_language_example: I had known her for a long time, but I didn’t know where she lived.

meaning: 'Do you know the boy in the (photo/picture)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone recognizes/knows a specific boy shown in a photo. Often you’ll see it as **Lo conosci, il ragazzo nella foto?** where **lo** = “him” repeats the direct object (**il ragazzo**) for emphasis (common in spoken Italian). **nella** = “in the” (nel + la), so it’s typically followed by **foto** or **fotografia**.
target_language_example: Scusa, lo conosci il ragazzo nella foto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know the boy in the photo?

meaning: met (got to know) some Canadian women.
additional_notes: Uses the past participle of "conoscere" in the passato prossimo (e.g., "hai/avete/ha conosciuto...") to mean "met" or "got to know" someone. "Delle canadesi" is a partitive expression meaning "some Canadian women" (female plural).
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto delle canadesi a Boston la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I met some Canadian women in Boston last week.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *conoscere* (to know/be familiar with). It usually refers to knowing a person well or being very familiar with something. You can add a direct object or pronoun: *Conosco molto bene tuo fratello* (I know your brother very well), *Ti conosco molto bene* (I know you very well), *Lo conosco molto bene* (I know him/it very well).
target_language_example: Conosco molto bene questo quartiere.
native_language_example: I know this neighborhood very well.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object (often a pronoun like gli/le/ti/vi) plus an infinitive to say what someone suggested another person should do: “Ho consigliato a Marco di riposare.” In the plural: “abbiamo consigliato di …” = “we advised/recommended to …” (context makes clear who was advised, or it can be said with “a + person”).
target_language_example: Il medico mi ha consigliato di bere più acqua.
native_language_example: The doctor advised/recommended that I drink more water.

additional_notes: "Consigliò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "consigliare" (to advise/recommend), 3rd person singular: "he/she advised." It’s commonly used in written Italian (stories, news, biographies), while in everyday speech you often hear "ha consigliato di" (past tense with "ha" + past participle). It’s followed by "di" + infinitive: "consigliò di bere" (advised to drink). To advise someone *not* to do something: "consigliò di non" + infinitive.
target_language_example: Il medico mi consigliò di riposare qualche giorno.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me to rest for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to say you can depend on a person for help, support, or trust. It’s followed by an indirect object pronoun with di: contare su di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro (also: su di lei for formal “you”). In everyday speech you’ll also hear contare su + name (e.g., contare su Marco).
target_language_example: Puoi contare su di me se hai bisogno di una mano.
native_language_example: You can count on me if you need a hand.

contatto in maniera frequente con degli studenti stranieri

target_language_multi_word_term: contatto in maniera frequente con degli studenti stranieri
additional_notes: In the examples this comes after the common verb phrase **entrare in contatto con** = “to come into contact with / to get in touch with.” It’s used with **essere** in the past (**sono entrato/a in contatto…**) and the past participle agrees with the subject (**entrato** = male, **entrata** = female). **In maniera frequente** means “frequently / often.”
target_language_example: Durante l’università sono entrata in contatto in maniera frequente con degli studenti stranieri.
native_language_example: During university I often came into contact with foreign students.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone (or describe someone) to keep doing an action: continua a + infinitive (continua a leggere = keep reading). It can be an instruction (imperative) or a statement in the present tense. Often translated as “keep on …” or “continue to …”.
target_language_example: Continua a parlare: ti sto ascoltando.
native_language_example: Keep talking: I’m listening to you.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb (continuare a + infinitive) to say you keep doing an action or don’t stop doing it: continuare a studiare/scrivere/fare/vivere. Very common after verbs like decidere (to decide), chiedere (to ask), dovere (must), volere (to want).
target_language_example: Per favore, continua a parlare più lentamente.
native_language_example: Please, keep talking more slowly.

additional_notes: Used to say someone keeps doing the activity of working, or will go on working in the future. It’s built from continuare (to continue) + a + lavorare (to work). Often followed by a place (qui, in ufficio) or a reason/purpose (per la famiglia...).
target_language_example: Devo continuare a lavorare domani.
native_language_example: I have to keep working tomorrow.

meaning: to keep going out with / to continue seeing (someone).
additional_notes: Used with a person (con + name/pronoun) to say you keep spending time with them; depending on context it can mean either “keep hanging out with” or “keep dating/seeing.” Grammatically it’s “continuare a/ad” + infinitive (uscire), and “ad” is common before a vowel (uscire).
target_language_example: Non so se voglio continuare ad uscire con lui.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I want to keep going out with him.

additional_notes: Used to tell more than one person (voi) to keep doing an action: continuate a + infinitive (continuate a ballare, continuate a cercarlo). For one person you’d say: continua a. Often used as an instruction/encouragement, sometimes as an order.
target_language_example: Continuate a parlare piano, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep speaking quietly, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb CONTINUARE + A + infinitive to say that someone keeps doing an action. In the past tense (ha continuato a...), it means they continued/kept doing it. The next verb stays in the infinitive (dire, leggere, mentire, litigare).
target_language_example: Ho continuato a studiare fino a tardi.
native_language_example: I kept studying until late.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “continuare a lavorare”: ho/ha/hanno continuato a lavorare = “I/he-she/they continued to work.” Used to say you kept doing an action (often despite being tired or for a long time).
target_language_example: Nonostante il mal di testa, ho continuato a lavorare fino alle sei.
native_language_example: Despite the headache, I continued to work until six.

meaning: you keep (doing something) / you continue to (do something).
additional_notes: "Continui" is the present tense of "continuare" for "you" (formal) and is also used with "Lei". It’s followed by "a" + an infinitive (e.g., continuare a fare). Often used in questions or complaints ("Perché continui a...?" = "Why do you keep ...?") and can sound like telling someone to stop or to persist, depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Continui a parlare così forte.
native_language_example: You keep talking so loudly.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say an action keeps happening or you keep doing it (often repeatedly or despite trying to stop). Conjugate only "continuare" (continuo, continui, continua, continuiamo, continuate, continuano) + a + infinitive: "Continuo a studiare". When the next verb normally takes "a" (e.g., "scrivere a qualcuno"), you can have both: "Continuo a scrivere a Tom".
target_language_example: Continuo a dimenticare il tuo nome, scusa.
native_language_example: I keep forgetting your name, sorry.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "continuare" used in storytelling and formal writing, especially for completed past events. It’s followed by "a" + infinitive (e.g., continuò a camminare = continued walking). In everyday spoken Italian you’ll often hear "ha continuato a" (passato prossimo) instead.
target_language_example: Dopo la pausa, continuò a parlare per altri dieci minuti.
native_language_example: After the break, he continued to speak for another ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to show opposition, criticism, or action directed at someone/something: protestare contro il piano (protest against the plan), urlare contro il computer (yell at the computer). With races/struggles it can mean "against" an enemy or challenge (una corsa contro il male = a race against evil). It’s simply contro + il (masculine singular "the"); compare: contro lo, contro la, contro i, contro gli, contro le.
target_language_example: Sono contro il fumo nei ristoranti.
native_language_example: I’m against smoking in restaurants.

additional_notes: Used for physical contact/position (something leaning or pressed against a wall). In commands (especially by police/guards), it can mean “up against the wall!”. Also appears in the common expression “con la schiena contro il muro” = “with your back against the wall,” which can be literal or figurative (feeling trapped/under pressure).
target_language_example: Metti la bici contro il muro, per favore.
native_language_example: Put the bike against the wall, please.

meaning: at his computer (angrily; used after verbs like “yell/shout”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like *urlare/gridare contro* (“to yell/shout at”) to show the target of the anger. Literally it’s “against his computer,” but in English you usually say “at his computer.” You can swap *suo* with other possessives: *contro il mio computer* (at my computer), *contro il tuo computer* (at your computer).
target_language_example: Ho gridato contro il mio computer quando si è bloccato.
native_language_example: I yelled at my computer when it froze.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la). Common meanings: (1) being opposed to something: "contro la violenza" = against violence; (2) competing/playing versus: "contro la Scozia" = against Scotland; (3) physical impact/movement into something: "sbattere/schiantarsi contro la banchina" = crash into the dock; (4) directing speech/anger at someone: "gridare contro la cassiera" = shout at the cashier. With masculine/singular or plural nouns you’ll see: contro il / contro lo / contro i / contro gli / contro le.
target_language_example: Siamo contro la guerra.
native_language_example: We are against the war.

additional_notes: Used to say you did something even though you didn’t want to (often because someone forced or pressured you). You can change the possessive: contro la tua/sua/nostra/vostra volontà (“against your/his/her/our/your will”).
target_language_example: Ho accettato contro la mia volontà.
native_language_example: I accepted against my will.

additional_notes: Used for keeping anger in check (not showing it or not letting it guide your actions). The possessive can change: controllare la mia/tua/sua/nostra/vostra/loro rabbia. You can also say simply “controllare la rabbia” (to control anger).
target_language_example: Respira profondamente e cerca di controllare la tua rabbia.
native_language_example: Take a deep breath and try to control your anger.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: “una copia del libro” (“a copy of the book”). It’s “copia” + “del” (= “di” + “il”). With other nouns you change “del”: “dello” (before s+consonant, z, gn, ps…), “dell’” (before a vowel), “della” (feminine singular), “dei/degli/delle” (plural).
target_language_example: Mi serve una copia del documento, per favore.
native_language_example: I need a copy of the document, please.

meaning: "copy the copy" (make a copy of an existing copy).
additional_notes: Used when talking about documents (certificates, contracts, wills) and you need to reproduce a photocopy/scan rather than the original. Often implies the result may be lower quality or less detailed, and it may be labeled as "copia di copia" (copy of a copy).
target_language_example: Per favore, copia la copia e scrivi sopra "copia di copia".
native_language_example: Please copy the copy and write "copy of a copy" on it.

meaning: “the thing that …” / “the thing which …” (a general way to refer to something, followed by a description).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with che (“that/which”). Often appears as la/una/ogni/quella cosa che… (“the/a/every/that thing that…”). In speech it can be a vague placeholder like “you know that thing that…”.
target_language_example: È una cosa che mi rende felice.
native_language_example: It’s something that makes me happy.

additional_notes: Used to ask about something a group of people has done, usually with a past participle (passato prossimo): "Cosa avete + participle?" (e.g., cantato, vinto, scoperto). "Avete" is the 2nd-person plural of *avere* (“you all have”) and is also the auxiliary for many past-tense verbs. It can also be literal "What do you have?" depending on context, but in these examples it introduces a past action/result.
target_language_example: Cosa avete deciso alla fine?
native_language_example: What did you decide in the end?

meaning: “What did you (plural) do / have you (plural) done?”
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (voi) what actions they did, often with a time expression (ad Halloween, questa estate) or with ad/ con/ per (“to/with/for”). In spoken Italian it’s often shortened to “Che avete fatto?”
target_language_example: Cosa avete fatto ieri sera dopo cena?
native_language_example: What did you all do last night after dinner?

meaning: "What should I do?" / "What am I supposed to do?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or the best course of action. "Dovrei" is the conditional of "dovere" (to have to/should), so it often sounds like seeking guidance or expressing uncertainty. It can be followed by details like "con..." (with/about), "dopo" (next/after), or "per..." (for someone).
target_language_example: Non so come rispondere: cosa dovrei fare?
native_language_example: I don’t know how to reply—what should I do?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone (or an organization/animal) does, either in general (habitual: job/regular activity) or right now/at a specific time (especially with words like "adesso" = now, "stasera" = tonight). The subject often comes right after: "Cosa fa Tom?" You can also use it on its own if the subject is clear: "Cosa fa?" (What is he/she doing?)
target_language_example: Cosa fa Marco in questo momento?
native_language_example: What is Marco doing right now?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say which action/plan is the right one, often after verbs like sapere (to know), decidere (to decide), dire (to tell), scoprire (to find out). Common in moments of uncertainty: Non so più cosa fare = “I don’t know what to do anymore.”
target_language_example: Se non sai cosa fare, chiedi aiuto.
native_language_example: If you don’t know what to do, ask for help.

additional_notes: Used in questions when the verb takes an indirect object (someone you speak to, give to, tell to). "Gli" is an unstressed pronoun meaning "to him" (also sometimes "to them" in informal spoken Italian). Word order is typically: Cosa + gli + verb (e.g., Cosa gli dici? = What are you telling him?).
target_language_example: Cosa gli hai detto ieri?
native_language_example: What did you tell him yesterday?

meaning: 'what (to her / to you [formal])' at the start of a question.
additional_notes: Used to ask “what” with an indirect object pronoun: le = “to her” (3rd person feminine singular) or “to you” in the formal polite form (Lei). Word order in English usually changes (e.g., “What did you tell her?” / “What do you like to do?”). Often followed by a verb like dire (“to tell”), piacere (“to like”), etc.
target_language_example: Cosa le posso dire?
native_language_example: What can I tell her? / What can I tell you (formal)?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or problem that happened to a woman/girl. Uses the polite/formal "Lei" form: "le" = “to her/to you (formal)”, and "è capitato" = “happened” (past). You can change the pronoun depending on who it happened to: "cosa gli è capitato?" (to him), "cosa ti è capitato?" (to you, informal), "cosa vi è capitato?" (to you all). Often said with concern after something seems wrong.
target_language_example: Scusi, cosa le è capitato? Sembra preoccupata.
native_language_example: Excuse me, what happened to you? You seem worried.

meaning: “What happened to her?” / “What happened to you?” (formal).
additional_notes: Uses the polite form (Lei). "le" means “to her” or “to you” (formal), and "è successo" is the past tense of succedere (“to happen”). In context it can be a direct question (“What happened…?”) or used after Guardi/Guardate (“Look what happened to her”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, cosa le è successo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what happened to you? (formal)

meaning: "what ... about it/of it" (used to ask what someone thinks, what to do, or what happened).
additional_notes: Used at the start of questions with the pronoun “ne” (= about it/of it/from it). Common patterns: “Cosa ne pensi di...?” = “What do you think of...?”; “Cosa ne dici di...?” = “What do you say to...?/How about...?”; “Cosa ne facciamo?” = “What do we do with it/them?”; “Cosa ne è stato di...?” = “What happened to...?”
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensi di questo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion. It’s often followed by di + noun/pronoun: "Cosa ne pensa di lui?" = "What do you think of him?" The "ne" refers back to the topic (“about it/that”). With "Lei" it’s polite/formal: "Lei cosa ne pensa?"
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensa di questo progetto?
native_language_example: What do you think of this project?

meaning: “What do you think of …?” (asking someone’s opinion about …).
additional_notes: Formal/polite way to ask for an opinion. The basic structure is: Cosa ne pensa di + [noun/infinitive]. With masculine singular nouns you often see “del” (= di + il): Cosa ne pensa del film? For feminine singular: “della” (della pizza). For plural: “dei/degli/delle”. Often used with “Lei” for extra politeness: Lei cosa ne pensa del libro?
target_language_example: Lei cosa ne pensa del nuovo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you think of the new restaurant?

meaning: 'What do you think of ...?' (asking for an opinion).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone’s opinion about a person, thing, plan, place, etc. It comes from "pensare" (to think) and normally takes "di" before the topic. Often used with the formal "Lei": "Lei cosa ne pensa di ...?" You can also use it on its own if the topic is clear: "Cosa ne pensa?" = "What do you think?".
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensa di questa idea?
native_language_example: What do you think of this idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. It’s addressed to “you” plural (voi): either a group of people, or (in some regions) as a polite/formal way to address one person. "Ne" means “about it/about that/about them,” and is often followed by a more specific topic with di: "Cosa ne pensate di questo ristorante?"
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensate di questo progetto?
native_language_example: What do you all think about this project?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about a topic. It addresses more than one person (voi). The structure is: Cosa + ne + pensate + di + il/lo/la/i/gli/le. With masculine singular nouns you often see del (= di + il): Cosa ne pensate del Brasile? You can also start with Voi for emphasis: Voi, cosa ne pensate del futuro?
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensate del nuovo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you think about the new restaurant?

meaning: "What do you (all) think of ...?" / "What’s your opinion of ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about a person, thing, or idea. It uses the 2nd person plural (pensate): you can use it to address a group ("you all"), or as a polite/formal "you" (especially in some contexts). "Ne" refers back to the topic: roughly "about it".
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensate di questa idea?
native_language_example: What do you think of this idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion. Often followed by a topic with **di** (e.g., *cosa ne pensi di lui?*) or **della/del/dei/degli/delle** (e.g., *cosa ne pensi della nuova professoressa?*). The little word **ne** refers back to “about it/about them,” so it can stand alone when the topic is already clear: *Allora, cosa ne pensi?* You’ll also hear it as *Tu cosa ne pensi?* or with emphasis like *veramente* (“really”).
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensi di questo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you think of this restaurant?

meaning: "what do you think of ...?" (asking someone’s opinion about something).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. It’s made of: cosa (what) + ne (about it/about that) + pensi (you think) + del (= di + il, of the). The "del" changes depending on the noun: della (fem. sing.), dell’ (before a vowel), dei/degli/delle (plural). Often you can add "tu" for emphasis: "Tu cosa ne pensi del..."
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensi del ristorante qui vicino?
native_language_example: What do you think of the restaurant nearby?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about a person, thing, or idea. It’s often followed by a noun (Cosa ne pensi di Tom?) or by an infinitive (Cosa ne pensi di andare al cinema?). The little word “ne” refers back to the topic (“about it/about that”) and is required in this common phrasing.
target_language_example: Cosa ne pensi di questa idea?
native_language_example: What do you think of this idea?

meaning: "What do you think" (followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion/guess about what is happening, what someone said/did, or what should be done. It’s typically followed by "che" + a verb (often in the subjunctive in Italian): "Cosa pensate che stia succedendo?" = “What do you think is happening?” You can change "pensate" depending on who you’re talking to: "cosa pensi che" (you, informal singular), "cosa pensa che" (you, formal), "cosa pensate che" (you all / polite plural).
target_language_example: Cosa pensate che sia la scelta migliore?
native_language_example: What do you think is the best choice?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about something. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo) because it introduces uncertainty or a personal opinion: "Cosa pensi che abbia detto?" = "What do you think he/she said?" You can also use it inside a longer sentence: "Dimmi cosa pensi che si debba fare" = "Tell me what you think should be done."
target_language_example: Cosa pensi che succederà domani?
native_language_example: What do you think will happen tomorrow?

additional_notes:
Used to offer help or ask for a solution. It’s often followed by:
- an infinitive with a goal: "Cosa possiamo fare per migliorare...?" (What can we do to improve...?)
- a person/pronoun: "Cosa possiamo fare per lei/loro/te?" (What can we do for you/her/them?)
Common in customer service, formal or neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Cosa possiamo fare per aiutarti oggi?
native_language_example: What can we do to help you today?

meaning: "What can I do to…?/What can I do for…?" (offering help).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or service politely. Often followed by an infinitive (per aiutare, per risolvere) = “to…”, or by a person/pronoun (per te/Lei/lei) = “for you/her.” Use "per Lei" (capital L) for formal “for you,” and "per te" for informal.
target_language_example: Buongiorno, cosa posso fare per Lei?
native_language_example: Good morning, what can I do for you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, or idea. Often followed by "in + language" (Cosa significa in inglese?) or "per + person" (Cosa significa per te? = what does it mean to you?). It can be a direct question (Cosa significa?) or part of a longer sentence (Non so cosa significa = I don’t know what it means).
target_language_example: Scusi, cosa significa "vietato"?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what does “vietato” mean?

meaning: "what is ... doing?" (right now), used before a gerund (-ando/-endo).
additional_notes: Used with the present progressive: "stare" (conjugated) + gerund to talk about an action in progress. Very common patterns: "Cosa sta facendo?" (What is he/she doing?), "Cosa stai facendo?" (What are you doing?), "Cosa stanno facendo?" (What are they doing?). Often followed by a verb in -ando/-endo: "cucinando, disegnando, pensando".
target_language_example: Cosa stai guardando?
native_language_example: What are you watching/looking at (right now)?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now (present continuous: "stare" + gerund). The subject is often understood from context (he/she), but you can add it: "Cosa sta facendo tuo figlio?" = "What is your son doing?". With "Mi scusi," it can sound like a polite but possibly disapproving challenge ("Excuse me, what are you doing?").
target_language_example: Cosa sta facendo Marco?
native_language_example: What is Marco doing?

additional_notes: A common question to ask what is happening right now. Literally “what is happening” (cosa = what; sta succedendo = is happening). You can add an adverb or place: esattamente (exactly), qui (here), laggiù (over there), in Francia (in France).
target_language_example: Scusa, cosa sta succedendo qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s going on here?

meaning: "what are you ...?" (used before a verb in the -ando/-endo form).
additional_notes: Used to ask or refer to what someone is doing right now: "cosa stai" + gerund (e.g., facendo, scrivendo, leggendo). It’s built with stare (tu: stai) + gerund to form the present continuous. In statements you’ll often see it after another verb: "So cosa stai facendo" = "I know what you’re doing."
target_language_example: Cosa stai facendo adesso?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: A very common question using the present continuous: "stai" (you are) + "facendo" (doing). Used to ask what someone is doing right now; the tone depends on context (can sound curious, surprised, or annoyed), often with a name or a term of endearment (e.g., "Tesoro").
target_language_example: Scusa, cosa stai facendo in cucina?
native_language_example: Sorry, what are you doing in the kitchen?

additional_notes: A question used to ask what a group of people is doing right now. It uses the Italian present progressive: "stare" (stanno = they are) + gerund (facendo = doing). You can add a subject before or after (e.g., "Loro cosa stanno facendo?" = "What are they doing?").
target_language_example: Cosa stanno facendo i bambini in giardino?
native_language_example: What are the kids doing in the garden?

meaning: “what are you (plural) …?” (used to ask what someone is doing, usually with a gerund).
additional_notes: Used with voi (you plural) and typically followed by a gerund (-ando / -endo) to form the present progressive: “Cosa state facendo?” = “What are you doing?” It can address a group (or, more rarely, one person in a very formal/old-fashioned voi). Note: Italian “state” here is from stare (“to be” in the progressive), not the English noun “state”.
target_language_example: Cosa state facendo in cucina?
native_language_example: What are you doing in the kitchen?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an action in progress in the past. It’s typically followed by a gerund (stare + -ando/-endo): "Cosa stava dicendo?" = "What was he/she saying?". With "capitando" it means "what was happening?". You can change the subject: "cosa stavi..." (you were), "cosa stavano..." (they were).
target_language_example: Cosa stava facendo quando l’hai chiamato?
native_language_example: What was he doing when you called him?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to an action in progress in the past. It uses the imperfect tense: "stava" (was) + gerund "facendo" (doing), like English "was doing". The subject is understood from context (e.g., Tom, Mary) and can be used in both questions and statements.
target_language_example: Non capivo cosa stava facendo quando sono entrato.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what he was doing when I came in.

meaning: “what was happening / what was going on”.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an event in progress in the past. It combines: “cosa” (what) + “stava” (was, from stare) + “succedendo” (happening, from succedere). Common after verbs like dire (to tell), vedere (to see), sapere (to know). Note: “succedere” means “to happen,” not “to succeed.”
target_language_example: Non capivo cosa stava succedendo.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what was happening.

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening right now or what will happen next. It can also appear inside a longer sentence to mean “what happens/what’s happening” (e.g., “Non so cosa succede” = “I don’t know what’s happening”). Often used to check what’s going on: “Cosa succede?” = “What’s going on?”
target_language_example: Scusa, cosa succede qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s going on here?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions when the verb takes the indirect object pronoun "ti" (= to you / for you), e.g. "Cosa ti devo?" (What do I owe you?), "Cosa ti rende felice?" (What makes you happy?). Often followed by a verb: "cosa ti ha detto...", "cosa ti impedisce...", "cosa ti va?" (What do you feel like doing/having?).
target_language_example: Cosa ti serve per il viaggio?
native_language_example: What do you need for the trip?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason/evidence behind someone’s belief or assumption. It’s often followed by a clause introduced by che ("that"). The verb form changes with the person: Cosa vi fa pensare che…? (you all), Cosa le fa pensare che…? (formal you).
target_language_example: Cosa ti fa pensare che non voglia venire?
native_language_example: What makes you think I don’t want to come?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask what caused or led to a result in someone. It’s followed by a past participle or verb phrase with "ha" (has): e.g., "cosa ti ha reso/a..." (what made you...), "cosa ti ha aiutato/a a..." (what helped you to...), "cosa ti ha tenuto/a..." (what kept you...). The participle often agrees with the person: "ti ha resa" (to a woman), "ti ha reso" (to a man).
target_language_example: Cosa ti ha convinto a venire?
native_language_example: What made you decide to come?

meaning: “what do you want?” (talking to more than one person, or formal “you”).
additional_notes: Uses volete (2nd person plural) to address a group (“you all”) or a single person politely/formally (common in shops, customer service, with strangers). Often followed by details: cosa volete adesso/dopo?; cosa volete da me? (“what do you want from me?”). In questions you may also hear “Che cosa volete…?” which is slightly more explicit but means the same.
target_language_example: Scusi, cosa volete ordinare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what would you like to order?

additional_notes: Literally 'what you want'. Used to ask what someone wants or expects; with 'E' (as in 'E cosa vuoi?') it often sounds impatient or rhetorical, like 'So what do you want/expect?'. Can come across as blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: Cosa vuoi da me?
native_language_example: What do you want from me?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone about their intention or plans. Often followed by a time word like adesso (now) or dopo (later), or used on its own as a question: Tu cosa vuoi fare? You can also use it inside a longer sentence (indirect question): Sta a te decidere cosa vuoi fare (It’s up to you to decide what you want to do).
target_language_example: Allora, cosa vuoi fare stasera?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, sign, symbol, or message. You can use it alone (Cosa vuol dire?) or followed by what you’re asking about (Cosa vuol dire questo segno?). Often used with "esattamente" for emphasis: "Cosa vuol dire esattamente?"
target_language_example: Scusa, cosa vuol dire “sconto”?
native_language_example: Sorry, what does “discount” mean?

meaning: "what do you want?" / "what does he/she want?"
additional_notes: Literally “what (someone) wants.” The verb form "vuole" can mean "he/she wants" or formal "you want" (Lei). Used both as a direct question (sometimes a bit abrupt: "Beh, cosa vuole?") and inside longer sentences: "Scoprite cosa vuole" = "Find out what he wants"; "Cosa vuole che + subjunctive" asks what someone wants you to do (e.g., "Cosa vuole che chieda...?" = "What do you want me to ask...?" ).
target_language_example: Scusi, cosa vuole che faccia adesso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you want me to do now?

meaning: “What do you want to do?” (formal) / “What does he/she want to do?”
additional_notes: Literally “what (someone) wants to do.” With "vuole" it commonly refers to a third person (he/she wants), but it can also be a formal/polite "you" (Lei) when talking to someone: "Cosa vuole fare, Signora?" The subject can be made explicit ("il suo amico", "la vostra amica").
target_language_example: Cosa vuole fare stasera?
native_language_example: What would you like to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing the things you mean: "cose che + verb". Very common after expressions like "ci sono" (there are), "ho" (I have), "molte" (many), "una lista di" (a list of). Often interchangeable with "cose da" when you mean tasks to do (e.g., "cose da fare" = things to do).
target_language_example: Ci sono cose che non capisco.
native_language_example: There are things that I don’t understand.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for duties, errands, or tasks you need to complete. Often used with expressions like "ho un sacco di..." (I have a lot of...), "troppe..." (too many...), or "lista di cose da fare" (to-do list).
target_language_example: Oggi ho molte cose da fare, quindi non posso uscire.
native_language_example: Today I have many things to do, so I can't go out.

additional_notes: Used to refer vaguely to situations, events, ideas, or topics similar to what was just mentioned. Common with verbs like succedere/accadere/capitare (“to happen”) and in questions like “Credi in…?” (“Do you believe in…?”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: cose del genere capitano a tutti.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: things like that happen to everyone.

meaning: things on my/your/his/her mind; a lot on one’s mind.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "avere" (e.g., "Ho molte cose per la testa") to say you’re mentally busy, preoccupied, or thinking about many things (often worries, responsibilities, problems). You can change the amount: "delle" (some), "molte" (many), "troppe" (too many).
target_language_example: Scusa se sono distratto: ho troppe cose per la testa oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry if I'm distracted: I have too much on my mind today.

meaning: “the coast costs (money)” (wordplay: costa = coast; costa = costs).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom; it’s a playful/striking repetition because Italian uses the same form “costa” for the noun “coast” (la costa) and the verb “to cost” in the 3rd person singular (costa = it costs). You’ll often see it in headlines or reports about the expenses of maintaining/protecting/cleaning the coastline. In normal speech you’d more commonly say: “La costa costa molto da mantenere” or simply “Costa molto.”
target_language_example: Dopo le mareggiate, la costa costa molto da riparare.
native_language_example: After the storms, the coast costs a lot to repair.

additional_notes: Used with a location after "in" (often countries/regions): "costruire negozi in Australia" = "to build shops in Australia." Very often follows "andare a" to mean "to go and build": "vado a costruire negozi in...". Use "non" to make it negative and "?" for questions.
target_language_example: Vogliono costruire negozi in centro.
native_language_example: They want to build shops downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier than expected or earlier than usual. Often with questions like "Perché sei venuto così presto?" (Why did you come so early?) or to comment on making a decision earlier than is typical ("decidere... così presto"). "Presto" can mean "early" (timing) or "soon" (in the near future); "così" intensifies it: "this/so".
target_language_example: Non pensavo che saresti arrivato così presto.
native_language_example: I didn’t think you would arrive so early.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a large number of things (facts, events, changes, topics). It’s the feminine plural form because "cose" is feminine plural. Often used with the verb before it: "sono cambiate così tante cose" = "so many things have changed".
target_language_example: Ho ancora così tante cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I still have so many things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a large amount of money. It’s built from così (“so”), tanti (“many”), and soldi (“money”). With soldi (plural), Italian often uses tanti (“many”) rather than tanto (“much”). Common in questions like Chi ti ha dato così tanti soldi? (“Who gave you so much money?”).
target_language_example: Perché hai speso così tanti soldi?
native_language_example: Why did you spend so much money?

meaning: “so much,” “so much/so many,” or “so much (that much).”
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a large degree or amount. Often with verbs of liking/loving (Ti amo così tanto = “I love you so much”) and with changes (È cambiato così tanto = “It changed so much”). With knowledge/quantity it can mean “so much/so many”: Sa così tanto di… = “He/She knows so much about…”.
target_language_example: Mi manchi così tanto.
native_language_example: I miss you so much.

meaning: so much; so much/so many; that much (to such a degree).
additional_notes: Used to express a large amount or a strong degree. With uncountable nouns: così tanto + noun (così tanto denaro = so much money). With countable plurals you often hear “così tanti/e” (così tanti soldi = so many dollars; così tante persone = so many people). It can also modify verbs/adjectives to mean “so much/so”: Mi fa così tanto male = It hurts so much; Come hai perso così tanto? = How did you lose so much? In negative/exclamations it can mean “not that much”: Non così tanto sale! = Not so much salt!
target_language_example: Non parlare così tanto, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t talk so much, please.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a duration feels very long. Often appears with verbs like aspettare (to wait) and with the expression "metterci" ("to take" time): "Ci mette così tanto tempo" = "It takes so long" / "He/She takes so long."
target_language_example: Non ci vediamo da così tanto tempo!
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in so long!

additional_notes: Used with the structure “avere una cotta per + person” to say you’re romantically interested in someone, often in a light, not-too-serious way. You can soften it with “una specie di cotta” (“kind of a crush”).
target_language_example: Ho una cotta per il mio compagno di corso.
native_language_example: I have a crush on my classmate.

meaning: “I think/believe that …” (used to introduce an opinion or assumption).
additional_notes: Used before a clause to soften what you say (it’s your view, not a fact). It’s very common in conversation. After “credo che”, Italian typically uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo): “credo che sia…”, “credo che vada…”. In casual speech you may also hear the indicative, especially with “credo che” + something that feels certain.
target_language_example: Credo che domani piova, quindi resto a casa.
native_language_example: I think it will rain tomorrow, so I’m staying home.

meaning: “I think/believe that it is…” (used to give an opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Often followed by the subjunctive: "sia" is the subjunctive of "essere" (to be) after expressions of opinion like "credo che..." and "non credo che...". Used when you’re not 100% sure, similar to “I think that…” / “I believe that…”. You can also use it to make a polite suggestion: "Credo che sia meglio..." = “I think it’s better to...”.
target_language_example: Credo che sia troppo tardi per chiamarlo adesso.
native_language_example: I think it’s too late to call him now.

meaning: to grow a beard (to let your beard grow).
additional_notes: Often used as "farsi crescere la barba" (= to let your beard grow / to grow yourself a beard). In the past, you’ll often see "si fece crescere la barba" (passato remoto) meaning "he grew/let his beard grow." You can add adjectives like "lunga" (long): "farsi crescere la barba lunga."
target_language_example: Quest’inverno mi faccio crescere la barba.
native_language_example: This winter I’m going to grow a beard.

additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase like "nulla / niente" to express having (or not having) a reason or purpose to keep living: "non ha nulla/niente per cui vivere" = “he has nothing to live for.” Literally "per cui" means “for which,” and it often follows what it refers to (e.g., "qualcosa per cui vivere").
target_language_example: Devo trovare qualcosa per cui vivere.
native_language_example: I have to find something to live for.

meaning: 'care of' / 'take care of (someone)' (used with prendere cura di).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the expression "prendersi cura di" (to take care of). The pronoun changes: "mi prendo cura di..." (I take care of), "ti prendi cura di..." (you take care of), "si prende cura di..." (he/she takes care of), "ci prendiamo cura di..." (we take care of). In the imperative you’ll often hear: "Prenditi cura di..." (take care of...), "Prendetevi cura di..." (take care of..., plural/formal). Used mainly for people (or animals), meaning to look after them.
target_language_example: Mi prendo cura di mia nonna quando sta male.
native_language_example: I take care of my grandma when she’s sick.

meaning: care of her; taking care of her.
additional_notes: Usually used in the expression "prendersi cura di (qualcuno)" = "to take care of (someone)". "Di lei" means "of her" (referring to a woman/girl). You’ll often hear it in different tenses: "mi sono preso/a cura di lei" (I took care of her), "mi stavo prendendo cura di lei" (I was taking care of her), and as a command: "prenditi cura di lei" (take care of her).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: mi prenderò cura di lei stasera.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll take care of her tonight.

meaning: “there is/there are”; also “what’s wrong?/what’s going on?” (in questions).
additional_notes: Contraction of “ci è” (from “esserci”, to be there). Used to say that someone/something is present or exists: “C’è la polizia.” Negative: “non c’è” = “there isn’t/aren’t”. Common with indefinites: “c’è qualcosa…” (there’s something…), “non c’è nessuno…” (there’s nobody…), “non c’è nulla…” (there’s nothing…). In questions like “Che c’è?” it means “What’s the matter?/What’s up?” rather than “What is there?” in most everyday contexts.
target_language_example: Scusa, c’è un problema?
native_language_example: Sorry, is there a problem?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “to drink” (e.g., acqua da bere = drinking water) or on its own to mean “(something) to drink,” especially when offering or requesting a drink (Vuoi da bere? / Mi porti da bere.). It can also follow an adjective to express “too/easy/hard + to drink” (troppo caldo da bere = too hot to drink).
target_language_example: Avete qualcosa da bere?
native_language_example: Do you have something to drink?

meaning: from my house; (starting) from where I live.
additional_notes: Used to indicate origin/distance relative to the speaker’s home. Often with verbs of movement (andare via, uscire) meaning “out of my house,” and with distance expressions (non lontano, a due isolati) meaning “from my place/home.” Note: “a casa mia” = “at my house/home,” while “da casa mia” emphasizes “from (my home/place).”
target_language_example: La fermata dell’autobus è a cinque minuti da casa mia.
native_language_example: The bus stop is five minutes from my house.

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone/something is from (Da che parte vieni? = Where are you from?/From which area?), and to talk about taking a side in a disagreement or decision (da che parte stare = which side to be on). Often followed by "di" + place (da che parte di Roma?) or used with verbs like "stare" (da che parte stai?).
target_language_example: Scusa, da che parte si va per il centro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, which way do you go to the city center?

da cui poter prendere in prestito

target_language_multi_word_term: da cui poter prendere in prestito
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person or source you could borrow something from. It combines: da cui = from whom/from which (referring back to someone/something mentioned), poter = to be able to, prendere in prestito = to borrow (literally “take on loan”). With people, Italian often uses “da cui” where English would say “from whom.”
target_language_example: Non ho nessuno da cui poter prendere in prestito una penna.
native_language_example: I don’t have anyone I could borrow a pen from.

meaning: to say; to tell (something to say).
additional_notes: Used after a noun/pronoun like qualcosa/niente/molto or quello to mean “to say/tell” as something that needs to be expressed: qualcosa da dire = “something to say,” niente da dire = “nothing to say,” quello che avevo da dire = “what I had to say.” The structure is often avere + [qualcosa/niente] + da dire.
target_language_example: Non ho niente da dire.
native_language_example: I have nothing to say.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the place of origin or starting point (physical or sometimes figurative): Da dove vieni? (Where are you from?). With verbs like prendere (to take/get), chiamare (to call), venire (to come). In indirect questions it keeps the same form: Non so da dove viene. (I don’t know where he/she comes from).
target_language_example: Da dove vieni?
native_language_example: Where are you from?

meaning: to read; for reading (something you should/can read).
additional_notes: Used after a noun (or pronoun like qualcosa) to mean “to be read” or “for you/someone to read.” It often implies a purpose or a task: un libro da leggere = “a book to read.” It’s a common pattern: qualcosa da + infinitive (qualcosa da mangiare = something to eat).
target_language_example: Cerco un articolo da leggere in treno.
native_language_example: I’m looking for an article to read on the train.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "da" + "lei". It often indicates the source of something (a pen borrowed from her; a call from her) or who you want to hear something from ("Lo voglio sentire da lei" = “I want to hear it from you/her”). With some verbs/adjectives it can also mark the person causing a reaction ("spaventato da lei" = “scared of her/you”). Note: "lei" can mean “her” OR the formal “you,” so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Preferisco sentirlo da lei, non da altri.
native_language_example: I’d rather hear it from you/her, not from others.

meaning: bedroom; for sleeping (used after a noun).
additional_notes: Most often used with a room noun to mean “bedroom,” especially: camera da letto / camere da letto (“bedroom(s)”). More generally, it can describe something intended for the bed/sleeping, e.g., lampada da letto (“bedside lamp”), tavolino da letto (“bed tray/table”).
target_language_example: L'appartamento ha una camera da letto e un soggiorno.
native_language_example: The apartment has one bedroom and a living room.

additional_notes: Uses "da" + stressed pronoun (lui) to refer to a male person. Common meanings: (1) "from him" with verbs like prendere/comprare/ricevere (e.g., "Ho preso un libro da lui" = I borrowed a book from him); (2) "by him" to show the agent in passive sentences (e.g., "Sono stato ingannato da lui" = I was fooled by him); (3) "by him" after some adjectives/participles expressing a reaction or feeling caused by someone (e.g., "disgustata da lui" = disgusted by him).
target_language_example: Il regalo è stato scelto da lui.
native_language_example: The gift was chosen by him.

additional_notes: Often used after words like niente/qualcosa ("nothing/something to eat"). It also appears in the common expression "dare da mangiare (a ...)" = "to feed (someone/animals)" (literally, "to give to eat").
target_language_example: Hai qualcosa da mangiare?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

meaning: to feed (something) to; to give food to (the...).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" (to give) in the expression "dare da mangiare a + [person/animal]" = "to feed". "ai" is the contraction of "a + i" meaning "to the" (plural masculine), e.g., ai polli = to the chickens, ai maiali = to the pigs. For singular you’ll see "al" (a + il), "alla" (a + la), etc.
target_language_example: Non dare da mangiare ai piccioni, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t feed the pigeons, please.

meaning: food for the dogs; to feed the dogs (with "dare").
additional_notes: Used most often with the verb "dare": "dare da mangiare a + [person/animal]" = "to feed [someone/animal]" (literally, "to give [them] something to eat"). Here "ai" = "a + i" (to the, plural masculine) and "cani" = dogs. Example: "Ho dato da mangiare ai cani" = "I fed the dogs."
target_language_example: Puoi dare da mangiare ai cani stasera?
native_language_example: Can you feed the dogs tonight?

meaning: fish food; to feed the fish.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" in the common structure "dare da mangiare a + [someone/animal]" = "to feed + [someone/animal]" (literally "to give to eat to..."). Here, "ai pesci" means "to the fish" (plural). Often appears in questions about how often you feed them: "Quante volte..." or "Quanto spesso...?"
target_language_example: Devo dare da mangiare ai pesci ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I have to feed the fish every day.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "dare" (to give): "dare da mangiare a" = "to feed" (literally, "to give to eat to"). "Al" = "a" + "il" and is used before masculine singular nouns (al gatto, al cavallo). For feminine singular you’ll usually see "alla" (alla gatta), and for plural "ai/alle".
target_language_example: Hai già dato da mangiare al cane?
native_language_example: Have you already fed the dog?

meaning: food for the dog; to feed the dog (in “dare da mangiare al cane”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" in the common expression "dare da mangiare al cane" = "to feed the dog" (literally, "to give [something] to eat to the dog"). You can also use it as a noun phrase: "(del) da mangiare" = "something to eat / food" (e.g., "C’è del da mangiare?").
target_language_example: Puoi dare da mangiare al cane prima di uscire?
native_language_example: Can you feed the dog before going out?

meaning: to feed his/her dog (to give food to his/her dog).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare": "dare da mangiare a [qualcuno]" = "to feed [someone]". Here, "al suo cane" means "to his/her dog" ("suo" agrees with what is owned—"cane"—not with the owner).
target_language_example: Non dimenticare di dare da mangiare al suo cane prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to feed his/her dog before going out.

meaning: "from me" / "by me" / "at my place" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used in several common ways: (1) source/origin: "Cosa vuoi da me?" = "What do you want from me?"; (2) agent in a passive sentence: "è stato fatto da me" = "it was done by me"; (3) location meaning "at my place" (often with verbs like venire/andare): "Vieni da me" = "Come to my place"; (4) after verbs like tenere lontano: "Tieni X lontano da me" = "Keep X away from me."
target_language_example: Vieni da me dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: Come to my place after work.

meaning: for a long time; in a long time (with a negative).
additional_notes: Uses da to mark how long something has been true/hasn’t happened up to now. Often with the imperfect to describe an ongoing situation in the past (Conoscevo... da molto tempo = I had known... for a long time). With a negative, it commonly means “in a long time” (Non... da molto tempo = I haven’t ... in a long time).
target_language_example: Non ci vediamo da molto tempo.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

additional_notes: Used when you ask someone to pass along a message, greeting, or thanks for you (e.g., "Tell Tom from me", "Thank them on my behalf"). It can also introduce who something comes from (a gift, invitation, etc.): "Questo regalo è da parte mia" = "This gift is from me". Variations: da parte tua/sua/nostra/vostra/loro.
