additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "i" (the, plural) + "loro" (their) + "genitori" (parents). Used to talk about the parents of more than one person, or of one person when "loro" is used as a general/neutral "their". For one child, you’ll often also hear "i suoi genitori" (his/her parents).
target_language_example: I loro genitori vivono lontano.
native_language_example: Their parents live far away.

additional_notes: “I” is the plural masculine article used for mixed groups or when gender is unknown; “loro” means “their” and doesn’t change for gender/number; “nomi” is the plural of “nome” (name). Used when referring to the names of more than one person.
target_language_example: Non ricordo i loro nomi, ma ricordo le loro facce.
native_language_example: I don’t remember their names, but I remember their faces.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase: "i" = "the" (masculine plural), "loro" = "their" (doesn’t change for gender/number), "ombrelli" = "umbrellas" (plural of "ombrello"). Used to talk about umbrellas that belong to them (Tom and Mary, the kids, etc.).
target_language_example: Non dimenticate i loro ombrelli prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Don’t forget their umbrellas before going out.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "i" (the) + "loro" (their) + "soldi" (money). Used for money belonging to more than one person (or to a group). Often appears after verbs like contare (to count), nascondere (to hide), perdere (to lose), mettere (to put).
target_language_example: Hanno speso i loro soldi in viaggio.
native_language_example: They spent their money on a trip.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to show possession: i miei cani (my dogs), i miei guanti (my gloves). Italian normally uses the definite article (i) with possessives, unlike English. It can also be used on its own to mean “my family/relatives/people,” depending on context: Devo chiamare i miei. (I have to call my family.)
target_language_example: Non trovo i miei documenti.
native_language_example: I can't find my documents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your friends as a group. "I" = "the" (plural masculine), "miei" = "my" (plural masculine), "amici" = "friends" (plural masculine). For an all-female group, say "le mie amiche".
target_language_example: Stasera esco con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with my friends.

additional_notes: Means “my hair” (literally “the my hairs”): in Italian, *capelli* is plural. Often used when talking about your hairstyle, hair color, or asking about your hair (e.g., in a salon or after swimming). The article *i* is commonly used with body parts and possessions, even when English would just say “my hair.”
target_language_example: Non toccare i miei capelli, per favore.
native_language_example: Don't touch my hair, please.

additional_notes: Literally “my tasks/duties.” In everyday school context, compiti usually means homework. You’ll often hear: fare i compiti (“to do homework”), finire i compiti (“to finish homework”), compiti di matematica (“math homework”).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire stasera: devo fare i miei compiti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: I have to do my homework.

additional_notes: Literally “the my mistakes.” Used when talking about faults or things you did wrong. Common with verbs like riconoscere (to admit/acknowledge), correggere (to correct), fare (to make), and imparare dai (to learn from).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare dai miei errori.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn from my mistakes.

meaning: my children / my kids (sons and/or daughters).
additional_notes: Literally “the my children.” Used when talking about your own children. With a possessive in Italian, you often include the definite article: i miei figli. Singular: mio figlio (my son) / mia figlia (my daughter).
target_language_example: I miei figli vanno a scuola in autobus.
native_language_example: My kids go to school by bus.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your brothers (plural, masculine). If you have sisters too, or a mixed group, you normally use the masculine plural "i miei fratelli" to mean "my siblings" in general. For only sisters, use "le mie sorelle."
target_language_example: Domani ceno con i miei fratelli.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I'm having dinner with my brothers.

additional_notes: Means “my parents” (mother and father). It’s plural, so it takes plural verbs and adjectives: “I miei genitori vivono…” (“My parents live…”). You can change the possessive: “i tuoi genitori” (your parents), “i suoi genitori” (his/her parents).
target_language_example: I miei genitori arrivano domani.
native_language_example: My parents arrive tomorrow.

meaning: "my parents have" (did to me) — used before a past participle.
additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the passato prossimo (present perfect) to say what your parents did to/for you. "Mi" = "me/to me" and comes before the verb: "I miei genitori mi hanno + past participle" (e.g., "aiutato/a", "proibito", "cresciuto/a"). The past participle may change ending for gender/number in some cases (e.g., "cresciuta" when the speaker is female).
target_language_example: I miei genitori mi hanno aiutato a scegliere l'università.
native_language_example: My parents helped me choose a university.

additional_notes: Used to describe your parents with an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., anziani = elderly, ricchi = rich, molto religiosi = very religious, sempre occupati = always busy). Remember agreement: genitori is plural, so adjectives usually take the masculine plural form (-i): religiosi, occupati. If your parents are both women, you can also use feminine plural: le mie madri sono… / i miei genitori sono… (adjectives: -e).
target_language_example: I miei genitori sono molto gentili, ma un po' severi.
native_language_example: My parents are very kind, but a bit strict.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: i (the, plural) + miei (my, plural masculine) + libri (books). You use it to talk about books that belong to you. If the group is mixed gender or all masculine, Italian uses the masculine plural form (miei).
target_language_example: Non trovo i miei libri da scuola.
native_language_example: I can't find my school books.

additional_notes: “I” = “the” (plural masculine), “miei” = “my” (plural), “nonni” = “grandparents” (or sometimes “grandfathers” depending on context). You can use it as the subject or object of a sentence: “I miei nonni sono…” (My grandparents are…), “Vado a trovare i miei nonni…” (I go visit my grandparents…).
target_language_example: Domani pranzo con i miei nonni.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m having lunch with my grandparents.

meaning: "my eyes"; in expressions, "with my own eyes" (personally, directly).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “my eyes.” Very common in the phrase “(con) i miei occhi” = “(with) my own eyes,” used to emphasize you want to see something yourself, not just hear about it.
target_language_example: Devo vederlo con i miei occhi prima di crederci.
native_language_example: I have to see it with my own eyes before I believe it.

additional_notes: Means the speaker’s own eyeglasses. It uses the plural article and plural possessive: "i" + "miei" + "occhiali" (glasses are plural in Italian). For a polite request you can say: "Mi dia i miei occhiali, per favore/per piacere."
target_language_example: Scusi, ho dimenticato i miei occhiali sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I forgot my glasses on the table.

additional_notes: Used when talking about directives you must follow (often in the military, police, or at work). It can imply you’re acting under authority: "Ho già i miei ordini" = "I already have my instructions."
target_language_example: Non posso fermarmi: ho già i miei ordini.
native_language_example: I can’t stop: I already have my orders/instructions.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own pants/trousers. "I" is the masculine plural definite article (the), "miei" means "my" (masculine plural), and "pantaloni" is plural in Italian (you normally say it in the plural, like "pants" in English).
target_language_example: Non trovo i miei pantaloni.
native_language_example: I can’t find my pants.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you’re thinking or reflecting on. Very common with verbs like interrompere (to interrupt) and tenere per me (to keep to myself). If you mean “my opinions,” Italians often use le mie opinioni or il mio parere.
target_language_example: Scusa, mi hai interrotto i miei pensieri.
native_language_example: Sorry, you interrupted my thoughts.

additional_notes: Used to describe the condition or characteristics of your feet, followed by an adjective (caldi, freddi, piccoli) or a comparison (più … dei tuoi/dei vostri, piccoli in confronto ai tuoi). Note: 'piedi' is plural, so it takes 'sono' (are), not 'è'.
target_language_example: I miei piedi sono stanchi dopo la camminata.
native_language_example: My feet are tired after the walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your emotional reactions or inner feelings. Common with verbs like esprimere (to express), ferire (to hurt), and tenere per me (to keep to myself). Often appears as part of the set phrase “ferire i miei sentimenti” = “hurt my feelings.”
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare dei miei sentimenti adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about my feelings right now.

additional_notes: Means money that belongs to the speaker. Uses the plural article and possessive: i (the, plural masculine) + miei (my, plural masculine) + soldi (money; literally “coins”). Often used to claim ownership, complain that someone took it, or ask if someone has it.
target_language_example: Non toccare i miei soldi!
native_language_example: Don’t touch my money!

additional_notes: Used to refer to a pair of glasses you used to wear (an older pair). In Italian, for plural items like glasses, you use the plural article and possessive: i + miei + occhiali. The adjective vecchi (“old”) usually comes between the possessive and the noun here: i miei vecchi occhiali.
target_language_example: Non riesco a trovare i miei vecchi occhiali.
native_language_example: I can’t find my old glasses.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: il vestito (a piece of clothing) → i vestiti (clothes). Often used when asking about or talking about your outfit, or when your clothes have a smell/stain (e.g., odorano di fumo = "smell like smoke").
target_language_example: Devo lavare i miei vestiti stasera.
native_language_example: I have to wash my clothes tonight.

additional_notes: Plural noun with the definite article: singular is "il musulmano" (a Muslim man) / "la musulmana" (a Muslim woman); plural feminine is "le musulmane" (Muslim women). Used to talk about Muslims as a group, so be mindful of generalizations.
target_language_example: In questa città vivono molti musulmani.
native_language_example: Many Muslims live in this city.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to show possession: i nostri + noun (e.g., i nostri soldi = our money). It agrees with the noun (gender/number). Related forms: il nostro (m. sg.), la nostra (f. sg.), le nostre (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Dov'è la nostra macchina? Non troviamo i nostri documenti.
native_language_example: Where is our car? We can’t find our documents.

additional_notes: Used when speaking about your own children. In everyday Italian, "figli" is commonly used in a gender-neutral way to mean “children” even though it literally means “sons”; “our daughters” is "le nostre figlie". With a mixed group, "i nostri figli" is standard.
target_language_example: Facciamo di tutto per i nostri figli.
native_language_example: We do everything for our children.

additional_notes: Definite plural form (“the pants”). Used when talking about pants in general or specific pants. Common with verbs like comprare (to buy), costare (to cost), mettersi (to put on), and with possessives: mi/ti/si + pantaloni (e.g., “si fissò i pantaloni” = he stared at his pants).
target_language_example: Devo comprare dei pantaloni nuovi.
native_language_example: I need to buy some new pants.

meaning: the dishes (plates; also dishware/what you wash after eating).
additional_notes: Plural of "il piatto". In everyday Italian, "lavare i piatti" means “to do the dishes” (wash the dishes). Used for plates specifically, but often includes all the dirty dishware after a meal.
target_language_example: Dopo cena faccio i piatti.
native_language_example: After dinner I do the dishes.

additional_notes: Used for the body part. Common with verbs like avere (Ho i piedi freddi = My feet are cold), fare male (Mi fanno male i piedi = My feet hurt), lavare/pulire (Si pulisca i piedi = Clean your feet). In warnings, it can mean “watch your step” (Guarda dove metti i piedi).
target_language_example: Dopo la camminata mi facevano male i piedi.
native_language_example: After the walk, my feet hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much things cost in general (e.g., in a shop, for certain products, or when prices go up/down). Often followed by “di/dei/delle …” to specify what: “i prezzi dei biglietti” = “ticket prices.”
target_language_example: Mi puoi dire i prezzi di questi due articoli?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the prices of these two items?

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about prices (often followed by an adjective or a past participle): i prezzi sono alti/bassi (prices are high/low), i prezzi sono aumentati/cresciuti (prices have increased), i prezzi sono scesi/diminuiti (prices have gone down). In Italian you must include the article: i prezzi (the prices).
target_language_example: In questo negozio i prezzi sono troppo alti.
native_language_example: In this shop the prices are too high.

additional_notes: Plural form of "proprio" used with a plural noun to mean “your/his/her/their own,” referring back to the subject of the sentence. It agrees with the noun: i propri (masc. plural), le proprie (fem. plural). Example: "Luca vede spesso i propri genitori" = Luca sees his own parents (not someone else’s).
target_language_example: Ognuno dovrebbe rispettare i propri limiti.
native_language_example: Everyone should respect their own limits.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a short summary of the most important ideas. Often follows verbs like "dammi" (give me, informal), "datemi" (give me, to you all/formal), or "mi dia" (give me, formal). You can also say "i punti chiave" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Puoi dirmi i punti principali della riunione?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the main points of the meeting?

meaning: the boys; the guys; (sometimes) the kids/young people.
additional_notes: Plural of "il ragazzo". Often refers to a group of boys/young men ("the guys"), but in some contexts it can mean "the kids/young people" in general. It’s masculine plural, and it can be used for mixed-gender groups when speaking generally.
target_language_example: I ragazzi sono già arrivati a casa.
native_language_example: The guys have already arrived home.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "il ragno" (a/the spider) → "i ragni" (the spiders). Used when talking about spiders in general or specific spiders in context; often appears with verbs like "mangiare" (eat) and "spaventare" (scare).
target_language_example: In giardino ci sono molti ragni.
native_language_example: In the garden there are many spiders.

additional_notes: Plural of "il risultato". Used for outcomes of tests, elections, experiments, etc. In sports, "i risultati" often means the final score(s) (e.g., match results). Common with adjectives like "finali" (final), "buoni" (good) and in questions like "Quali erano i risultati?" (What were the results?).
target_language_example: I risultati degli esami arrivano domani.
native_language_example: The exam results arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: Plural of "il segreto". Used to talk about hidden information or things you don’t want others to know. Often follows verbs like "amare" (to love) or "odiare" (to hate), as in the examples.
target_language_example: Non posso dirti i segreti della ricetta.
native_language_example: I can’t tell you the secrets of the recipe.

additional_notes: Plural of "il soldato" (a soldier). Used to refer to soldiers as a group; often appears with military duties or actions (obeying commanders, fighting, shooting). In Italian, "i" is the masculine plural definite article "the" used before most consonant sounds.
target_language_example: I soldati sono arrivati in città questa mattina.
native_language_example: The soldiers arrived in the city this morning.

additional_notes: Plural form with the article: il soldo (rare in everyday use) → i soldi. Very common for talking about having/owing/asking for money: i soldi che ti devo = 'the money I owe you'. Can refer to cash or money generally depending on context.
target_language_example: Hai i soldi per il biglietto?
native_language_example: Do you have the money for the ticket?

meaning: “the money that …” (introduces a relative clause describing the money).
additional_notes: Used when you add information about specific money: who it belongs to, where it came from, what it’s for, etc. Pattern: i soldi che + verb/clause (often with passato prossimo: che ho fatto / che ha vinto / che aveva rubato). Also common: i soldi che ho = “the money I have.”
target_language_example: Non spendere i soldi che ti ho dato.
native_language_example: Don’t spend the money that I gave you.

additional_notes: "Soldi" is plural in Italian, so it uses the plural verb "sono" (and plural adjectives): "i soldi sono spariti" = "the money is gone". In English we usually treat "money" as singular, but Italian commonly treats "soldi" as plural.
target_language_example: I soldi sono sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The money is on the table.

additional_notes: It’s the plural masculine form of the possessive adjective "suo" used with a plural masculine noun (or a mixed-gender plural). It usually comes with the definite article: "i suoi + noun" (e.g., "i suoi commenti" = his comments). It can also refer to the polite form "Lei" (your, formal), often written with a capital letter: "i Suoi".
target_language_example: Ho trovato i suoi documenti sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I found his documents on the table.

additional_notes: "Suoi" is the formal (Lei) possessive and agrees with the noun: "amici" (male or mixed group) vs. "amiche" (all-female group). It can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context (e.g., "lui" vs. "lei"). Often used in polite/formal situations, especially with "Lei": "i suoi amici".
target_language_example: Sta aspettando i suoi amici davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: He/She is waiting for his/her friends in front of the cinema.

meaning: his dogs (or her dogs, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Suoi" is a possessive that agrees with the noun: cane (sing.) → il suo cane; cani (pl.) → i suoi cani. It can refer to either 'his' or 'her'—Italian often doesn’t specify gender here, so you understand it from context. Common with verbs about pets (chiamare = to call, portare a fare una passeggiata = to take for a walk) and safety phrases like "Metta i suoi cani al guinzaglio" (Put your dogs on a leash).
target_language_example: Può tenere i suoi cani vicino a sé, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you keep your dogs close to you, please?

additional_notes: Italian usually uses the plural for hair on the head: i capelli. Suoi means “his/her” (formal: “their”), and it agrees with capelli (masculine plural). Often Italian uses the definite article instead of a possessive with body parts (e.g., Le lavo i capelli = “I wash her hair”), but i suoi capelli is used for emphasis, contrast, or clarity.
target_language_example: I suoi capelli sono ricci e castani.
native_language_example: His/Her hair is curly and brown.

additional_notes: Italian usually treats *capelli* (hair) as plural, so it uses *sono* (“are”): *I suoi capelli sono lunghi* (“His/her hair is long”). *Suoi* agrees with *capelli* (masculine plural) and can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context. Often followed by an adjective or a comparison: *più lunghi dei miei* (“longer than mine”).
target_language_example: I suoi capelli sono ricci e castani.
native_language_example: His/her hair is curly and brown.

meaning: his homework / his tasks (things he has to do).
additional_notes: "Compiti" most commonly means "homework" in a school context (often "compiti scolastici"). More generally, it can mean "tasks/duties". "I suoi" means "his" (plural), agreeing with the masculine plural noun "compiti". For "her homework," use "i suoi compiti" as well in modern Italian (or "i compiti di lei" if you need to be extra clear).
target_language_example: Ha già fatto i suoi compiti, poi è uscito con gli amici.
native_language_example: He already did his homework, then he went out with friends.

additional_notes: Means the homework (assignments) for French class. "i suoi" = "his/her" (can refer to a male or female person; the gender is shown by context or by using a name). "compiti" is plural in Italian, so it uses "i" (the). Often used with verbs like "fare" (to do) and "dimenticare/scordare" (to forget).
target_language_example: Ho finito i miei compiti di francese.
native_language_example: I finished my French homework.

additional_notes: "Suoi" is the possessive meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the thing owned: errori = masculine plural). Often used when talking about taking responsibility or blaming someone: pagare per i suoi errori (pay for his/her mistakes), ammettere i suoi errori (admit his/her mistakes), incolpare gli altri per i suoi errori (blame others for his/her mistakes).
target_language_example: Deve imparare dai suoi errori.
native_language_example: He/She has to learn from his/her mistakes.

meaning: his children / her children (depending on context).
additional_notes: "I" = "the" (plural masculine, used for mixed groups too). "Suoi" is the plural form of "suo" (his/her/its/your formal), agreeing with "figli" (children/sons). The phrase can mean "his children" or "her children"—Italian usually doesn’t show the owner’s gender here, so you infer it from context.
target_language_example: Parla spesso dei suoi figli.
native_language_example: He/She often talks about his/her children.

additional_notes: Means “his/her brothers” (brothers belonging to the person being talked about). It’s plural: il fratello → i fratelli. The possessive adjective suo/suoi agrees with the noun (fratello/fratelli), not with the owner. With family members in the plural, Italian normally uses the definite article: i suoi fratelli. For a single brother you often say suo fratello (no article), but in some contexts you may also see il suo fratello for emphasis/clarity.
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto i suoi fratelli ieri sera.
native_language_example: I met his/her brothers last night.

additional_notes: "I" = "the" (plural), "suoi" is the plural masculine form of the possessive "suo" and must match the noun: "il suo gatto" (his/her cat), "i suoi gatti" (his/her cats). In Italian, "suoi" can refer to either "his" or "her" depending on who owns them (the subject/context).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire stasera: devo dare da mangiare ai suoi gatti.
native_language_example: I can’t go out tonight: I have to feed his/her cats.

additional_notes: “I” is the plural masculine article used for mixed-gender groups; “genitori” is plural (“parents”). “Suoi” means “his/her” in the plural and agrees with “genitori,” not with the owner. Used for both “his parents” and “her parents”; the context clarifies whose parents they are. Can also refer formally to “your parents” (e.g., speaking politely to someone).
target_language_example: Non conosco i suoi genitori.
native_language_example: I don’t know his/her parents.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone’s parents were like, felt, did, or what their situation was in the past. "Suoi" agrees with "genitori" (masculine plural) and can refer to either his or her parents; "erano" is the imperfect of "essere" (to be), often used for ongoing states/background descriptions in the past.
target_language_example: I suoi genitori erano molto severi quando era piccolo.
native_language_example: His/Her parents were very strict when he was little.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person’s parents (relationship status, nationality/origin, feelings, etc.). "Suoi" agrees with the plural noun "genitori" (parents) and can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context. Often followed by an adjective ("divorziati", "orgogliosi") or by "di" to say where they’re from ("sono della Spagna").
target_language_example: Non so se i suoi genitori sono d'accordo.
native_language_example: I don’t know if his/her parents agree.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suoi" (his/its) with a masculine plural noun: "i" + "suoi" + "giocattoli". Italian possessives usually come with the definite article (i, il, la, etc.). "I suoi" can also mean "his family/relatives" in some contexts, but with "giocattoli" it’s clearly "his toys".
target_language_example: Dopo cena, ha messo a posto i suoi giocattoli.
native_language_example: After dinner, he put away his toys.

additional_notes: "I" = “the” (plural). "suoi" is the plural form of "suo" (“his/her/its/their” in formal address) and agrees with "guanti" (plural). Often used when talking about borrowing, wearing, or taking off gloves; in everyday Italian you may also hear "i guanti" without the possessive if it’s obvious whose they are.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato i suoi guanti sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I forgot his/her gloves on the table.

additional_notes: “Suoi” is a possessive meaning “his/her/its/your (formal)” and it agrees with the noun: here it’s plural masculine to match “libri.” Italian usually uses the definite article with possessives: “i suoi libri.” The meaning can be “his books” or “her books” depending on context; it can also mean “your books” when speaking formally to someone (Lei).
target_language_example: Puoi prendere i suoi libri dallo zaino?
native_language_example: Can you take his/her books from the backpack?

additional_notes: Literally “the his/her enemies.” Used to refer to enemies of a male or female person; Italian uses the same possessive “suoi” (plural) for both “his” and “her,” so context tells you which. “I” is the plural masculine article used with mixed groups or when the group is all male; for all-female enemies you’d say “le sue nemiche.”
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare con i suoi nemici.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk to his/her enemies.

meaning: his eyes / her eyes (literally: “the his/her eyes”).
additional_notes: Italian often uses the definite article with body parts. "Suoi" agrees with the plural noun "occhi". In singular it’s "il suo occhio" (his/her eye). "Suoi" can refer to either “his” or “her”; context tells you which.
target_language_example: I suoi occhi sono stanchi oggi.
native_language_example: His/Her eyes are tired today.

meaning: his glasses / her glasses / your glasses (formal).
additional_notes: “Occhiali” is plural in Italian, so it uses the plural article “i” and the plural possessive “suoi”. Depending on context, “suoi” can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or (when speaking politely to one person) “your” (formal, using “Lei”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ha dimenticato i suoi occhiali sul tavolo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you forgot your glasses on the table.

additional_notes: “Occhiali da lettura” means “reading glasses” (glasses used for reading). “I suoi” means “his/her” (their, singular), and it agrees with the plural noun “occhiali.” The phrase is commonly used with verbs like “perdere” (to lose), “trovare” (to find), or “mettere” (to put on).
target_language_example: Non trovo i suoi occhiali da lettura.
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her reading glasses.

additional_notes: Means “his plans.” In Italian, the possessive often agrees with the thing owned (here: piani = plural masculine), so suoi can sometimes refer to a female owner too (e.g., “Mary ha cambiato i suoi piani” = Mary changed her plans). Used often with verbs like cambiare (to change), fare (to make), raccontare (to tell).
target_language_example: Ho cambiato i suoi piani all’ultimo momento.
native_language_example: I changed his/her plans at the last moment.

additional_notes: "I" is "the" (plural masculine) and "suoi" is a possessive meaning "his/her/your (formal)" depending on context. Use it for multiple issues/difficulties someone has. Often refers to a man’s problems ("his"), but it can also mean "her" if the owner is a woman, or "your" when speaking formally to someone (Lei).
target_language_example: Non posso risolvere i suoi problemi al posto suo.
native_language_example: I can't solve his/her/your (formal) problems instead of him/her/you.

additional_notes: “I sentimenti” are feelings/emotions (often personal or romantic). “Suoi” is the possessive for a third person (“his/her/its”) and also for the formal “you” (Lei). It agrees with what is owned: sentiment*i* (masculine plural) → *i suoi*.
target_language_example: Non voleva mostrare i suoi sentimenti.
native_language_example: He/She didn’t want to show his/her feelings.

additional_notes: "I suoi" is the formal possessive (used with Lei) and can refer to “your” (formal), “his,” or “her,” depending on context. "Sforzi" is the plural of "sforzo" (effort) and is common with verbs like apprezzare (to appreciate), raddoppiare (to double), dare/portare frutti (to bear fruit), essere inutili (to be useless).
target_language_example: Grazie per i suoi sforzi.
native_language_example: Thank you for your efforts.

additional_notes: "I" = “the” (plural). "Suoi" is the possessive adjective used with masculine plural nouns like "soldi". Depending on context, it can mean “his money,” “her money,” “their money,” or (with Lei) the polite/formal “your money.” Often used to specify that it’s someone’s own money, not someone else’s.
target_language_example: Non spendere i suoi soldi per cose inutili.
native_language_example: Don’t spend his/her money on useless things.

additional_notes: Means “his/her studies” depending on context (Italian possessives agree with the thing owned: studi = masculine plural → suoi). You’ll also see: il suo studio (his/her study), la sua università (his/her university), le sue lezioni (his/her lessons). Often used with verbs like abbandonare (to drop/abandon), trascurare (to neglect), prendere sul serio (to take seriously).
target_language_example: Ha lasciato i suoi studi per lavorare a tempo pieno.
native_language_example: He/She quit his/her studies to work full-time.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suoi" with the plural noun "vestiti" (clothes). "Suoi" agrees with the thing owned (plural), not the owner. It can mean "his" or "her"; if it refers to "their" it’s usually formal (Lei/Loro).
target_language_example: Non trovo i suoi vestiti nell’armadio.
native_language_example: I can’t find his/her clothes in the closet.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: i tuoi soldi (your money), i tuoi bambini (your children). It agrees with the noun: il tuo (m. sg.), la tua (f. sg.), i tuoi (m. pl.), le tue (f. pl.). Sometimes "i tuoi" can also be used on its own to mean "your family / your loved ones," depending on context.
target_language_example: Porta con te i tuoi documenti, per favore.
native_language_example: Bring your documents with you, please.

additional_notes: Plural phrase used to refer to people who are your friends (male or mixed-gender group). It can be the subject or object of the sentence. Use "le tue amiche" for an all-female group, and "i tuoi amici" is also the default when the group includes at least one male.
target_language_example: Stasera esci con i tuoi amici?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your friends tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "tuoi" with the plural noun "capelli" (hair is plural in Italian), so it takes the plural article "i". Used when complimenting, describing, or referring to someone’s hair directly (e.g., "Mi piacciono i tuoi capelli" = "I like your hair"). For formal "you" (Lei), you’d say "i Suoi capelli".
target_language_example: I tuoi capelli sono bellissimi oggi.
native_language_example: Your hair is beautiful today.

additional_notes: Often used for schoolwork/homework (what a student has to do). Depending on context, it can also mean responsibilities or assigned tasks. Grammar: plural noun + possessive; you can also hear "i compiti" (the homework) or "i miei/ i suoi compiti" (my/his/her homework).
target_language_example: Hai già finito i tuoi compiti per domani?
native_language_example: Have you already finished your homework for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Literally “the your parents.” Used when addressing someone with tu. The plural noun genitori means “parents” (mother and father). For more formal/polite speech (Lei), use i Suoi genitori.
target_language_example: Come stanno i tuoi genitori?
native_language_example: How are your parents?

additional_notes: Used to refer to books belonging to the person you’re speaking to (tu). You can place it before or after the verb for emphasis (e.g., "Nessuno li vuole i tuoi libri!" = "Nobody wants your books!").
target_language_example: Ho preso i tuoi libri dallo scaffale.
native_language_example: I took your books from the shelf.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "i" (the) + "tuoi" (your, plural masculine) + "occhi" (eyes). Used to address someone directly or talk about their eyes. Often appears in romantic/poetic compliments (e.g., describing someone’s eyes).
target_language_example: Chiudi i tuoi occhi e rilassati.
native_language_example: Close your eyes and relax.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: **i** = “the” (plural masculine), **tuoi** = “your” (plural masculine), **vestiti** = “clothes.” Often used when talking about washing/drying clothes or commenting on what someone is wearing. You may also hear **i vestiti** (“the clothes”) without **tuoi** when the owner is clear from context.
target_language_example: Puoi mettere i tuoi vestiti nell’armadio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put your clothes in the closet, please?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "i" = "the" (masculine plural), "vecchi" = "old" (masculine plural), "film" is invariable (same in singular and plural). Often used with "piacere" to talk about what someone likes: "Ti piacciono i vecchi film?" = "Do you like old movies?"
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i vecchi film in bianco e nero.
native_language_example: I like old black-and-white movies.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun (singular: il vestito). Commonly used for clothes in general; in everyday Italian it can refer to what someone is wearing or to laundry (e.g., lavare i vestiti = to wash clothes). Often used with verbs like mettere (put on), togliere (take off), lavare (wash), strappare (tear).
target_language_example: Devo lavare i vestiti prima di domani.
native_language_example: I have to wash the clothes before tomorrow.

meaning: "clothes" + "so quickly" (usually in questions about changing clothes fast).
additional_notes: This chunk is most commonly used with the verb *cambiare/cambiarsi* (“to change (clothes)”), e.g. *Come ti cambi i vestiti così velocemente?* = “How do you change your clothes so quickly?” With *cambiarsi* you use a reflexive pronoun: *mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si* (often combined with *i vestiti*).
target_language_example: Come ti cambi i vestiti così velocemente?
native_language_example: How do you change your clothes so quickly?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “your” when speaking to more than one person (voi): i vostri messaggi = your messages. It can also mean “your (pl.)” in a polite/formal context (e.g., addressing customers). Feminine plural is "le vostre"; singular is "il vostro" (m.) / "la vostra" (f.).
target_language_example: Avete preso i vostri documenti?
native_language_example: Did you take your documents?

meaning: "your friends" (plural, talking to more than one person).
additional_notes: Uses the plural possessive "vostri" because you’re addressing multiple people (voi). The noun is masculine plural (amici); for a mixed group or all males. If the group is all female, you can say "le vostre amiche". Often appears in everyday requests/instructions: "Portate/Salutate i vostri amici."
target_language_example: Potete invitare anche i vostri amici alla festa.
native_language_example: You can invite your friends to the party too.

additional_notes: "I capelli" is plural in Italian (literally “the hairs”), so you say "sono" (they are). "Vostri" is the plural or polite/formal way to say “your” (to more than one person, or in formal address); in everyday speech to one person you’ll usually hear "i tuoi capelli".
target_language_example: Posso vedere i vostri capelli da vicino?
native_language_example: Can I see your hair up close?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person (voi = “you all”) or to one person in a polite/formal way. "Compiti" is plural and in school contexts usually means “homework”; it can also mean “tasks/duties” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non dimenticate di fare i vostri compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to do your homework before going out.

additional_notes: "I" is the plural masculine article (used for a mixed group or when gender is unknown). "Vostri" is the plural form of "your" and is used with plural nouns. It can refer either to one person addressed formally (Lei) or to more than one person (voi). For an all-female group you can also say "le vostre figlie".
target_language_example: I vostri figli sono già a scuola?
native_language_example: Are your children already at school?

additional_notes: “Vostri” agrees with the plural noun “genitori” (parents). It’s used when speaking to more than one person (you all) or to one person using the formal “Lei”; in informal singular you’d say “i tuoi genitori.”
target_language_example: I vostri genitori sono a casa?
native_language_example: Are your parents at home?

meaning: “your books” (plural; addressed to more than one person).
additional_notes: Uses the plural definite article (i) + plural possessive (vostri) to mean “your” when speaking to a group (voi). Common in classroom instructions (e.g., Aprite… / Mettete via…). With a masculine plural noun like libri, the form is vostri; for feminine plural it would be vostre (e.g., le vostre penne).
target_language_example: Ragazzi, prendete i vostri libri e aprite a pagina dieci.
native_language_example: Guys, take your books and open to page ten.

meaning: 'idea of' / 'any idea about…?'; often used as 'have (no) idea…'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive or with question words (chi, dove, quando, cosa) to talk about knowing/guessing something: “Hai idea di quando…?” = “Do you have any idea when…?” Very common in the negative: “Non ho idea di…” / “Non ne ho idea” = “I have no idea.”
target_language_example: Hai idea di dove sia il bagno?
native_language_example: Do you have any idea where the bathroom is?

additional_notes: Most often used with the expression "(non) avere idea di cosa…" to say you (don’t) know what something means or what is happening. It’s typically followed by "cosa" + a verb (often in the subjunctive in dependent clauses): "Non ho idea di cosa stia succedendo" = “I have no idea what’s happening.” You can also use it in questions: "Hai idea di cosa voglia dire?" = “Do you have any idea what it means?”
target_language_example: Non ho idea di cosa stia succedendo.
native_language_example: I have no idea what’s happening.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the afternoon of the previous day. Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also go at the beginning for emphasis (e.g., “Ieri pomeriggio ero occupato”).
target_language_example: Ieri pomeriggio ho studiato a casa.
native_language_example: Yesterday afternoon I studied at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the evening/night of the previous day. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., "Ieri sera ho..." or "Ho... ieri sera").
target_language_example: Ieri sera siamo andati al cinema.
native_language_example: Last night we went to the movies.

additional_notes: Definite article + holiday name: Italian usually says "il Natale" (literally "the Christmas"). Used with verbs like "passare/trascorrere il Natale" (to spend Christmas) and often followed by "con" (with): "il Natale con la famiglia". You’ll also hear it without the article in greetings: "Buon Natale!"
target_language_example: Quest'anno passiamo il Natale con i nonni.
native_language_example: This year we’re spending Christmas with our grandparents.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article (il) as an official title. It refers to the leader of the government in a country (not the president/monarch). You can add “di + country” to specify: “il Primo Ministro della Finlandia”. Capitalization is common in news and formal writing, but you may also see “il primo ministro”.
target_language_example: Ho visto il Primo Ministro in TV ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw the Prime Minister on TV last night.

additional_notes: Bambino means a young child; it’s often understood as “boy” (especially in contrast with bambina = “girl”), but it can also be used more generally like “child/kid.” In sentences like “Il bambino sta per nascere,” it can mean “the baby” (a child about to be born).
target_language_example: Il bambino dorme già.
native_language_example: The child is already sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article il when talking about the sport in general (like il calcio, il tennis). Often appears with piacere: A Tom piace il baseball = “Tom likes baseball.”
target_language_example: Ti piace il baseball?
native_language_example: Do you like baseball?

additional_notes: A common Italian way to say the sport “basketball” (masculine singular). You may also hear the more Italian term "la pallacanestro". Don’t confuse it with English “basket” (a container): in Italian, "basket" usually refers to the sport.
target_language_example: Gioco a basket due volte a settimana.
native_language_example: I play basketball twice a week.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a very young child. It’s masculine with the article (il bebè), and the plural is usually invariable: i bebè. You can also say il bambino / la bambina for “the child/boy/girl,” but bebè emphasizes that they’re very young.
target_language_example: Il bebè dorme nella carrozzina.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping in the stroller.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dare/dare il benvenuto (“to welcome someone”): Le do il benvenuto. It’s also used with essere (“to be welcome”): Sei/è/sarò il benvenuto qui (“You/he/I will be welcome here”). In this pattern, Italian often keeps the article: è il benvenuto/è la benvenuta (match gender), and the plural is: sono i benvenuti / sono le benvenute.
target_language_example: Siete i benvenuti a casa nostra.
native_language_example: You are welcome in our home.

additional_notes: With verbs like *studiare* (to study) and *usare* (to use), *il berbero* usually refers to the Berber language (also called *tamazight*), not a person. To refer to a person you can also say *un berbero / una berbera* (“a Berber man/woman”).
target_language_example: Sto imparando il berbero per parlare con i miei amici in Marocco.
native_language_example: I'm learning Berber to speak with my friends in Morocco.

additional_notes: Refers to a person’s arm (upper limb). Often used with body-part grammar: Italian commonly uses the definite article (il) instead of a possessive (e.g., "Mi ha preso per il braccio" = "He/she grabbed me by the arm"). Common phrases: "il braccio destro/sinistro" (right/left arm), "(avere) il braccio ingessato" (to have your arm in a cast), "rompersi/bruciarsi il braccio" (to break/burn your arm).
target_language_example: Mi fa male il braccio destro.
native_language_example: My right arm hurts.

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun: il caffè. In Italy, “un caffè” typically means an espresso by default. Common phrases: “Prendo un caffè” (I’ll have a coffee), “Il caffè è caldo/freddo” (The coffee is hot/cold), “con/senza zucchero” (with/without sugar).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe the state or quality of the coffee, usually followed by an adjective (e.g., caldo = hot, forte = strong) or a past participle to describe a condition (e.g., finito = finished/there’s no coffee left). "È" is the 3rd-person singular of essere (to be).
target_language_example: Il caffè è troppo amaro.
native_language_example: The coffee is too bitter.

additional_notes: Used with the article to refer to the sport (common in phrases like guardare il calcio “watch soccer” or essere interessato al calcio “be interested in soccer”). Note: calcio can also mean “calcium” in scientific/medical contexts, and it can mean “kick” in other contexts, but in everyday conversation il calcio usually means the sport.
target_language_example: La domenica guardiamo il calcio in TV.
native_language_example: On Sundays we watch soccer on TV.

additional_notes: Used for a gate you can open/close, often the entrance to a house, garden, courtyard, building, or driveway. Common with verbs like aprire/chiudere (to open/close), dipingere/pitturare (to paint). Not the same as il cancello in a train station (less common) vs. il cancelletto (a small gate).
target_language_example: Puoi chiudere il cancello quando esci?
native_language_example: Can you close the gate when you leave?

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "il" = "the" (masculine singular) + "cane" = "dog". Used to talk about a specific dog (or dogs in general in some contexts). Plural: "i cani" (the dogs).
target_language_example: Dov'è il cane?
native_language_example: Where is the dog?

meaning: “the dog is” (Il = the, cane = dog, è = is).
additional_notes: Used to describe the dog’s state, quality, or location with the verb essere (“to be”): Il cane è stanco (tired), Il cane è in casa (in the house). In questions, the word order is usually the same and you add a question mark/intonation: Perché il cane è qui? Note: Italian cane (“dog”) is a false friend with English “cane” (walking stick).
target_language_example: Il cane è tranquillo oggi.
native_language_example: The dog is calm today.

meaning: the captain of the (team) for … / the team captain of …
additional_notes: Used to say who leads a sports team. It’s followed by the sport or the team type: "il capitano della squadra di pallacanestro" (basketball team captain), "... di wrestling/lotta" (wrestling team captain). You can also use it with a specific team: "il capitano della squadra di Milano" (captain of Milan’s team).
target_language_example: Lei è il capitano della squadra di calcio.
native_language_example: She is the captain of the soccer team.

additional_notes: Refers to a castle/fortified building or royal residence; often used with a specific name using “di” (e.g., il castello di Neuschwanstein).
target_language_example: Domani visitiamo il castello con una guida.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re visiting the castle with a guide.

additional_notes: Common general word for food as a thing in general (what you eat), especially in contexts like restaurants, cooking, or food quality/availability. It’s masculine singular: il cibo. For “foods” as different types/items, you’ll often see the plural i cibi.
target_language_example: Il cibo in questo ristorante è davvero buono.
native_language_example: The food in this restaurant is really good.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning food from Chinese cuisine. Often used with the verb "piacere" to talk about what you like (e.g., "Mi piace il cibo cinese" = "I like Chinese food"). You can add "in generale" (“in general”) or intensifiers like "molto" (“a lot”).
target_language_example: Ti piace il cibo cinese?
native_language_example: Do you like Chinese food?

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning “Korean food/cuisine.” Used with the definite article: il cibo coreano. Common with verbs like piacere: Ti piace il cibo coreano? You can also say La cucina coreana (“Korean cuisine”), which sounds a bit more formal/restaurant-like.
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo il cibo coreano.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating Korean food.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: il cibo = “the food” + giapponese = “Japanese.” Often used with piacere (“to like”) as in Ti/Le/Vi piace il cibo giapponese? (“Do you like Japanese food?”). With mancare (“to miss”), it means you will miss Japanese food: Il cibo giapponese ti mancherà (“You’ll miss Japanese food”).
target_language_example: Quando viaggio, mi manca il cibo giapponese.
native_language_example: When I travel, I miss Japanese food.

additional_notes: Used to talk about food with a “hot”/spicy flavor (like chili peppers). "Il" is the definite article (“the”); "piccante" agrees with "cibo" (masculine singular). You can also say "cibo molto piccante" for “very spicy food.”
target_language_example: Non posso mangiare il cibo piccante.
native_language_example: I can’t eat spicy food.

additional_notes: Refers to unhealthy, highly processed food (e.g., burgers, fries, chips, sweets). Often used with verbs like evitare (to avoid) or mangiare (to eat). In Italian, cibo is masculine, so you say il cibo spazzatura.
target_language_example: Dovremmo mangiare meno cibo spazzatura.
native_language_example: We should eat less junk food.

meaning: "the food is" (used to describe food or say what’s true about it).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective or a detail: Il cibo è buono/piccante/halal/incluso. You can use it to give an opinion (ottimo, terribile, sublime) or to state a fact (incluso). For plural, use: I cibi sono… (less common in restaurants).
target_language_example: Il cibo è buonissimo, ma un po' caro.
native_language_example: The food is very good, but a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the sky” in everyday, literal contexts (weather, looking up): *Il cielo è nuvoloso/azzurro*. It can also mean “heaven” in religious or poetic contexts: *andare in cielo* (“to go to heaven”). Gender/number: masculine singular; plural *i cieli* (often poetic).
target_language_example: Oggi il cielo è molto azzurro.
native_language_example: Today the sky is very blue.

additional_notes: Used to describe the sky (weather, color, etc.). Depending on context, "il cielo" can also mean "heaven" in a religious or poetic sense (e.g., "il cielo è vuoto" = 'heaven is empty').
target_language_example: Il cielo è azzurro oggi.
native_language_example: The sky is blue today.

il cielo è pieno di stelle

target_language_multi_word_term: il cielo è pieno di stelle
additional_notes: A simple descriptive sentence you can use when talking about the night sky. "Il cielo" = "the sky"; "è pieno di" = "is full of"; "stelle" = "stars." Often paired with time words like "stanotte" (tonight) or "stasera" (this evening).
target_language_example: Qui in montagna il cielo è pieno di stelle.
native_language_example: Here in the mountains the sky is full of stars.

additional_notes: With "il" + adjective, Italian often names a language as a noun: "il cinese" = "Chinese". It’s used after verbs like "studiare" (to study), "parlare" (to speak), "scrivere" (to write), and "imparare" (to learn).
target_language_example: Sto imparando il cinese da sei mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning Chinese for six months.

additional_notes: A masculine noun with the definite article "il" (singular). Plural: "i computer" (often unchanged in Italian). Used for a PC/laptop in general; with "accendere/spegnere" (turn on/off), "lasciare acceso" (leave on), "riparare" (repair), "controllare" (check).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il computer acceso tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I left the computer on all night.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun: il concerto. It refers to a live musical event/performance. Common verbs with it include: andare bene (to go well), avere luogo (to take place), essere un successo (to be a success), cominciare (to start).
target_language_example: A che ora finisce il concerto?
native_language_example: What time does the concert end?

meaning: "the concert is …" (used to say when it is, or that it has started/ended).
additional_notes: Use it with essere (è = “is”, past participle = “has”) to give information about a concert. With a time expression: “Il concerto è domenica/lunedì prossimo” = “The concert is next Sunday/Monday.” With a past participle: “Il concerto è cominciato/finito” = “The concert has started/ended.”
target_language_example: Il concerto è sabato sera alle otto.
native_language_example: The concert is Saturday evening at eight.

additional_notes: Often means the restaurant bill/check: "Porti il conto, per favore." It can also mean a count/number ("Ho perso il conto" = I’ve lost track of how many). In business/email contexts, "mandami il conto" can mean “send me the invoice/bill.”
target_language_example: Scusi, può portarmi il conto, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you bring me the bill, please?

additional_notes: Used for a formal, written agreement (e.g., job, rental/lease, phone plan). Common verbs with it: firmare il contratto (to sign the contract), leggere il contratto (to read the contract), cambiare il contratto (to change/modify the contract). Gender/number: il contratto (sing.), i contratti (pl.).
target_language_example: Prima di firmare il contratto, voglio leggerlo bene.
native_language_example: Before signing the contract, I want to read it carefully.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun used with the definite article "il": "il couscous". It refers to the food dish (often made from steamed semolina) and can be modified with an adjective or regional style, e.g. "il couscous cabilo" (Kabyle-style couscous).
target_language_example: Stasera mangiamo il couscous con le verdure.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re eating couscous with vegetables.

additional_notes: Very vulgar word for “butt,” common in strong idioms. Often appears in fixed expressions: “farsi/fare il culo” = to work extremely hard; “salvare il culo” = to save someone’s ass; “prendere per il culo” = to make fun of / mess with someone; “spaccare il culo (a qualcuno)” = to kick someone’s ass (threat); “leccare il culo (a qualcuno)” = to kiss someone’s ass (insult). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Mi hai salvato il culo, grazie!
native_language_example: You saved my ass, thanks!

additional_notes: Literally the physical heart. Very common in figurative expressions: “metterci il cuore” = to put your heart into something (do it with passion/care); “mi sanguina il cuore” = it breaks my heart / I feel deep pain or sadness about something.
target_language_example: Ha messo il cuore in questo progetto.
native_language_example: He/She put their heart into this project.

additional_notes: Means “money” in a general sense, often referring to cash or an amount of funds. It’s more formal than "i soldi". Used with common verbs like avere (to have), prendere (to take/get), passare (to hand over), contare (to count).
target_language_example: Non ho il denaro per pagare adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t have the money to pay right now.

meaning: “the desire to be …” (wanting to become or be a certain way).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun after essere (“to be”) to express an aspiration or goal: il desiderio di essere ricco/a (“the desire to be rich”), il desiderio di essere libero/a (“the desire to be free”). It agrees only in the following adjective/noun (ricco/ricca/ricchi/ricche), not in desiderio (which stays masculine singular here).
target_language_example: Ho il desiderio di essere più indipendente.
native_language_example: I have the desire to be more independent.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled/allowed to do something, often in moral or legal contexts. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., "avere il diritto di sapere" = "to have the right to know"). With "non" it means someone does not have that right ("non hai il diritto di..."). Related: "diritto di voto" = "the right to vote."
target_language_example: Hai il diritto di dire di no.
native_language_example: You have the right to say no.

additional_notes: This phrase is typically used after a verb describing an accident or injury, especially with "tagliarsi" (to cut oneself): "Mi sono tagliato/a il dito con un coltello" = “I cut my finger with a knife.” Italian often uses "il" (the) where English uses "my" for body parts, and you add "mi/ti/si..." to show whose finger it is.
target_language_example: Mi sono tagliato il dito con un coltello mentre cucinavo.
native_language_example: I cut my finger with a knife while I was cooking.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun. Use it for a book (or app/tool) you use to look up words and meanings. Often used with verbs like servire (to need), restituire (to return), and passare (to pass/hand). Plural: i dizionari.
target_language_example: Puoi prestarmi il dizionario per un momento?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the dictionary for a moment?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to physical pain (e.g., after an injury), but it can also mean emotional pain or grief. Often used with verbs like "ignorare" (to ignore), "sopportare" (to endure/stand), and "ritornare" (to come back).
target_language_example: Non riesco più a sopportare il dolore.
native_language_example: I can’t stand the pain anymore.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male medical doctor. The feminine form is "la dottoressa". In Italy, "dottore" can also be used as a title for someone with a university degree (similar to “Dr.”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov'è lo studio del dottore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the doctor's office?

il dottore mi ha consigliato di

target_language_multi_word_term: il dottore mi ha consigliato di
meaning: 'the doctor advised/recommended that I...' / 'the doctor told me to...'.
additional_notes: Used to report medical advice. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (di + verb): "Il dottore mi ha consigliato di bere più acqua". The past tense "mi ha consigliato" means 'has advised'/'advised'.
target_language_example: Il dottore mi ha consigliato di riposare per qualche giorno.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me to rest for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause as a “fact” or reason, often after expressions like tenere in conto/accettare/negare/essere furioso per. The verb after che is frequently in the subjunctive (especially after emotions, opinions, or negation), but you may also see the indicative when stating something as objective.
target_language_example: Mi preoccupa il fatto che non risponda ai messaggi.
native_language_example: I’m worried about the fact that he/she isn’t replying to messages.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the key point or real explanation, often after a hesitation or as a correction/clarification. It’s common in spoken Italian to sound more natural or to soften what you’re about to say. It can be followed by a full sentence: “Il fatto è che + [sentence]”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma il fatto è che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but the fact is I can’t come today.

additional_notes: "Film" is a masculine noun; the singular definite article is "il". Used to talk about a specific movie already known from context. Plural: "i film" (same spelling).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto il film?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie?

additional_notes: Literally “the end of the week.” Used with the definite article (il) and often after prepositions like nel/il (on the weekend) or durante il (during the weekend). Common with verbs like trascorrere/passare (to spend) the weekend.
target_language_example: Cosa fai il fine settimana?
native_language_example: What do you do on the weekend?

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: il ("the") + fiume ("river"). Commonly used with expressions like lungo il fiume ("along the river") to talk about walking or places by the river. Plural: i fiumi ("the rivers").
target_language_example: Ci sediamo vicino al fiume e facciamo un picnic.
native_language_example: Let’s sit near the river and have a picnic.

additional_notes: Literal statement describing a river’s movement, often followed by where it flows: attraverso (through), tra/fra (between/among). Conjugation: scorrere → (lui/lei) scorre.
target_language_example: Il fiume scorre lentamente in primavera.
native_language_example: The river flows slowly in spring.

additional_notes: A common food noun. Uses the definite article "il" ("the") because "formaggio" is masculine singular. Often used generally (like English "cheese") or with a specific type: "il formaggio parmigiano", "il formaggio di capra".
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con il formaggio, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a sandwich with cheese, please.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (il) to talk about the language in general: Mi piace il francese (I like French). With parlare/studiare/imparare, you can say parlare/studiare/imparare il francese (“to speak/study/learn French”). Not the person from France—that’s un francese / una francese.
target_language_example: Studio il francese da sei mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been studying French for six months.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to check/confirm something you believe is true. Here it refers to the language ("il francese" = French). Often equivalent to English "..., right?" / "..., correct?".
target_language_example: Tu parli il francese, giusto?
native_language_example: You speak French, right?

meaning: 'French at school' (as a subject you study/learn).
additional_notes: Used when talking about studying the French language as a school subject. Italian often uses the definite article with languages (il francese, l’italiano, lo spagnolo). With verbs like imparare/studiare, it means you learn/study French at school.
target_language_example: Ho studiato il francese a scuola, ma ora lo parlo poco.
native_language_example: I studied French at school, but now I don’t speak it much.

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun with the definite article: il gatto = “the (male) cat,” but it’s also the default for “the cat” in general. Plural: i gatti (“the cats”). In the idiomatic expression «Vi è morto il gatto?» it literally means “Did the cat die there?”, used humorously to suggest a place smells bad.
target_language_example: Il gatto dorme sul divano.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

meaning: "the cat is" (and in some past tenses: "the cat has").
additional_notes: Uses the verb "essere" (to be): "è" = "is". It describes the cat’s state/quality/location (e.g., "Il gatto è al sicuro" = The cat is safe; "Il gatto è sulla sedia" = The cat is on the chair). With some verbs in the passato prossimo, Italian uses "essere" as the helper, so you’ll see patterns like "Il gatto è corso via" = The cat ran away (literally "is run away").
target_language_example: Il gatto è in giardino.
native_language_example: The cat is in the garden.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun with the definite article: il gelato (“the ice cream”). Often used when talking about ice cream in general (as a category) or a specific ice cream you mean in context. Plural: i gelati (“the ice creams/ice creams”).
target_language_example: Vorrei un gelato al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a chocolate ice cream, please.

additional_notes: A specific flavor of gelato. Use it when saying what you like/prefer or asking someone’s preference (Mi piace…?/Ti piace…?/Vi piace…?). In Italian menus, “al + ingredient” often means “flavored with” or “made with” that ingredient.
target_language_example: Per dessert, prendo il gelato al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For dessert, I’ll have chocolate ice cream.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (il) because it refers to a language. It can also mean “the Japanese person/man” depending on context, but in these examples it clearly means the language you study/speak.
target_language_example: Parli il giapponese?
native_language_example: Do you speak Japanese?

additional_notes: Usually means a daily newspaper (print or digital) you read for news. With the definite article (il), it often refers to a specific one in context (e.g., the one at home, or the one you usually read). You can also say "un giornale" for "a newspaper."
target_language_example: Ho comprato il giornale in edicola.
native_language_example: I bought the newspaper at the newsstand.

additional_notes: Literally "il" (the) + "giorno" (day). In Italian, you often use the definite article without a preposition to mean "on" a specific day/event: "il giorno di Natale" = "on Christmas Day". It can also be followed by adjectives to specify which day: "il giorno successivo" = "the following day".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo il giorno dopo.
native_language_example: See you the next day.

meaning: the next day; the day after.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the day following a specific event or a day already mentioned (often like “the next day” in a story). It can also mean “the day after” something: e.g., Il giorno dopo la festa = the day after the party.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo domani; il giorno dopo, invece, sono impegnato.
native_language_example: See you tomorrow; the next day, though, I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that specifies which day you mean: il giorno in cui + (event/action). It can refer to a specific remembered day (Ricordo il giorno in cui...), a scheduled day (Il giorno in cui arrivo...), or a future day that will come (Arriverà il giorno in cui...). Similar to "il giorno che" in some contexts, but "in cui" is very common in standard Italian.
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò mai il giorno in cui abbiamo traslocato.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day we moved.

meaning: the government; also 'government' as a form/system of rule.
additional_notes: Most often means the national government/administration (the people in power). It can also refer more generally to how a country is governed (e.g., democracy as a form of government). Gender/number: masculine singular; plural is "i governi".
target_language_example: Il governo ha annunciato nuove misure economiche.
native_language_example: The government announced new economic measures.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: *il* + *jazz* = “the jazz.” In Italian you typically use the article when talking about musical genres in general: *Mi piace il jazz* (“I like jazz”). Used with verbs like *amare* (to love) and *ascoltare* (to listen to).
target_language_example: A casa ascolto spesso il jazz.
native_language_example: At home I often listen to jazz.

additional_notes: A masculine noun used with the article (il). It’s a loanword and is usually invariable in Italian (often just "ketchup" in both singular and plural). Common in requests at the table: "Passami il ketchup" (informal, to a friend) vs. "Mi passa il ketchup?" / "Passi il ketchup" (more polite/formal).
target_language_example: Mi passi il ketchup, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you pass me the ketchup, please?

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun phrase: il ("the") + ladro ("thief"). Used for someone who steals. Plural: i ladri (the thieves). Feminine form: la ladra (the female thief). In Italian it’s common to stress identity with phrases like “Non sono io il ladro” (I’m not the thief) or “È lui il ladro!” (He’s the thief!).
target_language_example: Il ladro ha rubato il mio portafoglio.
native_language_example: The thief stole my wallet.

additional_notes: "Latte" is a masculine singular noun, so it usually takes the article "il" (il latte). Common in drinks: "caffè con il latte" (coffee with milk), "tè con il latte" (tea with milk), and "senza" to say without ("senza zucchero").
target_language_example: Vorrei un cappuccino, ma senza troppo latte.
native_language_example: I’d like a cappuccino, but without too much milk.

additional_notes: Used for both (1) a specific task to do (fare il lavoro, finire il lavoro) and (2) a job/employment (trovare il lavoro, ottenere il lavoro, abbandonare il lavoro). Masculine singular with the definite article: il lavoro = “the work/the job.”
target_language_example: Devo finire il lavoro prima di cena.
native_language_example: I have to finish the work before dinner.

additional_notes: "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), used before many masculine singular nouns. "Libro" means “book.” Used for a specific book known from context. In commands like "Chiuda il libro!" it means “Close the book!” (formal/Lei form).
target_language_example: Dov'è il libro?
native_language_example: Where is the book?

additional_notes: Used to identify/specify a particular book by adding extra information after it. "che" here means "that/which" and can be followed by a verb (e.g., "che ho comprato") or by a clause with an object pronoun (e.g., "che mi avete dato" = "that you gave me").
target_language_example: Il libro che hai consigliato è già esaurito.
native_language_example: The book that you recommended is already sold out.

additional_notes: Il = “the” (masculine singular). Libro = “book.” È is the 3rd person singular of essere (“to be”) and is used for descriptions (Il libro è fantastico.) or to ask where/with whom something is (Il libro è con te? = “Is the book with you?”). Note the accent: è (“is”) vs e (“and”).
target_language_example: Il libro è sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

additional_notes: Used for legal/posted maximum driving speed. Common with verbs like rispettare (to respect/obey) and superare (to exceed): “superare il limite di velocità” = “to go over the speed limit.”
target_language_example: Non superare il limite di velocità: qui è 50 km/h.
native_language_example: Don’t exceed the speed limit: it’s 50 km/h here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to sign language as a whole (a way of communicating with hand signs), often with the verb "conoscere" (to know). In Italy you may also see "LIS" (Lingua dei Segni Italiana) for Italian Sign Language.
target_language_example: Mio fratello conosce il linguaggio dei segni.
native_language_example: My brother knows sign language.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: il loro treno (their train), il loro caffè (their coffee), il loro segreto (their secret), il loro eroe (their hero). It agrees with the noun owned, not with the owners. Other forms: la loro (fem. sing.), i loro (masc. pl.), le loro (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ho visto il loro cane al parco.
native_language_example: I saw their dog at the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a dog that belongs to more than one person (e.g., a couple or a family). "Loro" is the plural possessive adjective (“their”) and it doesn’t change for gender/number of what’s owned, but the article does: il loro cane (their dog), i loro cani (their dogs).
target_language_example: Ho visto il loro cane nel giardino.
native_language_example: I saw their dog in the yard.

additional_notes: Used to describe what a group of people’s job or task consists of. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamare, costruire, lavare) or sometimes by "di" + infinitive in more formal/older usage ("Il loro lavoro è di aggiungere...").
target_language_example: Il loro lavoro è controllare le prenotazioni ogni mattina.
native_language_example: Their job is to check the reservations every morning.

meaning: on Mondays; on Monday (as a regular day).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone usually does on Mondays (habit/routine). In Italian, days of the week often take the definite article (il, la) when you mean “on (that day) regularly.” Without the article (e.g., “lunedì”), it can refer to a specific Monday depending on context.
target_language_example: Il lunedì vado in palestra dopo lavoro.
native_language_example: On Mondays I go to the gym after work.

additional_notes: Means the specific place where people have agreed to meet. Uses the French loanword “rendez-vous,” which in Italian can sound a bit dramatic or “spy-movie-like” compared to the common words “appuntamento” or “incontro.” Often used with verbs like: sapere/dare (know/give) il luogo, trovare (find) il luogo, essere (be) lo stesso di sempre (be the same as always).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle otto: il luogo del rendez-vous è davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at eight: the meeting place is in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (to have): "Ho il mal di gola" = "I have a sore throat." It’s a common health complaint, often mentioned together with other symptoms like fever (la febbre).
target_language_example: Ho il mal di gola, quindi oggi non vado al lavoro.
native_language_example: I have a sore throat, so I’m not going to work today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho il mal di stomaco" = "I have a stomachache." Often shortened in speech to "mal di stomaco" without the article.
target_language_example: Ho il mal di stomaco da ieri sera.
native_language_example: I’ve had a stomachache since last night.

additional_notes: Literally “the pain of head.” Most often used with the verb avere (“to have”): Ho il mal di testa. You can also use venire (“to come on”): Mi viene il mal di testa (“I’m getting a headache”).
target_language_example: Ho il mal di testa, posso prendere un'aspirina?
native_language_example: I have a headache—can I take an aspirin?

additional_notes: Used before verbs like "può" (can) or "riesce" (manages/succeeds) to say someone is doing as well as possible given the circumstances: "Fare il meglio che puoi" = "Do the best you can." It often expresses effort and limitation (they’re trying hard, even if results aren’t perfect).
target_language_example: Sto facendo il meglio che posso.
native_language_example: I'm doing the best I can.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (e.g., "Il mese prossimo parto..." / "Parto... il mese prossimo").
target_language_example: Il mese prossimo iniziamo il corso di italiano.
native_language_example: Next month we start the Italian course.

additional_notes: Time expression used to say something happened in the previous month. It often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis (e.g., "Il mese scorso, ...").
target_language_example: Il mese scorso ho iniziato un nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: Last month I started a new job.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken, written, or digital communication (e.g., a note, announcement, text/DM). It’s masculine singular; plural: i messaggi.
target_language_example: Ti mando il messaggio più tardi.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the message later.

meaning: the best (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Short form of "il migliore" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "il miglior posto", "il miglior modo"). You can also use the fuller form "il migliore" after the noun or on its own (e.g., "Questo posto è il migliore").
target_language_example: È il miglior ristorante della città.
native_language_example: It’s the best restaurant in the city.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns: **il mio** + noun (e.g., *il mio invito*, *il mio ex*). Italian possessives usually take the definite article (*il/la/i/le*), unlike English. It can also be used as a possessive pronoun meaning “mine” when the noun is understood: *È il mio* = “It’s mine.”
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Where is my phone?

additional_notes: Used before the platform/service name: "il mio account di Facebook/Instagram/Google". In Italian, "account" is commonly used (especially for online services). You’ll often see it with verbs like "controllare" (to check), "cancellare" (to delete), "creare" (to create), "accedere al" (to log in to).
target_language_example: Domani voglio cambiare la password del mio account di Google.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I want to change the password of my Google account.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants, asks for, or needs your help: "Vuoi il mio aiuto?" = "Do you want my help?". Note that aiuto is masculine (il), so the possessive is mio (not mia). You can also use it after verbs like chiedere (to ask for) and volere (to want).
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno, posso darti il mio aiuto.
native_language_example: If you need it, I can give you my help.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend who is male (or when "amico" is used as the default masculine form). It’s a noun phrase: "il" (the) + "mio" (my) + "amico" (friend). For a female friend, you usually say "la mia amica". In the plural: "i miei amici" (my friends, mixed/masculine) and "le mie amiche" (my friends, all female).
target_language_example: Domani esco con il mio amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going out with my friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe your (male) friend with an adjective (Il mio amico è loquace), a nationality/profession/noun (Il mio amico è indiano / medico), or a location (Il mio amico è qui). "è" is the 3rd-person singular of "essere" (to be). For a female friend: "la mia amica è"; for plural: "i miei amici sono" / "le mie amiche sono".
target_language_example: Il mio amico è molto gentile.
native_language_example: My friend is very kind.

meaning: "my love" (a term of affection; also "my love" for something).
additional_notes: Used either as (1) a romantic/affectionate way to refer to a person (similar to “my love/darling”), or (2) to talk about the love you feel for someone or something: “il mio amore per …” = “my love for …”. With a person, Italian often uses the vocative without the article: “Amore mio!” or “Mio amore!”.
target_language_example: Amore mio, mi sei mancato tanto.
native_language_example: My love, I missed you so much.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own lawyer. Often appears with verbs like chiamare (to call) and parlare con (to speak with). In formal/polite speech you may use the imperative form with Lei: "Parli con il mio avvocato" (Speak with my lawyer).
target_language_example: Prima di firmare, voglio parlare con il mio avvocato.
native_language_example: Before signing, I want to speak with my lawyer.

additional_notes: Literally “the my dog,” but in Italian you normally use a definite article (il/lo/la/i/gli/le) before a possessive + noun: il mio cane, la mia casa. Here it’s masculine singular (cane), so you use il mio. Plural: i miei cani (“my dogs”).
