target_language_example: Domani il tempo è bello, quindi andiamo al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the weather is nice, so let’s go to the park.

meaning: the test; the exam; the trial/check.
additional_notes: Used for an exam (school/qualification) or a practical/technical test (e.g., testing a new engine). Common verbs: fare/sostenere un test (take a test), superare un test (pass a test), fallire un test (fail a test), iniziare il test (start the test). In Italian you often keep the English loanword “test” with the masculine article “il”.
target_language_example: Domani ho il test di italiano.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have the Italian test.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like prendere (to take/catch) and perdere (to miss): prendere il treno, perdere il treno. You may also see it with times: il treno delle otto (the 8 o’clock train). In schedules, in orario means “on time.”
target_language_example: Scusi, a che ora parte il treno per Milano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does the train to Milan leave?

additional_notes: Used to say a train arrived or left later than expected. Often followed by the amount of delay with “di” (e.g., “in ritardo di dieci minuti”) and/or a reason with “a causa di” (because of). “Era” is past tense (imperfect) of “essere” (to be), common for describing a situation in the past.
target_language_example: Scusi, il treno era in ritardo, quindi sono arrivato tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, the train was delayed, so I arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the train whose destination is the place that follows “per”. You’ll often see/hear it in stations and announcements: “Questo è il treno per…” = “This is the train to…”. Related common phrase: “perdere il treno per [città]” = “to miss the train to [city]”.
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è il treno per Milano?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train to Milan?

additional_notes: Possessive with the definite article. Used with masculine singular nouns: "il tuo cibo" = "your food". It can also stand alone to mean "yours" when the noun is understood: "È il tuo" = "It’s yours" (referring to a masculine singular item). For feminine singular use "la tua", masculine plural "i tuoi", feminine plural "le tue".
target_language_example: È il tuo libro o il mio?
native_language_example: Is it your book or mine?

additional_notes: Means help coming from the person you’re speaking to (informal singular tu). It’s commonly used with verbs like: mi serve il tuo aiuto (I need your help), grazie per il tuo aiuto (thanks for your help), apprezzo il tuo aiuto (I appreciate your help). For polite/formal singular, use il Suo aiuto; for talking to more than one person, use il vostro aiuto.
target_language_example: Mi serve il tuo aiuto con questo esercizio.
native_language_example: I need your help with this exercise.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend of the person you’re talking to: il = “the”, tuo = “your”, amico = “friend (male)”. For a female friend, say “la tua amica”. In Italian, the article (il/la) is often included before possessives (il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue), especially with family/friends and many everyday nouns.
target_language_example: Il tuo amico parla inglese?
native_language_example: Does your friend speak English?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s love/affection (romantic, but can also be very deep affection in general). It’s a noun phrase: il (the) + tuo (your) + amore (love). Often used with verbs like volere (to want), mancare (to miss/lack), or ricordare (to remind).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del tuo amore e del tuo supporto.
native_language_example: I need your love and your support.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s dog, addressing one person informally (tu). The article changes with gender/number: il tuo cane (m. sing.), la tua cagna (f. sing., less common; often people still say "il mio/tuo cane" for a female dog), i tuoi cani (pl.), le tue cagne (pl.). In questions like "Come si chiama...?" it means “What’s your dog’s name?”
target_language_example: Dov'è il tuo cane?
native_language_example: Where is your dog?

additional_notes: Used when talking directly to someone about their computer. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article, and "tuo" agrees with the noun (computer is masculine in Italian). Often appears in questions and requests: "Posso usare/prendere in prestito il tuo computer?"
target_language_example: Non posso usare il tuo computer adesso.
native_language_example: I can’t use your computer right now.

meaning: "your heart" (literally; often meaning your feelings/inner voice).
additional_notes: Used literally for the physical heart (especially with verbs like battere/sentire) and figuratively in expressions like ascoltare/seguire il tuo cuore (“listen to/follow your heart”), meaning to trust your feelings or intuition. In romantic/dramatic contexts, "Dammi il tuo cuore!" can mean “Give me your love/yourself.”
target_language_example: A volte è difficile, ma devi ascoltare il tuo cuore.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard, but you have to listen to your heart.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular noun "lavoro" (work/job) with the possessive adjective "tuo" (your). It can refer to your job (employment) or more generally to the work you do, depending on context. Often used after prepositions like "con" (with), "a" (at), or "nel" (in the).
target_language_example: Come va con il tuo lavoro?
native_language_example: How’s it going with your job?

additional_notes: Uses the definite article + possessive: il (the) + tuo (your) + libro (book). In Italian, possessives usually take an article (il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue). Here it’s masculine singular (libro). You can use it in questions or statements when talking directly to someone about their book.
target_language_example: Scusa, dov'è il tuo libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your book?

additional_notes: Used to address one person informally (tu). In more formal situations (to a stranger, customer, older person), use “il suo nome” instead. Often appears in questions when asking for someone’s details.
target_language_example: Qual è il tuo nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used when asking for someone’s phone number. You can use it after verbs like: dare (“Dammi…”, give me…), avere (“Posso avere…?”, can I have…), dire (“Mi diresti…?”, would you tell me…). Often paired with “il tuo nome” (your name) in more polite/form-style requests.
target_language_example: Scusa, posso avere il tuo numero di telefono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have your phone number?

additional_notes: Literally "the your plan". Used when talking about someone’s idea/strategy (un piano) or, in some contexts, someone’s schedule (il piano, e.g., a work plan). Often followed by verbs like è (is), sembra (seems), funziona (works), fallisce (fails).
target_language_example: Il tuo piano è interessante, ma costa troppo.
native_language_example: Your plan is interesting, but it costs too much.

additional_notes: Means “your phone” when talking to one person you address with tu. It’s masculine singular: il (the) + tuo (your) + telefono (phone). Used in everyday situations: losing your phone, it ringing, borrowing it, charging it, or asking how often someone uses it. For “your phone” in the formal singular (Lei), use: il Suo telefono.
target_language_example: Scusa, dov'è il tuo telefono? Sta suonando.
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your phone? It’s ringing.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun meaning “tea.” You often hear it with flavor/ingredients: il tè al limone (lemon tea), il tè con il latte (tea with milk), il tè senza zucchero (tea without sugar). In some contexts “per il tè” can mean “for tea / for tea time” (staying to have tea).
target_language_example: Vorrei un tè caldo, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot tea, please.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun phrase: il (the) + vento (wind). Often used with weather verbs like soffiare (to blow): “Il vento soffia” = “The wind is blowing.” You can modify it with adverbs/adjectives (forte = strong) to describe how windy it is.
target_language_example: Oggi c'è il vento, quindi fa più freddo.
native_language_example: Today it’s windy, so it feels colder.

additional_notes: Uses the present continuous (stare + gerund) to describe what’s happening right now: “sta soffiando” = “is blowing.” Often followed by a direction. “da + (direction)” means “from” (where the wind comes from): da est/da nord/da ovest. “verso + (direction)” means “toward” (where it’s blowing to): verso est/verso sud.
target_language_example: Oggi il vento sta soffiando forte.
native_language_example: Today the wind is blowing hard.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun meaning a trip/journey (travel from one place to another). Often followed by “a/in + place” to say where you’re going (e.g., “il viaggio a Parigi”). Plural: “i viaggi”.
target_language_example: Il viaggio in treno è durato tre ore.
native_language_example: The train trip lasted three hours.

additional_notes: Used for a video clip/movie recording (online or offline). With "video" the singular article is usually "il" (il video), plural "i video". Common with verbs like vedere (to watch), mettere in pausa (to pause), caricare (to upload).
target_language_example: Puoi mandarmi il video?
native_language_example: Can you send me the video?

additional_notes: Used in instructions or ads to suggest using a video to make a declaration—most commonly completed as “il video per dichiarare il tuo/vostro/suo amore” (“the video to declare your/his/her love”). The verb “dichiarare” here means “to declare/proclaim” (e.g., feelings), not “to declare” in the sense of customs/taxes.
target_language_example: Ho usato il video per dichiarare il mio amore.
native_language_example: I used the video to declare my love.

additional_notes: Noun with the definite article: il = “the”, vino = “wine”. Use it when talking about wine in general or a specific wine already known from context (e.g., at the table). Common with verbs like bere (to drink) and versare (to pour). Plural: i vini (“the wines”).
target_language_example: Possiamo ordinare il vino della casa?
native_language_example: Can we order the house wine?

additional_notes: Used to talk about or order white wine. Often contrasted with il vino rosso (“red wine”). The article changes with quantity: un vino bianco (“a white wine”), del vino bianco (“some white wine”).
target_language_example: Per me un bicchiere di vino bianco, grazie.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of white wine, please.

meaning: “wine or beer” (a choice between the two).
additional_notes: Used in questions to offer a simple choice, often with the verb "preferire" (to prefer): "Preferisci/Preferisce/Preferite il vino o la birra?". Literally it includes the articles ("the"), but in English you usually just say "wine or beer?".
target_language_example: Per cena preferisci il vino o la birra?
native_language_example: For dinner, do you prefer wine or beer?

additional_notes: Common in restaurants and at home. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). You’ll often hear it contrasted with "il vino bianco" (white wine). With preferences you can use: "Preferisco il vino rosso" (I prefer red wine) and comparisons like "Preferisce il vino rosso al vino bianco" (He/She prefers red wine to white wine).
target_language_example: Al ristorante prendo il vino rosso, grazie.
native_language_example: At the restaurant I’ll have red wine, thanks.

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun. Used with verbs like suonare (to play) and sapere suonare (to know how to play). Plural: i violini.
target_language_example: Mia sorella studia il violino da due anni.
native_language_example: My sister has been studying the violin for two years.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "il" (the, masculine singular) + "virus". Used for a disease-causing virus; in Italian, "virus" is invariable in the singular and plural (il virus / i virus).
target_language_example: Secondo il medico, il virus è molto contagioso.
native_language_example: According to the doctor, the virus is very contagious.

meaning: "your" (plural or formal), referring to a masculine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used to talk to more than one person (voi) or to one person in formal situations. It agrees with the noun: il vostro libro (m. sing.), la vostra casa (f. sing.), i vostri libri (m. pl.), le vostre case (f. pl.). In many everyday situations, Italians use possessives with an article (il/la/i/le).
target_language_example: Scusate, dov'è il vostro hotel?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is your hotel?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "vostro" to address more than one person ("your" plural) or to address someone formally ("your" polite). Often used with verbs like "servire" (to need) and "apprezzare" (to appreciate), and in expressions like "senza il vostro aiuto" (without your help).
target_language_example: Grazie per il vostro aiuto: senza di voi non ce l’avrei fatta.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help: without you I wouldn’t have made it.

meaning: "your dog" (addressing more than one person, or using polite/formal 'you').
additional_notes: “Il” is “the” and “vostro” means “your” for plural “you” (voi) or for polite/formal address in some contexts. It agrees with the masculine singular noun “cane” (dog). You can also hear “il cane vostro,” but “il vostro cane” is more common.
target_language_example: Il vostro cane è molto simpatico, ma abbaia troppo.
native_language_example: Your dog is very nice, but it barks too much.

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (“you all”) or as a polite/formal way to address one person (“your,” formal). It agrees with the noun: computer is masculine singular, so it takes il vostro. Often used in instructions or customer support contexts.
target_language_example: Potete salvare il file sul vostro computer?
native_language_example: Can you save the file on your computer?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive vostro (“your”) with the article il (“the”). It’s used when speaking to more than one person (you all) or to one person formally (like “your” in a polite context). Common with verbs like dare (to give) and dire (to tell): “Datemi/Ditemi il vostro indirizzo” = “Give/Tell me your address.”
target_language_example: Può scrivermi il vostro indirizzo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you write me your address, please?

additional_notes: "Vostro" is the possessive for "you" plural (voi) and also a polite/formal "your" when addressing someone (often with titles like Signore/Signora). "Lavoro" can mean both the job/profession and the work someone is doing. Used when talking to a group or speaking formally to one person.
target_language_example: Mi interessa molto il vostro lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm very interested in your work.

meaning: “your book” (addressing more than one person, or one person formally).
additional_notes: “Il” = “the”; “vostro” is the possessive for “your” used with (1) multiple people (“you all/you guys”) or (2) formal “you” in some contexts; it agrees with the noun: libro (masculine singular) → vostro. Often used when talking about something that belongs to the people you’re speaking to or referring to.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito il vostro libro per un giorno?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your book for one day?

additional_notes: "Vostro" is the formal "your" (to one person you address as "Lei"), or "your" to more than one person ("you all"). It’s often used in polite questions: "Posso chiedere il vostro nome?".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, qual è il vostro nome?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name?

additional_notes: Used with the possessive "vostro" to address more than one person ("you all") or, in some contexts, as a formal/polite "your". In everyday conversation with one person, you’ll more often hear "il tuo numero di telefono" (informal) or "il Suo numero di telefono" (formal).
target_language_example: Può ripetere il vostro numero di telefono, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat your phone number, please?

meaning: "your plan" (addressing more than one person, or using formal "you").
additional_notes: "Vostro" agrees with the noun: "il vostro piano" (masc. singular). You can also say "il piano vostro", but "il vostro piano" is much more common. Used when speaking to a group ("your" plural) or to one person in a polite/formal way (Lei).
target_language_example: Capisco il vostro piano, ma credo che serva più tempo.
native_language_example: I understand your plan, but I think we need more time.

additional_notes: "Il" = "the" and "vostro" = "your" when speaking to more than one person (voi) or in formal contexts. Used for giving instructions or addressing a group: "Caricate/Usate/Utilizzate il vostro telefono". Often alternates with "il tuo telefono" (your phone, informal singular).
target_language_example: Per favore, spegnete il vostro telefono durante la riunione.
native_language_example: Please, turn off your phone during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to express an assumption or a guess about something. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially in more careful/formal Italian: "Immagino che sia...", "Immagino che tu abbia...". In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, but learners should recognize the subjunctive pattern.
target_language_example: Immagino che tu sia stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: I imagine you’re tired after the trip.

additional_notes: From the verb "imparare" (to learn). "Imparando" is the gerund, commonly used with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno imparando il francese" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you (pl.) are/they are learning French."
target_language_example: In questo periodo sto imparando il francese online.
native_language_example: These days I’m learning French online.

meaning: to learn to play the piano.
additional_notes: Used to talk about learning the skill of playing an instrument. The pattern is: imparare a + verb (to learn to do something). “Suonare” means “to play” (an instrument), and “il pianoforte” is “the piano.” Often appears with polite or friendly questions like “Ti piacerebbe…?” (Would you like…?) or “Vorresti…?” (Would you want…?/Would you like…?).
target_language_example: Sto imparando a suonare il pianoforte da sei mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning to play the piano for six months.

meaning: to learn to ride a bike.
additional_notes: Used with a form of dovere (deve/devi) or dovrebbe (“should”) to say someone needs/ought to learn. The structure is imparare a + infinitive (“to learn to do something”). In bici is short for in bicicletta and means “by bike/on a bike.”
target_language_example: Ho imparato ad andare in bici quando avevo sei anni.
native_language_example: I learned to ride a bike when I was six years old.

additional_notes: Imparare = “to learn.” Lingue = “languages.” The partitive plural “delle” means “some,” so imparare delle lingue is often used in a general sense (“learn (some) languages”), not necessarily specific ones. With a specific language, you usually say: imparare l’italiano / imparare l’inglese. You can also say: imparare le lingue straniere (“to learn foreign languages”).
target_language_example: Vorrei imparare delle lingue per viaggiare più facilmente.
native_language_example: I’d like to learn some languages to travel more easily.

meaning: “to learn (a/the) …” (used before a masculine singular noun, often a language).
additional_notes: In Italian, languages often take a definite article: imparare il coreano / il polacco. Here il = “the” for masculine singular nouns. With feminine singular languages you’ll use la (imparare la lingua italiana / imparare la grammatica). In English you usually omit “the” before languages (“learn Korean”), but Italian commonly includes it.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare il giapponese.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn Japanese.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like volere (to want), piacere (to like), aiutare (to help), or avere bisogno di (to need): e.g., “Voglio imparare il berbero.” “Berbero” is a language name and is capitalized less consistently in Italian than in English; both “berbero” and “Berbero” may be seen.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un corso per imparare il berbero.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a course to learn Berber.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "imparare" (to learn) + the language name with the definite article: "il francese" (French). It often appears with another verb to talk about starting/trying to learn: "iniziare a imparare", "provare a imparare", "cercare di imparare".
target_language_example: Sto imparando il francese per lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m learning French for work.

additional_notes: Imparare = “to learn”; il tedesco = “German (language)”. Used for talking about studying the German language. You’ll often see it with time questions: “Quanto tempo ti/le serve per…?” (How long do you need to…?), and with “iniziare a…” (to start to…).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare il tedesco per lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn German for work.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase meaning “to learn the Berber vocabulary/words.” It commonly follows verbs like “cerca di…” (try to…) and “prova a…” (try to…), and can be adapted with other languages (e.g., imparare il vocabolario italiano/francese).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare il vocabolario berbero per il mio viaggio.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Berber vocabulary for my trip.

additional_notes: Common way to talk generally about studying/learning foreign languages. Uses the infinitive imparare (“to learn”) + le lingue (“the languages”). Often follows verbs like piacere (Mi piace...), amare (Amo...), and volere (Voglio...).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un corso per imparare le lingue.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a course to learn languages.

additional_notes: Common infinitive phrase used as the subject of a sentence (e.g., “Imparare una lingua straniera è…”). You can change the person/tense: “voglio imparare…”, “sto imparando…”, “ho imparato…”. “Lingua” = language; “straniera” agrees with it (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare una lingua straniera per il lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb (usually "avere") to form the passato prossimo of "imparare" + "a" + infinitive: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno imparato a + verb". It talks about acquiring a skill or learning how to do something.
target_language_example: Ho imparato a guidare l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I learned to drive last year.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *imparare* (“to learn”) in the *passato prossimo*: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno imparato il berbero*. With *avere*, *imparato* usually doesn’t change for gender/number. *Il berbero* refers to the Berber language (Tamazight); you can replace it with other languages: *imparato l’italiano / il francese*.
target_language_example: Ho imparato il berbero durante un corso in Marocco.
native_language_example: I learned Berber during a course in Morocco.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb "avere" to talk about having learned French in the past (passato prossimo: "ho/abbiamo imparato il francese"; pluperfect: "avevo/avevamo imparato il francese"). Italian normally uses the article with languages ("il francese"), while English usually says just "French".
target_language_example: Ho imparato il francese a scuola.
native_language_example: I learned French at school.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern (Non) importa quanto + adjective/adverb + verb to say something doesn’t change regardless of degree: “Non importa quanto (io) sia stanco…” = “No matter how tired I am…”. It can refer to quantity (“how much”) or degree (“how + adjective/adverb”). Often appears with the subjunctive (sia, possa essere, etc.).
target_language_example: Non importa quanto sia difficile, ci proverò.
native_language_example: No matter how difficult it is, I’ll try.

meaning: important to me / important for me.
additional_notes: Used to say that something matters personally to you (your feelings, priorities, values). Common with "essere": "È importante per me". You can also start with "Per me" for emphasis: "Per me è importante". "Importante" doesn’t change here because it refers to the thing/person that is important, not to you.
target_language_example: Questa amicizia è molto importante per me.
native_language_example: This friendship is very important to me.

meaning: “(that) I care whether he likes me.”
additional_notes: Used with **importare (a qualcuno)** = “to matter / to care (to someone)”. In sentences like **Pensi che…?** (“Do you think that…?”), Italian uses the **subjunctive**: **importi**. **A me** and **mi** both mean “to me” here (you may see either or both for emphasis). **Gli** = “to him,” and **piaccio** = “I am pleasing/likable (to him)” → “he likes me.” Often used rhetorically: **Pensi che mi importi se gli piaccio?** = “Do you think I care if he likes me?”
target_language_example: Non mi importa se gli piaccio: voglio solo essere me stessa.
native_language_example: I don’t care if he likes me: I just want to be myself.

meaning: “(that) I care whether she likes me.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb **importare (a qualcuno)** = “to matter / to care (to someone).” Here **importi** is the subjunctive (often after *pensi/pensa/pensate che…*). **se** means “whether/if” in an indirect question. **le piaccio** literally means “I’m pleasing to her” → “she likes me.” You may also hear **mi importi** instead of **a me importi** (“that I care”).
target_language_example: Pensi che mi importi se le piaccio?
native_language_example: Do you think I care if she likes me?

additional_notes: Used to say something negative happens suddenly to someone, especially an illness: *essere attaccato da una malattia* = to be struck by an illness. It’s often used in the passive (*è stato/fu...*) and is followed by a feminine noun after *una* (e.g., *una malattia*, *una febbre*).
target_language_example: È stato improvvisamente attaccato da una febbre alta.
native_language_example: He was suddenly struck by a high fever.

additional_notes: Used to say something is shown/broadcast on television. With verbs like vedere/guardare (to see/watch): “Vederlo in TV” = “to see him on TV”; “guardare … in TV” = “to watch … on TV.”
target_language_example: Stasera c'è un film interessante in TV.
native_language_example: Tonight there's an interesting movie on TV.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel using an airplane, or to ask/how long a trip takes by plane. Often used with verbs like andare/viaggiare/arrivare (to go/travel/arrive) and with time questions: Quanto tempo ci vuole in aereo?
target_language_example: Andiamo a Roma in aereo perché è più veloce.
native_language_example: We’re going to Rome by plane because it’s faster.

meaning: a rented apartment; used with prendere: “to rent an apartment.”
additional_notes: Most often used in the expression “prendere in affitto un appartamento” (to rent an apartment, i.e., to become the tenant). You can also see “un appartamento in affitto” meaning “an apartment for rent/available to rent.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo preso in affitto un appartamento vicino al centro.
native_language_example: We rented an apartment near the city center.

meaning: in advance; ahead of time; early.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens before the expected time (essere in anticipo = to be early) or before another action/deadline (pagare in anticipo = to pay in advance). Common with apologies: scusarsi in anticipo = “to apologize in advance.”
target_language_example: Per favore, avvisami in anticipo se non puoi venire.
native_language_example: Please let me know in advance if you can’t come.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, revealed, or expressed using the Arabic language. Very common with verbs like essere (to be), parlare (to speak), scrivere (to write), and phrases like tutto in arabo (“all in Arabic”). In questions, it often means “in Arabic, what does it mean?”
target_language_example: Puoi scriverlo in arabo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write it in Arabic, please?

meaning: by bus (using the bus as transport).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/coming/traveling (and similar) to say you are traveling by bus: andare/venire/arrivare/partire in autobus. Compare: “con l’autobus” is also possible but less common in everyday speech for this meaning. You can add destinations with a or in: “Vado in stazione in autobus.”
target_language_example: Domani andiamo in centro in autobus.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going downtown by bus.

meaning: “by bus or by …” (asking which means of transport).
additional_notes: Used to offer/ask between two travel options. In Italian you often use **in + vehicle** to mean “by (that vehicle)”: *in autobus, in auto, in treno*. This phrase typically continues with a second option: *in autobus o in auto?*
target_language_example: Andiamo in autobus o in metro?
native_language_example: Are we going by bus or by subway?

meaning: at the bank; (money) in the bank.
additional_notes: Used for being physically at/going to the bank (e.g., “Sono andata in banca”) and for money kept in a bank account (e.g., “ho dei soldi in banca”). With verbs like "andare" it often implies going to the bank building; with amounts of money it means deposited/saved in a bank.
target_language_example: Ho dei soldi in banca, ma oggi devo andare in banca a prelevare.
native_language_example: I have money in the bank, but today I have to go to the bank to withdraw (some).

additional_notes: Used with verbs like parlare (to speak), comunicare (to communicate), fare conversazioni (to have conversations) to indicate the language being spoken. Like other language phrases with "in" (e.g., in italiano, in inglese).
target_language_example: In casa parliamo spesso in berbero con i nonni.
native_language_example: At home we often speak in Berber with our grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or happening inside a library. Common with verbs like essere/stare (to be), studiare (to study), andare (to go), entrare (to enter).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in biblioteca alle cinque per studiare.
native_language_example: See you in the library at five to study.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel using a bicycle (like “by car/on foot”). Very common with verbs of movement such as andare, venire, tornare: “Vado in bici.” You can also hear “in bicicletta” (same meaning, more explicit).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo al parco in bici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the park by bike.

meaning: in the countryside; out in a rural area.
additional_notes: Used to say someone lives or is located outside the city, in a rural setting (fields, small towns, farmland). Often contrasts with in città (“in the city”).
target_language_example: Nel fine settimana andiamo spesso in campagna.
native_language_example: On the weekend we often go to the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned or will be sent to prison/jail. Often follows verbs like essere (to be), andare (to go), mettere/mandare (to put/send). You can add a place after it: in carcere a Roma / a Boston. In Italian, carcere is more like “prison” (not a vehicle), but it’s also commonly used where English might say “jail.”
target_language_example: È finito in carcere per furto.
native_language_example: He ended up in prison for theft.

meaning: in my house; at my place.
additional_notes: Means inside your home or at your place in general. Often used with surprise or annoyance in questions like "Che fai in casa mia?" (What are you doing in my house?). Can also appear in firmer statements about rules or welcome: "Non sei più il benvenuto in casa mia."
target_language_example: Non fumare in casa mia, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t smoke in my house, please.

in case di vetro non dovrebbero

target_language_multi_word_term: in case di vetro non dovrebbero
meaning: "people who live in glass houses shouldn't..." (you shouldn't criticize others if you have the same faults).
additional_notes: Part of the proverb: "Quelli/Chi abita(no) in case di vetro non dovrebbe(ro) lanciare/tirare pietre (o sassi)." It’s used to warn someone not to judge or attack others when they’re also vulnerable or guilty of similar things. "Non dovrebbe" (singular) and "non dovrebbero" (plural) both occur.
target_language_example: Dai, in case di vetro non dovrebbero lanciare pietre: anche tu hai fatto lo stesso errore.
native_language_example: Come on, people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones: you made the same mistake too.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone should do if an emergency happens. Often placed at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma), or after the instruction. Common in signs and instructions. Can be followed by a command in the tu form (premi/mettiti) or the formal Lei form (prema/si metta).
target_language_example: In caso di emergenza, chiama il 112.
native_language_example: In case of emergency, call 112.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or infinitive to say someone is searching for something (often abstract like "aiuto" or "avventura"). Common with verbs of movement or purpose (andare/venire/partire/essere) and can introduce a motivation: "Siamo qui in cerca di...".
target_language_example: Sono in cerca di lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a job.

meaning: "what kind of" (asking for the type/category of something).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask what category or kind something belongs to. It’s followed by a noun: In che tipo di casa/città/ranch...? You can often also say Che tipo di...?, which is slightly shorter and very common.
target_language_example: In che tipo di ristorante vuoi andare stasera?
native_language_example: What kind of restaurant do you want to go to tonight?

meaning: “what kind/type of apartment” (do you live in).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the category or style of someone’s apartment (e.g., monolocale/studio, bilocale/one-bedroom, attico/penthouse). It’s typically followed by a verb like abita/abiti/abitate (“live” in the sense of reside) or vive/vivete.
target_language_example: In che tipo di appartamento vivi, un monolocale o un bilocale?
native_language_example: What kind of apartment do you live in, a studio or a one-bedroom?

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of being/meeting (essere, vedersi) to mean “in the church building,” and with verbs of going (andare, venire) to mean “to church” (often implying going for a service). Italian often drops the article here; you can also hear "nella chiesa" when emphasizing a specific church building.
target_language_example: Domenica mattina andiamo in chiesa con i nonni.
native_language_example: On Sunday morning we go to church with our grandparents.

meaning: to/at church on the eve of (a holiday).
additional_notes: Used to say someone goes to church on the evening/day before an important celebration, most commonly "la Vigilia di Natale" (Christmas Eve). The structure is: "in chiesa" (to/at church) + "la Vigilia di" + holiday (Natale, Pasqua, ecc.). Often used with "andare" (to go): "andare in chiesa la Vigilia di Natale".
target_language_example: Siamo in chiesa la Vigilia di Pasqua.
native_language_example: We’re at church on Easter Eve.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone goes to church regularly on Sundays. Often follows a verb like andare (vado/andiamo/va/vanno/andava) + in chiesa + ogni domenica.
target_language_example: Da bambino andavo in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: As a child, I went to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located within the city (often contrasted with being outside the city, e.g., in the countryside or suburbs). In Italian it’s common to say "in città" without an article (not *"nella città"*), especially when speaking generally about being/going to town.
target_language_example: Domani devo andare in città per fare la spesa.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to go into town to do the shopping.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens while you are in a classroom during a lesson (studying, speaking, being present, rules like not eating). Often refers to the time/context of the lesson rather than a specific physical place.
target_language_example: Oggi in classe facciamo un quiz.
native_language_example: Today in class we’re doing a quiz.

meaning: in a coma for three years.
additional_notes: Used to say someone remained in a coma for a period of time. Often with essere in the past: "Sono stato/a in coma per tre anni" (I was in a coma for three years) or "È stato/a in coma per tre anni" (He/She was...). "stato" changes to "stata" for a female speaker/subject.
target_language_example: Mio nonno è stato in coma per tre anni, poi si è svegliato.
native_language_example: My grandpa was in a coma for three years, then he woke up.

meaning: with his/her mother; accompanied by his/her mother.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived or is present together with their mother. "In compagnia di" means "in the company of / accompanied by" and is slightly formal; in everyday speech you can also say "con sua madre" (or "con la madre"). Note: "sua" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: È arrivata in compagnia di sua madre.
native_language_example: She arrived with her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say you pay with physical money (coins/bills), not by card or bank transfer. Common with verbs like pagare (to pay) and sometimes with “preferisci pagare in contanti o con la carta?”
target_language_example: Posso pagare in contanti?
native_language_example: Can I pay in cash?

meaning: in touch with; in contact with.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere (to be), mettersi (to get), entrare (to come), rimanere (to stay) to talk about communicating or having a connection with someone. Common in both everyday and more formal contexts (e.g., emergencies: “mettersi in contatto con…”).
target_language_example: Sono ancora in contatto con i miei ex colleghi.
native_language_example: I’m still in touch with my former colleagues.

meaning: in touch with her; in contact with her.
additional_notes: Often used with reflexive verbs like tenersi/mantenersi/mettersi: “tenersi/mantenersi in contatto con lei” = “to stay/keep in touch with her”; “mettersi in contatto con lei” = “to get in touch with her.” “Lei” is the formal/polite way to say “you” (so it can also mean “with you” in formal situations), but it can also literally mean “with her” from context. In questions with the passato prossimo, the past participle agrees: messo (masc. sing.), messa (fem. sing.), messi (masc. pl.), messe (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Mi sono messo in contatto con lei ieri per confermare l’appuntamento.
native_language_example: I got in touch with her yesterday to confirm the appointment.

additional_notes: Used to say you keep communicating with a man (by phone, messages, email, etc.). Common with verbs like essere/restare/rimanere (“to be/stay/remain”) and mettersi (“to get in touch”): e.g., "Ti sei messa in contatto con lui?" = "Did you get in touch with him?". For a woman, use "con lei"; plural: "con loro".
target_language_example: Sono ancora in contatto con lui, ci scriviamo spesso.
native_language_example: I'm still in contact with him; we message often.

in contatto con me, per ogni evenienza

target_language_multi_word_term: in contatto con me, per ogni evenienza
meaning: “in touch with me, just in case.”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to keep communicating/available (phone, text, email) as a precaution in case something unexpected happens. Often follows verbs like restare (“to stay”), rimanere (“to remain”), or tenersi (“to keep oneself”) in contatto. “Per ogni evenienza” is similar to “in case of anything / just in case.”
target_language_example: Resta in contatto con me, per ogni evenienza.
native_language_example: Stay in touch with me, just in case.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is or where an action happens. Often with verbs like essere (to be), mangiare (to eat), portare (to bring), preparare (to prepare).
target_language_example: Il caffè è in cucina.
native_language_example: The coffee is in the kitchen.

meaning: 'in which' / 'when' (refers to a time or place).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause to refer back to a noun like a place (il ristorante in cui...) or a time/moment (il momento in cui... = 'the moment when...'). Often interchangeable with "dove" for places and "quando" for time in casual speech, but "in cui" is more general and works in formal writing too.
target_language_example: È una città in cui vorrei vivere un giorno.
native_language_example: It’s a city where I’d like to live one day.

additional_notes: Used after a noun like luogo/posto/casa/città to describe it as the place where someone lives or could live. Often follows descriptions like sicuro, migliore, bello: “a safe/better/best place to live.”
target_language_example: Cerco un appartamento in cui vivere vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for an apartment to live in near work.

meaning: in disagreement with; not agreeing with.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (to be): "essere in disaccordo con [person/idea]". It’s a fairly formal/neutral way to say you disagree, especially in discussions or opinions. Similar meaning to "non essere d’accordo con".
target_language_example: Sono in disaccordo con questa decisione.
native_language_example: I disagree with this decision.

in discoteca per tutta la notte

target_language_multi_word_term: in discoteca per tutta la notte
additional_notes: Literally “in the nightclub for the whole night.” Used to say someone spends the entire night at a club, often implying partying/dancing. Common with verbs like "andare" (to go), "stare" (to stay), "ballare" (to dance), and "rimanere" (to remain).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti in discoteca per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: We stayed at the nightclub all night.

additional_notes: Use "in + language" to say something is done using that language, especially with verbs like parlare (to speak), scrivere (to write), tradurre (to translate), leggere (to read), and sometimes pensare (to think).
target_language_example: Puoi scriverlo in esperanto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write it in Esperanto, please?

meaning: in line for the promotion; next to be promoted.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is next (or among the next) to receive a promotion, based on order/priority. Often appears with "il/la prossimo/a" or "i/le prossimi/e": "il prossimo in fila per la promozione" = "the next in line for the promotion."
target_language_example: Marco è in fila per la promozione, ma non è ancora sicuro quando arriverà.
native_language_example: Marco is in line for the promotion, but he’s not sure yet when it will happen.

meaning: the bread in the oven; (with a verb) to bake/cook the bread in the oven.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like mettere (to put), cuocere (to cook/bake), or sfornare (to take out of the oven). Often placed after the verb: "Ho cotto in forno il pane" = "I baked the bread in the oven."
target_language_example: Ho messo in forno il pane e tra mezz’ora è pronto.
native_language_example: I put the bread in the oven and in half an hour it’ll be ready.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done using the French language (speaking, writing, singing, presenting), or to refer to the school subject French (e.g., grades in French). Often used after verbs like parlare/scrivere/cantare, or after adjectives like forte (good at).
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere in francese, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat in French, please?

meaning: “in French with” (speaking in French to/with someone).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like parlare/parlarsi (“to speak”) to say the language you use with a specific person. Structure: parlare in + [language] + con + [person]. Example: “Parlo in francese con Maria” = “I speak in French with Maria / I speak French with Maria.” In English you often drop “in” (“I speak French with…”).
target_language_example: Parlo in francese con i clienti, ma in italiano con i colleghi.
native_language_example: I speak in French with customers, but in Italian with colleagues.

meaning: 'in the future' (from now on; at a later time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen later than now. Common after verbs like accadere (to happen) and with advice/requests: “in futuro, sii…” = “in the future/from now on, be…”.
target_language_example: In futuro vorrei vivere vicino al mare.
native_language_example: In the future I'd like to live near the sea.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like andare/finire/essere in galera (“go/end up/be in jail”). It’s fairly colloquial; in more formal contexts you may hear in prigione or in carcere.
target_language_example: Se continui così, finirai in galera.
native_language_example: If you keep this up, you'll end up in jail.

meaning: in the garden / in the yard.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the garden (outdoors, usually at/behind a house). With verbs like essere/stare it answers “Where?” (Dov’è?). With action verbs it means the action happens there (e.g., piantare in giardino = to plant in the garden).
target_language_example: I bambini stanno giocando in giardino.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the garden.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (in grado di + infinitive) to say someone has the ability/capacity to do something. Often appears in questions and negatives: Non sono in grado di... = “I’m not able to...”. With essere in the right tense: ero/sono/sarai in grado di...
target_language_example: Non sono ancora in grado di guidare da solo.
native_language_example: I’m not able to drive alone yet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability/capacity to help. It’s built from: essere in grado di (“to be able to”) + aiutare (“to help”). Often used with different tenses: ero in grado di aiutare (I was able to help), sarai in grado di aiutare (you will be able to help). Similar in meaning to “poter aiutare” (can help), but “essere in grado di” can sound a bit more formal/explicit about capability.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non sono in grado di aiutare.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m not able to help.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **essere in grado di + infinitive** to say someone is capable/able to do something. The person changes with the verb **essere** (e.g., *sono/sei/è/siete in grado di…*). Often appears with **non** for “not able to” and with conditional/subjunctive for politeness or uncertainty (e.g., *sarebbe/sareste in grado di aiutarmi?*).
target_language_example: Siete in grado di aiutarmi con questo modulo?
native_language_example: Are you able to help me with this form?

meaning: able to do it; capable of doing it.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability, skills, or possibility to do something. It’s built from the expression "essere in grado di" (to be able/capable of) + "farlo" (to do it). Often used with different tenses: "sono" (I am), "ero" (I was), "sia" (is, subjunctive), "non era" (was not).
target_language_example: Non sono ancora in grado di farlo da solo.
native_language_example: I’m not able to do it by myself yet.

additional_notes: "Essere in grado di" means "to be able/capable of." "Farlo" = "do it" (refers to an action already understood). "Se" introduces a condition ("if"). Often used with the conditional/subjunctive to talk about what someone could do in certain circumstances: "sarebbe in grado di farlo se…" = "would be able to do it if…".
target_language_example: Sarei in grado di farlo se mi dessi un po’ di tempo.
native_language_example: I’d be able to do it if you gave me a bit of time.

meaning: able to read; capable of reading.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere": "essere in grado di" + infinitive means "to be able/capable of" doing something. It often implies having the skill or capacity (sometimes after learning or with enough conditions). You can replace "leggere" with other verbs: "Sono in grado di capire" (I’m able to understand).
target_language_example: Non sono ancora in grado di leggere un romanzo in italiano.
native_language_example: I’m not able to read a novel in Italian yet.

meaning: able to swim / capable of swimming.
additional_notes: "Essere in grado di" means "to be able to" or "to be capable of" doing something; it’s followed by the preposition "di" + an infinitive verb (here: "nuotare"). Often used to talk about ability/competence in a more formal or careful way than "sapere" (e.g., "So nuotare").
target_language_example: Non sono in grado di nuotare molto lontano dalla riva.
native_language_example: I’m not able to swim very far from the shore.

meaning: in serious danger; in grave danger.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is facing a very serious risk or threat. Often used with the verb "essere" (è/sono/era) to describe a critical situation: "La sua vita è in grave pericolo" (His/Her life is in serious danger). "Grave" here means "serious" (not "grave" like a tomb).
target_language_example: Senza aiuto, i bambini sono in grave pericolo.
native_language_example: Without help, the children are in serious danger.

additional_notes: Used with essere (“to be”) to say someone is in big trouble (often because of a problem, mistake, or danger). "Guai" is usually plural in this expression. You may also hear: "mettersi nei guai" (to get into trouble) and "finire nei guai" (to end up in trouble).
target_language_example: Se lo scoprono, siamo in guai seri.
native_language_example: If they find out, we’re in serious trouble.

additional_notes: Used to say something is expressed/written in English, or that someone is good at English. Often with verbs like parlare/scrivere/dire (“to speak/write/say”) or with school subjects: essere bravo/a in inglese (“to be good at English”).
target_language_example: Come si dice questo in inglese?
native_language_example: How do you say this in English?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is crying or very close to crying. Common with verbs like essere (era in lacrime = he was in tears), venire/tornare (è venuto a casa in lacrime = he came home crying), and especially scoppiò/scoppiare in lacrime (to burst into tears).
target_language_example: Quando l’ha sentito, è scoppiata in lacrime.
native_language_example: When she heard it, she burst into tears.

additional_notes: Used either to say how you travel (equivalent to “by car”: Andiamo a Roma in macchina) or where someone is (equivalent to “in the car”: Sono/ero in macchina). Often contrasts with other transport: in treno (by train), in autobus (by bus).
target_language_example: Preferisco andare in macchina perché è più comodo.
native_language_example: I prefer to go by car because it’s more convenient.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how someone behaves/feels, usually followed by an adjective or an adverb phrase: in maniera terribile (in a terrible way), in maniera eccessiva (in an excessive way), in maniera diversa (in a different way). Often interchangeable with "in modo".
target_language_example: Spiegalo in maniera semplice, per favore.
native_language_example: Explain it in a simple way, please.

meaning: less than; fewer than; ... younger than (by).
additional_notes: Used with numbers to compare amounts or time. With time expressions it means “in under …” (in less than ten minutes). With age it can mean “... years younger than” (quattro anni in meno di lui = four years younger than him). Often follows the number: “dieci minuti” + “in meno di” + reference, or “in meno di” + number + unit.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in meno di mezz’ora.
native_language_example: We arrived in under half an hour.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone does something or how something happens, usually followed by an adjective (in modo incredibile = in an incredible way). You can also add a modifier like molto/abbastanza (in modo molto gentile = in a very kind way). Often translates like "in a way" or "...ly" in English (in modo strano = strangely).
target_language_example: Parla in modo molto chiaro.
native_language_example: He/She speaks in a very clear way.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone does something or thinks/sees something differently from before or from other people. Often follows the verb: vedere/guardare le cose in modo diverso (“to see/look at things differently”), fare qualcosa in modo diverso (“to do something differently”).
target_language_example: Proviamo a risolvere il problema in modo diverso.
native_language_example: Let’s try to solve the problem differently.

in molti negozi a cercare il libro

target_language_multi_word_term: in molti negozi a cercare il libro
meaning: to (go) to many shops to look for the book.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like andare/andare in or essere andato/a (past tense) to say you went to several stores with the purpose of searching for a specific book. Often appears as: (sono) andato/a in molti negozi a cercare il libro.
target_language_example: Sono andata in molti negozi a cercare il libro, ma non l’ho trovato.
native_language_example: I went to many shops to look for the book, but I didn’t find it.

meaning: in the hospital; to the hospital.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of being/staying (essere/stare) to mean “in the hospital” and with verbs of motion (andare/portare) to mean “to the hospital.” Often implies someone is there for medical care (as a patient), but it can also be used for visiting someone there (e.g., “andare in ospedale a visitarlo”).
target_language_example: Devo andare in ospedale per un controllo.
native_language_example: I have to go to the hospital for a check-up.

meaning: in the hospital for a week.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was staying in the hospital for one week. Often follows verbs like stare/restare/rimanere/essere (“to be/stay/remain”).
target_language_example: Mia madre è stata in ospedale per una settimana dopo l’operazione.
native_language_example: My mother was in the hospital for a week after the operation.

additional_notes: Used both literally (a country is at peace: "essere in pace con...") and in everyday requests meaning “leave (someone/something) alone” ("lasciare in pace"). Also used in condolences or about death: "riposare in pace" (“rest in peace”) and "morire in pace" (“die peacefully”).
target_language_example: Per favore, lasciami in pace: devo studiare.
native_language_example: Please, leave me alone: I have to study.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/being (andare, andare a, venire, essere) to say you go to the gym or you’re at the gym. Common with frequency phrases: "due volte alla settimana" (twice a week).
target_language_example: Dopo lavoro vado in palestra.
native_language_example: After work I go to the gym.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is retired (no longer working) or has entered retirement. Often with essere (to be): “Sono in pensione” = “I’m retired.” With andare in pensione it means “to retire” (to stop working and start receiving a pension).
target_language_example: Mio padre è in pensione da due anni.
native_language_example: My father has been retired for two years.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to say someone/something is in danger: "Sono in pericolo" (I’m in danger). It can also be used with mettere (“to put”) or mettere in pericolo (“to endanger”): "Lo metti in pericolo" (You put him in danger). You may also hear "in pericolo immediato" for “in immediate danger.”
target_language_example: Sei in pericolo? Chiamo la polizia.
native_language_example: Are you in danger? I’ll call the police.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at the pool or going there, often with verbs like essere (to be), andare (to go), and portare (to take/bring). You can also use it for pool-related events: una festa in piscina = a pool party.
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio andiamo in piscina con gli amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon we’re going to the pool with friends.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb "prendere" → "prendere in prestito" = "to borrow". It implies you will give it back. The opposite is "dare in prestito" = "to lend". You can use it for objects (books, pens) and money.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito la tua penna?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your pen?

meaning: (some) money as a loan; borrowed money.
additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "prendere" ("prendere in prestito dei soldi" = to borrow money) and the opposite is "dare dei soldi in prestito" (= to lend money). You can add who you borrow from with "da": "prendere in prestito dei soldi da un amico".
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito dei soldi da te?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money from you?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "prendere" ("prendere in prestito") to mean "to borrow" something and then return it. You can add who you borrow from with "da/dal/dai/dalle": "Prendo in prestito dei gioielli da un’amica" (I borrow some jewelry from a friend). "Dei gioielli" means "some jewelry" (unspecified quantity).
target_language_example: Ho preso in prestito dei gioielli da mia sorella per la festa.
native_language_example: I borrowed some jewelry from my sister for the party.

meaning: (to borrow) some money; money on loan.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "prendere" (or "chiedere") to mean borrowing money (often implying you will pay it back). Common patterns: "prendere in prestito dei soldi (da qualcuno)" = to borrow some money (from someone); "venire a prendere in prestito dei soldi" = to come to borrow money.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito dei soldi da te fino a domani?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money from you until tomorrow?

additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb phrase "prendere in prestito" (to borrow). You’ll usually say: "prendere in prestito del denaro" = to borrow some money. The lender would say "prestare del denaro" = to lend money.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito del denaro fino a domani?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money until tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently detained (essere in prigione) or to describe spending time there (passare X giorni in prigione). With verbs like mettere/mandare in prigione it means “to put/send (someone) in prison.”
target_language_example: Non voglio finire in prigione.
native_language_example: I don’t want to end up in prison.

additional_notes: Used to say someone spent a total duration of three years in prison. With essere, the past participle agrees with the subject: sono stato (male) / sono stata (female). You can swap the time: in prigione per due mesi, per cinque anni, etc.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è stato in prigione per tre anni, ma ora lavora e sta bene.
native_language_example: My brother was in prison for three years, but now he works and is doing well.

meaning: in public; in front of other people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about actions done where others can see/hear you (e.g., in the street, at a party, on stage). Often contrasts with "in privato" (in private).
target_language_example: Preferisco non discutere in pubblico.
native_language_example: I prefer not to argue in public.

additional_notes: Used when the exact method or reason is unknown, unspecified, or not important. It can mean “somehow (I’ll manage)” in problem-solving contexts, or “in some way” to say something is partly/indirectly true (e.g., “limited in some way”). Common in offers of help: “Posso aiutarti in qualche modo?”
target_language_example: Non so come, ma in qualche modo ce la faremo.
native_language_example: I don’t know how, but somehow we’ll make it.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen or be done at an unspecified time, without restrictions. Often with the future tense to mean “any moment now” (e.g., something is expected to happen soon).
target_language_example: Puoi chiamarmi in qualsiasi momento.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

meaning: at any time; whenever you like.
additional_notes: Used to say there is no restriction on timing (you can do it now, later, day or night). Common with invitations or permission, often with the verb in the present or future: “puoi chiamarmi in qualunque momento,” “sarai/ sarà il benvenuto/a in qualunque momento.” Similar to “in qualsiasi momento.”
target_language_example: Puoi scrivermi in qualunque momento se hai domande.
native_language_example: You can write to me at any time if you have questions.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to point to a specific place/time/thing already known or indicated: in quel periodo (in that period), in quel caso (in that case), in quel villaggio (in that village). It’s the contraction of "in" + "quel" (from "quello"). Feminine: "in quella"; plural: "in quei" / "in quegli" / "in quelle".
target_language_example: Non voglio entrare in quel negozio.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go into that shop.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific way of speaking, behaving, doing something, or even looking at someone—often with a negative or disapproving tone depending on context (e.g., "Don’t talk to me like that"). Can also refer to leaving a situation "that way" (unresolved, messy, etc.).
target_language_example: Non guardarmi in quel modo, mi metti a disagio.
native_language_example: Don’t look at me like that, you’re making me uncomfortable.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific point in time being talked about (in the past, present, or in a story). Often appears with past tenses (e.g., imperfetto) to describe what was happening then. Similar to "in quel momento" = "at that moment" and "in quel periodo" = "during that period" (longer time span).
target_language_example: In quel momento non potevo rispondere al telefono.
native_language_example: At that moment I couldn't answer the phone.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific shop (usually one you’ve mentioned already or can indicate in context). Often answers “Where?” (Dove?): *Hai comprato la penna dove?* → *In quel negozio.* You can swap in other determiners: *in questo negozio* (in this shop), *in quel supermercato* (in that supermarket).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in quel negozio alle cinque.
native_language_example: See you in that shop at five.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific feminine noun already known from context (e.g., foto, città, parte, stanza, moschea, biblioteca). It often means either being inside a place (“in that room/library/city”) or within a context/area (“in that part of the country”). You’ll also see: in quel (masc. sing.), in quei (masc. plural), in quelle (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Non posso parlare in quella sala, c’è una riunione.
native_language_example: I can’t talk in that room, there’s a meeting.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being inside a specific house already identified in context. "Quella" is the feminine singular demonstrative (“that”) and matches "casa" (feminine). Often implies the house is not the one near the speaker (contrast with "in questa casa" = “in this house”).
target_language_example: Non voglio entrare in quella casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go into that house.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being inside/attending a specific school already known from context. "Quella" = "that" (not "this"), pointing to a particular school (often not the one you’re in right now). Common with verbs like andare (to go), studiare (to study), trasferirsi (to transfer).
target_language_example: Mio fratello studia in quella scuola da due anni.
native_language_example: My brother has been studying at that school for two years.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to indicate location or context: “in this library / factory / season / room / church.” It’s the preposition “in” + “questa” (“this,” feminine singular). With masculine nouns you usually use “in questo” (e.g., in questo ufficio).
target_language_example: C'è il Wi‑Fi gratuito in questa zona.
native_language_example: There is free Wi‑Fi in this area.

meaning: in this house; in this home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is (or happens) inside this specific house. Often used when talking about where you lived or grew up ("Sono cresciuto in questa casa"), or when setting a rule about what/who is allowed inside ("Non la voglio in questa casa!" = “I don’t want her/it in this house!”).
target_language_example: In questa casa non si fuma.
native_language_example: In this house, no one smokes / Smoking is not allowed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or stays/lives) within the current city being talked about. Common with verbs like abitare (to live), restare (to stay), vivere (to live), and rimanere (to remain). You can swap questa with other demonstratives: in quella città = in that city.
target_language_example: Non lavoro più in questa città.
native_language_example: I don’t work in this city anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside/part of the particular class you’re talking about. Often follows phrases like “Ci sono…” (There are…), “Quanti sono…” (How many are…), or “essere in…” (to be in…). “Classe” can mean a school class, a course group, or sometimes a category/grade level—context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Oggi in questa classe siamo in venti.
native_language_example: Today in this class there are twenty of us.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is located inside the room you are currently in (or the room being referred to). Common with "essere/ci sono" (to be/there are) and with action verbs like "succedere" (to happen) or "rimanere" (to stay). "Questa" agrees with the feminine noun "stanza".
target_language_example: Non fumare in questa stanza, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t smoke in this room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening or existing nearby (in the local area). Common in questions about whether something has been seen/found locally, or statements about what people are like in the area.
target_language_example: C'è un buon ristorante in questa zona?
native_language_example: Is there a good restaurant in this area?

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to mean being located/doing something inside a place or within a time/moment: in questo lago, in questo letto, in questo istante. With abstract nouns it can mean “in this (situation/case)”: In questo caso…. For feminine singular, use "in questa" (e.g., in questa città).
target_language_example: In questo momento non posso parlare.
native_language_example: At this moment I can’t talk.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is located or happens inside this specific building (often one you’re in or have just mentioned). Common with verbs like vivere (to live), lavorare (to work), trovarsi (to be located), and fare (to do).
target_language_example: C'è un ascensore in questo edificio?
native_language_example: Is there an elevator in this building?

additional_notes: Used to describe the way something happens or is done, often referring to a specific situation (sometimes with a negative tone: “treated me like this”). It can also mean “end up like this” (finire in questo modo) or mean “it doesn’t have to be like this” (non deve essere in questo modo).
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare con me in questo modo.
native_language_example: Please, don’t talk to me like this.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening or true at the present time. Often answers the question “Quando?” (When?) and can go at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Non posso parlare in questo momento.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now.

meaning: in this country (or: in this town/village).
additional_notes: Means “in this place” with paese most often understood as “country,” but in some contexts it can also mean “town/village” (especially when talking about a small local place). Used for location or being present/absent in that place.
target_language_example: Non ho mai vissuto in questo paese prima d’ora.
native_language_example: I’ve never lived in this country before.

additional_notes: Used to say where an action happens (a place). With restaurants you typically use "in" (in/at) to mean you eat there. You can change the noun: "in questo bar" (in this bar), "in questo hotel" (in this hotel).
target_language_example: Non ho mai mangiato in questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I’ve never eaten in this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with essere (e.g., sono/sei/è/eravamo) to say you are late for an event, appointment, meeting, school, work, etc. It’s often followed by an article + noun (per il lavoro, per una riunione, per gli appuntamenti).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo per la lezione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late for class.

additional_notes: Used with essere (to be) or arrivare (to arrive) to say someone won’t make it to dinner on time. You can replace la cena with another event: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work), in ritardo per l'appuntamento (late for the appointment).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo per la cena.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (to be): essere in ritardo per la scuola = to be late for school. Common in talking about schedules and obligations. You can swap the destination: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work), in ritardo per l’appuntamento (late for the appointment).
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo per la scuola, devo andare subito!
native_language_example: I’m late for school, I have to go right away!

meaning: late for class / late for lessons.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives after the scheduled start time of their classes. Common pattern: "essere in ritardo per ..." (to be late for ...) + what you’re late for (e.g., le lezioni, la scuola, una riunione).
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo per le lezioni perché l'autobus non è arrivato.
native_language_example: I'm late for class because the bus didn't come.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (or similar) to say someone is doing well health-wise: "Sono in salute" = "I’m in good health." It often implies “healthy/doing well” rather than just “not sick,” and can be strengthened with words like "molto" or contrasted with age/conditions ("per la sua età").
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, è finalmente in salute.
native_language_example: After the operation, he’s finally in good health.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays or does something quietly, without talking or making noise. Often with verbs like essere/stare (to be/stay), rimanere (to remain), andare/uscire/entrare (to go out/in).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti in silenzio durante il film.
native_language_example: We stayed silent during the movie.

meaning: at the beach; to the beach.
additional_notes: Means being/doing something at the beach (location), or going to the beach with verbs of movement like andare (“to go”). Often used without an article: in spiaggia (more general) vs. nella/alla spiaggia (more specific, less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Andiamo in spiaggia domani mattina?
native_language_example: Are we going to the beach tomorrow morning?

meaning: at the train station; to the train station.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to mean “to the station” (andare/arrivare/portare qualcuno in stazione). With verbs describing being somewhere, it means “at the station” (essere/vedere qualcuno in stazione). In Italian, "stazione" usually refers to the train station unless specified (e.g., stazione degli autobus).
target_language_example: Puoi accompagnarmi in stazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take me to the train station, please?

meaning: in three days; within three days (time needed to finish).
additional_notes: Used with completed actions to say how long it took to finish something (duration needed), often with verbs like fare, completare, leggere. It answers “How long did it take?” or “Can you do it in X days?” For time spent doing something without focusing on completion, Italian often uses "per" (e.g., "per tre giorni" = for three days).
target_language_example: Abbiamo preparato tutto in tre giorni.
native_language_example: We prepared everything in three days.

meaning: by train; on the train (as a means of travel).
additional_notes: Used to say you travel using the train as your transportation method, especially with verbs like andare/venire/partire/arrivare (e.g., andare in treno = to go by train).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a Milano in treno.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to Milan by train.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true everywhere in the world. Often follows verbs like vivere/viaggiare (to live/travel) or expressions like essere famoso (to be famous). Similar options: "nel mondo" = in the world (more general), "in giro per il mondo" = around the world.
target_language_example: Questo film è conosciuto in tutto il mondo.
native_language_example: This movie is known all over the world.

meaning: in the office; at the office (at work).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at their workplace/office or that something happens there. Very common with verbs like essere/stare (to be), andare/venire (to go/come), arrivare (to arrive), aspettare (to wait). Contrast: "a casa" (at home).
target_language_example: Oggi lavoro in ufficio fino alle sei.
native_language_example: Today I’m working in the office until six.

meaning: "in a" / "in an" (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside a place or within a time/moment (e.g., *in un ospedale*, *in un istante*). **un** is the masculine singular indefinite article. Variations: **in una** (feminine: *in una casa*), **in uno** (before *s+consonant*, *z*, *ps*, *gn*, etc.: *in uno stadio*).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in un minuto.
native_language_example: See you in a minute.

meaning: in an apartment / in a flat.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "abitare" or "vivere" to say where someone lives. "In" + a place (here, an apartment) expresses location. You can add details after it, e.g. "in un appartamento sopra un negozio" (in an apartment above a shop).
target_language_example: Vivo in un appartamento in centro.
native_language_example: I live in an apartment in the city center.

meaning: "in a way" / "in a certain sense" (partly; from one point of view).
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement: you agree only to some extent, or only from a particular perspective. Often followed by a contrast like "però/ma" (but).
target_language_example: In un certo senso ti capisco, ma non posso essere d'accordo su tutto.
native_language_example: In a way I understand you, but I can’t agree with everything.

meaning: in one day; within a day.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be done in the time span of a single day (a 24-hour period). Often answers “How long does it take?” (Quanto ci vuole?). Can also be used in fixed expressions like “Roma non è stata costruita in un giorno” (“Rome wasn’t built in a day”).
target_language_example: Non posso finire questo lavoro in un giorno.
native_language_example: I can’t finish this work in one day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was staying, working, or located at a hotel. Often appears with verbs like essere (to be), stare (to stay), soggiornare (to stay), and lavorare (to work). Note: in Italian, hotel is masculine, so you say un hotel (not *una*).
target_language_example: Abbiamo dormito in un hotel vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: We slept in a hotel near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often injury or death) happened as the result of an accident. Very common with verbs like "morire/perdere la vita" (to die), "rimanere ucciso" (to be killed), and "ferirsi" (to get injured). You can specify the type: "in un incidente stradale" (in a road accident), "in un incidente di caccia" (in a hunting accident).
target_language_example: È rimasto ferito in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: He was injured in a road accident.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened as a result of a traffic accident (often serious, e.g., injuries or death). You’ll also see related phrases like "essere coinvolto in un incidente stradale" (to be involved in a traffic accident) and "morire/perdere la vita in un incidente stradale" (to die in a traffic accident).
target_language_example: Due persone sono rimaste ferite in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: Two people were injured in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "stare", "restare", "rimanere" to say you are staying/living temporarily at a motel. "Un" is the masculine indefinite article (“a”).
target_language_example: Stiamo in un motel vicino all’aeroporto per una notte.
native_language_example: We’re staying in a motel near the airport for one night.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere portato/a (to be taken) or essere mandato/a (to be sent) to say someone is taken/sent to a psychiatric hospital for mental health care. The preposition “in” is used for being taken/sent into institutions/places. “Ospedale psichiatrico” is a formal term; in everyday language you may also hear “ospedale/clinica psichiatrica” or “reparto di psichiatria” (psychiatry ward).
target_language_example: Dopo la crisi, l'hanno portato in un ospedale psichiatrico.
native_language_example: After the crisis, they took him to a psychiatric hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being/going/staying abroad. It’s often used with travel/life-experience questions like “Sei mai stato/a…?” (“Have you ever been…?”). Note agreement in questions: stato (male), stata (female), stati (mixed/plural male), state (plural female).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto in un paese straniero per un anno.
native_language_example: I lived in a foreign country for a year.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives or grew up. Often followed by extra detail with "di..." (e.g., "un villaggio di pescatori" = a fishing village) or by a place name.
