target_language_example: Sono nato in un piccolo villaggio vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I was born in a small village near the sea.

meaning: in a place; to a place.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of being/staying (è/sta/tenere) to mean “in a place,” and with movement verbs (andare/portare) to mean “to a place.” Often followed by an adjective: in un posto tranquillo/carino/fresco. In phrases like “in un posto migliore,” it can mean “in a better place” (sometimes said about someone who has died).
target_language_example: Mettilo in un posto sicuro.
native_language_example: Put it in a safe place.

meaning: in a place like this / in such a place.
additional_notes: Used to describe the kind of place you’re in, often followed by an adjective (e.g., così buio = so dark, così freddo = so cold, così bello = so beautiful, così rumoroso = so noisy). It can also be used on its own (“in un posto così”) when the context makes the description clear, often expressing surprise or emphasis.
target_language_example: Non pensavo di finire in un posto così lontano.
native_language_example: I didn’t think I’d end up in a place this far away.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located somewhere safe, or will be taken somewhere safe. Common with verbs like essere (to be) and portare (to take/bring).
target_language_example: Metti i documenti in un posto sicuro.
native_language_example: Put the documents in a safe place.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens inside/at a restaurant. Very common with verbs like mangiare (to eat), lavorare (to work), andare (to go). You can change the article depending on the restaurant: in un ristorante (a restaurant), nel ristorante (in the/the specific restaurant), in un ristorante asiatico/costoso (in an Asian/expensive restaurant).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in un ristorante vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you in a restaurant near the station.

meaning: 'in a' / 'into a' (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns after "in". It can mean being located inside something (state/location: "abitare in una…", "essere in una…") or moving into something (direction: "mettere/portare in una…"). The noun that follows is usually a place, group, family, or situation (e.g., "in una palude", "in una band", "in una famiglia", "in una situazione").
target_language_example: Siamo in una stanza molto piccola.
native_language_example: We’re in a very small room.

meaning: in a bank (inside a bank / at a bank).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically inside a bank or works at a bank. Often follows verbs like lavorare (to work), entrare (to enter), andare (to go), aprire un conto (to open an account).
target_language_example: Vado in una banca per prelevare contanti.
native_language_example: I’m going to a bank to withdraw cash.

meaning: in a house; into a house.
additional_notes: Uses "in" + indefinite article "una" (a/an) + "casa" (house/home). With verbs like "abitare" it means being/living in a house (location). With verbs of movement/change like "trasferirsi" it can mean moving into a (different) house. "Casa" can mean either "house" or "home" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vivono in una casa vicino al mare.
native_language_example: They live in a house near the sea.

meaning: in a city; living/being in an (unspecified) city.
additional_notes: Uses "in" + a place to say where someone lives, is, or grew up. "Una" is the indefinite article, so it often means an unspecified city (not naming which one). You can add adjectives or details: "in una città grande" (in a big city), "in una città vicino a Boston" (in a city near Boston).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto per anni in una città molto rumorosa.
native_language_example: I lived for years in a very noisy city.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives or where something happens. "In" is used with most cities in Italian (e.g., "abito in una grande città").
target_language_example: Lavoro in una grande città, ma vivo in periferia.
native_language_example: I work in a big city, but I live in the suburbs.

meaning: in a small town (in a small city).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives/lived or grew up. Italian often uses "città" even when English would say "town." You can change the adjective or size: "in una grande città" (in a big city), "in una città tranquilla" (in a quiet town/city).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto per anni in una piccola città vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I lived for years in a small town near the sea.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like andare (“to go”) to say you went to/into an Italian pizza place. The preposition in is common for places you go inside (restaurants, shops). You’ll often see it with the past tense: Siamo andati/e in una pizzeria italiana (“We went to an Italian pizzeria”).
target_language_example: Ieri sera siamo andati in una pizzeria italiana vicino a casa.
native_language_example: Last night we went to an Italian pizzeria near home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to say you are/were in a relationship where the partners live far apart. Often appears in questions like “Sei mai stata/o…?” (“Have you ever been…?”). You can also say “una relazione a distanza” without “in.”
target_language_example: Sono in una relazione a distanza da due anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been in a long-distance relationship for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something is placed inside a box. Often follows verbs like mettere (to put), mettere via (to put away), or tenere (to keep).
target_language_example: Metti questi libri in una scatola, per favore.
native_language_example: Put these books in a box, please.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or happens inside a zoo. Italian uses "uno" (not "un") before words that start with z (zoo), s+consonant, ps, gn, x, etc.: "in uno zoo".
target_language_example: I bambini si divertono in uno zoo.
native_language_example: The kids have fun at a zoo.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "andare" (to go) to talk about going on vacation: "andare in vacanza". It can also describe your current status: "Sono in vacanza" = "I’m on vacation." You can add the destination with "a" (city) or "in" (country/region): "in vacanza a Roma", "in vacanza in Italia".
target_language_example: Siamo in vacanza in Italia per due settimane.
native_language_example: We’re on vacation in Italy for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with "essere") to describe a species, language, or other thing that is disappearing and may die out soon. Common pattern: "una specie in via di estinzione" / "X è in via di estinzione".
target_language_example: Questo animale è in via di estinzione e va protetto.
native_language_example: This animal is endangered and must be protected.

indicarmi la strada per la stazione

target_language_multi_word_term: indicarmi la strada per la stazione
meaning: “to show/tell me the way to the station”.
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for directions. "indicarmi" is "indicare" (to indicate/show) + "mi" (to me). It’s often used with courtesy phrases like "per favore" and "(sia/sii/siate) gentile". You can swap the destination: "indicarmi la strada per il museo / per l’hotel".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, potrebbe indicarmi la strada per la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you show me the way to the station?

additional_notes: Used to ask for, give, or talk about someone’s email address. Often with verbs like avere (to have), perdere (to lose), cambiare (to change), and essere (to be): "Il mio indirizzo e-mail è..."
target_language_example: Mi può dare il suo indirizzo e-mail, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me your email address, please?

additional_notes: Used for putting on/wearing a necktie, often in contexts like work, formal events, or dress codes. With dovere/bisogno di it expresses obligation or necessity (e.g., "Devo/Ho bisogno di indossare una cravatta?").
target_language_example: Per la cerimonia devi indossare una cravatta.
native_language_example: For the ceremony you have to wear a tie.

additional_notes: Used when you try to estimate someone’s age without knowing it for sure. The pronoun "sua" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with "età," not with the person). Often used with verbs like "cercare di" (to try to) or as a question: "Riesci a... ?" (Can you...?).
target_language_example: Non riesco a indovinare la sua età: sembra molto più giovane.
native_language_example: I can’t guess his/her age: he/she looks much younger.

inglese mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri

target_language_multi_word_term: inglese mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri
meaning: (My) English (teacher) recommended that I read these books.
additional_notes:
In real usage you normally include who the person is: "Il mio/la mia insegnante di inglese mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri." 
- "mi ha raccomandato di + infinitive" = "recommended that I + verb" / "recommended to me to + verb".
- Use "insegnante" (common), "maestro/maestra" (more for primary school), "professore/professoressa" (middle/high school/university).
target_language_example: Il mio insegnante di inglese mi ha raccomandato di leggere questi libri prima dell’esame.
native_language_example: My English teacher recommended that I read these books before the exam.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (e.g., capire, preoccuparsi). Often appears in the progressive: stare + iniziando a + infinitive (sto/stai/sta; stavo/stava, etc.) to mean “I/you/he/she was starting to…”. You can also use it without stare (e.g., Iniziavo a capire = “I was starting to understand”).
target_language_example: Sto iniziando a capire come funziona.
native_language_example: I'm starting to understand how it works.

additional_notes: Past participle of "iniziare" used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno iniziato a" + infinitive. It means someone began an action; often used with time words like "già" (already) or questions about whether something has begun.
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a lavorare alle otto.
native_language_example: I started working at eight.

additional_notes: Used after the verb "iniziare" (to start/begin) in the past (e.g., "ho iniziato", "ha iniziato", "hanno iniziato"). "Ad" is used before an infinitive verb to mean "to" (e.g., "ad andare", "ad arrabbiarmi"). You also see "a" instead of "ad"; "ad" is commonly used before vowels for easier pronunciation ("ad avere", "ad andare"), while "a" is common before consonants ("a parlare").
target_language_example: Abbiamo iniziato ad ascoltare musica italiana.
native_language_example: We started listening to Italian music.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "iniziare" used in storytelling and in written Italian, especially for completed past events. It is followed by "a" + infinitive: "iniziò a piangere" = "started to cry". In everyday conversation, you’ll often hear "ha iniziato a" instead.
target_language_example: Quando sentì la notizia, iniziò a tremare.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he started to shake.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "iniziare" + "a" + infinitive. It’s used especially in narratives and written storytelling; in everyday speech you’ll more often hear "ha iniziato a urlare" (passato prossimo). "Urlare" can mean to shout (often angrily) or to scream (from fear/pain). You can add details like "contro [someone]" (at someone) or "dal dolore" (from pain).
target_language_example: Quando vide il cane, iniziò a urlare.
native_language_example: When she saw the dog, she started to scream.

meaning: in love with (said by/for a woman).
additional_notes: Used with "di" + a person (or sometimes something) to say someone is in love. "Innamorata" is feminine; masculine is "innamorato di". Often used with "essere": "Sono/era innamorata di..."
target_language_example: Sono innamorata di lui da anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with him for years.

meaning: "in love with him" (said by/about a woman).
additional_notes: Uses the feminine form "innamorata". A man would say "innamorato di lui". Often used with "essere": "Sono/era/è innamorata di lui". "Di" is used before a person/pronoun (di lui = of him).
target_language_example: Lei è innamorata di lui da anni.
native_language_example: She has been in love with him for years.

additional_notes: Used with a person (or sometimes something) you love: *innamorato di te/lei/lui/voi*, *innamorato di Maria*. It agrees with the subject: **innamorato** (male), **innamorata** (female); plural **innamorati/innamorate**. Common with **essere** (“to be”): *Sono innamorato/a di te.*
target_language_example: Lei è innamorata di lui da anni.
native_language_example: She’s been in love with him for years.

additional_notes: Used by a male speaker: “innamorato” agrees with the speaker (female: “innamorata di lei”). “di lei” means “with her” / “of her” in this expression, referring to a woman; you can also say “innamorato di lui” (“in love with him”).
target_language_example: Sono innamorato di lei da mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with her for months.

additional_notes: From the verb "insegnare" (to teach) + "il francese" (French). It agrees with the subject: "insegno il francese" (I teach French), "insegni il francese" (you teach French), "insegnano il francese" (they teach French). You can add who the student is with "a" (e.g., "insegna il francese a Tom") or an indirect object pronoun ("mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi"), and you can add frequency/time ("due volte la settimana").
target_language_example: Mia sorella insegna il francese online.
native_language_example: My sister teaches French online.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject someone teaches. It agrees with the teacher’s gender and number: insegnante (m./f. sing.), insegnanti (plural). Common patterns: "il mio insegnante di matematica", "la mia insegnante di inglese".
target_language_example: La mia insegnante di italiano è molto paziente.
native_language_example: My Italian teacher is very patient.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person who teaches the French language. "Insegnante" is gender-neutral in form; the article or context can indicate who you mean (e.g., "il mio insegnante" / "la mia insegnante"). You can swap "francese" for other subjects/languages: "insegnante di inglese" (English teacher).
target_language_example: La mia insegnante di francese parla molto lentamente.
native_language_example: My French teacher speaks very slowly.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone whose job is teaching English. Insegnante is gender-neutral in many contexts, but you may also see the feminine forms: una insegnante (common) or un'insegnante; sometimes professoressa (more typical for middle/high school). You can change the language: insegnante di italiano, insegnante di matematica, ecc.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è un'insegnante di inglese in una scuola superiore.
native_language_example: My sister is an English teacher at a high school.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher who teaches mathematics. "Insegnante" can be masculine or feminine depending on the person (e.g., *il nostro insegnante* / *la nostra insegnante*). Often used with a possessive (e.g., *il mio/il nostro insegnante di matematica*).
target_language_example: Domani abbiamo un compito in classe e il nostro insegnante di matematica ci farà ripassare le frazioni.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we have a test and our math teacher will have us review fractions.

meaning: to teach children / to teach kids.
additional_notes: Used to talk about teaching kids in general. "Insegnare" = "to teach"; "ai" is the contraction of "a + i" meaning "to the" (plural masculine); "bambini" means "children/kids" (often mixed or boys; for a group of girls you can also say "alle bambine"). You can add what you teach with "a" + infinitive: "insegnare ai bambini a..." (to teach children to...).
target_language_example: È importante insegnare ai bambini a condividere.
native_language_example: It’s important to teach children to share.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity/job of teaching the French language. "Insegnare" is the verb (to teach) and "francese" is the language being taught; it can follow verbs like "piacere" (to like), "odiare" (to hate), "iniziare" (to start), or expressions like "avere intenzione di" (to intend to).
target_language_example: Vorrei insegnare francese in una scuola superiore.
native_language_example: I’d like to teach French in a high school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity/job of teaching the French language. "Insegnare" (to teach) is followed by the language name with the definite article: "il francese" (French). You can add who you teach with "a" (e.g., "insegnare il francese agli studenti").
target_language_example: Mi piacerebbe insegnare il francese in una scuola.
native_language_example: I’d like to teach French in a school.

additional_notes: From the verb *insegnare* (to teach). Most commonly it’s used as **insegnare a + person + infinitive**: *Ho insegnato a mia moglie a guidare* (“I taught my wife to drive”). It can also be used in the passive with a place: *Il francese viene insegnato a scuola* / *Questo è insegnato a scuola* (“French is taught at school / This is taught at school”). Word order can vary: *Gli ha insegnato a suonare...* (“He/She taught him to play...”).
target_language_example: Mi hanno insegnato a cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: They taught me to cook pasta.

additional_notes: Past participle of *insegnare* used with *avere* to say who taught French: *Mi ha insegnato il francese* = “He/She taught me French.” With reflexive *si è insegnato*, it means “to teach oneself / be self-taught”: *Si è insegnato il francese* = “He taught himself French.” In questions you’ll often see *Chi ti/vi ha insegnato il francese?* (“Who taught you French?”).
target_language_example: Me lo ha insegnato il francese a scuola, ma poi mi sono insegnato molto da solo.
native_language_example: I was taught French at school, but then I taught myself a lot on my own.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *insegnare* (“to teach”) with *avere*: *ho/hai/ha insegnato...* The thing taught is the direct object (*il francese*), and the person taught is introduced by *a* (“to”): *insegnare [qualcosa] a [qualcuno]*.
target_language_example: Ho insegnato il francese a mia sorella per due mesi.
native_language_example: I taught French to my sister for two months.

meaning: to intend to; to plan to (have the intention to).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (intenzione di + infinitive) to express a plan, intention, or firm decision. Often appears with “avere” (avere intenzione di…). Negation is common: “non ho intenzione di…” = “I have no intention of…/I’m not going to…”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo intenzione di partire domani mattina.
native_language_example: We intend to leave tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere" (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno intenzione di...) to say you plan or mean to go somewhere or to do something. It’s followed by "andare" + destination (a/in/da) or an activity (e.g., "andare a pescare"). Often implies a plan or firm intention.
target_language_example: Ho intenzione di andare al mare domani.
native_language_example: I intend/plan to go to the beach tomorrow.

meaning: to intend to do; to plan to do.
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere: "avere intenzione di + infinitive" = "to intend/plan to + verb". It describes someone’s intention (often a plan for the near future). It can appear in different tenses (ho/abbiamo, aveva, hanno) and after question words (cosa/che cosa) or in indirect questions.
target_language_example: Ho intenzione di fare una passeggiata dopo pranzo.
native_language_example: I intend to take a walk after lunch.

meaning: "the intention to do it" / "planning to do it."
additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere intenzione di..." (= to intend to / to plan to). "Farlo" means "to do it" and refers back to an action already mentioned or understood from context. Often appears after verbs like "dire", "pensare", "credere" in statements or questions.
target_language_example: Non ho intenzione di farlo oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t intend to do it today.

additional_notes: Used with forms of avere (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno intenzione di...) to express a plan or intention. Often followed by a place or a time period: “rimanere qui”, “rimanere per tre giorni”.
target_language_example: Non ho intenzione di rimanere a lungo.
native_language_example: I don’t intend to stay long.

meaning: “(foreign languages) interest (someone)” / “to be interested in foreign languages.”
additional_notes: With the verb interessare, the thing that interests you is the grammatical subject. So “le lingue straniere” (plural) + “interessano”. The person interested is expressed with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: Ti interessano…? (Are you interested…?), Le interessano…? (formal “you”), Vi interessano…? (you all). You can also say: A te/A lei/A voi interessano le lingue straniere?
target_language_example: Mi interessano molto le lingue straniere.
native_language_example: I’m very interested in foreign languages.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *invitare* to say that one or more women/girls were invited to dinner. *Invitate* agrees with the people being invited (feminine plural). In the examples, pronouns like *le* (“them,” fem. pl.) and *vi/ci* (“you/us”) often appear before the verb.
target_language_example: Le abbiamo invitate a cena per sabato.
native_language_example: We invited them to dinner for Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live or who you live with. Often followed by a place ("Io abito a Roma") or by "con" + people ("Io abito con mia madre"). In everyday speech, Italian often drops the subject pronoun: "Abito con la mia famiglia."
target_language_example: Io abito a Milano, vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I live in Milan, near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live. "Abito" is the 1st-person singular of "abitare" (to live/reside). With most cities you use "a" (e.g., "abito a Roma"); with countries/regions you usually use "in" ("abito in Italia").
target_language_example: Io abito a Milano, ma lavoro a Torino.
native_language_example: I live in Milan, but I work in Turin.

meaning: “I love” (I really like / I’m fond of).
additional_notes: “Io” (I) is often optional in Italian because the verb already shows who is speaking; you can also just say “Amo…”. Used for strong liking (food, places, hobbies, things) and for romantic love (“Amo lei/ti amo”). With people, “ti amo” is usually romantic; for friends/family you may also hear “ti voglio bene” (I care about you).
target_language_example: Io amo questo posto, ci torno ogni estate.
native_language_example: I love this place; I come back every summer.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: io amo i + noun (e.g., i dolci, i viaggi). The article i is the masculine plural form of "the". For feminine plural, use "io amo le" (e.g., le mele). In everyday Italian you can also drop "io" and just say "Amo i...".
target_language_example: Io amo i film italiani.
native_language_example: I love Italian movies.

meaning: “I love the …” (talking about a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you love/like something. “Io” (I) is often optional in Italian (e.g., “Amo il caffè”). “Il” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) used before many consonant sounds (il caffè, il Vietnam). With other masculine nouns it can change to “lo” (lo sport) or “l’” (l’amore).
target_language_example: Io amo il caffè.
native_language_example: I love coffee.

meaning: “I love the …” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you love something. "La" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it goes with feminine singular nouns (e.g., la California, la Russia, la letteratura). With masculine singular nouns, you’d say "Io amo il / lo ...".
target_language_example: Io amo la musica italiana.
native_language_example: I love Italian music.

meaning: "I love the" (before a feminine plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you love something in general. "Le" is the feminine plural form of "the" and is used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., le farfalle, le sfide, le tagliatelle). Swap in the thing you love after "le".
target_language_example: Io amo le montagne.
native_language_example: I love the mountains.

meaning: "I went to" / "I went to (do something)" (simple past).
additional_notes: "Andai" is the passato remoto (remote past) of *andare* for "io". It’s common in books, stories, and historical narration, and in some regions in everyday speech. In most spoken Italian, you’ll often hear *sono andato/a a...* instead. Use *a* before a place (*andai a Boston*) or before an infinitive to mean "went to do" (*andai a fare escursionismo*, *andai a trovarla*).
target_language_example: Io andai a casa presto quella sera.
native_language_example: I went home early that evening.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude or to say you value a person, action, comment, help, or quality. Often followed by a noun (io apprezzo il gesto, il sostegno) or by “quello che…” + past action (io apprezzo tutto quello che ha fatto). You can also drop “io” in most contexts: “Apprezzo davvero la tua visita.”
target_language_example: Apprezzo molto il tuo aiuto, grazie.
native_language_example: I really appreciate your help, thank you.

meaning: “I had” / “I used to have” (imperfect past of avere).
additional_notes: Used to describe an ongoing situation in the past ("I had/there was") or a habitual state ("I used to have"). Common with nouns (Io avevo tre cani), with "bisogno di" (Io avevo bisogno di aiuto = I needed help), and in comparisons like "io avevo torto" (I was wrong). Often the subject pronoun "io" is omitted in Italian: "Avevo tre cani".
target_language_example: Quando ero piccolo, io avevo paura del buio.
native_language_example: When I was little, I was afraid of the dark.

meaning: “I should have / I was supposed to (but didn’t).”
additional_notes: Used to talk about an obligation or the right thing to do in the past, often with regret or criticism because it didn’t happen. Structure: io + avrei dovuto + infinitive (dire, mentire, pagare, sapere, scrivere, tenere...). Often implies “but I didn’t” (e.g., Io avrei dovuto pagare… ma non l’ho fatto).
target_language_example: Io avrei dovuto chiamarti ieri, ma mi sono dimenticato.
native_language_example: I should have called you yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: "I know" / "I’m familiar with" (a person, place, thing, sound).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *conoscere* to talk about being familiar with someone or something (people, places/areas, routes, sounds, etc.). It’s different from *io so*, which is for knowing facts/information (e.g., *Io so la risposta* = “I know the answer”).
target_language_example: Io conosco bene questa città.
native_language_example: I know this city well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or belief. After "credo che", Italian typically uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo): e.g., "conosca", "stia", "sia". In everyday speech some people may use the indicative, but the standard form is the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Io credo che sia una buona idea.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you have an obligation, necessity, or something you really need to do. In Italian, the subject pronoun is often dropped, so you’ll very commonly hear just “devo …” (same meaning). It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., devo andare = I have to go).
target_language_example: Io devo andare adesso.
native_language_example: I have to go now.

meaning: I have to go / I must go.
additional_notes: Used to say you need to leave or go somewhere (often because of an obligation or urgency). It’s commonly followed by a destination or purpose (e.g., “a lavorare” = to work, “in stazione” = to the station). In everyday speech, Italians often drop “io” and just say “Devo andare…”.
target_language_example: Scusa, io devo andare: è tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go: it’s late.

meaning: "I have to go to" / "I need to go to" (a place) or "I have to go" + infinitive (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave for a destination (io devo andare a Boston; io devo andare a un funerale) or that you must go do an action (io devo andare a chiederlo; io devo andare a mangiare). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun: "Devo andare a...".
target_language_example: Scusa, io devo andare a prendere il treno.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go catch the train.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement. It is normally followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): e.g., "dubito che sia", "dubito che abbia", "dubito che ci siano". In everyday speech you may also hear indicative, but subjunctive is standard, especially in writing.
target_language_example: Io dubito che lui venga domani.
native_language_example: I doubt that he’ll come tomorrow.

meaning: “I and …” (used to join yourself with someone else as the subject).
additional_notes: Used before another person’s name/noun: “Io e Tom…”. In more formal Italian, it’s often preferred to put the other person first (“Tom e io…”), but “io e …” is common in everyday speech. The verb is plural because there are two subjects.
target_language_example: Io e mia sorella andiamo al cinema stasera.
native_language_example: My sister and I are going to the movies tonight.

meaning: “I was” (first person singular, imperfect past of essere).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past state, feeling, or ongoing situation/background in the past (not a single completed event). Often the subject pronoun “io” is omitted because the verb form already shows the person (e.g., “Ero alla festa.”). Agree adjectives with the speaker: ero preoccupato (male) / preoccupata (female).
target_language_example: Io ero stanco, quindi sono tornato a casa presto.
native_language_example: I was tired, so I went home early.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of essere (ero = “I was”) to describe a past state/feeling or an ongoing background situation. It’s usually followed by an adjective, which agrees with the speaker: ero molto curioso/curiosa, fiero/fiera, scioccato/scioccata, ubriaco/ubriaca.
target_language_example: Io ero molto stanco ieri sera.
native_language_example: I was very tired last night.

additional_notes: Used to say you were 'too' + adjective in the past. Often followed by an infinitive with per: "Ero troppo stanco per uscire" = "I was too tired to go out." The adjective usually agrees with the speaker (e.g., troppo impegnato/occupato/spaventato/ubriaco = masculine; troppo impegnata/occupata/spaventata = feminine). Note: in everyday Italian you can also drop the subject pronoun: "Ero troppo...".
target_language_example: Io ero troppo stanco per uscire.
native_language_example: I was too tired to go out.

meaning: "I have" / "I did" (used with the passato prossimo: "I have" + past participle).
additional_notes: "Io" (I) + "ho" (I have) is the 1st-person singular of "avere". With a past participle it forms the passato prossimo to talk about completed actions: "Io ho ascoltato" = "I listened / I have listened." In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often omitted: "Ho ascoltato".
target_language_example: Io ho mangiato troppo ieri sera.
native_language_example: I ate too much last night.

meaning: “I have just …” (something happened a moment ago).
additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo to say something happened very recently: “ho appena + past participle” (e.g., ho appena visto, ho appena sentito). In everyday Italian you often drop the subject pronoun, so you’ll usually hear “Ho appena …” rather than “Io ho appena …”.
target_language_example: Ho appena finito il lavoro.
native_language_example: I’ve just finished work.

additional_notes: Used to express a necessity/need and is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "sapere", "uscire", "vedere") or by a noun ("ho bisogno di aiuto"). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun and just say "Ho bisogno di...".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con il dottore.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the doctor.

meaning: "I bought" / "I have bought" (past tense of "to buy").
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: "ho" (present of avere) + past participle "comprato". "Io" is often optional in Italian because the verb already shows the subject; you can usually just say "Ho comprato...". Common add-ons: "per te" (for you), "a Tom" (for Tom; can mean for him), "a un prezzo basso" (at a low price), "al negozio" (at the shop).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per mia sorella ieri.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my sister yesterday.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of dire (“to say/tell”). It’s followed by the person you spoke to, introduced by a: Io ho detto a Maria… (“I told Maria…”). You can then add what you said with che (“that…”) or another clause.
target_language_example: Io ho detto a Laura che arrivavo tardi.
native_language_example: I told Laura that I was arriving late.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "dormire" (to sleep), using the auxiliary "avere": (io) ho dormito. Often used to say you slept (once) in the recent past or to report a completed action. Context can change the meaning: "Ho dormito con X" can mean you slept in the same bed/place with someone, but it can also imply you had sex with them.
target_language_example: Ieri sera io ho dormito otto ore.
native_language_example: Last night I slept eight hours.

meaning: I had to / I have had to (I was forced/required to).
additional_notes: "Ho dovuto" is the passato prossimo of "dovere" (to have to, must). It’s used for a necessary action in the past, often something you didn’t really want to do. It’s followed by an infinitive: "ho dovuto + verb" (e.g., "ho dovuto aspettare"). You can drop the subject pronoun in Italian: "Ho dovuto aiutare Tom" is more common than "Io ho dovuto...".
target_language_example: Ho dovuto annullare la prenotazione.
native_language_example: I had to cancel the reservation.

additional_notes: “Io” (I) + “ho fatto” is the passato prossimo of fare (to do/make). It’s used for actions completed in the past, often with an object: ho fatto dei piani (I made plans), ho fatto una chiamata (I made a call), ho fatto un sogno (I had a dream), ho fatto molti soldi (I made a lot of money). In everyday Italian, the subject “io” is often omitted unless you want emphasis or contrast: Ho fatto dei piani.
target_language_example: Io ho fatto tutto quello che potevo.
native_language_example: I did everything I could.

meaning: "I met" / "I ran into" (past: passato prossimo of incontrare).
additional_notes: Used to say you met someone or came across someone/something in the past. Literally "I have met" (io + ho + incontrato), but it’s usually translated as simple past in English. You can add where/when: "ieri", "in Europa", etc.
target_language_example: Io ho incontrato un turista alla stazione.
native_language_example: I met a tourist at the station.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "leggere": "ho letto" means you finished reading something in the past (often translated as either "I read" or "I have read," depending on context). The subject pronoun "io" is often omitted in Italian: "Ho letto il tuo libro."
target_language_example: Ho letto la tua email stamattina.
native_language_example: I read your email this morning.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo (past tense) of "mangiare" (to eat): "ho" (I have) + "mangiato" (eaten). In Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often optional, so you’ll also commonly hear just "ho mangiato". Used for a completed action in the past (often with a time like "ieri", "stamattina").
target_language_example: Oggi non ho fame perché io ho mangiato già.
native_language_example: Today I’m not hungry because I already ate.

additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of perdere (“to lose”). Often used with a noun to say you lost something or no longer have a feeling/quality: ho perso interesse (I lost interest), ho perso la speranza (I lost hope). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun io is often omitted: ho perso...
target_language_example: Ho perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: I lost my keys.

meaning: “I took / I got / I had” (past: I got/bought/ordered, depending on context).
additional_notes: First-person singular of the passato prossimo of prendere (“to take”). Used for things you took physically (I took two bottles), things you got/bought (I got a new hat), things you ordered/had (I had a coffee / I got a bowl of spaghetti), and also fixed expressions like prendere una decisione (“to make a decision”). Often in real speech you can drop the subject “io” because the verb already shows who is speaking: “Ho preso…”.
target_language_example: Oggi ho preso un panino e una bottiglia d’acqua.
native_language_example: Today I got a sandwich and a bottle of water.

meaning: "I tried to / I have tried to".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (provare a + verb) to say you made an attempt to do something, often without saying whether you succeeded. In everyday English it’s usually translated as “I tried to…”.
target_language_example: Io ho provato a chiamarti ieri, ma non rispondevi.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you weren’t answering.

meaning: I wrote a letter / I have written a letter.
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (ho scritto) to talk about a completed action in the past. Often followed by a + person to say who you wrote to: “Ho scritto una lettera a mia madre.” In everyday Italian you can often drop the subject pronoun “io” because the verb already shows who is doing the action: “Ho scritto una lettera…”.
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera a un amico ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to a friend last night.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: "io" (I) + "ho" (I have) + "sentito" (heard). It can mean you heard a sound ("Ho sentito il telefono suonare") or that you heard some information/rumor ("Ho sentito che..."). Often the subject "io" is omitted in Italian: "Ho sentito..."
target_language_example: Ho sentito che domani piove.
native_language_example: I've heard that it's going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: “I found” / “I have found”; also “I found (that)…” (I thought/considered).
additional_notes: Past tense of trovare with the subject “io” (“I”). It can mean finding something physically (“I found your diary”), discovering something (“I found Tatoeba on Google”), or giving an opinion with an adjective (“I found the book interesting” = “I thought the book was interesting”). You can also use it with che + clause: “Ho trovato che…” = “I found that… / I felt that…”. In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject: “Ho trovato…”.
target_language_example: Io ho trovato questo ristorante per caso e l’ho trovato ottimo.
native_language_example: I found this restaurant by chance and I thought it was great.

meaning: "I saw" / "I have seen" (past of vedere, "to see").
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: io + ho (auxiliary avere) + visto (past participle of vedere). Often translates as simple past in English (“I saw”). With another verb (e.g., piangere, attraversare) it can mean “I saw someone/something do ...”.
target_language_example: Io ho visto Marco uscire di casa.
native_language_example: I saw Marco leave the house.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess something or have something (including receiving something like a message). In Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often optional because "ho" already means "I have"; adding "io" can give emphasis or contrast (e.g., "Io ho un cane, ma tu hai un gatto").
target_language_example: Io ho due sorelle.
native_language_example: I have two sisters.

additional_notes: Used to state a need or necessity. Often followed by **di + noun/pronoun**: *Ho bisogno di una giacca* (“I need a jacket”), *Ho bisogno di te/lei* (“I need you/her”). With a verb, use **ho bisogno di + infinitive**: *Ho bisogno di parlare* (“I need to talk”). With a full clause, you’ll often see **ho bisogno che + (subjunctive)**: *Ho bisogno che mi venga restituito…* (“I need it to be returned to me…”).
target_language_example: Io ho bisogno di aiuto adesso.
native_language_example: I need help right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. Follow it with a noun (io ho bisogno di tempo) or with an infinitive verb to say what you need to do (io ho bisogno di sapere). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun: "Ho bisogno di...".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di aiuto.
native_language_example: I need help.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. "Ho bisogno di" = "I need"; "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (before a masculine noun). If the noun is feminine, use "una" (e.g., "Ho bisogno di una penna"). Often you can omit "io" because the verb already shows who it is: "Ho bisogno di un interprete."
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un biglietto, per favore.
native_language_example: I need a ticket, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. "Ho bisogno di" means "I need"; add "una" before a singular feminine noun (una busta, una distrazione, una nuova automobile). With a masculine noun, use "un": "Ho bisogno di un biglietto". In everyday Italian you can drop the subject "io": "Ho bisogno di una...".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di una penna, per favore.
native_language_example: I need a pen, please.

meaning: “I have some …” (talking about having certain things, in a general/unspecified amount).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say you have some of something: **io ho dei + noun**. **dei** is the partitive article for masculine plural nouns (e.g., *dei dolori, dei parenti*). Variants: **degli** before vowels or certain consonant clusters (e.g., *io ho degli amici*), and **delle** for feminine plural (e.g., *io ho delle idee*). Often in everyday speech you can also omit it: *Ho dolori terribili*.
target_language_example: Io ho dei problemi con la macchina.
native_language_example: I have some problems with the car.

meaning: "I have some..." / "I have a few..." (before a plural noun).
additional_notes: "Io ho" = "I have." "Delle" is the partitive article used with plural feminine nouns to mean "some" (an unspecified quantity). It’s often used to introduce something you have (things, news, letters, information, difficulties). In negatives, you often see "non ho delle..." changed to "non ho..." or "non ho nessuna..." depending on meaning.
target_language_example: Io ho delle domande per te.
native_language_example: I have some questions for you.

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to say you possess or have two of something. In Italian, "ho" = "I have" (from *avere*), and "due" means the number 2. Note: Italian "due" can look like English "due" (payable), but it means "two."
target_language_example: Io ho due biglietti per il concerto.
native_language_example: I have two tickets for the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a plan or intention to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "ho intenzione di partire"). You can drop the subject pronoun in Italian: "Ho intenzione di..." is more natural than "Io ho intenzione di..." in most contexts.
target_language_example: Ho intenzione di chiamarti domani.
native_language_example: I plan to call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a large number of something. "Molti" agrees with a masculine plural noun (e.g., molti gatti, molti dischi). With feminine plural nouns, use "molte" (e.g., molte amiche). In Italian you often drop the subject pronoun, so "Ho molti..." is very common.
target_language_example: Ho molti amici in Italia.
native_language_example: I have many friends in Italy.

meaning: "I have some / I have a few."
additional_notes: Used to say you have a small number or an unspecified amount of something. With "qualche", Italian typically uses a singular noun ("qualche amico", "qualche idea", "qualche libro") even though the meaning is plural. "Io" is often optional in Italian, so you may also hear just "Ho qualche...".
target_language_example: Io ho qualche minuto per parlare.
native_language_example: I have a few minutes to talk.

meaning: “I have three …” (to say you have three of something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to state quantity: io (I) + ho (I have) + tre (three). The verb is avere: io ho (I have). Add the plural noun after tre (e.g., tre biglietti). Often you can drop “io” because it’s understood: “Ho tre bagagli.”
target_language_example: Ho tre prenotazioni per stasera.
native_language_example: I have three reservations for tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you possess something or that you ‘have’ a condition/situation. "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (like “a/an”) used before most masculine nouns (e.g., un negozio). With masculine nouns starting with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y, use "uno" (e.g., uno studente). For feminine nouns, use "una" or "un'" before a vowel (e.g., un'idea). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun and just say "Ho un...".
target_language_example: Ho un problema con la prenotazione.
native_language_example: I have a problem with the reservation.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a friend and then add more information about them. After che (“who/that”), Italian uses a normal verb clause: Io ho un amico che abita a Londra (“…who lives in London”). In everyday conversation, people often drop the subject pronoun io and just say Ho un amico che….
target_language_example: Ho un amico che parla tre lingue.
native_language_example: I have a friend who speaks three languages.

meaning: "I have a lot of" / "I have lots of".
additional_notes: Common, fairly informal way to say you have many things/people or a large amount of something. It’s usually followed by a plural noun (un sacco di amici) or by something like "cose da + infinitive" (un sacco di cose da fare). In everyday speech Italian often drops the subject pronoun: "Ho un sacco di lavoro".
target_language_example: Ho un sacco di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: "I have a" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you possess or have something. "Una" is the feminine singular form of "a/an" (e.g., una moglie, una sorpresa, una bici). In everyday speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun "io" and just say "Ho una...". For masculine nouns, use "io ho un" (or "ho un...").
target_language_example: Io ho una domanda.
native_language_example: I have a question.

meaning: “I feel like / I want to (do something).”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re in the mood to do something (often right now or in general). It’s followed by an infinitive verb: ho voglia di + mangiare/uscire/studiare. The negative is common too: non ho voglia di… (“I don’t feel like…”). You can also say it without “io” in normal conversation: ho voglia di…
target_language_example: Oggi ho voglia di stare a casa.
native_language_example: Today I feel like staying at home.

meaning: “I + her/it” (feminine direct object pronoun before the verb).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker (“io”) is the subject and the object is “la” = “her” or “it” (referring to a feminine noun, e.g. la macchina, la lettera). In Italian, object pronouns like la usually come before the conjugated verb: “Io la compro” = “I buy it.” It can also appear before a modal/verb phrase: “Io la riesco a fare” = “I can do it.” In “Io la penso così”, “la” is part of the fixed expression “la penso” = “I think (about it) / I see it (that way).”
target_language_example: Io la vedo domani.
native_language_example: I’ll see her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Subject + verb: "io" (I) + "lavoro" (I work). In Italian the subject pronoun is often dropped, so you’ll also hear just "lavoro". It can describe your job in general (Io lavoro in uno zoo) or what you’re doing these days (Io lavoro ancora in Australia). Common patterns: "lavoro a tempo pieno" (full-time), "lavoro per + [person/company]" (I work for), "lavoro sodo" (I work hard), "lavoro velocemente" (I work quickly), "persino (la) domenica" (even on Sunday).
target_language_example: Io lavoro in centro, vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I work downtown, near the station.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (sometimes "that"), used with verbs like: Io lo amo (I love him/it), Io lo so (I know it), Io lo ricordo (I remember him/it). In Italian the subject pronoun "io" is often omitted (e.g., "Lo amo"), so "io lo" sounds more emphatic/contrasting ("I do, at least"). "Lo" normally comes before the verb: "Io lo avviserò" (I’ll warn him).
target_language_example: Io lo capisco, ma non sono d’accordo.
native_language_example: I understand it, but I don’t agree.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already knew or suspected. "Lo" is an anticipatory pronoun meaning "it" (referring to the whole following idea), so in English you often just say "I knew (that)…" or, more emphatically, "I knew it!". Word order can vary in real speech (e.g., "Lo sapevo che…", "Sapevo che…").
target_language_example: Io lo sapevo che avrebbe detto di no.
native_language_example: I knew he/she would say no.

additional_notes: Used to say you know something. "Lo" means "it" (referring to a fact, situation, or what was just said). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun "io" is often dropped ("Lo so"), but keeping it can add emphasis ("I do know"). You can add words like "già" (already) or "bene" (well) for nuance: "Io lo so già" = "I already know".
target_language_example: Tranquillo, io lo so già.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I already know.

additional_notes: "Io" = "I" and "mangio" is the 1st-person singular present of "mangiare" (to eat). In Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted ("Mangio..."), but "io" is used for emphasis or contrast (e.g., "Io mangio carne, ma lei no"). The present tense can mean a habit ("I eat every day") or something happening now ("I'm eating").
target_language_example: Scusa, adesso io mangio e non posso parlare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm eating right now and I can't talk.

meaning: "I ... (of it / from there)" with the pronouns "me" + "ne" before a verb (often: "I’m leaving").
additional_notes:
"Io" means “I,” and "me ne" is a common pronoun combo used before the verb. "Me" refers back to the speaker (“to/for myself”), and "ne" usually means “of it/about it” or “from there,” depending on the verb. Very common with:
- andare: "Io me ne vado / me ne sono andato(a) / me ne volevo andare" = “I’m leaving / I left / I wanted to leave.”
- scusarsi: "Io me ne scuso" = “I apologize for it.”
Also appears in the idiom "me ne lavo le mani" = “I wash my hands of it” (I don’t want to be involved / take responsibility). In real speech, "io" is often dropped: "Me ne vado."
target_language_example: Scusa, ma io me ne vado adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I’m leaving now.

meaning: I'm leaving / I'm going away (from here).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "andarsene" (to go away, to leave). "me ne" are pronouns that go with this verb and often don’t translate word-for-word in English. Commonly used to say you’re leaving a place right now ("Io me ne vado!" can sound firm: "I’m leaving!"), or that you’re leaving at a certain time (e.g., "domani", "dopodomani"). Often you can drop "io" because Italian already implies the subject: "Me ne vado".
target_language_example: Scusa, è tardi: io me ne vado.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s late: I’m leaving.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is explicitly stated (io = I) and the verb is reflexive, so you also need the reflexive pronoun mi (myself/me). In Italian, io is often omitted because the verb ending already shows who is doing the action (e.g., Mi lavo i capelli. = I wash my hair.). With some verbs it means doing something to yourself (mi lavo), and with others it’s more like “I find myself / I consider myself” (mi considero) or “I ran into” (mi sono imbattuta).
target_language_example: Io mi preparo un caffè prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I make myself a coffee before going out.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. Often shortened to just “Mi chiamo …” (the “io” = “I” is optional because the verb ending already shows who is speaking). “Chiamarsi” is a reflexive verb meaning “to be called.”
target_language_example: Ciao, io mi chiamo Sara.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Sara.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question (who/what/when/how, etc.) to express curiosity or uncertainty. It’s followed by words like che cosa, come, quando, and often uses the subjunctive in more formal or careful Italian (e.g., quando sia successo).
target_language_example: Io mi chiedo se Tom venga stasera.
native_language_example: I wonder if Tom is coming tonight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question when you’re unsure or curious about something. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "se sia", "se siano"), especially in more formal/standard Italian, though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Io mi chiedo se abbia già chiamato.
native_language_example: I wonder if he/she has already called.

meaning: "I was wrong about…" / "I was mistaken about…"
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of the reflexive verb "sbagliarsi" ("mi sbagliavo") to say you had an incorrect opinion/assumption in the past. It’s followed by "su" + a person/thing: "su Tom" or, with a pronoun, usually "su di lui/lei" (also common in speech: "su lui/lei"). You can also say "su me stesso/a" = "about myself."
target_language_example: Mi sbagliavo su di te.
native_language_example: I was wrong about you.

additional_notes: From the verb **sentirsi** (“to feel” in terms of emotions/conditions). **Mi** is reflexive (“myself”), and **sentivo** is the **imperfetto** (imperfect past), used for an ongoing feeling or background situation in the past (“I was feeling…”, “I used to feel…”). It’s commonly followed by an adjective: *a mio agio* (comfortable), *solo/sola* (alone), *isolato/a* (isolated), *indesiderato/a* (unwanted).
target_language_example: Quando sono arrivato in città, io mi sentivo perso.
native_language_example: When I arrived in the city, I felt lost.

meaning: "I feel" (talking about your physical or emotional state).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "sentirsi". It’s commonly followed by an adjective ("io mi sento triste" = I feel sad) or by an expression like "a mio agio" (comfortable) or "in cima al mondo" (on top of the world). In everyday speech Italians often drop "io" because it’s understood: "Mi sento stanco".
target_language_example: Oggi mi sento meglio.
native_language_example: Today I feel better.

additional_notes: Used to describe how you feel (emotionally or physically). Follow it with an adjective, which changes for gender/number (e.g., rilassatO/ rilassatA, traditO/traditA, vecchiO/vecchiA). In everyday speech you often drop the subject pronoun: "Mi sento molto..."
target_language_example: Mi sento molto stanco oggi.
native_language_example: I feel very tired today.

meaning: "I have" / "I did" with reflexive verbs in the past (passato prossimo).
additional_notes: Used before a past participle to form the passato prossimo of reflexive (or pronominal) verbs: io + mi + sono + participio (e.g., mi sono adattato/a = I adapted). With reflexive verbs, Italian uses essere, and the past participle agrees with the subject: adattato (male) / adattata (female). In informal speech, Italians often drop the subject pronoun: "Mi sono adattato rapidamente".
target_language_example: Io mi sono svegliato presto stamattina.
native_language_example: I woke up early this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of the reflexive verb sentirsi (“to feel”). Use it to describe how you felt emotionally or physically. Feminine form: sentita (speaker is female); masculine form: io mi sono sentito. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: mi sono sentita sola/persa/isolata.
target_language_example: Dopo il trasloco, io mi sono sentita un po' spaesata.
native_language_example: After the move, I felt a bit out of place.

meaning: "I have (some/of it/of them)" — "ne" refers to something already mentioned.
additional_notes: Used when you have a certain amount of something or some items previously mentioned. "Ne" can mean “some” (quantity) or “of it/of them” (replacing a noun). It’s followed by "ho" + past participle in the examples (passato prossimo): "io ne ho visto uno" = “I saw one of them.” Agreement: the past participle usually agrees in gender/number with what "ne" refers to when it’s a direct object: "ne ho portata dentro una" (feminine), "ne ho portato dentro uno" (masculine). Often you can drop "io" in Italian: "Ne ho ordinato uno."
target_language_example: Ne ho comprati due, ma me ne serve ancora uno.
native_language_example: I bought two of them, but I still need one more.

additional_notes: Italian negation uses **non** before the verb: *non guardo*, *non ho*, *non sto lavorando*. **Io** ("I") is often optional because the verb ending already shows the subject; adding **io** can sound more emphatic or contrastive (e.g., "I don't, but someone else does").
target_language_example: Io non capisco questa parola.
native_language_example: I don't understand this word.

additional_notes: "Io" (I) + "non" (not) + "ho" (I have). Used to negate having something ("I don't have any regrets") or to form the negative present perfect with a past participle ("I have not done" / "I haven't said"). In everyday Italian, "io" is often omitted: "Non ho...".
target_language_example: Non ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: I don't have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something up to now. It’s the negative past of experience: "non" + "ho" (I have) + "mai" (ever/never) + past participle (fatto, detto, ferito, mentito, perso, ecc.). In everyday speech you often drop "io": "Non ho mai...".
target_language_example: Non ho mai visitato Roma.
native_language_example: I’ve never visited Rome.

io non ho mai detto che

target_language_multi_word_term: io non ho mai detto che
additional_notes: Used to deny having said something (often to correct a misunderstanding or defend yourself). It’s followed by a clause with che + verb: "Io non ho mai detto che + [statement]". You can drop the subject "io" in normal speech: "Non ho mai detto che…".
target_language_example: Non ho mai detto che non volevo venire; ho solo detto che ero stanco.
native_language_example: I never said I didn’t want to come; I just said I was tired.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never seen something (up to now). It’s formed with the present perfect (passato prossimo): "ho visto" (I have seen) + the negative "non" and "mai" (never). In Italian, "non" goes before the verb and "mai" usually comes after it: "non ho mai visto...".
target_language_example: Io non ho mai visto un posto così bello.
native_language_example: I've never seen a place this beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to say you do not possess something or you lack something. In Italian, the negation "non" goes directly before the verb: "non ho" (I don’t have). The subject pronoun "io" is often omitted because the verb ending already shows who it is: "Non ho tempo" is more common than "Io non ho tempo".
target_language_example: Non ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: I don't have time today.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say you have none of something (a strong negation). With "non", "alcun" works like "any" but translates as "no" in English: "Non ho alcun tempo" = "I have no time." It agrees with the noun: "alcun" (masc. sing.), "alcuna" (fem. sing.), "alcuni/alcune" (plural). In everyday speech, "io" is often omitted: "Non ho alcun..."
target_language_example: Non ho alcun dubbio: hai ragione.
native_language_example: I have no doubt: you're right.

meaning: "I don’t have any" / "I have no" (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny having something. "Alcuna" is the feminine form of "alcun/alcuna" (= any/none) and is used with a negative verb ("non ho"). It must agree with a feminine singular noun: "alcuna amica", "alcuna informazione", "alcuna scusa". For masculine nouns, use "io non ho alcun ..." (e.g., "io non ho alcun problema").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma io non ho alcuna disponibilità oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t have any availability today.

meaning: “I have nothing to … / I don’t have anything to …”
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (chiedere, dire, scrivere, fare, etc.) to say you have nothing to do/say/ask/write. In everyday Italian, you’ll also hear the less formal double-negative form “Non ho niente da …” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Io non ho niente da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do today.

additional_notes: Common negative structure (Italian uses double negation: non + nulla). Often followed by an infinitive phrase: "nulla da fare" (nothing to do), "nulla di + adjective" (nothing + particular/special), or expressions like "nulla a che fare con..." (nothing to do with...) and "nulla per cui..." (nothing to live for / nothing to ... for).
target_language_example: Io non ho nulla da perdere.
native_language_example: I have nothing to lose.

meaning: "I have never..." / "I never have..." (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Common pattern for saying you’ve never done something, especially with reflexive verbs or verbs that use essere in the passato prossimo: io + non + mi + sono + mai + past participle. The past participle often agrees with the subject (especially with reflexive verbs): aspettat**o** (male speaker), aspettat**a** (female speaker). You can replace "mi" with other reflexive pronouns: ti/se/ci/vi (e.g., "Tu non ti sei mai...", "Lei non si è mai...").
target_language_example: Io non mi sono mai svegliato così presto.
native_language_example: I have never woken up this early.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something or not allowed to do it. It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., *io non posso approvare / toccare*). In the special structure **non posso che + infinitive**, it means “I can only…” (there’s no other option), as in *Io non posso che crederle* = “I can only believe you.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, io non posso venire oggi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t come today.

meaning: "I can't" / "I can’t manage to" (I’m unable to).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (io non riesco a + verb) to say you can’t manage to do something—because it’s too hard, you lack strength/ability, or the situation makes it impossible. Often implies effort or trying, similar to “I can’t manage to…” or “I can’t bring myself to…” in emotional contexts.
target_language_example: Io non riesco a capire questa regola di grammatica.
native_language_example: I can’t understand this grammar rule.

additional_notes: Used to deny or state the opposite of something about yourself. Follow it with an adjective (Io non sono romantica), a noun (Io non sono un uomo), or other complements. Often dropped in speech (Non sono...), since the verb ending already shows the subject.
target_language_example: Io non sono pronto adesso.
native_language_example: I’m not ready now.

meaning: “I am/was never …” / “I have never been …” (for states).
additional_notes: Used with essere (“to be”) + mai (“never”) to say you are/were never in a certain state or situation. Tense changes with context: present (sono) = “I’m never …”; passato prossimo (sono stato/a) = “I have never been …”. With the past participle after essere (piaciuto/a, riuscito/a, scivolato/a, stato/a), it agrees with the subject (io): -o (male), -a (female). In negative sentences, non comes before the verb and mai usually goes after it.
target_language_example: Io non sono mai stato a Venezia.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Venice.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of essere with "mai" to say something has never happened/been true up to now (often meaning “never in my life”). "Stata" agrees with a female speaker; a male speaker says "io non sono mai stato". It’s commonly followed by an adjective or phrase: "… bella", "… brava in…", "… innamorata di…".
target_language_example: Io non sono mai stata a Roma.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome.

meaning: “I have never been …” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve never been to a place or never had an experience up to now. Because the verb is **essere** in the passato prossimo, the past participle agrees with the speaker: **stato** (man), **stata** (woman). Often followed by a place: **a** + city (a Roma), **in** + country/region or some places (in Italia, nel deserto).
target_language_example: Io non sono mai stata in Giappone, ma vorrei andarci.
native_language_example: I have never been to Japan, but I’d like to go there.

io non sono mai stata in

target_language_multi_word_term: io non sono mai stata in
meaning: "I have never been to/in …" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve never visited a place. It uses the auxiliary essere in the passato prossimo: sono stata (female speaker). A man would say: io non sono mai stato in…. Often you can drop io: Non sono mai stata in…. With countries/regions/cities you typically use in + place name (in America, in Cina, in Europa).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata in Italia, ma vorrei andarci.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Italy, but I’d like to go there.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never been to a place (or never been in a situation) up to now. Often followed by a place introduced by in/nel/nella/nei/negli (e.g., in quella città, nel deserto) or a situation with dentro (e.g., dentro una prigione). Literally it’s “I am never been,” but Italian uses essere + stato to form the past of “to be.”
target_language_example: Io non sono mai stato a Roma, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome, but I’d like to go there.

additional_notes: Used to deny being something. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (un + noun): “Io non sono un mercenario / un panda.” For feminine nouns use “Io non sono una …” (e.g., “Io non sono una dottoressa.”). Often “Io” is optional in Italian: “Non sono un …”.
target_language_example: Non sono un turista, sono uno studente.
native_language_example: I’m not a tourist, I’m a student.

additional_notes: Used to express strong dislike. Often followed by a noun ("Io odio il traffico") or by an infinitive ("Io odio aspettare"). In conversation, Italian often drops the subject pronoun: "Odio questa parte della città."
target_language_example: Io odio aspettare in fila.
native_language_example: I hate waiting in line.

meaning: "I hate the ..." (used before masculine plural nouns that take "gli").
additional_notes: "Io" = "I" and "odio" = "(I) hate." "Gli" is the masculine plural form of "il/lo" used before nouns starting with a vowel (gli ospedali) or with s+consonant / z / gn / ps / x / y (gli scacchi, gli zoo). Often "io" is optional in Italian: "Odio gli scacchi" also means "I hate chess."
target_language_example: Io odio gli insetti.
native_language_example: I hate insects.

meaning: "I hate the" (talking about masculine plural things/people).
additional_notes: Used to say you strongly dislike a category of things or people. "i" is the masculine plural definite article (= "the") and is followed by a masculine plural noun: "i weekend", "i pomodori", "i poliziotti". (For feminine plural you’d use "le": "Io odio le bugie".)
target_language_example: Io odio i compiti.
native_language_example: I hate homework.

meaning: "I hate the" (talking about a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express very strong dislike: io = I, odio = I hate, il = the (masculine singular). Often sounds harsh in everyday conversation; a softer alternative is "non mi piace" (I don’t like). Change the article depending on the noun: "io odio la..." (feminine), "io odio i/gli..." (masculine plural), "io odio le..." (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Io odio il traffico del lunedì mattina.
native_language_example: I hate Monday morning traffic.

meaning: “I hate the …” (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express strong dislike. "La" is the feminine singular definite article, so it must match a feminine noun (e.g., la politica, la marmellata). With other nouns you’ll change the article: "io odio il…" (masc.), "io odio lo…", or "io odio l’…" (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Io odio la pioggia quando devo uscire.
native_language_example: I hate the rain when I have to go out.

additional_notes: Used to say you hate a specific category of things expressed with a feminine plural noun. Structure: "Io odio le" + plural noun (e.g., le zanzare). If the noun is masculine plural, you usually use "io odio i" (e.g., io odio i rumori). "Io" is often optional in Italian: "Odio le zanzare."
target_language_example: Io odio le code lunghe.
native_language_example: I hate long lines.

additional_notes: From the verb *parlare* (to speak). In Italian you can usually drop the subject pronoun and just say *parlo*; adding *io* emphasizes "I" (e.g., in contrast with someone else). Often followed by a language (*Io parlo italiano*) or by *in* + language when talking about the language you use in a situation (*Io parlo in francese con Tom*).
target_language_example: Io parlo un po' di italiano, ma capisco bene lo spagnolo.
native_language_example: I speak a little Italian, but I understand Spanish well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed in the past (often an opinion or expectation that may turn out to be wrong). After "che" it commonly takes the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., fosse/fossero) in more formal/standard Italian; in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative.
target_language_example: Io pensavo che fosse già arrivata.
native_language_example: I thought she had already arrived.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past belief/assumption, often something you later found out was different. In Italian this pattern commonly uses the imperfect (pensavo) + che + subjunctive (fosse). You can continue with an adjective (fosse giusto/eccellente) or with a place/role/situation (fosse qui, fosse di mia responsabilità).
target_language_example: Io pensavo che fosse più facile, ma mi sbagliavo.
native_language_example: I thought it was easier, but I was wrong.

additional_notes:
Often followed by:
- **a + person/thing** = “to think about” (Io penso a te = I think about you).
- **che + verb** = “I think that …” to give an opinion (Io penso che sia vero = I think it’s true).
- **di + infinitive** = “I think (that) / I plan” with an action (Io penso di andare = I’m thinking of going).
In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun **io** is often omitted: **Penso che…**
target_language_example: Io penso che domani pioverà.
native_language_example: I think it will rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used before a clause to express what you believe or think. After "penso che" Italian commonly uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo), e.g. "debba", "sia". In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, but the standard form is with the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Io penso che oggi piova.
native_language_example: I think it will rain today.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion and make a suggestion about what the group (we = noi) ought to do. After "penso che" Italian commonly uses the conditional ("dovremmo" = "we should/we ought to"), followed by an infinitive (e.g., aiutare, lavorare, ridurre). You can also drop "io" in conversation: "Penso che dovremmo..."
target_language_example: Penso che dovremmo partire presto.
native_language_example: I think we should leave early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you think about something feminine singular (la = “the”). After "penso che" Italian often uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially for opinions/uncertainty: "penso che la grammatica sia…". You can swap "la" for other articles depending on the noun: "io penso che il…", "io penso che le…", etc.
target_language_example: Io penso che la pizza sia migliore a Napoli.
native_language_example: I think that pizza is better in Naples.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or make a guess about something. After "penso che" Italian normally uses the subjunctive mood (congiuntivo), so you often see forms like "sia" (from "essere" = to be). In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative ("io penso che questo è"), but "sia" is the standard/grammar-correct form.
target_language_example: Io penso che questo sia il posto giusto.
native_language_example: I think this is the right place.

meaning: “I think (that) I…” + verb (I believe / I plan to).
additional_notes: Used with **di + infinitive** to express your opinion/belief about what you can/will do, or your intention: *Penso di capire* (“I think I understand”), *Penso di andare* (“I’m thinking of going / I plan to go”). In everyday Italian the subject is often dropped: **Penso di…**. Not the same as English “think of” (Italian usually uses **pensare a** for “think of/about”).
target_language_example: Penso di arrivare in ritardo.
native_language_example: I think I’m going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability, permission, or possibility to do something. In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun “io” is often omitted because the verb form already shows who it is: “Posso farlo oggi.”
target_language_example: Io posso venire domani, se vuoi.
native_language_example: I can come tomorrow, if you want.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional tense of potere (potrei) to talk about a possibility or something you would be able to do. It’s also common for being polite/less direct than "posso" (e.g., asking permission or making a request). Often followed by an infinitive: "Io potrei + verbo".
target_language_example: Io potrei venire più tardi, se vuoi.
native_language_example: I could come later, if you want.

additional_notes: Used to say what you like better than something else. Often followed by an infinitive (Io preferisco camminare = I prefer walking) or a noun (Io preferisco i film divertenti = I prefer funny movies). For comparisons, use "preferire X a Y" (Io preferisco le automobili inglesi a quelle straniere = I prefer English cars to foreign ones). The subject pronoun "io" is optional and is mainly used for emphasis or contrast.
target_language_example: Io preferisco prendere un caffè invece del tè.
native_language_example: I prefer to have a coffee instead of tea.

meaning: "I prefer the…" (used to choose one thing over another).
additional_notes: "Preferisco" means "I prefer." Add the article + noun (e.g., il caffè). Often used with comparisons: "preferisco X a Y" (I prefer X to Y) or "fra/tra X e Y, preferisco…" (between X and Y, I prefer…). "Il" changes with the noun (il/lo/la/l’/i/gli/le): e.g., "io preferisco la pasta", "io preferisco l’acqua". You can also drop "io" because the verb already shows the subject: "Preferisco il caffè."
target_language_example: Tra tè e caffè, preferisco il caffè.
native_language_example: Between tea and coffee, I prefer coffee.

meaning: “I can / I manage to …” (I succeed in doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: “io riesco a + infinito” (e.g., riesco a capire = I can understand). It often implies it’s difficult but possible, like “I manage to” rather than a simple ability (which is often expressed with “posso”). In speech, Italians often drop “io” and just say “riesco a …”.
target_language_example: Oggi non riesco a venire al lavoro.
native_language_example: Today I can’t manage to come to work.

additional_notes: "Io" is often optional in Italian because the verb ending already shows the subject; you’ll frequently just hear "So...". Use "io so" for emphasis or contrast (“I know, not you”). Patterns: "Io so + (che / chi / quale...)" = “I know that / who / which…”. "Io so + infinitive" means “I know how to / I can” (e.g., "so suonare" = “I can play”). "So di…" / "so di te/voi" = “I know about… / I know of you.” "So già" = “I already know.”
target_language_example: Io so dove abiti.
native_language_example: I know where you live.

additional_notes: Used to talk about who you are (identity/role), where you’re from (often with di: “Io sono di…”), and states/qualities with adjectives or past participles (“Io sono stanco/a”, “Io sono ferito/a”). In everyday speech, Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so “Sono…” is very common; “Io sono…” adds emphasis (“I am…”).
target_language_example: Io sono pronto/a.
native_language_example: I am ready.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare" using the auxiliary "essere". "Andata" agrees with the speaker: a woman says "(io) sono andata"; a man says "(io) sono andato". Often followed by a place ("sono andata a Roma"), or by "a" + infinitive to say what you went to do ("sono andata a nuotare", "a vedere"). You can also use "in" for institutions/places like schools ("sono andata in una scuola...").
target_language_example: Ieri io sono andata al supermercato.
native_language_example: Yesterday I went to the supermarket.

meaning: "I went to" / "I have gone to" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare" using "essere": "sono andata". The past participle agrees with the speaker: a woman says "sono andata", a man says "sono andato". Often followed by a place or event ("a Roma", "a un concerto") or by an infinitive to express purpose ("sono andata a trovarlo" = "I went to visit him").
target_language_example: Io sono andata a Roma l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I went to Rome last year.

meaning: "I went to / I went in(to)" (female speaker).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "andare" using "essere": "sono andata" agrees with a female speaker (male: "sono andato"). "In" is commonly used with countries/regions (in America, in Australia, in Iran) and with some activities/places like "in campeggio" (camping).
target_language_example: Io sono andata in Spagna l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I went to Spain last year.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "andare" with the auxiliary "essere". The past participle agrees with the subject: a man says "(io) sono andato"; a woman says "(io) sono andata". Often "io" is omitted because the verb already shows the person: "Sono andato al parco."
target_language_example: Sono andato a casa dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I went home after work.

additional_notes: Used to say where you went in the past.
