Non comes before the verb to make it negative: “Lei non + verb” = “You don’t / You aren’t / You won’t …”. With a lowercase l (lei), it usually means “she,” but in many sentences the meaning is clear from context.
target_language_example: Lei non parla italiano?
native_language_example: Don’t you speak Italian? (formal)

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman has never done something up to now. "Lei" is the formal/polite "you" (female or generic in formal address), so the phrase can also mean "you have never" in formal situations. Often followed by a past participle: "Lei non ha mai + participio" (e.g., "visto", "detto", "avuto").
target_language_example: Lei non ha mai visto questo film.
native_language_example: She has never seen this movie.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”) in the present tense: lei (she, formal “you”) + non (not) + ha (has). Often followed by a noun: “Lei non ha molti soldi” = “She doesn’t have much money.” In conversation, Lei (capital L) can also mean formal “you,” but in this example it means “she.”
target_language_example: Lei non ha tempo oggi.
native_language_example: She doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: "Lei" is the feminine singular subject pronoun meaning "she". It can also mean the polite/formal "you" (capitalized "Lei"), so "Lei non è..." may mean either "She isn’t..." or "You (formal) aren’t..." depending on context. Used to state that someone is not something or doesn’t have a quality: "Lei non è alta" = "She isn’t tall."
target_language_example: Lei non è pronta per l’esame.
native_language_example: She isn’t ready for the exam.

additional_notes: "Lei" with a capital L is the formal "you" (used with strangers, customers, older people). In questions like "Lei pensa che...?", it means "Do you think that...?" and is followed by "che" + the subjunctive (e.g., sia, stia, aspetterebbe). With "lei" lowercase, it can also mean "she": "Lei pensa che..." = "She thinks that...".
target_language_example: Lei pensa che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you think it's a good idea?

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the person who is liked is the grammatical subject (lei), and the person who likes is introduced with a + indirect object (a lui, a Mary, a tutti). In English we flip it: "Mary likes her" = "Lei piace a Mary". You can replace lei with a name or pronoun: "Maria piace a tutti".
target_language_example: Lei piace molto a Marco.
native_language_example: Marco likes her a lot.

additional_notes: Uses the formal subject pronoun Lei (“you”, polite) + riuscire a + infinitive to ask if someone manages/is able to do something. Often translates as “can you…?” but emphasizes ability/success (managing to do it), sometimes with difficulty. In the present tense: Lei riesce a + verb (infinitive).
target_language_example: Lei riesce a venire domani alle 9?
native_language_example: Can you make it tomorrow at 9?

meaning: formal “you know” / “do you know…?” (talking to someone politely).
additional_notes: “Lei” (capital L in writing) is the polite/formal way to say “you” in Italian. So “Lei sa” literally looks like “she knows,” but it usually means “you know” when addressing someone formally (e.g., a stranger, an older person, or in customer service). In questions you often keep the same order and use intonation: “Lei sa…?” = “Do you know…?”. You can also add “per caso” to sound softer: “Lei sa per caso…?” = “Do you happen to know…?”.
target_language_example: Scusi, Lei sa dov’è la stazione?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know where the station is?

meaning: "she … herself" or "you (formal) … yourself" (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: "Lei" can mean "she" (normal 3rd-person singular feminine) or "you" in the polite/formal form (often written with a capital L: "Lei"). "Si" is the reflexive pronoun used with many verbs to mean doing something to/for oneself (e.g., "guardarsi" = to look around, "meritarsi" = to deserve, "rifiutarsi" = to refuse, "suicidarsi" = to commit suicide, "registrarsi" = to register, "sposarsi" = to get married, "divertirsi" = to have fun). With formal "Lei", past participles and adjectives usually agree with the real person’s gender: "Lei si è registrato" (male) / "Lei si è registrata" (female).
target_language_example: Lei si è già svegliata?
native_language_example: Have you (formal) already woken up?

meaning: "she" + "(to) herself" + "has/is" (used to form the past tense with reflexive verbs).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb in the passato prossimo (e.g., lei si è svegliata, lei si è lavata). Reflexive verbs use essere as the auxiliary, and the past participle usually agrees with the subject: feminine singular -> -a (si è addormentata, si è coperta). In some cases it can express something she "got" done or "had" done (lei si è fatta fare una foto = she had a photo taken of herself).
target_language_example: Lei si è svegliata presto stamattina.
native_language_example: She woke up early this morning.

additional_notes: “Lei” is the subject pronoun for “she,” but it’s also used as the polite/formal “you” when speaking to one person (often capitalized: “Lei”). “È” is the verb “to be” (third-person singular: he/she/it is). In the past tense with movement verbs like “andare” (to go), you’ll also see “Lei è + past participle” (e.g., “Lei è andata” = “She went/has gone”).
target_language_example: Lei è pronta per la riunione?
native_language_example: Are you (formal) ready for the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion in a formal/polite way (Lei = “you”). It’s often followed by a + noun/idea: “Lei è favorevole o contrario a questo?” In correct agreement, contrary changes with the person: “Lei è favorevole o contrario” (to a man) / “Lei è favorevole o contraria” (to a woman). You can also say: “È favorevole o contrario al piano?”
target_language_example: Lei è favorevole o contrario a questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of or against this proposal?

additional_notes: Used to ask (politely/formally) whether someone has ever done something. It’s typically followed by a past participle in the passato prossimo: “Lei è mai andato/a…?” Note the agreement: andato (male) / andata (female), caduto/caduta, scivolato/scivolata, stato/stata, ecc. “Lei” is the formal “you” (written with a capital L), not “she.” “Mai” means “ever” in questions, and “never” with “non” (e.g., “Non sono mai stato…” = “I’ve never been…”).
target_language_example: Lei è mai stato in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

meaning: 'Have you ever been to…?' (formal, to a woman).
additional_notes: Used to ask if a woman has ever been in/visited a country or place. "Lei" is the formal "you" (used with strangers, customers, older people) and "stata" agrees with a female person; for a man you’d say "Lei è mai stato in…?". Common answers: "Sì, ci sono stata" (Yes, I have) / "No, non ci sono mai stata" (No, I’ve never been).
target_language_example: Lei è mai stata in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

additional_notes: Used to ask (politely/formally) if someone has ever visited a place. It uses the formal “Lei” = “you” and the adverb “mai” = “ever.” With “essere” in the passato prossimo, the past participle agrees with the person: to a man you say “Lei è mai stato…?”, to a woman “Lei è mai stata…?”. Often followed by “in” + country/region (e.g., in Italia, in Africa).
target_language_example: Lei è mai stato in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Italy?

meaning: “Is she for it or against it?” (asking someone’s position).
additional_notes: Uses the loanwords pro/contro to ask if someone supports or opposes an idea, plan, war, etc. Lei is the formal “you,” but it can also literally mean “she,” depending on context. You can also say: Sei pro o contro…? (informal “you”) or È pro o contro…? (he/she/it).
target_language_example: Lei è pro o contro questa proposta?
native_language_example: Are you for or against this proposal?

additional_notes: Uses the auxiliary essere in the passato prossimo with lei (“she”): è stata is feminine singular (masculine would be è stato). Very common with passive sentences (Lei è stata accettata = “She was accepted”) and with expressions like “è stata di grande aiuto” (“she was a great help”).
target_language_example: Lei è stata molto gentile con me ieri.
native_language_example: She was very kind to me yesterday.

meaning: 'she is a' (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: "Lei" is the formal/polite "you" in Italian, but in these examples it means "she." Use "Lei è una" to identify a woman’s role or category (profession, relationship, characteristic) before a feminine singular noun: "Lei è una professoressa." With a masculine noun, use "Lei è un" (or "uno" before s+consonant, z, gn, etc.): "Lei è un medico."
target_language_example: Lei è una studentessa italiana.
native_language_example: She is an Italian student.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to speak or repeat more slowly (common in conversations, customer service, and language-learning situations). Often appears as “(più) lentamente, per favore” after a verb like parlare (to speak) or ripetere (to repeat). You can use informal tu forms (Puoi/Potresti…) or formal Lei forms (Può/Potrebbe…).
target_language_example: Può parlare più lentamente, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down—especially when they’re speaking too fast. You can say it by itself (“Lentamente, per piacere.”) or after a verb: “Parla/Parlate lentamente, per piacere.” (tu = parla; voi/Lei polite = parli; voi plural = parlate).
target_language_example: Può parlare lentamente, per piacere?
native_language_example: Could you speak slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno letto il libro" = "I/you/he… read (have read) the book". "Letto" is the past participle of "leggere" (to read).
target_language_example: Non ho ancora letto il libro che mi hai consigliato.
native_language_example: I still haven’t read the book you recommended to me.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle letto (“read”) with the helper verb avere (e.g., ho letto questo libro = “I read/I have read this book”). Often appears with time words like appena (“just”) or in questions like Chi ha letto questo libro? (“Who has read this book?”). You may also see it after verbs like ricordare: Ricordo di avere letto questo libro (“I remember having read this book”).
target_language_example: Hai mai letto questo libro?
native_language_example: Have you ever read this book?

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *leggere* (“to read”). You’ll often see it in the *passato prossimo*: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno letto un libro* (“I/you/he… read (or have read) a book”).
target_language_example: Ho letto un libro molto interessante ieri.
native_language_example: I read a very interesting book yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "andare" (or "andarsene") to talk about going to bed early: "andare a letto presto". "Letto" = bed, "presto" = early. Very common in advice/commands: "Vai/Andate a letto presto".
target_language_example: Domani mi alzo presto, quindi vado a letto presto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m getting up early, so I’m going to bed early.

additional_notes: "Li" is the direct object pronoun (them, masculine plural or mixed group) and it usually comes before the auxiliary verb: "li abbiamo". It’s very common in the passato prossimo: "Li abbiamo cercati" = "We looked for them." When "li" refers to a masculine plural group, the past participle often agrees: "catturati", "cercati", "guardati".
target_language_example: Li abbiamo già chiamati, ma non rispondono.
native_language_example: We already called them, but they’re not answering.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the passato prossimo (e.g., "Li avete chiamati?" = "Have you called them?"). "Li" is a direct object pronoun placed before the verb. With avere, the past participle often agrees in gender/number with "li" when the pronoun comes before it (li = masculine plural; le = feminine plural). Can also appear as a standalone "you have them" when the rest is understood from context.
target_language_example: Li avete già trovati?
native_language_example: Have you already found them?

meaning: "Have you seen them?" / "Did you see them?"
additional_notes: Uses the direct object pronoun "li" (= them, masculine plural or mixed group) before the verb. "Avete" is "you (plural) have" (voi), and "visti" is the past participle of "vedere"; it agrees in gender/number with "li" (so with "le" you’d say "le avete viste"). In questions it’s often used when asking if someone spotted people somewhere or at a certain time.
target_language_example: Li avete visti uscire dal cinema?
native_language_example: Did you see them leave the movie theater?

meaning: "has them" / "(he/she) did ... them" (them + has), used before a past participle.
additional_notes: "Li" is the direct object pronoun meaning "them" (usually masculine plural, but often used for mixed groups too). In the passato prossimo, Italian puts this pronoun before the auxiliary: "li ha + past participle" = "(he/she) has/did + verb + them" (e.g., "Li ha visti" = "He/She saw them"). It can refer to people or things, depending on context.
target_language_example: Li ha già chiamati.
native_language_example: He/She already called them.

meaning: "he/she has seen them" / "have you (formal) seen them?"
additional_notes: "Li" is the direct object pronoun meaning "them" (masculine plural, or mixed-gender group). "Ha" is the present of *avere* (3rd person singular), used with the past participle "visti" to form the past tense (*passato prossimo*). With a direct object pronoun before the verb, the past participle often agrees in gender/number: *visti* (masc. pl.), *viste* (fem. pl.). In questions like "Li ha visti?", "ha" can also be the formal "you" (Lei).
target_language_example: Li ha visti stamattina davanti alla stazione?
native_language_example: Did you (formal) see them this morning in front of the station?

meaning: "you have them" / "did you … them?" (masculine plural direct object).
additional_notes: `li` is the direct object pronoun meaning “them” (usually masculine plural, or mixed group). It comes *before* the verb: `Li hai visti?` = “Did you see them?” It’s very common with the passato prossimo (`hai` + past participle). With `li`, the past participle often agrees in masculine plural: `li hai letti`, `li hai comprati`, `li hai minacciati`.
target_language_example: Li hai visti ieri?
native_language_example: Did you see them yesterday?

meaning: “have you seen them?” (masculine plural direct object).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has seen a group of people/things referred to by "li". It’s the passato prossimo of "vedere" with "avere": "hai visto" (you saw / you have seen). You can add time words like "recentemente" or places like "in giro". If the group is feminine, use "le hai viste".
target_language_example: Li hai visti stamattina al bar?
native_language_example: Did you see them this morning at the café?

meaning: 'I have them' / 'I … them' (with a past action).
additional_notes: "Li" is the direct-object pronoun meaning "them" (masculine plural, or mixed group). It usually comes before the verb. With "ho" it’s commonly the start of the passato prossimo: li ho visto/i = "I saw them." In this tense, the past participle often agrees with "li": li ho seguiti, li ho uccisi, li ho sposati.
target_language_example: Li ho visti ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw them last night.

meaning: "I met them" / "I got to know them".
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of conoscere with the direct object pronoun li (“them”). Conosciuti agrees with li (masculine plural, or a mixed group). In Italian, conoscere in the past often means “to meet (for the first time),” even though the literal English translation would be “I have known them.” Common with time/place phrases: Li ho conosciuti a una festa (at a party), di recente (recently), stasera (tonight).
target_language_example: Li ho conosciuti in ufficio l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I met them at the office last year.

meaning: "I saw them" / "I've seen them" (referring to them, masculine plural).
additional_notes: "Li" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "them" (masculine plural; for a mixed group, Italian usually uses the masculine plural). "Ho visti" is the passato prossimo of vedere (to see). With a direct-object pronoun (li/le), the past participle often agrees: visti (masc. pl.), viste (fem. pl.). Used both for "I saw them" (finished time like yesterday) and "I’ve seen them" (experience/recent past), depending on context.
target_language_example: Li ho visti stamattina in centro.
native_language_example: I saw them this morning downtown.

meaning: "you have them" / "you (all) did ... to them" (with a past participle).
additional_notes: "Li" is the direct object pronoun meaning "them" (usually masculine plural, or mixed group). "Avete" is "you have" (2nd person plural; also used as polite "you" in some contexts). Together they often appear with the passato prossimo: "li avete visti" = "you saw them". The pronoun "li" normally comes before the auxiliary verb (avete).
target_language_example: Li avete già chiamati?
native_language_example: Have you called them already?

meaning: 'has them' (li = them + ha = has), used to form the past tense with a past participle.
additional_notes: In Italian, object pronouns like li (“them,” masculine plural) usually come before the verb. With the passato prossimo, you often get: li ha + past participle (e.g., li ha chiamati = “he/she called them”). In questions it’s the same order: Chi li ha chiamati? (“Who called them?”). The past participle may agree with li (li ha chiamati/uccisi/convinti), especially in careful/written Italian.
target_language_example: Non so dove li ha messi.
native_language_example: I don’t know where he/she put them.

meaning: “you have” + “them” (direct-object pronoun), as in “you have done/said/brought them.”
additional_notes: Used when the object is plural masculine (or mixed gender) “them” and it comes before the verb. It’s made of: **li** = “them” + **hai** = “you have” (tu, present of *avere*), typically used with the *passato prossimo* (e.g., *li hai portati* = “you brought them”). The past participle often agrees with **li**: *portati, lasciati, licenziati* etc.
target_language_example: Dove li hai messi?
native_language_example: Where did you put them?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase for books whose genre is adventure. Often used after verbs like leggere (to read) or comprare (to buy). You may also hear the singular: un libro di avventura (an adventure book).
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i libri di avventura, soprattutto quelli ambientati in mare.
native_language_example: I like adventure books, especially ones set at sea.

additional_notes: Used for school/university books used in a course. Usually plural (libri di testo); singular: libro di testo. Often appears with verbs like comprare/vendere (buy/sell), costare (cost), and with places like la libreria (bookstore).
target_language_example: Devo comprare i libri di testo per il corso di matematica.
native_language_example: I have to buy the textbooks for the math course.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for a book, often after the noun or object you want. In full requests you’ll usually hear/see it with an article or possessive (e.g., "il libro, per favore", "questo libro, per favore", "il tuo libro, per favore"). It commonly follows an imperative or request form: "Passami...", "Mi dia...", "Mi presti...".
target_language_example: Il libro, per favore.
native_language_example: The book, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (è) to say where a book is or describe it. Very often you’ll see it with possessives (Il tuo libro è… = Your book is…) and location words: qui (here), lì/là (there), and prepositions like su (on) + article (sul/sulla) for surfaces.
target_language_example: Il libro è sul tavolo.
native_language_example: The book is on the table.

additional_notes: Used to talk about any language that isn’t your own/native language. Common in school contexts with verbs like studiare (to study): “studiare una lingua straniera.” The plural is “lingue straniere.”
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera per lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Plural phrase used to talk about languages that are not your native language. Very common in questions with conoscere (to know) and studiare (to study). Often appears with the preposition a: interessato/a alle lingue straniere (interested in foreign languages).
target_language_example: A scuola ho studiato due lingue straniere.
native_language_example: At school I studied two foreign languages.

additional_notes: Used before a time word like anno (year), mese (month), agosto, autunno (autumn), settimana (week), semestre (semester) to mean the one immediately before now. It agrees in gender/number with the time noun: lo scorso anno/autunno/semestre; la scorsa settimana; il mese scorso; le scorse vacanze; gli scorsi anni. Note: with months you often hear both forms, e.g., lo scorso agosto or agosto scorso.
target_language_example: Ho iniziato questo lavoro lo scorso mese.
native_language_example: I started this job last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately before this one. Often interchangeable with "il fine settimana scorso"; in everyday speech you may also hear "lo scorso weekend".
target_language_example: Che cosa hai fatto lo scorso fine settimana?
native_language_example: What did you do last weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the previous winter season (the winter before the current one). It’s a time expression and usually goes after the verb, but it can also be moved for emphasis (e.g., "Lo scorso inverno, ...").
target_language_example: Lo scorso inverno abbiamo preso lezioni di sci.
native_language_example: Last winter we took ski lessons.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the month immediately before the current one. It often comes after the verb (e.g., “Eri… lo scorso mese?”), but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ho iniziato questo corso lo scorso mese.
native_language_example: I started this course last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately before the current one. It’s a time expression that can go at the end of the sentence (common) or near the beginning. "Scorso" agrees with "weekend" in the masculine singular: lo scorso weekend.
target_language_example: Che cosa hai fatto lo scorso weekend?
native_language_example: What did you do last weekend?

additional_notes: Usually refers to someone’s gaze or where they are looking. Often used with verbs like alzare/abbassare/volgere lo sguardo (“raise/lower/turn your gaze”).
target_language_example: Ha abbassato lo sguardo e non ha detto niente.
native_language_example: He lowered his gaze and didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "lo" because "spagnolo" starts with s + consonant (sp-). Used after verbs like parlare (to speak), studiare (to study), imparare (to learn), insegnare (to teach): e.g., "parlo lo spagnolo". Can also mean "the Spanish man" in other contexts, but in these examples it clearly refers to the language.
target_language_example: Parlo lo spagnolo abbastanza bene.
native_language_example: I speak Spanish fairly well.

lo spagnolo, ma anche il francese

target_language_multi_word_term: lo spagnolo, ma anche il francese
meaning: 'Spanish, but also French' (i.e., 'not only Spanish, but also French').
additional_notes: Used in the pattern "non solo/soltanto/solamente X, ma anche Y" to add extra information: someone/something is not limited to X; Y is true too. Often used to list languages, skills, activities, etc. The subject can be repeated or left implied: "(Lui) non parla solo...".
target_language_example: Non capisco solo lo spagnolo, ma anche il francese.
native_language_example: I don’t understand only Spanish, but also French.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event you watch (a theater performance, concert, show, etc.). It often comes up with verbs like piacere (“to like”) and amare (“to love”).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto lo spettacolo di ieri sera?
native_language_example: Did you like last night’s show?

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "lo" because "sport" starts with s + consonant. Often refers to sport as an activity or category in general, not a single match; you can also say "fare sport" = "to play/do sports".
target_language_example: Faccio sport tre volte a settimana.
native_language_example: I do sports three times a week.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "pitturare" (to paint): "pitturare (qualcosa) di + colore" = "to paint (something) + color". So "lo steccato di verde" means the fence in green / painted green. "Steccato" is a fence (often wooden).
target_language_example: Hanno pitturato lo steccato di verde scuro.
native_language_example: They painted the fence dark green.

additional_notes: Used when someone makes an identical mistake again (often with verbs like commettere/fare “to make,” ripetere “to repeat,” rifare “to do again”). Note: *stesso* agrees with the noun (e.g., *lo stesso errore*; *la stessa cosa*).
target_language_example: Per favore, non fare lo stesso errore un'altra volta.
native_language_example: Please, don’t make the same mistake again.

lo stesso giorno in cui noi

target_language_multi_word_term: lo stesso giorno in cui noi
additional_notes: Used to say two events happened on the same day. It introduces a time clause with a relative expression: "il giorno in cui..." = "the day when/that...". "Stesso" agrees with the noun: "lo stesso giorno" (m. sing.), "la stessa sera" (f. sing.), "gli stessi giorni" (m. pl.), "le stesse ore" (f. pl.). "Noi" can be omitted because the verb ending already shows "we" (e.g., "lo stesso giorno in cui siamo arrivati").
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti lo stesso giorno in cui noi siamo arrivati in città.
native_language_example: We met on the same day that we arrived in the city.

meaning: "the same"; in this context: "the same (thing)" / "the same way" = "do the same".
additional_notes: Often used after verbs like fare (“to do/make”) to mean “do the same (thing)” or “do it too”: fare lo stesso. It refers back to an action already mentioned. It can also mean “the same one” (e.g., lo stesso giorno = the same day), depending on context.
target_language_example: Non so cosa fare, ma probabilmente farò lo stesso.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to do, but I’ll probably do the same.

additional_notes: Common with expressions about hunger/digestion or pain: avere lo stomaco pieno (to have a full stomach), avere lo stomaco vuoto (to have an empty stomach), lo stomaco mi fa male (my stomach hurts). It can refer to the organ or, in everyday speech, the general belly area.
target_language_example: Mi fa male lo stomaco dopo aver mangiato.
native_language_example: My stomach hurts after eating.

additional_notes: A common noun (masculine singular) used for psychological/physical tension or pressure: gestire/affrontare/ridurre lo stress (“manage/cope with/reduce stress”). It takes the definite article “lo” because it starts with s + consonant (st-).
target_language_example: Cerco di ridurre lo stress facendo una passeggiata ogni sera.
native_language_example: I try to reduce stress by taking a walk every evening.

additional_notes: A food item. "Yogurt" is masculine in Italian, so it takes the article "lo" (and becomes "l'yogurt" before a vowel). Used in questions like "Ti/Vi/Le piace...?" to ask if someone likes frozen yogurt.
target_language_example: Vorrei lo yogurt gelato alla fragola, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like strawberry frozen yogurt, please.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article "lo" (not "il") because "zoo" starts with "z". Used to talk about a specific zoo (e.g., in your city or one you’re visiting).
target_language_example: Andiamo allo zoo domenica?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the zoo on Sunday?

additional_notes: A common food ingredient. Uses the masculine singular definite article "lo" because the noun starts with "z" (like "lo zaino"). Often used when ordering or talking about ingredients: "e adesso lo zucchero" = "and now the sugar"; "abbiamo finito lo zucchero" = "we’ve run out of sugar".
target_language_example: Per il caffè, preferisci lo zucchero o no?
native_language_example: For your coffee, do you prefer sugar or not?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for sugar at the table (e.g., in a café). Often said with verbs like passare (“to pass”): "Mi passi lo zucchero, per favore?" (“Could you pass me the sugar, please?”) or avere (“to have”): "Posso avere lo zucchero, per favore?" (“Can I have the sugar, please?”). "Per favore" = “please.”
target_language_example: Mi passi lo zucchero, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you pass me the sugar, please?

additional_notes: Used when "we" is the subject and "lo" ("it" or "him") is a direct object pronoun placed before the verb. Very common with the passato prossimo: "lo abbiamo" + past participle (e.g., lo abbiamo visto = we saw him/it). The past participle can sometimes agree with "lo" (especially in more careful/written Italian): lo abbiamo visto / lo abbiamo vista (if referring to a feminine noun previously mentioned).
target_language_example: Lo abbiamo visto ieri al supermercato.
native_language_example: We saw him yesterday at the supermarket.

meaning: 'you help him' / 'you help it' (often: 'that you help him/it').
additional_notes: “Lo” is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” or “it.” “Aiuti” is the form of aiutare used with tu (“you”) and also with Lei (“you” formal) in many contexts. After expressions like “ha bisogno che… / si aspetta che… / vuole che…”, Italian typically uses the subjunctive: “che lo aiuti” = “that you help him/it.”
target_language_example: Mi serve qualcuno che lo aiuti a trovare casa.
native_language_example: I need someone to help him find a place to live.

additional_notes: Made of the direct-object pronoun "lo" (it / him) + "avete" (you all have). Very common in the passato prossimo: "lo avete visto" = "you (all) saw it/him" / "you (all) have seen it/him". "Lo" goes before the auxiliary verb (avere) and refers to something already known from context.
target_language_example: Lo avete già pagato?
native_language_example: Have you (all) already paid for it?

meaning: “(he/she/you formal) has to do it / must do it.”
additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun **lo** (“it”) plus **dovere** (**deve** = “must/has to”) + **fare** (“do”). The subject is understood from context (e.g., *Tom lo deve fare* = “Tom has to do it”). Often refers back to something already mentioned (“it”). Can be made into a question by intonation or a question mark: *Lo deve fare?* = “Does he/she have to do it?”
target_language_example: Se è urgente, lo deve fare oggi.
native_language_example: If it’s urgent, he/she has to do it today.

meaning: “I should tell (it) to … / I ought to tell …”.
additional_notes: Used to say you think it would be the right thing to tell someone something. "Lo" = “it” (the thing you’re going to say), "dovrei" is the conditional of "dovere" (“should/ought to”), and "dire a" introduces the person you tell it to (a + name/pronoun: a Tom, a lei, a loro). Often implies uncertainty or asking for confirmation (e.g., "giusto?").
target_language_example: Forse lo dovrei dire a Maria.
native_language_example: Maybe I should tell Maria.

additional_notes: Used when the action is understood from context. "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or sometimes "him"), placed before the verb: "fa" (does). Often refers back to something previously mentioned (e.g., a task, an activity). You may also see it as one word in the infinitive form: "farlo" = "to do it".
target_language_example: Non so chi lo fa, ma lo fa molto bene.
native_language_example: I don't know who does it, but they do it very well.

additional_notes: "Lo" is the direct object pronoun meaning "it." "Faccia" is from the verb "fare" (to do/make): it can be (1) the present subjunctive after phrases like "voglio che..." ("I want that...") or "si assicuri che..." ("make sure that..."); and (2) the formal (Lei) command form used for polite requests (similar to "please do it").
target_language_example: Per favore, lo faccia subito.
native_language_example: Please do it right away.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or sometimes “him,” referring to a masculine person/thing already understood from context). It usually comes before the verb: "lo faccio" = “I do it.” Depending on context, it can also mean “I’ll do it.” In expressions like "Te lo faccio vedere!" it’s used for emphasis and can mean “I’ll show you!” (often said as a challenge or warning).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: lo faccio io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll do it.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning "it" (or "that"), placed before the verb. "Fanno" is "they do" (present tense of *fare*). The subject can be explicit (*lo fanno loro* = "they do it") or implied (*lo fanno tutti* = "everyone does it"), and it’s often used to talk about what people in general do.
target_language_example: Se lo fanno tutti, non significa che sia giusto.
native_language_example: If everyone does it, it doesn’t mean it’s right.

additional_notes: Used when the action has already been mentioned and you refer to it with the direct object pronoun "lo" (= "it"). "Lo" normally comes before the verb: "lo farà" (not *"farà lo"*). The subject can be explicit ("Tom lo farà") or implied ("Lo farà domani" = "He/She will do it tomorrow").
target_language_example: Non so se lo farà oggi.
native_language_example: I don't know if he/she will do it today.

additional_notes: Future tense of fare (to do/make) with the direct object pronoun lo (“it”). Used to promise/decide to do something already mentioned or understood. Negation: non lo farò (“I won’t do it”).
target_language_example: Va bene, lo farò domani.
native_language_example: Okay, I’ll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Made of the direct object pronoun "lo" (“it/him”) + "fece" (passato remoto of "fare", “to do/make”). It refers back to something already mentioned (“it”). "Fece" is a literary/storytelling past tense; in everyday conversation people often use "l'ha fatto" instead.
target_language_example: Non so perché lo fece, ma lo fece.
native_language_example: I don’t know why he did it, but he did it.

meaning: “(he/she) did it for …” (for the sake of / because of).
additional_notes: Used to say the reason or purpose for an action. “Lo” = “it” (refers to something already understood), “fece” is the past tense of fare (to do/make), and “per” introduces the motive/beneficiary (e.g., per soldi = for money, per la sua famiglia = for his/her family).
target_language_example: Non l’ha detto a nessuno: lo fece per proteggere sua sorella.
native_language_example: He didn’t tell anyone: he did it to protect his sister.

additional_notes: Made of lo (“it/him”), ha (“has”), fatto (“done”). It refers to something already known from context (lo = “it/that”). Often corresponds to English simple past (“did it”), even though Italian uses the present perfect (ha fatto). Can also mean “made (someone) do/feel” in patterns like lo ha fatto + infinitive/adjective (e.g., lo ha fatto sorridere = “made him smile”).
target_language_example: Perché lo ha fatto?
native_language_example: Why did he/she do it?

additional_notes: "Lo" means “it” (a direct object pronoun) and comes before the verb: può fare = “can do.” The subject is often implied by context (he/she/you/they). It can be used in statements and questions, and you can add details like when/how: "lo può fare più tardi" (can do it later), "lo può fare a mani nude" (can do it with bare hands).
target_language_example: Se vuole, lo può fare domani.
native_language_example: If you want, you can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it/that” (a fact, answer, or thing already mentioned or understood). "Sa" is the present tense of *sapere* (“to know”). It often appears with *Lei* (formal “you”): *Lei lo sa?* = “Do you know (it)?” It can also introduce an indirect question: *Lo sa cosa vuol dire?* = “Do you know what it means?”
target_language_example: Non lo sa nessuno, ma lei lo sa.
native_language_example: Nobody knows it, but you (formal)/she knows it.

additional_notes: From "sapere" (to know). "Lo" is a pronoun meaning "it" and refers forward to the whole "che..." clause: "Lo sa che..." = "(He/She/You) knows that...". Often used to state that someone is aware of a fact, and it can sound slightly emphatic ("you know that..., right?").
target_language_example: Lei lo sa che oggi è festa, vero?
native_language_example: You know that today is a holiday, right?

additional_notes: Used to say someone already knows something (“as you know”) or to check/confirm that they know. Very common in conversation, including as a tag at the end of a sentence: “..., lo sai?” = “..., you know?” / “..., right?” The pronoun "lo" means “it” (the thing you know).
target_language_example: Domani c’è l’esame, lo sai?
native_language_example: The exam is tomorrow, you know?/right?

meaning: "you know that…" (often used to introduce a fact or a reminder).
additional_notes: Literally "you know it, that…". Used to point out something the speaker thinks the listener already knows, or to emphasize/surprise: "Lo sai che…?" can be a rhetorical question or a way to introduce new information. Very common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Lo sai che domani è festa?
native_language_example: You know that tomorrow is a holiday?

additional_notes: Used with a following clause introduced by “che”. The “lo” is a dummy pronoun that refers to the whole idea that follows (like “it” in “Did you know it…?”). In questions it often means “Were you aware that…?”. You’ll also hear other forms: “Lo sa che…?” (formal you), “Lo sai che…?” (informal you), “Lo sapevo che…” (I knew that).
target_language_example: Lo sapeva che domani il museo è chiuso?
native_language_example: Did you know that the museum is closed tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce information the speaker thinks might be surprising or unknown. It’s the past tense of sapere (“to know”) with voi (you all). Literally it’s “did you know it, that…”, but in English you typically just say “Did you know that…?”.
target_language_example: Lo sapevate che domani è festa?
native_language_example: Did you know that tomorrow is a holiday?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact or piece of information (often surprising or interesting). It’s the imperfect of sapere (“to know”): sapevi = “you knew/you did know,” but in this pattern it functions like “did you know…?”. You can also add “tu” for emphasis: “Tu lo sapevi che…?”.
target_language_example: Lo sapevi che domani è festa?
native_language_example: Did you know that tomorrow is a holiday?

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew something would happen or was true. Often expresses confirmation or “called it!” feeling. Literally it’s “I knew it that…”, but in English it’s usually “I knew (that)… / I knew it!”. The verb is in the imperfect (sapevo), referring to what you knew at that time.
target_language_example: Lo sapevo che avresti dimenticato le chiavi!
native_language_example: I knew you’d forget the keys!

additional_notes: Common way to say you already know something. The pronoun "lo" means “it/that” (referring to a fact or situation). Often used by itself as a response (“Lo so.” = “I know.”) or followed by a clause: "Lo so che..." (“I know that...”), "Lo so cosa..." (“I know what...”). You can add emphasis with "bene": "lo so bene" = “I know it well / I’m well aware.”
target_language_example: Lo so, ma non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: I know, but I can’t come tonight.

meaning: "I know, but…" (used to introduce a disagreement or objection).
additional_notes: Common in conversation to acknowledge what someone just said and then add a contrasting point. Often followed by a reason or preference ("…ma preferisco…", "…ma non voglio…"). Related pattern: "Non lo so, ma…" = "I don’t know, but…" (you’re unsure, yet you still have an opinion/guess).
target_language_example: Lo so, ma oggi non mi va di uscire.
native_language_example: I know, but I don’t feel like going out today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with che (“that”) after stating you know something. Often used to acknowledge information the other person is saying or feeling: Lo so che hai ragione (“I know you’re right”). In everyday speech, che is sometimes dropped: Lo so. / Lo so, ma…
target_language_example: Lo so che sei stanco, ma dobbiamo partire adesso.
native_language_example: I know you’re tired, but we have to leave now.

meaning: "is doing it" / "has been doing it" (right now).
additional_notes: Uses the present continuous in Italian: **stare + gerundio** (**sta facendo** = “is doing”). **Lo** is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (or “him,” depending on context) and comes before **sta**. In a question with **da quanto...**, it often implies “how long (has he/she been) doing it?”
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare: lo sto facendo adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk: I’m doing it right now.

additional_notes: Lo is a direct-object pronoun meaning “him” or “it.” Vidi is the passato remoto (remote past) of vedere (“to see”), common in stories, books, and historical narration (and also in some regions in everyday speech). In most everyday conversation, you’ll more often hear l’ho visto/a (“I saw him/it”). In sentences like “Lo vidi entrare...”, it means “I saw him enter...”.
target_language_example: Lo vidi attraversare la strada e poi sparire tra la folla.
native_language_example: I saw him cross the street and then disappear into the crowd.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is someone (often already known from context) and you refer back to an action with the direct object pronoun lo (= “it/that”). Common with names: “Tom lo vuole fare” = “Tom wants to do it.” You can add time/place/with whom: “oggi”, “con me”, etc.
target_language_example: Giulia lo vuole fare domani.
native_language_example: Giulia wants to do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express physical distance ("far from") or to tell someone to keep away from a person/thing ("stay away from"). It agrees with the subject: lontano da (masc.), lontana da (fem.), lontani da (masc. pl.), lontane da (fem. pl.). Common with verbs like stare/tenere (e.g., "stai lontana da...", "tienila lontana da...").
target_language_example: Tieni i bambini lontani dal fuoco.
native_language_example: Keep the children away from the fire.

additional_notes: Used to indicate distance from a place or person, often after verbs like portare (to take/bring) and tenere (to keep): "portare/tenere [someone/something] lontano da [place/person]" = to take/keep someone/something away from [place/person]. "Da" can mean "from" or "away from" depending on context.
target_language_example: Tieni il cane lontano dai bambini, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep the dog away from the children, please.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone is at a distance from your current location. Often appears with intensifiers like molto (“very”): “molto lontano da qui.” You can also negate it: “non lontano da qui” = “not far from here / nearby.” It can be a full short answer by itself: “Lontano da qui.”
target_language_example: La stazione è lontano da qui?
native_language_example: Is the station far from here?

additional_notes: “Loro” is a possessive meaning “their.” It usually comes before the noun with an article: “il loro cane” = “their dog.” With “loro” you don’t change the form for gender/number of the owners (Tom and Mary = “il loro cane”). If the dog is plural: “i loro cani” = “their dogs.”
target_language_example: Hanno portato il loro cane dal veterinario.
native_language_example: They took their dog to the vet.

additional_notes: "Loro" before a noun means "their" (it doesn’t change for gender/number): i loro cani (their dogs), le loro case (their houses). Don’t confuse it with "loro" as a pronoun meaning "them/to them" (e.g., "a loro" = to them).
target_language_example: I loro cani sono molto amichevoli.
native_language_example: Their dogs are very friendly.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the parents of “they” (or of a plural group mentioned). With family members you often use the definite article: i loro genitori (“their parents”). Common preposition combinations: ai loro genitori (to their parents), coi loro genitori (with their parents).
target_language_example: Non vogliono parlare coi loro genitori stasera.
native_language_example: They don’t want to talk with their parents tonight.

meaning: 'them not to…' (telling/asking them not to do something).
additional_notes: This is a common structure with verbs like dire (to tell) and chiedere (to ask): verb + loro (to them) + di + infinitive. With a negative infinitive, non goes right before the infinitive: di non + verb (e.g., di non parlare). In English you usually translate it as “(I told/asked) them not to …,” not word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ho chiesto loro di non parlare durante il film.
native_language_example: I asked them not to talk during the movie.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean you should deal with *them only* (and not other people). Often used after an instruction: “Parla con loro e basta” = “Talk to them, and that’s it (no one else).”
target_language_example: Per questa decisione, parla con loro e basta.
native_language_example: For this decision, talk to them and that’s it (only them).

additional_notes: Used to describe what people were like, how they felt, or what situation they were in in the past (ongoing/background description). Often the subject pronoun *loro* is optional because *erano* already implies “they.” Adjectives agree in number and gender: *spaventati* (mixed/masc. plural), *spaventate* (fem. plural). You can also place *tutti/e* with it: *loro erano tutti...* / *tutti loro erano...* = “they were all...”.
target_language_example: Quando li ho conosciuti, loro erano già inseparabili.
native_language_example: When I met them, they were already inseparable.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject (“loro” = “they”) plus the present tense of avere (“hanno” = “have”). Very often in Italian you can drop the subject pronoun and just say “hanno …” because the verb ending already shows it’s “they”. It’s also commonly used as the auxiliary verb to form the passato prossimo: “hanno” + past participle (e.g., “hanno bevuto” = “they drank / they have drunk”).
target_language_example: (Loro) hanno finito il lavoro.
native_language_example: They finished the work.

additional_notes: Used to say what 'they' possess or what they 'have' in a broader sense. Common with nouns (Loro hanno un figlio = They have a child) and with fixed expressions with avere to talk about states/feelings: avere bisogno di (to need), avere paura di (to be afraid of), avere speranza (to have hope). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun 'loro' is often omitted: Hanno bisogno di aiuto.
target_language_example: Loro hanno fame, ma non hanno soldi.
native_language_example: They are hungry, but they don't have money.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people needs something. "Avere bisogno di" is followed by a noun ("di un taxi") or an infinitive verb ("di parlare"). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun "loro" is often omitted: "Hanno bisogno di...".
target_language_example: Hanno bisogno di aiuto.
native_language_example: They need help.

meaning: "they" + reflexive/reciprocal "si" + past auxiliary "are/have" (used to form the past tense of reflexive/reciprocal verbs).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs in the passato prossimo (e.g., fermarsi, sposarsi, innamorarsi, prendersi gioco di). It corresponds to English "they ...ed" / "they have ...ed" when the action is done to themselves or to each other. With "essere" in the past tense, the past participle agrees with the subject: loro si sono fermate (all female) / fermati (all male or mixed). In everyday Italian, "loro" is often omitted: si sono fermate.
target_language_example: Loro si sono salutati e poi se ne sono andati.
native_language_example: They said goodbye to each other and then left.

additional_notes: Used to say what a group of people/animals/things is like or is doing. Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so you’ll also commonly hear just "sono" (e.g., "Sono già pronti?"). "Loro" is added for emphasis or to make clear who you’re talking about.
target_language_example: Loro sono italiani, ma vivono in Canada.
native_language_example: They are Italian, but they live in Canada.

meaning: sunlight; the light from the sun.
additional_notes: Literally “light of the sun.” Used to talk about natural sunlight (often in general, or as something plants need). Common with verbs like amare (to love), essere riconoscente per (to be grateful for), crescere in direzione di (to grow toward), and senza (without).
target_language_example: Apri la finestra: entra molta luce del sole.
native_language_example: Open the window: a lot of sunlight comes in.

additional_notes: Common setup in the passato prossimo: **lui** = “he”; **ci** is a clitic pronoun meaning **“us / to us”** (as in *Lui ci ha chiamati* = “He called us”, *Lui ci ha portato…* = “He brought us…”). It can also sometimes mean **“there”**, but in these examples it clearly means **“us/to us.”** The main verb is completed by the past participle after **ha**. With some verbs, the past participle may agree in gender/number with **ci** when it functions as a direct object (e.g., *ci ha chiamati/chiamate*).
target_language_example: Lui ci ha scritto ieri sera.
native_language_example: He wrote to us last night.

additional_notes: Made of the subject pronoun "lui" (he) + "era" (imperfect past of "essere", to be). It’s often used to describe a past state/condition or background description. Including "lui" can add emphasis or contrast (e.g., "He was..., not someone else"); in Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted when it’s clear from the verb ("era" can also mean "I/he/she was" from context).
target_language_example: Lui era molto stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He was very tired after the trip.

meaning: "he has" / "he did" (used to form past tenses and to express possession).
additional_notes: “Lui” is the subject pronoun “he,” and “ha” is the 3rd-person singular of avere (“to have”). It’s very often used with a past participle to form the passato prossimo (a common past tense): lui ha acceso = “he lit/has lit.” In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted because the verb ending already shows the subject (e.g., “Ha acceso le candele.”).
target_language_example: Lui ha finito il lavoro alle sei.
native_language_example: He finished the work at six.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb "fare" (to do/make): "lui" (he) + "ha" (has) + "fatto" (done/made). Used to talk about completed actions in the past; in English it can be translated as either "he did" or "he has done" depending on context. Often followed by a noun ("ha fatto degli errori" = he made some mistakes) or by a clause ("ha fatto quello che..." = he did what...).
target_language_example: Lui ha fatto la spesa ieri sera.
native_language_example: He did the grocery shopping last night.

additional_notes: A complete sentence. "Lui" = “he” (often used for emphasis; Italian commonly drops the subject pronoun). "Ha scritto" is passato prossimo of "scrivere" and can mean “has written” or “wrote,” depending on context. "Una lettera" = “a letter.” If you want to say “he wrote a letter to him/her,” you’d typically add "a lui/a lei" or a recipient like "a Maria".
target_language_example: Lui ha scritto una lettera al direttore ieri sera.
native_language_example: He wrote a letter to the director last night.

additional_notes: “Lui” is the subject pronoun (“he”) and “ha” is the 3rd-person singular of *avere* (“to have”). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted because the verb ending already shows the subject, so you’ll very often hear just “Ha…”. Using “lui” can add emphasis or contrast (e.g., “Lui ha…, ma lei no”). *Avere* is also used in expressions like “avere paura” (“to be afraid”) and “avere una cotta” (“to have a crush”).
target_language_example: Lui ha sempre ragione.
native_language_example: He is always right.

additional_notes: This is the pattern "avere bisogno di" (literally “to have need of”). Use "di" + a noun ("ha bisogno di acqua") or "di" + an infinitive to say “needs to” ("ha bisogno di studiare"). The subject can change: "io ho bisogno di", "lei ha bisogno di", "loro hanno bisogno di", etc.
target_language_example: Lui ha bisogno di parlare con il medico.
native_language_example: He needs to talk to the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy has something or has a certain trait/feature (appetito, senso di responsabilità, naso lungo, un iPhone, ecc.). The article changes with gender/number and sound: un (masc. sing., most nouns), uno (masc. sing. before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y), una (fem. sing.), un’ (fem. sing. before a vowel). In everyday Italian you often drop the pronoun and just say "Ha un..." if it’s clear who you mean.
target_language_example: Lui ha un cane molto gentile.
native_language_example: He has a very friendly dog.

meaning: “he has a” (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that a man has/owns something or has a characteristic. It’s the subject pronoun “lui” (he) + “ha” (has) + “una” (a/an, feminine singular). Often in Italian the subject pronoun is omitted: “Ha una piscina.” Use “un” instead of “una” with a masculine singular noun (e.g., “Lui ha un fratello.”).
target_language_example: Lui ha una macchina nuova.
native_language_example: He has a new car.

additional_notes: "Lui" is the subject pronoun (“he”), often used for emphasis or contrast (e.g., ‘HE did it’). "Mi" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “me” (direct or indirect depending on the verb). In many sentences you can drop "lui" because the verb ending already shows the subject: "Mi aiutò" = “He helped me.”
target_language_example: Lui mi ha detto la verità.
native_language_example: He told me the truth.

additional_notes: Common structure: subject pronoun + indirect object pronoun + auxiliary verb. "Lui" = he, "mi" = to me/me, "ha" = has (present of avere, used to form the passato prossimo). It’s used with a past participle: "lui mi ha detto" (he told me), "lui mi ha aiutato" (he helped me). In everyday Italian, the subject pronoun "lui" is often omitted if it’s clear from context: "Mi ha detto..."
target_language_example: Lui mi ha detto la verità.
native_language_example: He told me the truth.

meaning: “he doesn’t / he didn’t / he is not” (with emphasis on “he”).
additional_notes: Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so you usually just say “non …” (e.g., “Non mi ama.”). Adding “lui” is used for emphasis or contrast (like “HE doesn’t…” / “Not him…”), often when comparing with someone else: “Io sì, lui no.” The exact English tense depends on the verb that follows (present: “he doesn’t…”, past: “he didn’t…”, etc.).
target_language_example: Io vengo, ma lui non può.
native_language_example: I’m coming, but he can’t.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man (lui = “he”) does not possess something or does not have something (time, ideas, sleepiness, etc.). In Italian, the negative word non comes directly before the verb: non ha. Very often, Italian can drop the subject pronoun, so you may also hear just non ha…. It’s common with negative words like nessuno/nessuna (“no one”, “none”) or alcun/alcuna (“any”, used with non to mean “no/none”).
target_language_example: Lui non ha soldi per uscire stasera.
native_language_example: He doesn’t have money to go out tonight.

meaning: "he is not" (used to say what he isn’t).
additional_notes: Built from **lui** (“he”) + **non** (“not”) + **è** (“is”). In Italian, the subject pronoun (**lui**) is often optional because the verb ending already shows the subject, so you’ll also commonly hear **non è** (“he isn’t / it isn’t”) depending on context. Used with adjectives, nouns, and origins: **lui non è sposato** (he isn’t married), **lui non è italiano** (he isn’t Italian).
target_language_example: Lui non è pronto per uscire.
native_language_example: He isn’t ready to go out.

meaning: “he” + reflexive “si” (≈ “he … himself,” used with reflexive verbs).
additional_notes: Used when the verb is reflexive (verbs ending in -si in the dictionary), where the subject does the action to himself: alzarsi (to get up), farsi crescere (to grow for oneself), fidarsi (to trust), inchinarsi (to bow), stancarsi (to get tired), decidersi (to decide). In Italian you often include both the subject pronoun (lui) for emphasis/contrast and the reflexive pronoun (si) because the verb requires it.
target_language_example: Lui si alza presto ogni giorno.
native_language_example: He gets up early every day.

meaning: 'he has' / 'he ...ed' (passato prossimo with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs in the past: subject pronoun (lui) + reflexive pronoun (si) + auxiliary essere (è) + past participle. Common in actions done to oneself (Lui si è tagliato) or changes of state/feelings (Lui si è stancato). With essere, the past participle usually agrees with the subject: lui si è stancatO, lei si è stancatA.
target_language_example: Lui si è svegliato tardi stamattina.
native_language_example: He woke up late this morning.

additional_notes: Used when you want to explicitly state or emphasize the subject "he" (lui). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted because the verb form already shows the subject, so you’ll also commonly hear just "è" (e.g., "È vecchio" = "He’s old"). "È" is the present tense of "essere" and is used both for identity/description ("He is a teacher") and to form certain past tenses ("He has grown up", "He has burst out laughing").
target_language_example: Lui è molto gentile con tutti.
native_language_example: He is very kind to everyone.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of **andare** (auxiliary **essere**): **lui è andato**. It’s followed by **a** + a city/place (**è andato a Parigi**) or **a** + an infinitive to express purpose (**è andato a stare da…** = “he went to stay at …’s place”).
target_language_example: Ieri lui è andato a Roma per lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday he went to Rome for work.

additional_notes: Past tense with essere (passato prossimo): "è morto". In context it often translates as "he died" (an event, often with a time reference like "dieci anni fa"), but it can also mean "he is dead" (a current state). You can replace "lui" with a name or another subject: "Mio nonno è morto..."
target_language_example: Lui è morto nel 2015, ma lo ricordiamo ancora con affetto.
native_language_example: He died in 2015, but we still remember him fondly.

meaning: "he was" / "he has been" (often used to form the passive: "he was/has been + past participle").
additional_notes: Uses the auxiliary essere in the passato prossimo with the subject lui (“he”). Very commonly followed by a past participle to make the passive voice: lui è stato condannato/criticato/mandato = “he was/has been sentenced/criticized/sent.” In context, English usually chooses simple past (“he was…”) for finished events.
target_language_example: Lui è stato licenziato la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: He was fired last week.

meaning: "he is a" (used to say what someone is).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a male person’s role/profession/nationality, etc. In Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted (e.g., "È un cantante"), but "lui" can be included for emphasis or contrast. Use "un" before most masculine singular nouns; use "uno" before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y (e.g., "lui è uno studente"). For feminine, use "lei è una".
target_language_example: Non è un dilettante: lui è un professionista.
native_language_example: He’s not an amateur: he’s a professional.

additional_notes: Simple sentence used to identify or describe someone. Common pattern: "Lui è un uomo + adjective" (e.g., timido = shy, malvagio = evil, virtuoso = virtuous) or "Lui è un uomo di cui ci possiamo fidare" (= a man we can trust). Often "lui" is omitted because the verb already shows the subject: "È un uomo" or "È un uomo timido."
target_language_example: Lui è un uomo gentile e onesto.
native_language_example: He is a kind and honest man.

meaning: "he is a man of …" (used to describe someone’s qualities).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by a noun that describes a trait or characteristic. Very frequent: "un uomo di parola" = a man of his word (reliable, keeps promises). You can also use it with other nouns: "un uomo di pochi bisogni" = a man with few needs (simple lifestyle). You can change "lui" to another subject: "Lei è una donna di…", "Marco è un uomo di…".
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: Marco è un uomo di parola.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: Marco is a man of his word.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the Monday of the following week (relative to today). Often used for plans, meetings, or deadlines. You can also use it after a preposition like "fino a lunedì prossimo" (until next Monday).
target_language_example: Possiamo vederci lunedì prossimo alle 9?
native_language_example: Can we meet next Monday at 9?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the Monday of the previous week (relative to today or another reference point). Often used as a time expression with the past tense; can also be used as a starting point with “da” (e.g., “da lunedì scorso” = “since last Monday”).
target_language_example: Lunedì scorso abbiamo cenato insieme.
native_language_example: Last Monday we had dinner together.

meaning: along the road/street; down the road.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is located along the length of a road (often while moving). With verbs of movement it can mean “as you go along the road” or “down the road.” It’s a preposition phrase: lungo + la strada.
target_language_example: Abbiamo visto un bar lungo la strada per l’hotel.
native_language_example: We saw a café along the way to the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes or is in a place without anyone accompanying them. Agreement changes with the person: da sola (female), da solo (male). Often used with verbs of going/being (andare, venire, stare). You may also hear lì da sola (“there” in a more specific/nearby sense).
target_language_example: Non ci vado là da sola la sera.
native_language_example: I don’t go there alone in the evening.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was/goes/works in that place without anyone else. "Là" means “there” (often a bit distant). It agrees with the person: "là da sola" (female), "là da soli" (plural masculine/mixed), "là da sole" (plural female).
target_language_example: Perché sei là da solo?
native_language_example: Why are you there alone?

additional_notes: Used to say you went to a place many times. In natural Italian you more often hear: “Sono andato/a lì dozzine di volte” or “Ci sono andato/a dozzine di volte” (with lì/ci = “there”). “Dozzine” is the plural of “dozzina” (a dozen).
target_language_example: Ci sono andato dozzine di volte.
native_language_example: I went there dozens of times.

additional_notes: Used to say a woman/girl goes somewhere alone. It agrees with the person: a man would say "lì da solo"; for more than one person: "lì da soli" (mixed/men) or "lì da sole" (all women). Often used with verbs like andare (to go): "è andata lì da sola" = "she went there alone."
target_language_example: Non voglio andarci: lei è andata lì da sola.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go there: she went there by herself.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at that place without anyone else. "lì" = "there" and "da solo" = "alone / by yourself" (for a man; for a woman: "lì da sola"). Often used with verbs like "andare" (to go), "stare" (to be), "lavorare" (to work), "vivere" (to live).
target_language_example: Non voglio andare lì da solo di notte.
native_language_example: I don't want to go there alone at night.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific place that is not where the speaker is (lì = “there”, as opposed to qui = “here”). Often used when the place is already clear from context (e.g., a room, a building, a car, a box).
target_language_example: Non entrare lì dentro, è pericoloso.
native_language_example: Don’t go in there, it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: A very common exclamation used to show strong surprise, anger, frustration, or disbelief. Often said on its own ("Ma che cazzo!") or followed by a question ("Ma che cazzo ti prende?" = "What the fuck is wrong with you?/What’s gotten into you?"). It’s vulgar (cazzo = literally "dick"), so avoid it in polite situations; use milder options like "Ma che cavolo?" or "Ma che diavolo?".
target_language_example: Ma che cazzo fai?!
native_language_example: What the fuck are you doing?!

meaning: "but not" / "but" + a negation (to correct or contrast).
additional_notes: Used to add a contrast while denying something: you state one fact, then correct it or limit it with a negative idea (non + verb/adjective). Common in explanations and clarifications: "..., ma non era..." (but it wasn’t...), "..., ma non si..." (but it didn’t...).
target_language_example: Vorrei venire, ma non posso oggi.
native_language_example: I’d like to come, but I can’t today.

additional_notes: Used to contradict or correct what was just said. The subject (lui/lei/esso/questa, etc.) is often omitted and understood from context. With rising intonation it’s a question (“But isn’t it…?”); with flat intonation it’s a statement (“But it isn’t…”).
target_language_example: Sembra facile, ma non è così.
native_language_example: It looks easy, but it isn’t like that.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask if someone has ever smelled a particular perfume before. With avere + mai + past participle (annusato) it corresponds to English “ever” questions: “Have you ever…?”. Common in shops when offering a fragrance. You’ll often hear it as: “Ha mai annusato questo profumo?” (formal), “Hai mai annusato questo profumo?” (informal), or “Avete mai annusato questo profumo?” (plural/formal).
target_language_example: Hai mai annusato questo profumo? È molto delicato.
native_language_example: Have you ever smelled this perfume? It’s very delicate.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere in the passato prossimo: hai/ho/avete mai avuto… = “have you/I/you (plural) ever had…?” In negative sentences, non + mai means “never”: non ho mai avuto… = “I’ve never had…”. Common in questions about past experiences: Avete mai avuto un problema/animale domestico…?
target_language_example: Hai mai avuto paura di volare?
native_language_example: Have you ever been afraid of flying?

meaning: 'ever like a sad panda?' (a humorous way to say 'ever really sad/down?').
additional_notes: Used almost always with sentirsi/si sente/ti senti (“to feel”) to ask if someone ever feels very sad or low, in a joking, playful tone. Grammatically, mai in questions often means “ever.” You can change the person: Ti senti mai…? (you), Si sente mai…? (formal you), Vi sentite mai…? (you all).
target_language_example: Ti senti mai come un panda triste quando piove?
native_language_example: Do you ever feel like a sad panda when it rains?

additional_notes: Used as a warning/advice, usually with verbs like andare (“to go”): **non andare mai da nessuna parte da solo/a** = “never go anywhere alone.” The **da** here belongs to **da solo/a** (“alone”), which agrees with the person: **da solo** (male), **da sola** (female), **da soli/da sole** (plural). **Da nessuna parte** in negative sentences means “anywhere” (literally “to no place”).
target_language_example: Non uscire mai da nessuna parte da solo, è troppo tardi.
native_language_example: Never go out anywhere alone; it’s too late.

additional_notes: Used with the past participle detto (“said”). In negative sentences (non... mai) it means “never”: Non ho mai detto nulla. In questions, mai often means “ever”: Mi hai mai detto la verità? Usually refers to something that has (or hasn’t) happened at any time up to now.
target_language_example: Non l’ho mai detto a nessuno.
native_language_example: I’ve never said it to anyone.

additional_notes: In questions, **mai** often means **'ever'** (not 'never'). This phrase is typically used with the present perfect: **Hai mai giocato a golf?** = 'Have you ever played golf?' You can add **con + person** to say who you played with: **Hai mai giocato a golf con Tom?**
target_language_example: Hai mai giocato a golf in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever played golf in Italy?

meaning: "ever read" (have you read at any time up to now?).
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (avere + letto) to ask or state whether someone has read something at any point in their life/so far: «Hai mai letto…?». In negative sentences, Italian usually uses «non … mai» = “never” («Non l’ho mai letto.»).
target_language_example: Hai mai letto questo libro?
native_language_example: Have you ever read this book?

additional_notes: Used in questions with the passato prossimo to ask if someone has had the experience of reading poems at least once (often translated as “Have you ever read any poems…?”). "mai" = “ever” in questions; "delle" often means “some/any” in this context. You’ll typically see it as "(Tu/Lei) hai/ha mai letto delle poesie…?".
target_language_example: Hai mai letto delle poesie italiane?
native_language_example: Have you ever read any Italian poems?

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions with "avere" to ask about someone’s life experience: "Hai/Ha/Avete mai letto…?" = “Have you ever read…?” Here "mai" means “ever” (not “never”) because it’s in a question, and "delle poesie" means “some poems / any poems” (partitive article). You can add a language or adjective: "in francese", "francesi", or an author: "di Tennyson".
target_language_example: Hai mai letto delle poesie di Dante?
native_language_example: Have you ever read any poems by Dante?

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo to talk about life experience. In questions, "Hai mai mangiato...?" means "Have you ever eaten...?". With "non" it becomes negative: "Non ho mai mangiato..." = "I have never eaten...".
target_language_example: Hai mai mangiato il sushi?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

additional_notes: Used in questions with the present perfect (avere + past participle) to ask if someone has ever done something. "Mai" means “ever” in questions (and “never” in negative sentences). Often followed by extra details like "con il/col ketchup".
target_language_example: Hai mai mangiato le uova con il formaggio?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten eggs with cheese?

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo (avere + participle) to ask about someone’s experience. In questions, **mai** usually means **“ever”**: *Hai mai…?* = “Have you ever…?”. It can be used with different subjects/formality: *Tu hai…?* (informal), *Lei ha…?* (formal), *Voi avete…?* (plural).
target_language_example: Hai mai pronunciato questa parola in italiano?
native_language_example: Have you ever pronounced this word in Italian?

additional_notes: Used with the past participle of *sentire* to say you have never heard something (*non ho mai sentito...* = “I’ve never heard...”) or, with *sentirsi* (“to feel”), that you have never felt a certain way (*non mi sono mai sentito...* = “I’ve never felt...” / “I’ve never felt better”). Often appears with superlatives: *la cosa più ... che io abbia mai sentito* (“the most ... thing I’ve ever heard”).
target_language_example: Una cosa così non l’ho mai sentita prima.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard something like that before.

meaning: “ever plucked a chicken?” (i.e., ever done that before).
additional_notes: Used in questions with "mai" (“ever”) to ask if someone has had the experience of doing something. Here it’s a very concrete example (plucking a chicken) and can sound a bit humorous or folksy, but the grammar pattern is common: "Hai mai + past participle...?" / "Ha mai + past participle...?".
target_language_example: Hai mai spennato un pollo?
native_language_example: Have you ever plucked a chicken?

additional_notes: Used in questions with the passato prossimo to ask about life experience: “Sei mai stata a…?” = “Have you ever been to…?” It’s feminine singular because of “stata” (a woman speaking or being addressed). For a man you say “mai stato a”. Often used with places (cities, countries): “Sei mai stata a Roma?”
target_language_example: Sei mai stata a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

additional_notes: Used with essere in the passato prossimo (or subjunctive, as in non siano mai stati) to say someone has never visited a place. The word order is typically non + essere + mai + stati/e + a + place (agreement: stati for masculine/mixed plural, state for feminine plural).
target_language_example: Non siamo mai stati a Roma, ma ci andremo quest’estate.
native_language_example: We’ve never been to Rome, but we’ll go this summer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (past participle: stato) to talk about whether something has ever happened or existed up to now. With a negative it means “never been” (e.g., non è mai stato = “has never been”); in questions it often means “ever been” (e.g., Sei mai stato…? = “Have you ever been…?”).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato a Roma.
native_language_example: I've never been to Rome.

additional_notes: Used with forms of **essere** (è/sei/sono…): **Sei mai stato…?** = “Have you ever been…?” With negation **non … mai stato** = “have never been / was never.” It can also appear with **ci** to mean “(would) never have been there/existed,” e.g. **non ci sarebbe mai stato**.
target_language_example: Sei mai stato a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

meaning: “(have) ever been to” / “(have) never been to”.
additional_notes: Used with the verb **essere** in the passato prossimo to talk about visiting a place at least once. In negatives, **non … mai stato/a a** = “have never been to” (e.g., *Non sono mai stato a…*). In questions, **Sei mai stato/a a…?** = “Have you ever been to…?”. The past participle agrees with the subject: **stato** (male), **stata** (female); plural **stati/state**. Often followed by **vero?** (“right?”) in tag questions.
target_language_example: Sei mai stata a Roma?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Rome?

mai una biografia su di me

target_language_multi_word_term: mai una biografia su di me
meaning: "never a biography about me" / "you’ll never see a biography of me."
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something will never happen. "mai" = "never"; "una biografia" = "a biography"; "su di me" = "about me". Often appears with a future tense verb (e.g., "non vedrai/vedrete mai...").
target_language_example: Tranquillo: non leggerai mai una biografia su di me.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll never read a biography about me.

meaning: “never something like that / never such a thing.”
additional_notes: Used to strongly deny that you would ever do something (often with the conditional: non farei mai…, non faresti mai…). Literally “never a thing of this kind,” and it refers back to something mentioned or implied in the conversation.
target_language_example: Tranquillo: non direi mai una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I would never say something like that.

additional_notes: Built from mai (“never/ever”) + visto (“seen”, past participle of vedere). Common with the auxiliary avere: non l’ho mai visto = “I’ve never seen it/him.” In questions, mai often means “ever”: Lo avete mai visto? = “Have you ever seen it/him?” It can be followed by an infinitive to mean “seen someone do something”: Non lo aveva mai visto ridere = “He had never seen him laugh.”
target_language_example: Non ho mai visto un film così bello.
native_language_example: I've never seen such a beautiful movie.

meaning: 'ever seen an elephant' (used in questions with "hai/ha mai...").
additional_notes: Used as part of a question like "Hai mai visto... ?" / "Lei ha mai visto... ?" meaning "Have you ever seen...?". In questions, "mai" often means "ever" (not "never"). "visto" is the past participle of "vedere" (to see).
target_language_example: Hai mai visto un elefante in Italia?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen an elephant in Italy?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "volere" in the past (usually passato prossimo): "(non) ho/hai/ha mai voluto...". In negative sentences, "non... mai" means "never". In questions without "non", "hai mai voluto...?" means "have you ever wanted...?". It can be followed by an infinitive ("mai voluto ascoltare") or a noun ("mai voluto il mio aiuto").
target_language_example: Non ho mai voluto litigare con te.
native_language_example: I never wanted to argue with you.

meaning: 'ever wanted to be' / 'never wanted to be'.
additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary avere + past participle (avere/ha/ho… voluto) + infinitive essere to talk about whether someone has ever had the desire to be something. With "mai" in a question, it often means "ever" (Avete mai…? = Have you ever…?). With "non" it means "never" (Non ho mai… = I have never…). Agreement: voluto (masc./mixed) vs voluta (fem.) may change based on the subject in some contexts.
target_language_example: Hai mai voluto essere medico?
native_language_example: Have you ever wanted to be a doctor?

additional_notes: Used to talk about stomach pain or discomfort. Very common with the verbs avere (to have): “Ho/avevo mal di stomaco” and soffrire di (to suffer from): “Soffro di mal di stomaco.” You can add an adjective like terribile/brutto/forte to emphasize how bad it is.
target_language_example: Ho mal di stomaco da stamattina.
native_language_example: I’ve had a stomachache since this morning.

meaning: stomach pain; a stomachache (“my/your/his stomach hurts”).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase "fare male": "mi fa male lo stomaco" (my stomach hurts), "gli fa male lo stomaco" (his stomach hurts), "ti fa male lo stomaco?" (does your stomach hurt?). It can be caused by illness, food, or even laughing a lot.
target_language_example: Mi fa male lo stomaco, credo di aver mangiato troppo.
native_language_example: My stomach hurts; I think I ate too much.
