non mi hanno mai detto che

target_language_multi_word_term: non mi hanno mai detto che
additional_notes: Used to say you were never informed about a fact. Common pattern: non + indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) + hanno mai detto + che + clause. Often implies surprise or complaint.
target_language_example: Non mi hanno mai detto che la riunione era stata annullata.
native_language_example: They never told me that the meeting had been canceled.

meaning: “I don’t like it / I don’t like.”
additional_notes: Used to express dislike. Italian often phrases “to like” as “to be pleasing,” so it literally means “it doesn’t please me,” with mi = “to me.” You can add emphasis with words like mica (“not really / not at all,” often colloquial) or per niente (“not at all”): Non mi piace mica; Non mi piace per niente.
target_language_example: Non mi piace questo ristorante, è troppo caro.
native_language_example: I don’t like this restaurant; it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done/experienced something up to now. It’s made of: non (not) + mi (myself) + sono (I am / I have, auxiliary) + mai (ever/never). It’s typically followed by a past participle: non mi sono mai accorto/a (I never noticed), non mi sono mai fidato/a (I never trusted), non mi sono mai sentito/a (I never felt). The past participle often changes for gender/number: accorto (male), accorta (female).
target_language_example: Non mi sono mai svegliato così presto.
native_language_example: I’ve never woken up this early.

non mi sono mai preoccupato per

target_language_multi_word_term: non mi sono mai preoccupato per
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb preoccupare (preoccuparsi) in the passato prossimo: mi sono preoccupato/a = “I got worried / I worried.” Add mai to mean “never,” and per + person/thing you’re worried about. Change preoccupato to preoccupata if the speaker is female. Often used to emphasize you didn’t feel concern about someone/something.
target_language_example: Non mi sono mai preoccupato per l'esame.
native_language_example: I have never worried about the exam.

meaning: 'it has never (happened) to me' / 'I have never'.
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere to express that something has never happened/occurred to you, or that you have never had a certain experience. The full pattern is often: “Non mi è mai + past participle” (e.g., capitato, successo, passato per la testa, piaciuto/piaciuta). “Mi” = to me, “è” = has/is, “mai” = ever/never.
target_language_example: Non mi è mai venuto in mente di farlo.
native_language_example: It never occurred to me to do it.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve never liked someone or something, from the past up to now. It literally means “it has never pleased me,” so the thing/person you didn’t like is the grammatical subject (e.g., Non mi è mai piaciuto Tom/il Natale). With plural subjects, use piaciuti/piaciute (e.g., Non mi sono mai piaciute le feste). You can also follow it with an infinitive to talk about an activity: Non mi è mai piaciuto andare a scuola (“I never liked going to school”).
target_language_example: Non mi è mai piaciuto questo ristorante, anche se tutti lo adorano.
native_language_example: I’ve never liked this restaurant, even though everyone loves it.

meaning: “not … about it / of it / any (of it)” (with the pronoun *ne*).
additional_notes: *Ne* is a pronoun that often replaces **di + noun/pronoun** (“of it/them”, “about it”, “any of it”). With **non**, it forms very common negatives like **non ne so nulla** (“I don’t know anything about it”) and **non ne ho idea** (“I have no idea”). The exact English translation depends on the verb: *saperne* = “know about it”, *averne idea* = “have an idea”, etc.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ne so niente.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about it.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is impossible, not allowed, or not feasible for “us” (the speaker + others). It’s simply the negation of “possiamo” (“we can”). Often followed by an infinitive: “Non possiamo farlo” = “We can’t do it.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non possiamo venire stasera.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t come tonight.

meaning: "I can't" / "I’m not able to" (sometimes: "I’m not allowed to").
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: "non posso + verbo" (non posso farlo = I can’t do it). It can express inability (physical/practical), impossibility, or lack of permission depending on context. For other persons: non puoi (you can’t), non può (he/she can’t), non possiamo (we can’t), non possono (they can’t).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse something (a gift, an apology, an offer) or to say you can’t come to terms with a situation/fact (“I can’t accept the fact that…”). Often followed by a noun (non posso accettare il regalo / una scusa) or by “che …” / “il fatto che …”. Can also stand alone: “Non posso accettare.” = “I can’t accept it.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non posso accettare questa offerta.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I can’t accept this offer.

meaning: “I can’t agree/consent to (the fact) that…” / “I can’t allow that…”
additional_notes: Used to express strong refusal or non-approval. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), as in: che andiate / che vada. Common in formal or serious contexts (rules, authority, moral objection).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso acconsentire che tu esca così tardi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t allow you to go out that late.

meaning: "I can't do without" / "I can't help (doing something)".
additional_notes:
Used to say something is indispensable or unavoidable.

Common patterns:
- Non posso fare a meno di + infinitive = “I can’t help (doing) …” (e.g., Non posso fare a meno di ridere.)
- Non posso fare a meno di + noun/article (di/del/della/dei…) = “I can’t do without …” (e.g., Non posso fare a meno del caffè.)

Often implies a strong habit, need, or an emotional reaction you can’t control.
target_language_example: Non posso fare a meno di pensare a te.
native_language_example: I can't help thinking about you.

meaning: I could never / I would never (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express that you would be unable to do something or would never do it (often for moral/emotional reasons). It’s built from: non (not) + potrei (I could, conditional of potere) + mai (ever/never). Usually followed by an infinitive: non potrei mai farlo (I could never do it).
target_language_example: Non potrei mai mentire ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I could never lie to my friends.

additional_notes: Second-person singular negative of potere (“can/to be able to”). Used to say something is impossible, not allowed, or not acceptable: Non puoi entrare. / Non puoi farlo. Often followed by an infinitive (non puoi + verb) or used alone for emphasis.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non puoi entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: Sorry, but you can’t come in without a ticket.

additional_notes: Negative form of the verb "potere" (to be able to / can). "Può" is 3rd person singular (lui/lei) and is also used with the polite form "Lei" (formal "you"): e.g., "Lei non può entrare" = "You can’t enter." Often used for rules/prohibitions ("Non può fumare" = "You can’t smoke").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non può entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: Sorry, today you can’t enter without a ticket.

meaning: “it can’t be” / “it cannot be” (impossible or not true).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is impossible or cannot happen (non può essere + past participle/passive: “cannot be + done”), or to express disbelief that something is true (non può essere vero/reale: “can’t be true/real”). In the past, you may see non può essere stato/a (“it can’t have been”).
target_language_example: Non può essere vero quello che hai detto.
native_language_example: What you said can’t be true.

additional_notes: From "riuscire a" = "to manage to". "Non riesce a" is the 3rd person singular present (he/she/it doesn't manage to). It’s followed by an infinitive: "non riesce a + verb". You can change the subject: "non riesco a" (I can’t), "non riesci a" (you can’t), "non riusciamo a" (we can’t).
target_language_example: Scusa, non riesce a venire oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she can’t make it today.

meaning: "I can't" / "I’m not able to" (I can’t manage to).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (non riesco a + verb) to say you can’t do something—because it’s too hard, not working, or you’re unable (mentally/physically) at the moment. Often implies difficulty or failure to succeed (similar to “I can’t manage to…”). Conjugates with the person: non riesci a (you), non riesce a (he/she), non riusciamo a (we), etc.
target_language_example: Scusa, non riesco a trovare le chiavi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t find my keys.

meaning: "we can't / we aren't able to" (to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb "riuscire a" = "to manage to / to be able to" + an infinitive. "Non riusciamo a" is the negative, used when something is impossible or difficult (because of circumstances, ability, time, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: "non riusciamo a dormire". It can imply struggling rather than a simple lack of permission.
target_language_example: Scusa, non riusciamo a venire stasera.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t make it tonight.

meaning: “couldn’t / wasn’t able to” (he/she wasn’t managing to).
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "non riuscire a" + infinitive, used for an ongoing difficulty or repeated inability in the past. It can mean physical inability (non riusciva a camminare) or not being able to bring yourself to do something (non riusciva a dire di no / non riusciva a credere...). Often translated as “couldn’t manage to.”
target_language_example: Era troppo stanco e non riusciva a concentrarsi.
native_language_example: He was too tired and couldn’t concentrate.

additional_notes: From riuscire a (“to manage to / be able to”) + non (not) + più (anymore). Used to say someone has reached a limit and can’t keep doing something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., reggere, sopportare, contenere, nascondere). Tense can change: non riesco più a… (I can’t anymore), non riuscivo più a… (I couldn’t anymore), non riuscirà più a… (he/she won’t be able to anymore).
target_language_example: Dopo ore di lavoro, non riusciva più a tenere gli occhi aperti.
native_language_example: After hours of work, he couldn’t keep his eyes open anymore.

additional_notes: Uses the present tense of sapere (“to know”) with non ... niente (“not ... anything”). Often followed by di/su (“about”): non sa niente di/su di lui = “he/she doesn’t know anything about him.” You can change the subject: io non so niente, tu non sai niente, loro non sanno niente.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non sa niente di questa storia.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she doesn’t know anything about this story.

additional_notes: A common way to start a sentence with a reason or situation. It uses the gerund (sapendo) and often means “since/because I/they didn’t know what to do.” Usually the subject is the same as in the main clause (e.g., “Non sapendo cosa fare, ho chiesto aiuto.”).
target_language_example: Non sapendo cosa fare, ho chiamato un amico.
native_language_example: Not knowing what to do, I called a friend.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb *essere* (“to be”) with an implied subject *tu* (“you”). It can be followed by a noun (*Non sei mio padre!* = “You’re not my father!”) or an adjective (*Non sei stanco* = “You’re not tired”). It also appears in comparisons like *più … di quanto non …* where *non* can be part of the comparison structure, not a separate extra negation.
target_language_example: Non sei obbligato a venire oggi.
native_language_example: You’re not required to come today.

meaning: 'not' with "si" (impersonal/passive or reflexive), often meaning 'you/one can't/doesn't' or 'it isn't done'.
additional_notes:
Used before the verb in several common patterns:
- Impersonal "si": general statements about people in general. "Non si + verb" ≈ “you/one don’t…” / “you can’t…”. Example: "La felicità non si compra" (“You can’t buy happiness”).
- "Si" with a reflexive verb: "non si + verb" can mean “(he/she/they) doesn’t … himself/herself/themselves”, depending on context. Example: "Tom non si sbaglia" (“Tom doesn’t make mistakes”).
Meaning depends on whether "si" is impersonal or reflexive in the sentence.
target_language_example: In Italia non si fuma nei ristoranti.
native_language_example: In Italy you don’t smoke in restaurants.

additional_notes: Impersonal form used for general rules or situations, not directed at a specific person. Often means something is forbidden (“Non si può fumare…” = “No smoking”). With an infinitive, it means something can’t be done: “Non si può + verb”.
target_language_example: Qui non si può parcheggiare.
native_language_example: You can’t park here. / No parking here.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened up to now. It’s common with the passato prossimo: "non" + "si è" (or "si sono") + "mai" + past participle. With reflexive verbs you’ll often see it with a pronoun too: "Non si è mai perdonato" = “He never forgave himself.” For plural: "Non si sono mai sposati" = “They never got married.”
target_language_example: Non si è mai lamentato del lavoro.
native_language_example: He has never complained about work.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something or you’re unsure. Often followed by an indirect question (e.g., "non so cosa fare" = "I don’t know what to do"). You can add words like "più" (anymore) or "quasi" (almost) to nuance it: "non so più" = "I don’t know anymore"; "non so quasi niente" = "I know almost nothing."
target_language_example: Scusa, non so dove sia la stazione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know where the station is.

meaning: "I am not" / "they are not" (present tense of *essere* with *non*).
additional_notes: Used to negate the verb *essere* (“to be”). It can mean **I am not** (io non sono) or **they are not** (loro non sono)—Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so context tells you which. Follow it with a noun/adjective: *Non sono sicuro* (“I’m not sure”), *Non sono nel panico* (“I’m not panicking / I’m not in a panic”), or with **più** to mean “not anymore”: *Non sono più sposati* (“They’re not married anymore”).
target_language_example: Non sono pronto adesso.
native_language_example: I'm not ready right now.

meaning: 'I am/they are never' or 'I/they have never' (with essere).
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (present: sono; past: sono stato/a/i/e) to express 'never'. The exact English meaning depends on tense and context: present + a place/habit = 'I’m never…' (Non sono mai a casa la domenica.); past participle = 'I’ve never…' / 'I never…' (Non sono mai uscito/a…). Note agreement in the past participle with essere: sono mai tornata, sono mai cambiato.
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato a Roma.
native_language_example: I've never been to Rome.

meaning: “I have never been” / “I was never” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used by a female speaker to say she has never been something (a quality/state) up to now. It’s the negative of the passato prossimo of “essere” with “mai” (never): non + sono stata + mai. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: “brava” (good at), “coraggiosa” (brave), “innamorata di…” (in love with…), “sfortunata” (unlucky). For a man: “non sono mai stato”.
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata a Roma.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome.

meaning: "I've never been to/in" (said by a woman).
additional_notes:
Used to say you have never visited a place. 
- donna: non sono mai stata in… 
- uomo: non sono mai stato in… 
With countries, regions, and cities you usually use “in” (in America, in Cina, in Florida).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata in Italia, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I've never been to Italy, but I'd like to go there.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never had an experience or never been in/to a place. It’s the passato prossimo of "essere" with "mai" (ever/never): "non" + "sono" + "mai" + "stato". "Stato" agrees with the speaker: a woman says "non sono mai stata". With places you’ll often add a preposition: "non sono mai stato in Italia / nel deserto" (I've never been to/in Italy / the desert).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato a Roma, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I've never been to Rome, but I'd like to go there.

meaning: "I've never been to / I've never been in (a place)."
additional_notes: Used to say you have never been somewhere. Literally “I have never been in.” Use **sono stato** (not *ho stato*) because *stato* uses the auxiliary **essere**. Follow with a country/city without an article (e.g., *in America, in Cina*) or with a place that takes an article (e.g., *in una moschea*). You can change the subject: *non sei mai stato/a in…*, *non siamo mai stati/e in…*; add **-a/-e** for feminine forms.
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato in Italia, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I've never been to Italy, but I'd like to go there.

meaning: "I'm not a" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to deny identity/profession/category: non sono un + noun (e.g., non sono un barista). For feminine nouns, use "non sono una" (non sono una studentessa). Before a vowel or silent h, "un" becomes "un'": non sono un'amica (feminine).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non sono un medico.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm not a doctor.

additional_notes: Used before a verb: "non" makes the verb negative, and "ti" is the unstressed pronoun meaning "to you" (sometimes "you" depending on the verb). Common in questions and statements: "Non ti dice niente?" = "Doesn’t it tell you anything?" / "Does it mean nothing to you?" and "Non ti darò..." = "I won’t give you...".
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, va tutto bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something to someone (ti = “to you”; ho = “I have”; mai = “ever/never”). It’s commonly followed by a past participle: non ti ho mai dimenticata/o (I’ve never forgotten you), non ti ho mai incolpato/a (I never blamed you). The past participle can agree with the person being addressed when a direct object pronoun is involved (e.g., dimenticata when speaking to a woman).
target_language_example: Non ti ho mai mentito.
native_language_example: I have never lied to you.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to be concerned. It’s an informal, friendly form because it uses ti (to you). You can add di + something: Non ti preoccupare di quello. For a more formal version (to a stranger), use: Non si preoccupi.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, ti aiuto io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll help you.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or express unwillingness. It’s the negative of "voglio" ("I want"). Often followed by an infinitive verb: "Non voglio parlare" (I don’t want to talk). You can also use it with a noun/pronoun: "Non voglio questo" (I don’t want this). In conversation, the subject "io" is usually omitted: "Non voglio..."
target_language_example: Non voglio uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out tonight.

meaning: "I don't want (that)…" (used to introduce what you don’t want to happen).
additional_notes: Followed by the subjunctive to express something you don’t want: non voglio che + (io/tu/lui...) verb in the subjunctive. Common after this phrase: sia, vada, venga, faccia, dica, etc. For giving a direct order to someone, you can also use the imperative: Non parlare! (= Don’t talk!).
target_language_example: Non voglio che tu lo dica a nessuno.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used to negate statements with the verb essere (to be) in the present tense: non + è. It can be followed by an adjective (non è commestibile), a noun phrase (non è colpa mia), a place/state (non è a casa), or in questions (Non è stanca?). Often translated as “isn’t” in English.
target_language_example: Oggi non è possibile.
native_language_example: Today it isn’t possible.

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened or isn’t finished so far (up to now). It’s the negative form of “è già” (“already is”). It can be followed by an adjective (“non è ancora pronto”) or by a past participle to form “has/have not yet” (“non è ancora arrivato/a”). Agreement: arrivato (male), arrivata (female), arrivati/e (plural). You can replace “è” with other forms of essere: “non sono ancora”, “non era ancora”, etc.
target_language_example: Non è ancora pronto, ma tra dieci minuti lo sarà.
native_language_example: It’s not ready yet, but it will be in ten minutes.

meaning: “it’s not like that / it’s not so.”
additional_notes: Used to correct or disagree with a statement or impression (often meaning “that’s not the case”). It can also mean “not that + adjective/adverb” when followed by a description (e.g., non è così alto = not that tall; non è così romantico = not that romantic).
target_language_example: No, non è così: non è così semplice come sembra.
native_language_example: No, it’s not like that: it’s not as simple as it seems.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult or challenging. You can follow it with an infinitive to say what is hard: “Non è facile + verb (in the infinitive)” (e.g., non è facile imparare…, non è facile sbarazzarsi di…). You can also add “nemmeno” to mean “not even” / “not… either”: “Non è facile nemmeno per lui” = “It’s not easy for him either.”
target_language_example: Non è facile trovare casa a Milano.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to find a home in Milan.

meaning: "it’s not my…" / "it’s not my thing (my style/strength/type)."
additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t suit you or isn’t typical of you. It’s usually followed by a noun or expression, e.g. "non è il mio forte" (it’s not my strength), "non è il mio tipo" (not my type), "non è il mio solito..." (not my usual...). Literally it means “it’s not mine,” but in these contexts it often matches English “it’s not my thing.”
target_language_example: Grazie, ma ballare non è il mio forte.
native_language_example: Thanks, but dancing isn’t my strong point.

meaning: “(he/she/it) is not able to” / “cannot” (is not capable of).
additional_notes: Used to say someone lacks the ability, capacity, or means to do something (temporary or more general). It’s a more formal/neutral alternative to “non può”. Conjugate “essere” for other subjects: “non sono in grado di” (I’m not able to), “non siamo in grado di” (we’re not able to), etc. Followed by an infinitive verb: “non è in grado di + fare/andare/parlare…”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non siamo in grado di aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, we’re not able to help you today.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened (past experience) or is never true (a habitual/always-negative statement). It’s most common with “essere” (è) but the pattern works with other verbs too: “non ho mai… / non sono mai… / non torna mai…”. Word order: “non” goes before the verb; “mai” typically comes after it.
target_language_example: Tom non è mai stato a Roma.
native_language_example: Tom has never been to Rome.

additional_notes: Uses the negative (non) + "ever" (mai) + past participle of essere (stato) to say something never happened or was never true up to a point in time. Common with adjectives (e.g., bravo, generoso) and with past participles in the passive (e.g., catturato, scoperto). Can refer to a person (lui) or a thing (it).
target_language_example: Il mio computer non è mai stato così lento.
native_language_example: My computer has never been this slow.

additional_notes: Negative past with "mai" (“never”) + "è stato" (past of essere). Used to say someone has never been somewhere (Non è mai stato a/in...), or that something/someone never was a certain thing (Non è mai stato il mio ragazzo; non è mai stato un grande ballerino). With a thing/idea as subject it can mean “has never been” in the sense of “has never been part of” (Viaggiare non è mai stato nei suoi piani). Changes with person/number: non sono mai stato/a, non sei mai stato/a, non siamo mai stati/e, etc.
target_language_example: Non è mai stato a Roma.
native_language_example: He has never been to Rome.

meaning: “he never came back / he has never returned.”
additional_notes: Used to say that a (male) person did not return after going somewhere or doing something. Common with places introduced by da/dal/dalla (“from”) or in (“to/in”): “Non è mai tornato dal viaggio” = he never came back from the trip; “Non è mai tornato in Iraq” = he never returned to Iraq. Often implies the return was expected and (depending on context) can sound serious or dramatic.
target_language_example: Dopo la guerra, non è mai tornato a casa.
native_language_example: After the war, he never came back home.

additional_notes: Used to say something has changed and is not true anymore: “Tom non è più uno studente” = “Tom is no longer a student.” It’s also used in comparisons with “di quanto (non) …”: “Non è più X di quanto …” = “It’s no more X than …” (meaning: not X).
target_language_example: Da quando è andata in pensione, non è più stressata.
native_language_example: Since she retired, she’s not stressed anymore.

meaning: "has not been" / "was not" (often used in the passive).
additional_notes: Made of non + è ("is/has") + stato (past participle of essere, "been"). Very common in passive sentences: non è stato + past participle (presentato, approvato, tradotto) = "was/has not been presented/approved/translated." Often the subject is understood (e.g., "il progetto"), so English may need "it" or "the project." For feminine/plural subjects, stato changes: non è stata, non sono stati/e.
target_language_example: Il pagamento non è stato ricevuto.
native_language_example: The payment has not been received.

additional_notes: Used to say that nothing occurred, often to reassure someone or to emphasize that there were no consequences. It can refer to a specific time (“today”, “so far”) or to a person (“Nothing happened to him/her”). The tense is passato prossimo (è successo), which in English can be either past simple (“nothing happened”) or present perfect (“nothing has happened”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: non è successo nulla.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: nothing happened.

additional_notes: Used to negate a noun phrase with the indefinite article un (masculine singular). Structure: [subject] + non è un + [noun/adjective]. For feminine singular, use non è una; for plural, use non sono (dei/delle) depending on context.
target_language_example: Questo non è un problema.
native_language_example: This is not a problem.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone does not belong to a category or is not what someone claims. It’s the negative form of “è una” (= “it’s a…”) and must be followed by a feminine singular noun/adjective used as a noun (e.g., “una verdura”, “una strategia”). For masculine, use “non è un … / non è uno …”.
target_language_example: Questo non è una buona idea.
native_language_example: This isn’t a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to state that someone is not a student. You can add details after "studente" (e.g., "universitario" = university student) or describe the kind of student (e.g., "così pigro" = that lazy, "ordinario" = ordinary). "È" (is) changes with the subject: "non sono uno studente" (I’m not a student), "non sei uno studente" (you’re not a student), "non siamo studenti" (we’re not students). In the plural, drop "uno": "non sono studenti".
target_language_example: Lei non è uno studente, è un’insegnante.
native_language_example: She isn’t a student; she’s a teacher.

meaning: “that’s not true” / “isn’t it true?” (tag question: “isn’t it?”).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) as a statement to deny something: “Non è vero.” = “That’s not true.” (2) at the end of a sentence as a tag question to seek confirmation or agreement, often like “isn’t it?” / “right?”: “È splendido, non è vero?” In speech it can sound slightly insistent depending on tone.
target_language_example: Domani vieni anche tu, non è vero?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow too, aren’t you?

meaning: “despite the rain” / “in spite of the rain.”
additional_notes: Used to say something happened even though it was raining. It typically comes before the clause it modifies (e.g., “Nonostante la pioggia, siamo usciti”) or after it (as in the examples). You can swap in other nouns: nonostante il freddo (despite the cold), nonostante il traffico (despite the traffic).
target_language_example: Nonostante la pioggia, abbiamo fatto una passeggiata.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "avere" or "sentire" (e.g., "Ho nostalgia di casa", "Sento nostalgia di casa") to say you miss your home/your country/your usual place. In English, "nostalgia" is often about the past in general, but in Italian this phrase specifically means being homesick.
target_language_example: Dopo una settimana all’estero, ho nostalgia di casa.
native_language_example: After a week abroad, I’m homesick.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a house or home that belongs to “us.” It agrees with the feminine noun casa, so you say nostra (not nostro). Often used with the definite article: la nostra casa = “our house/home.” Can be used for location (di fronte alla nostra casa = “in front of our house”) or comparison (Rispetto alla nostra casa… = “Compared to our house…”).
target_language_example: Stasera ceniamo nella nostra casa.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re having dinner at our house.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular possessive: nostra + squadra (f.). Common for sports teams, work groups, school teams, or any organized group. Often follows a preposition: nella nostra squadra (in our team), alla nostra squadra (to our team).
target_language_example: Siamo orgogliosi della nostra squadra.
native_language_example: We’re proud of our team.

additional_notes: Plural of "la nostra vita". Used to talk about the lives of a group that includes the speaker (noi). Often appears after a preposition (e.g., "nelle nostre vite" = "in our lives"). In dramatic contexts, "salvare le nostre vite" means "to save our lives."
target_language_example: Questo viaggio ha cambiato le nostre vite.
native_language_example: This trip changed our lives.

additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase to talk about help coming from “us” (the speaker and others). Often appears with verbs like offrire (to offer), chiedere (to ask for), ringraziare per (to thank for), avere/avere bisogno di (to need), and rifiutare (to refuse). You’ll usually see it with an article or preposition: il nostro aiuto (our help), del nostro aiuto (of our help / some of our help), per il nostro aiuto (for our help).
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno, ti diamo il nostro aiuto.
native_language_example: If you need it, we’ll give you our help.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "nostro" (our) with the noun "insegnante" (teacher). In Italian, possessives are usually used with the definite article: "il nostro insegnante" (our teacher), "la nostra insegnante" (our (female) teacher). "Insegnante" can refer to a male or female teacher; the article often shows gender.
target_language_example: Il nostro insegnante arriva sempre in orario.
native_language_example: Our teacher always arrives on time.

meaning: to have nothing to do with; no involvement/connection with.
additional_notes: Used to deny any link, responsibility, or involvement with something/someone. Very common with verbs like: “avere nulla a che fare con …” (I have nothing to do with …) and “non c’entra nulla con …” (similar meaning). You can also use it to say you don’t want any dealings with a person: “Non voglio nulla a che fare con lui/lei.”
target_language_example: Questa decisione non ha nulla a che fare con te.
native_language_example: This decision has nothing to do with you.

meaning: “nothing to …” (e.g., nothing to do / nothing to hide).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say there is nothing to do/see/say, etc.: “nulla da + infinitive.” Common in negatives: “non ho nulla da …” = “I have nothing to ….” Fixed phrase “Non c’è nulla da fare” means “There’s nothing we can do” (often implying a situation can’t be changed).
target_language_example: Non ho nulla da aggiungere.
native_language_example: I have nothing to add.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere" (to have): "(non) avere nulla da perdere" = "to have nothing to lose." It often expresses that there’s no risk or no worse outcome possible, so you might as well try. You can change the subject and tense: "Non ho nulla da perdere" (I have nothing to lose), "Non avevamo nulla da perdere" (we had nothing to lose).
target_language_example: Proviamo: non abbiamo nulla da perdere.
native_language_example: Let’s try: we have nothing to lose.

additional_notes: Used to deny having done/said/seen something like that, often after an accusation or misunderstanding. It commonly follows negatives like non… (e.g., Non ho detto nulla del genere). Can also be used after mai (non ho mai visto nulla del genere).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non intendevo nulla del genere.
native_language_example: Relax, I didn’t mean anything like that.

meaning: “nothing to” (worry about / be ashamed of / complain about, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (often with essere + adjective/noun) to mean there is no reason or no thing that justifies the feeling/action: “nulla di cui preoccuparsi” (nothing to worry about), “nulla di cui vergognarsi” (nothing to be ashamed of), “nulla di cui lamentarsi” (nothing to complain about). It refers back to an implied reason/cause (“di cui” = “about which/of which”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non c’è nulla di cui aver paura.
native_language_example: Relax, there’s nothing to be afraid of.

additional_notes: Used after negation (non) to say someone did nothing wrong: “non ho fatto nulla di sbagliato.” It’s also common with (non) vedere + nulla di sbagliato to mean “(not) see anything wrong (with it)”: “Non ci vedo nulla di sbagliato.” The “di” is required here after nulla.
target_language_example: Non vedo nulla di sbagliato nel chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: I don’t see anything wrong with asking for help.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things share no similarities or interests. Very common with the verb avere: “(Non) avere nulla in comune (con qualcuno/qualcosa)” = “to have nothing in common (with someone/something).” It’s a negative expression; in Italian you typically keep the negative “non” in the sentence (e.g., “Non ho…”).
target_language_example: Io e Marco non abbiamo nulla in comune.
native_language_example: Marco and I have nothing in common.

additional_notes: "Nuotando" is the gerund (-ing form) of "nuotare" (to swim). It’s commonly used with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno nuotando nel fiume" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you all are/they are swimming in the river."
target_language_example: Stanno nuotando nel fiume vicino al ponte.
native_language_example: They are swimming in the river near the bridge.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "nuotare" (to swim) + "nel" (= in the, in the + masculine singular) + "fiume" (river). It refers to swimming in a river (as opposed to a pool or the sea). You can change the place: "nuotare nel lago" (in the lake), "nuotare nel mare" (in the sea).
target_language_example: In estate mi piace nuotare nel fiume con gli amici.
native_language_example: In summer I like to swim in the river with friends.

additional_notes: Used to describe a car that is newly bought or new to the speaker. Agree gender/number: una nuova auto (a new car), le nuove auto (the new cars). The adjective usually comes before the noun here, but you may also hear un’auto nuova.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di una nuova auto perché la mia è vecchia.
native_language_example: I need a new car because mine is old.

additional_notes: Used to describe a car that is newly bought or brand new. It’s a noun phrase: "nuova" (new) agrees in gender/number with "automobile" (feminine), so you’ll also see plural "nuove automobili". In everyday speech, Italians often say "una nuova macchina" instead of "una nuova automobile".
target_language_example: Sto cercando una nuova automobile, ma è troppo cara.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a new car, but it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Means a house or home that is newly bought/rented/built for someone. Often used in welcome phrases like "Benvenuto/a nella tua/sua/vostra nuova casa" (Welcome to your/his-her/your [plural/formal] new home). "Casa" can mean both "house" (the building) and "home" (the place you live).
target_language_example: Siamo felici della nostra nuova casa.
native_language_example: We’re happy with our new home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s new position/work, often after they’ve started a new job. Common in formal or neutral contexts; in everyday speech you’ll also hear "nuovo lavoro". With a possessive it’s usually "il mio/il tuo/il suo nuovo impiego"; with congratulations: "Congratulazioni per il tuo/vostro nuovo impiego".
target_language_example: In bocca al lupo per il tuo nuovo impiego!
native_language_example: Good luck with your new job!

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s recently started or recently changed job. Often appears with a possessive: il mio/il tuo/il suo nuovo lavoro (“my/your/his-her new job”). You can ask about it with: Ti piace il tuo nuovo lavoro? (“Do you like your new job?”) or speak about it with: parlare/chiedere del suo nuovo lavoro (“to talk/ask about his/her new job”).
target_language_example: Sono felice del mio nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m happy with my new job.

meaning: "or not?" (to press for a clear yes/no answer).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a question after a statement to emphasize that the speaker wants a definite answer. It can sound insistent or impatient depending on tone. Often pairs with a verb phrase: "Vuoi venire o no?"
target_language_example: Andiamo al cinema stasera, sì o no?
native_language_example: Are we going to the movies tonight, yes or no?

additional_notes: Used after an example to mean you’re not being exact, or you don’t know/remember the precise thing. Common in casual speech to keep the list open ("…or something similar").
target_language_example: Prendiamo un caffè o qualcosa del genere dopo pranzo.
native_language_example: Let’s grab a coffee or something like that after lunch.

meaning: eyes open; keep your eyes open / watch out.
additional_notes: Often used as **a occhi aperti** (“with eyes open”), especially in **sognare a occhi aperti** = “to daydream.” On its own (**Occhi aperti!**) it’s a warning meaning “Keep your eyes open / Pay attention.”
target_language_example: Occhi aperti: qui le biciclette passano veloci.
native_language_example: Keep your eyes open: bikes go by fast here.

additional_notes: Glasses used for reading/close-up work. Often used with the verb servire (e.g., A me servono degli occhiali da lettura = I need reading glasses). You can say occhiali da lettura with or without an article; miei/tuoi/suoi can be added (i miei occhiali da lettura).
target_language_example: Non riesco a leggere il menù: ho dimenticato gli occhiali da lettura.
native_language_example: I can’t read the menu: I forgot my reading glasses.

additional_notes: "Odi" is the 2nd-person singular (tu) present of "odiare" (to hate). "Così tanto" means "so much/so much like this" and intensifies the verb. It’s often used in questions like "Perché mi/ci/la/lo odi così tanto?" where the object can be a pronoun (mi = me, ci = us, la = her/it f., lo = him/it m.) or a noun.
target_language_example: Non capisco perché mi odi così tanto.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why you hate me so much.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the intensity of hate. It’s the verb "odia" (he/she hates) + "così tanto" (so much). Often appears in questions with "Perché...?" (Why...?) or with a pronoun/object after it (e.g., "mi", "ti", "i cani"). You can change the subject by changing the verb: "odio così tanto" (I hate so much), "odi così tanto" (you hate so much), "odiano così tanto" (they hate so much).
target_language_example: Perché lo odia così tanto?
native_language_example: Why does he/she hate him so much?

additional_notes: Used to say you dislike being in a certain state or situation. "Odio" is the 1st-person singular ("I hate"); the subject pronoun "io" is often omitted. It’s followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: "Odio essere stanco" (tired), "Odio essere un problema" (a problem). You can change the person: "odi essere" (you hate being), "odia essere" (he/she hates being), etc.
target_language_example: Odio essere in ritardo.
native_language_example: I hate being late.

meaning: “I hate the …” (used before masculine plural nouns).
additional_notes: "Odio" is the 1st person singular of *odiare* (“to hate”). "Gli" is the masculine plural definite article used before nouns starting with a vowel (e.g., *gli amici*) or with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, y (e.g., *gli studenti*, *gli zaini*). With other masculine plural nouns you use *i* (e.g., *odio i cani*).
target_language_example: Odio gli studenti che non ascoltano.
native_language_example: I hate the students who don’t listen.

additional_notes: Used to say you strongly dislike a category of things/people (often in general). It’s the verb *odiare* (to hate) + the masculine plural definite article *i* (the). Use it before masculine plural nouns: *odio i topi* (mice), *odio i politici* (politicians).
target_language_example: Odio i film dell'orrore.
native_language_example: I hate horror movies.

meaning: "I hate the" (used before feminine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used to express strong dislike. "Odio" is the 1st-person singular of "odiare" (to hate). "Le" is the feminine plural definite article (the). With masculine plural nouns you use "odio i" (e.g., "Odio i rumori"), and with singular nouns "odio il/la" depending on gender.
target_language_example: Odio le code al supermercato.
native_language_example: I hate the lines at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a situation or action you strongly dislike. The subject pronoun is often omitted in Italian, so you’ll frequently see just “Odio quando …”. The verb in the “quando” clause matches who does the action (e.g., “odio quando mente” = I hate it when he/she lies).
target_language_example: Odio quando la gente parla ad alta voce sul treno.
native_language_example: I hate it when people talk loudly on the train.

meaning: "I hate … as much as …" (to hate equally much).
additional_notes: Used to compare how much you hate two people/things. It’s built from: "odio" = "I hate" + "tanto quanto" = "as much as". Often used with object pronouns before the verb (la/le/li = her/them; ti/te = you). You can also replace "odio" with other verbs (e.g., "amo tanto quanto" = "I love as much as").
target_language_example: Odio questo film tanto quanto il primo.
native_language_example: I hate this movie as much as the first one.

additional_notes: A very solemn, dramatic phrase (often religious/ritual or literary), used to express offering one’s own death as a sacrifice. The person you’re offering it to is shown with an indirect object pronoun: ti (to you, informal singular), vi (to you, plural or formal), le (to her / to you formal feminine). Word-for-word it’s clear: offro = I offer, la mia morte = my death.
target_language_example: Per la tua salvezza, ti offro la mia morte.
native_language_example: For your salvation, I offer you my death.

meaning: anything else; everything else (often: “more than anything else”).
additional_notes: Used to compare priorities or preferences. Common patterns: “più di ogni altra cosa” = “more than anything else”; “prima di ogni altra cosa” = “before anything else/above all.” Without “più/prima,” it can mean “everything else” in a broader sense (e.g., “Ogni altra cosa…” = “Everything else…”).
target_language_example: Per me, la salute viene prima di ogni altra cosa.
native_language_example: For me, health comes before anything else.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens once a year or repeats year after year. Often placed at the end of the sentence (as in the examples), but it can also go near the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Andiamo in Italia ogni anno ad agosto.
native_language_example: We go to Italy every year in August.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on Sundays (a recurring habit). You can add more detail after it, e.g. "ogni domenica mattina" (every Sunday morning).
target_language_example: Andiamo al mercato ogni domenica.
native_language_example: We go to the market every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each weekend. You can also say "ogni weekend" (more informal/loanword).
target_language_example: Andiamo al mercato ogni fine settimana.
native_language_example: We go to the market every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens daily with one or more exceptions. Put the excluded day/date/thing after "tranne" (e.g., "tranne la domenica", "tranne oggi").
target_language_example: Sono aperti ogni giorno tranne il lunedì.
native_language_example: They’re open every day except Monday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly on Mondays (a routine or habit). With ongoing routines in the present: "Ogni lunedì vado..."; in the past for repeated actions: "Ogni lunedì andavo/giocavo...".
target_language_example: Ogni lunedì ho lezione di italiano alle sei.
native_language_example: Every Monday I have an Italian lesson at six.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a routine or repeated action that happens each morning. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence (e.g., “Ogni mattina…” / “…ogni mattina”).
target_language_example: Ogni mattina prendo l’autobus alle otto.
native_language_example: Every morning I take the bus at eight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly in the evenings. Often placed at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Vado a letto alle dieci ogni sera"), but it can also appear at the beginning for emphasis ("Ogni sera, ..."). Note: it refers to the evening time; for "every night" meaning nighttime, Italians also commonly say "ogni notte."
target_language_example: Studio un po' di italiano ogni sera.
native_language_example: I study a bit of Italian every evening.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a weekly routine or frequency. It can modify a verb directly (e.g., "Vado... ogni settimana") and often answers the question "Quanto spesso?" (How often?).
target_language_example: Faccio la spesa ogni settimana.
native_language_example: I do the grocery shopping every week.

additional_notes: Introduces a repeated situation: something happens each time another action/event happens. It’s usually followed by a verb phrase (often in the present tense). Common in routines and habits.
target_language_example: Ogni volta che piove, porto l’ombrello.
native_language_example: Whenever it rains, I bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Used to show surprise, shock, frustration, or strong emotion, often followed by a noun like Dio ("Oh, mio Dio!" = "Oh my God!") or amore ("Oh, mio amore" = "Oh, my love"). In speech it’s very common; punctuation (comma, exclamation) can vary.
target_language_example: Oh, mio Dio, che paura!
native_language_example: Oh my God, that was scary!

meaning: "Oh no!" (expression of surprise, worry, disappointment; also used to refuse politely).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation reacting to bad news or a problem (Oh, no!). It can also be used before a refusal: "Oh, no, grazie" = "Oh no, thank you." Often repeated for emphasis: "Oh, no, no, no." Punctuation varies ("Oh, no!", "Oh no!", "Oh, no.").
target_language_example: Oh, no! Ho dimenticato le chiavi a casa.
native_language_example: Oh no! I forgot my keys at home.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of **ordinare** (“to order/tell”) with **avere** (e.g., *ho/ha/abbiamo/hanno ordinato*). Structure: **ordinare a + someone + di + infinitive** → *Ho ordinato al cane di sedersi* (“I told the dog to sit”). You can swap the subject to change who gave the command (io, lei, loro, Mary, etc.).
target_language_example: Il veterinario ha ordinato al cane di sedersi prima della visita.
native_language_example: The vet ordered/told the dog to sit before the checkup.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ordinare" (to order, e.g., food). "Ordinato" is the past participle, typically used in the passato prossimo with "avere" (e.g., "Ho/Abbiamo/Hanno ordinato..."). "Della" is a partitive meaning "some" (unspecified amount) + feminine singular noun "pizza". In other contexts, "ordinare" can also mean "to tidy/put in order," but here it clearly means ordering food.
target_language_example: Stasera abbiamo ordinato della pizza a domicilio.
native_language_example: Tonight we ordered some pizza for delivery.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ordinare" (to order). In these examples it’s in the passato prossimo (present perfect): "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno ordinato" + the thing ordered. Common when ordering food at a restaurant, by phone, or online (e.g., "Ho ordinato una pizza al telefono").
target_language_example: Abbiamo ordinato una pizza da asporto.
native_language_example: We ordered a pizza to take away.

meaning: "hours a day" / "per day" (talking about a daily number of hours).
additional_notes: Used after a number to say how many hours something happens each day: "otto ore al giorno" = "eight hours a day." Common with routines and habits (sleeping, working, studying). You can also see the same pattern with other units: "volte al giorno" (times a day), "litri al giorno" (liters a day).
target_language_example: Cerco di camminare almeno un'ora al giorno.
native_language_example: I try to walk at least an hour a day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels pride about a person or thing: "essere orgoglioso/a di + noun/pronoun". The form changes with the subject: orgoglioso (man), orgogliosa (woman), orgogliosi (mixed/men plural), orgogliose (women plural). Often followed by pronouns like "di me" (of me), "di te" (of you), "di sé" (of himself/herself/themselves).
target_language_example: Sono orgogliosa di te per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I'm proud of you for what you did.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel pride about someone or something. It’s often followed by a person (orgoglioso di te/lei/lui) or a noun (orgoglioso di mia figlia). It can also refer to yourself: orgoglioso di me stesso/a (adjust the ending for gender: orgoglioso = male, orgogliosa = female).
target_language_example: Sono orgogliosa di quello che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I'm proud of what I did.

additional_notes: Literally “to observe the birds.” Used for the activity/hobby of birdwatching; often with piacere (“to like”) or as an infinitive subject: “Osservare gli uccelli è…”.
target_language_example: Nel fine settimana mi piace osservare gli uccelli al parco.
native_language_example: On the weekend I like to watch birds in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone's father is (job/nationality/qualities) or where he is. In real sentences you usually include an article or possessive: *il padre è…* (“the father is…”), *suo padre è…* (“his/her father is…”), *mio padre è…* (“my father is…”).
target_language_example: Mio padre è medico.
native_language_example: My father is a doctor.

additional_notes: Used for paying rent for an apartment/home. In real conversation, Italians often say "pagare l’affitto" (without "suo") when it’s clear whose rent it is. Possessives agree with the person: "il mio affitto" (my rent), "il tuo affitto" (your rent), "il suo affitto" (his/her/your formal rent), "il nostro/vostro/loro affitto".
target_language_example: Ricordati di pagare il tuo affitto entro fine mese.
native_language_example: Remember to pay your rent by the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used when choosing a payment method (especially in shops, restaurants, hotels). Often contrasted with paying by card: "in contanti" = cash, "con la carta"/"con carta di credito" = by card. You can use it in questions ("Vuole pagare in contanti?") or to state your preference ("Vorrei pagare in contanti.").
target_language_example: Scusi, posso pagare in contanti?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I pay in cash?

meaning: a couple of; a pair of.
additional_notes: Used with a number (usually "un") to mean an approximate small quantity ("un paio di minuti" = a couple of minutes). It can also mean a literal pair of things that come in twos, especially clothing/items like socks, boots, scissors: "un paio di calze/stivali/forbici". With people, "un paio di amici/amiche" means “a couple of friends” (approx. two).
target_language_example: Aspetta un paio di minuti, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait a couple of minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one set of two shoes. "Un paio di..." is a very common pattern meaning "a pair of..." (e.g., un paio di calzini = a pair of socks). Often followed by extra details: "un paio di scarpe da tennis" = a pair of tennis shoes/sneakers; "un altro paio di scarpe" = another pair of shoes.
target_language_example: Mi serve un paio di scarpe nuove.
native_language_example: I need a new pair of shoes.

additional_notes: Literally “ball for soccer/football.” In Italy, *calcio* means soccer, so *palla da calcio* is the ball used to play soccer. You’ll often see the pattern *[noun] da [sport]* to mean “(something) for (a sport)” (e.g., *scarpe da calcio* = soccer shoes).
target_language_example: Hai visto la mia palla da calcio?
native_language_example: Have you seen my soccer ball?

additional_notes: “Per colazione” means “for breakfast” (literally “for breakfast/at breakfast time”). Often you’ll hear it with an article and plural: “dei pancake per colazione” = “(some) pancakes for breakfast.” You can also say “a colazione” to mean “for breakfast/at breakfast”: “pancake a colazione.”
target_language_example: Domani voglio i pancake per colazione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I want pancakes for breakfast.

additional_notes: A simple grocery/food list. Often used with verbs like “servire” (to need): “Ti serve/ti servono…?” = “Do you need…?” Use “serve” for a singular item and “servono” for multiple items; here it’s usually “servono” because it’s a list of several things.
target_language_example: Mi servono pane, salsiccia e formaggio per la cena.
native_language_example: I need bread, sausage, and cheese for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person speaks the French language. It can appear in statements (e.g., “Nessuno di noi parla il francese”) or in questions (“Qualcuno qui parla il francese?”). With "si" it becomes general/impersonal: “Si parla il francese in Francia” = “French is spoken in France.” You can swap in other languages: “parla l’italiano / parla l’inglese / parla lo spagnolo.”
target_language_example: Mi scusi, lei parla il francese?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used to say you are in conversation with someone. Often appears with "stare" to form the present/past continuous ("sto/stai/sta... parlando con..." = "I am/you are/he is... talking with..."). You can also use it after verbs like "pensavo di stare" ("I thought I was...").
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare adesso: sto parlando con il dottore.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now: I'm talking with the doctor.

meaning: 'speaking/talking about' or 'as for/when it comes to' (introducing a topic).
additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun to say what the conversation is about: "parlare di + [person/thing]". At the start of a sentence, "Parlando di…" works like "Speaking of…" to introduce or shift to a topic.
target_language_example: Parlando di viaggi, sei mai stato in Sicilia?
native_language_example: Speaking of travel, have you ever been to Sicily?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is using the French language. Often follows verbs like "stare" (stanno/stava/stessero parlando) or appears in questions: "Stanno parlando in francese?". You can swap in other languages: "parlando in italiano / in inglese / in spagnolo".
target_language_example: Scusa, state parlando in francese?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you speaking in French?

additional_notes: Used with a person or group you are having a conversation with: parlare con + someone (e.g., parlare con Tom, parlare con la gente). In Italian it can translate as either “talk to” or “talk with” depending on context. It’s a common verb phrase and is followed directly by the person (no extra preposition like “a”).
target_language_example: Posso parlare con te un attimo?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

meaning: to talk/speak with her; or (formal) to talk/speak with you.
additional_notes: "Lei" can mean "her" (referring to a woman) or the polite/formal "you" (often written "Lei" capitalized, but not always). Used when you want to speak directly to that person: "devo parlare con lei" = "I need to speak with her/you (formal)."
target_language_example: Posso parlare con lei un momento?
native_language_example: Can I speak with you for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that you want to communicate directly with a group of people ("them"). "Parlare" can mean "to speak" or "to talk"; "con" = "with"; "loro" is the stressed pronoun meaning "them" (used after prepositions like "con"). Common in questions and polite requests: "Posso parlare con loro, per piacere?"
target_language_example: Se hai un problema, puoi parlare con loro dopo la riunione.
native_language_example: If you have a problem, you can talk with them after the meeting.

meaning: 'to talk to him' / 'to speak with him'.
additional_notes: Used when you want to have a conversation with a male person (lui = him). Often appears with polite requests (Potresti…? / Può…?) or suggestions (Dovremmo…).
target_language_example: Devo parlare con lui prima della riunione.
native_language_example: I need to talk to him before the meeting.

meaning: to talk to me; to speak with me.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants/needs to have a conversation with you. Often follows verbs like volere (to want), dovere (to have to), potere (to be able to): “Vuoi parlare con me?” = “Do you want to talk to me?” You can swap “me” for other pronouns: parlare con te (you), con lui/lei (him/her), con noi (us), con loro (them).
target_language_example: Scusa, puoi parlare con me un attimo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you talk to me for a moment?

meaning: to talk to us; to speak with us.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants or is asked to have a conversation with “us.” It can be about any topic or language (e.g., “in francese”). You’ll often see it with verbs like volere (to want), dovere (should), potere (could), provare (to try). Pronouns can change: parlare con me/te/lui/lei/voi/loro.
target_language_example: Se hai domande, puoi parlare con noi dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: If you have questions, you can talk to us after the lesson.

meaning: to talk to you / to speak with you.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants a conversation with the person they’re addressing. It can sound neutral (“talk with you”) or more serious depending on tone and context (e.g., “I need to talk to you”). Often appears after verbs like volere (to want), dovere (to have to), potere (can), or in reported speech (ha detto che…).
target_language_example: Dopo la lezione, devo parlare con te un momento.
native_language_example: After class, I have to talk to you for a moment.

meaning: to speak/talk with you (plural or formal).
additional_notes: "Voi" can mean "you" when talking to more than one person. In some contexts it can also be used as a formal/polite "you" (though "Lei" is more common in standard modern Italian). Often used after verbs like "desiderare" (to wish) or "vorrei" (I would like) to express wanting to talk with someone.
target_language_example: Vorrei parlare con voi un momento.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with you for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "parlare" (to speak) + the language with the definite article: "il francese" (French). It’s common with modal verbs like "potere" (can) and "sapere" (know how to): "posso parlare il francese", "so parlare il francese". You can also say "parlare francese" without the article, but beginners will often hear it with the article.
target_language_example: Sai parlare il francese?
native_language_example: Can you speak French?

additional_notes: Used before the name of a language to say what language someone uses. Common with verbs like potere/preferire/volere: “Posso parlare in…”, “Preferisco parlare in…”. In everyday Italian you’ll also often hear “parlare + language” without “in” (e.g., “Parlo italiano”), but “parlare in + language” is correct especially when emphasizing the language being used.
target_language_example: Scusi, può parlare in inglese, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you speak in English, please?

additional_notes: Used with "parlare" + "in" + language to say what language you speak (similar to "parlare in italiano/inglese"). You may also hear "parlare berbero" without "in".
target_language_example: Lei sa parlare in berbero molto bene.
native_language_example: She can speak Berber very well.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "parlare in + language" to say what language you speak (e.g., parlare in italiano/inglese). Often used with verbs like "riuscire a" (to manage to/can) and in questions like "Riesci a parlare in…?"
target_language_example: Non riesco a parlare in esperanto, ma lo capisco un po'.
native_language_example: I can’t speak in Esperanto, but I understand it a little.

additional_notes: Used to say someone can/does speak the French language. Often follows verbs like potere (can), riuscire a (manage to), and sapere (know how to): e.g., Posso parlare in francese; Sai parlare in francese?
target_language_example: Non so parlare in francese, ma capisco un po'.
native_language_example: I can't speak French, but I understand a little.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone's French ability/style to a male person previously mentioned (“lui” = “him”). Often appears in questions about ability, especially with modal/ability verbs like potere (can), riuscire (manage to), sapere (know how to). You can change the person: come lei (like her), come loro (like them).
target_language_example: Non credo di poter parlare in francese come lui.
native_language_example: I don’t think I can speak French like him.

additional_notes: Used to say that the language you’re speaking is English. After "parlare" (to speak), Italian often uses "in + [language]": "parlare in italiano", "parlare in francese". It can be used for a general ability ("Parlare in inglese è difficile") or in a specific situation ("parlare in inglese con Mary").
target_language_example: Posso parlare in inglese, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I speak in English, please?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "parlare" + a language name. You can use it after verbs like "sapere" (to know how to) and "potere" (to be able to): "Sai parlare inglese?" / "Posso parlare inglese". The subject pronoun is often omitted: "Parli inglese?" is very common.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non parlo inglese.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak English.

meaning: to badmouth others; to speak badly about other people.
additional_notes: Uses the pattern "parlare male di + person" (to speak badly about someone). "Degli altri" means "about others / about other people". It often implies criticizing or gossiping about people in an unkind way.
target_language_example: Non mi piace parlare male degli altri.
native_language_example: I don't like to badmouth other people.

meaning: to speak more than three languages.
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone can speak more than three languages. Often appears in questions with verbs like potere (puoi/può), sapere (sai/sapete), or riuscire a (riesci/riesce a), all meaning “can/be able to” with slightly different nuance (riuscire a = manage to).
target_language_example: Mia sorella sa parlare più di tre lingue.
native_language_example: My sister can speak more than three languages.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to slow down their speech (common in shops, at offices, or in language-learning situations). Often appears in requests like "Può/Potrebbe parlare più lentamente?" and can be made even more polite with "per favore".
target_language_example: Scusi, può parlare più lentamente? Non capisco bene.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you speak more slowly? I don’t understand well.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary avere in the passato prossimo: ho/hai/ha parlato con + person (e.g., "Ho parlato con Marco"). It means you spoke with someone; in English it’s often translated as “talked to” or “spoke with.”
target_language_example: Ieri ho parlato con la professoressa dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: Yesterday I talked to the teacher after class.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo (e.g., ho/hai/avete parlato con lei) to say you already spoke to someone. “Lei” can mean “her,” but it’s also the polite form of “you” (so “parlato con Lei” can mean “spoken with you,” formal).
target_language_example: Ho già parlato con lei, ma non mi ha risposto.
native_language_example: I already spoke to her, but she didn’t answer me.

additional_notes: "Parlato" is the past participle of "parlare" (to speak/talk). It’s commonly used with the auxiliary "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/abbiamo/avete/hanno parlato con loro" = "I/you/we/you(pl.)/they spoke (have spoken) with them." "Con loro" means "with them" (loro = them). In questions you’ll often see it with "mai" to mean "ever": "Hai mai parlato con loro?"
target_language_example: Ho già parlato con loro, ma non mi hanno risposto.
native_language_example: I’ve already spoken with them, but they didn’t answer me.

meaning: spoken to him / talked to him.
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho parlato con lui" (I talked to him). "Con" is often used for "to/with" when talking with someone. Common in questions like "Hai parlato con lui?" (Have you talked to him?).
target_language_example: Ho già parlato con lui, ma non mi ha risposto.
native_language_example: I already talked to him, but he didn’t answer me.

additional_notes: Uses the formal "Lei" form of the verb parlare (parli). Common in polite requests/commands: "Per favore, parli con..." = "Please, talk to...". The person you speak with comes after con (con lei/lui/Tom).
target_language_example: Scusi, parli con il direttore, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please speak with the manager.

additional_notes: Form of "parlare" + "con loro" ("with them"). In these examples it’s often used after "Lascia che..." or "Vuoi che...?" to mean "let me/him/her speak with them" or "do you want me/him/her to speak with them?". "Parli" can also be a formal command (Lei) meaning "Speak with them."
target_language_example: Vuole che parli con loro adesso?
native_language_example: Do you want me to speak with them now?

additional_notes: Used to say what language you speak. In Italian you can say either “parlo berbero” (without “in”) or “parlo in berbero” (with “in”), both meaning you speak Berber. You can add who you speak with (“con…”) or where (“a casa”, “in pubblico”).
target_language_example: Scusi, parlo in berbero e un po’ di italiano.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I speak Berber and a little Italian.

meaning: “I speak in Klingon with …” / “I speak Klingon with …”.
additional_notes: Used to say what language you speak when talking with someone: "parlare in + (lingua)" (in Klingon) + "con" (with). You then add the person: "con te" (with you, informal), "con lei" (with you, formal / with her), "con voi" (with you all / with you, formal in some regions).
target_language_example: Parlo in klingon con te quando giochiamo.
native_language_example: I speak Klingon with you when we play.

meaning: “(He/She) spoke with a full mouth” (while eating).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone talking while their mouth is full of food (often considered bad table manners). The base expression is "parlare con la bocca piena" and you can change the verb for different tenses/persons: "parla", "parlavo", "non parlare con la bocca piena".
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare con la bocca piena.
native_language_example: Please, don’t talk with your mouth full.

additional_notes: Used as an invariable English loanword in Italian (often with a hyphen). It can describe a job, worker, or how someone works: lavorare part-time (to work part-time), un lavoro part-time (a part-time job), un lavoratore part-time (a part-time worker).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un lavoro part-time per finire l'università.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job to finish university.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a portion/section of a larger whole. Often followed by a noun introduced by the fused preposition+article: del = di + il (“of the”); also possible: della, dei, degli, delle depending on the noun (e.g., parte della città). Common in questions like “Which part of the country/tour…?” and in statements like “Only part of the bridge…”.
target_language_example: Ho visto solo parte del film.
native_language_example: I only watched part of the movie.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to or makes up a portion of something else: "fare parte della" = "to be part of" (belong to a group/family/team). It can also mean "some of" when talking about a quantity or an aspect: "parte della storia" = "part of the story." You may also see "da parte della" meaning "from (on behalf of)": "un messaggio da parte della mamma" = "a message from Mom."
target_language_example: Vorrei far parte della squadra.
native_language_example: I’d like to be part of the team.

additional_notes: Used when asking or stating a train’s departure time. You’ll often see it in questions like “A che ora parte il treno…?” (What time does the train leave?) or with places: “parte il treno per Milano” (the train to Milan leaves). Related: “Da quale binario parte…?” (From which platform does it leave?) and “Da quale stazione parte…?” (From which station does it leave?).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, a che ora parte il treno per Roma?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does the train to Rome leave?

additional_notes: Used for taking part in a meeting (in person or online). In the examples, "avresti/avreste dovuto" means "you should have" (a past obligation/regret). "Partecipare" is followed by "a" + the event (a una lezione, a una festa, a una riunione).
target_language_example: Domani non posso partecipare alla riunione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I can’t attend the meeting.

meaning: (has/have) attended the conference; participated in the conference.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "partecipare" (to participate/attend) and the preposition "a" + article (a + la = alla). Often refers to being present at an event like a conference. In questions, it commonly appears as "Chi ha partecipato alla conferenza?" (Who attended the conference?).
target_language_example: Abbiamo partecipato alla conferenza ieri mattina.
native_language_example: We attended the conference yesterday morning.

meaning: "(have) attended the meeting" / "taken part in the meeting".
additional_notes: "Partecipato" is the past participle of "partecipare" (to participate/attend). It’s commonly used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "(io) ho partecipato...", "(loro) hanno partecipato...". "Alla" = "a" + "la" and means "to the" in this context (i.e., going to/being present at the meeting).
target_language_example: Non ho partecipato alla riunione perché ero malato.
native_language_example: I didn’t attend the meeting because I was sick.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a soccer game as an event (watching it on TV, going to it, when it is). In Italy, "calcio" refers to soccer (called "football" in British English).
target_language_example: Andiamo allo stadio per la partita di calcio stasera?
native_language_example: Are we going to the stadium for the soccer match tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone spends a lot of time doing an activity or in a place. Common patterns: passare molto tempo a + infinitive (Passa molto tempo a studiare = He spends a lot of time studying) and passare molto tempo + place (Passa molto tempo a casa/al telefono = He spends a lot of time at home/on the phone).
target_language_example: Passo molto tempo a studiare italiano.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Italian.

passa tutto il suo tempo a

target_language_multi_word_term: passa tutto il suo tempo a
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject (often lui/lei or a name) plus a verb in the infinitive introduced by a: passa tutto il suo tempo a studiare / a chattare. The possessive changes with the person: passo tutto il mio tempo a… (I), passi tutto il tuo tempo a… (you), passiamo tutto il nostro tempo a… (we), passano tutto il loro tempo a… (they). Often implies “always/constantly doing it,” sometimes with a mildly critical tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Ultimamente passa tutto il suo tempo a giocare ai videogiochi.
native_language_example: Lately he spends all his time playing video games.

additional_notes: Used to say you are with someone during a period of time (hanging out, being together). Con is followed by a person/pronoun: con me (with me), con te, con lui/lei, con noi, con voi, con loro. The verb passare changes with the subject (passo, passi, passa, passiamo, passate, passano).
target_language_example: Stasera voglio passare del tempo con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I want to spend time with my friends.

additional_notes: Common way to say you enjoy/want to be with someone socially. Uses the verb "passare" (to spend/pass) + "del tempo" (some time). "Con lei" means "with her" (formal/polite or “her” in general). For "with him" you’d say "con lui"; for "with you" (informal) "con te"; for "with you" (formal) "con Lei".
target_language_example: Mi piace passare del tempo con lei nel fine settimana.
native_language_example: I like spending time with her on the weekend.

meaning: “spent a lot of time” / “a lot of time has passed.”
additional_notes: With **avere** (e.g., *ho passato molto tempo...*), it means **to spend a lot of time** somewhere/doing something (*in Australia*, *assieme*, *a studiare*). With **essere** (e.g., *è passato molto tempo*), it means **a lot of time has gone by / has passed** (often like “it’s been a long time”).
target_language_example: È passato molto tempo da quando ci siamo visti.
native_language_example: A lot of time has passed since we saw each other.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "passare" (to spend, as in spending time) in the past tense, with "tutta la mattinata" = the entire morning (from early morning until lunchtime). Often followed by "con" + person (with someone) or "a" + infinitive (doing something): "Ho passato tutta la mattinata con..." / "Ho passato tutta la mattinata a...".
target_language_example: Abbiamo passato tutta la mattinata in centro.
native_language_example: We spent the whole morning downtown.

meaning: 'had a good summer' / 'spent a good summer'.
additional_notes: From the verb "passare" meaning "to spend" (time) in expressions like "passare una buona giornata/serata/estate". It’s usually used in the past (passato prossimo): "Hai passato una buona estate?" = "Did you have a good summer?" Note: "estate" means "summer" in Italian (not an "estate" in the English sense).
target_language_example: Sì, ho passato una buona estate al mare.
native_language_example: Yes, I had a good summer at the seaside.

meaning: 'afraid of' (with plural masculine nouns) / 'fear of the'.
additional_notes: Used after "avere paura" + "di" to say what someone is afraid of. "Dei" = "di" + "i" and is used before masculine plural nouns (e.g., i topi, i serpenti). For feminine plural, use "delle" (paura delle api); for singular, "del/dello/della".
target_language_example: Ho paura dei cani, ma non dei gatti.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of dogs, but not of cats.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere paura dei cani" = "to be afraid of dogs." You can intensify it with words like "molta" (a lot of) or "particolarmente" (particularly). "Dei" here means "(of) the/some" and is commonly used before a plural noun after "paura di".
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha paura dei cani, quindi attraversiamo la strada quando ne vediamo uno.
native_language_example: My brother is afraid of dogs, so we cross the street when we see one.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere paura dei ragni" = "to be afraid of spiders." You can add intensifiers like "così" (so) or "molta" (a lot of) and time words like "ancora" (still).
target_language_example: Io ho paura dei ragni, soprattutto quelli grandi.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of spiders, especially big ones.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase “avere paura di” (to be afraid of). “del” is “di + il” and introduces a masculine singular noun: “paura del fuoco” (afraid of fire). For feminine singular use “della” (paura della notte), for plural use “dei / degli / delle” (paura dei cani, paura degli insetti, paura delle altezze).
target_language_example: Ho paura del buio.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase. It uses the noun "paura" (fear) + "del" (= di + il, “of the”) + "buio" (darkness/dark). Often used with "avere" (to have): "avere paura del buio" = “to be afraid of the dark.”
target_language_example: Da piccolo avevo paura del buio, ma ora non più.
native_language_example: When I was little I was afraid of the dark, but not anymore.

additional_notes: Used after forms of "avere paura (di)" (to be afraid of). With "della" (= di + la), it means you’re afraid of death as a general concept: "avere paura della morte". You can also say "paura di morire" (“fear of dying”).
target_language_example: Non ho paura della morte, ma ho paura di soffrire.
native_language_example: I’m not afraid of death, but I’m afraid of suffering.
