additional_notes: Used with the verb avere: avere paura di + noun/pronoun/infinitive. With a noun/pronoun it means being afraid of someone/something (Ho paura di quel cane). With an infinitive it means being afraid to do something / afraid of doing something (Ho paura di dirlo; Ho paura di morire). Often shortened in speech to Ho paura + infinitive when the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Ho paura di parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: I'm afraid to speak in public.

meaning: "(he/she/you formal) thinks that" / "do you think that...?"
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with che (“that”). In questions it often means “do you think…?”; with Lei it’s a polite/formal “do you think…?”. The verb in the che-clause is often in the subjunctive (e.g., pensa che sia…), especially for opinions/uncertainty.
target_language_example: Pensa che sia una buona idea partire domani?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea to leave tomorrow?

meaning: (he/she/you formal) thinks he/she/you can manage to…
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone believes they will be able to do something successfully. It combines: "pensare di" (to think/believe that you will…) + "riuscire a" (to manage to / succeed in) + an infinitive verb.
target_language_example: Pensa di riuscire a finire il lavoro oggi?
native_language_example: Do you think you can manage to finish the work today?

additional_notes: Used to question or emphasize someone’s belief/opinion. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo) in Italian (e.g., “pensa veramente che sia…” = “do you really think that he is…?”). You can also use it in statements: “Penso veramente che…” = “I really think that…”.
target_language_example: Pensa veramente che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause expressing an opinion or belief: "Penso che..." = "I think that...". With pensare che, Italian commonly uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo) in the following clause, especially when it’s an opinion or uncertainty (e.g., "Penso che lui abbia torto"). It can also appear in the structure "A pensare che..." meaning "To think that..." / "Imagine that..." (often expressing surprise, regret, or disbelief).
target_language_example: Penso che domani piova.
native_language_example: I think it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: "do you (all) think that...?" / "what do you (all) think...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or assumption. "Pensate" is 2nd-person plural (voi) of "pensare" (to think), so it addresses a group or is used as a polite/formal plural. Very often followed by "che" + subjunctive (e.g., "pensate che stia...") when expressing doubt/uncertainty, or by "che" + future/indicative when it feels more like a prediction (e.g., "pensate che arriverà...").
target_language_example: Pensate che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you (all) think it’s a good idea?

meaning: "do you (all) think that this is…" / "you (all) think that this is…"
additional_notes: Used to ask for or state someone’s opinion/belief. "Pensate" is 2nd-person plural (you all), and it introduces a clause with "che" + subjunctive: "che questo sia" (that this is). Often followed by an adjective or past participle: "troppo costoso" (too expensive), "divertente" (funny), "reale" (real), "sbagliato" (wrong). In questions, intonation or a question mark shows it’s a question.
target_language_example: Pensate che questo sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you all think this is a good idea?

meaning: "do you think (that) it is...?" / "do you think it might be...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess. It’s addressed to more than one person (voi). It’s usually followed by the subjunctive (sia), common after verbs like pensare/credere in questions or uncertain statements: e.g., "Dove pensate che sia?" = "Where do you think it is/has gone?"
target_language_example: Quale pensate che sia la soluzione migliore?
native_language_example: Which solution do you think is the best?

meaning: "Do you really think that...?" (asking if someone truly believes something).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or double-check someone’s opinion/belief. It’s addressed to more than one person ("pensate" = "you all think" / formal "you" plural). It’s normally followed by "che" + a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "sia", "fosse").
target_language_example: Pensate davvero che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

meaning: “do you really think that …?” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or confirm someone’s opinion (often with a skeptical tone). It introduces a clause with **che**; after **pensare che**, Italian commonly uses the **subjunctive (congiuntivo)**, especially in questions or when expressing doubt (e.g., *abbia, sia*).
target_language_example: Pensate veramente che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used after the verb "pensare" in the past (usually passato prossimo: "ho/ha/hanno pensato che...") to introduce what someone believed or assumed. Very often the verb after "che" is in the subjunctive, especially when the idea is uncertain or just someone’s opinion (e.g., "Ho pensato che fosse...", "Ha pensato che non ci fosse...").
target_language_example: Ho pensato che fosse chiuso, quindi sono tornato a casa.
native_language_example: I thought it was closed, so I went back home.

additional_notes: Imperfect tense of *pensare* + *che*, used to report what someone believed/assumed in the past. After *pensare che*, Italian often uses the subjunctive (*pensava che fosse…*, *pensava che stessi…*), especially when the thought is uncertain or reported as someone’s opinion.
target_language_example: Pensava che fossi già arrivato.
native_language_example: He/She thought that I had already arrived.

additional_notes: Imperfect past: pensava = “(he/she) was thinking / used to think.” It introduces a clause with che, and the verb is in the subjunctive imperfect (fosse) after pensare (to think). Used to report someone’s belief or assumption in the past: Pensava che fosse vero / che fosse una buona idea.
target_language_example: Pensava che fosse già troppo tardi per chiamare.
native_language_example: He/She thought it was already too late to call.

additional_notes: Used to report someone’s belief/opinion in the past: *pensava* = “(he/she) thought” (imperfect), and after *pensare che* Italian normally uses the subjunctive, here *fossi* (imperfect subjunctive of *essere* = “to be”). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context or stated earlier (e.g., *Mary disse che…*). Follow it with an adjective/noun phrase: *pensava che fossi pigro / più giovane / mio fratello*.
target_language_example: Pensavo che fossi italiano.
native_language_example: I thought you were Italian.

additional_notes: Used to report someone’s belief/opinion in the past. After *pensare che* (“to think that”), Italian typically uses the subjunctive: *fossi* is the imperfect subjunctive of *essere* (“to be”), roughly “that I was/were.” What comes after it agrees with the speaker (“io”): *pigro/pigra*, *stupido/stupida*, etc.
target_language_example: Pensava che io fossi italiano, ma sono americano.
native_language_example: He/She thought I was Italian, but I’m American.

meaning: 'I thought (that)…' (introduces what you believed in the past).
additional_notes: Used to report a past belief or expectation. It’s very often followed by the subjunctive in Italian (e.g., pensavo che fosse/avessi), and sometimes by the conditional to express an expectation about what would happen (e.g., pensavo che sarebbe…).
target_language_example: Pensavo che oggi fosse domenica, invece è lunedì.
native_language_example: I thought today was Sunday, but it’s Monday.

meaning: "I thought it was…" (I believed it was…).
additional_notes: Used to express a past belief/assumption, often later corrected (e.g., you were wrong or surprised). It combines the imperfect of pensare (pensavo) with che + the subjunctive of essere (fosse). You can follow it with an adjective or a noun: pensavo che fosse facile / malata / tutto uno scherzo.
target_language_example: Pensavo che fosse oggi, invece è domani.
native_language_example: I thought it was today, but it’s tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe a past belief, assumption, or impression that may or may not be true. It often introduces an opinion about a situation (“it was…”) or someone (“he/she was…”). In Italian, after “pensavo” (imperfect of *pensare*), you commonly use the subjunctive “fosse” (from *essere*). In English you usually just say “I thought it was…” or “I thought he/she was…”.
target_language_example: Pensavo fosse più facile, ma mi sbagliavo.
native_language_example: I thought it was easier, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say you had a belief/assumption in the past about someone’s state, location, or situation, often later corrected. It’s short for "pensavo che fossi..." and uses the imperfect subjunctive ("fossi") after a past-tense verb of thinking ("pensavo"). Often followed by an adjective or place: "Pensavo fossi a casa / in camera / arrabbiato".
target_language_example: Scusa, pensavo fossi già a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought you were already at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an opinion or guess, often followed by the subjunctive in Italian (e.g., Pensi che sia…, Pensi che abbia…). It can be a real question (Pensi che…?) or part of a longer question like Chi pensi che…? (“Who do you think…?”).
target_language_example: Pensi che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea?

meaning: "you think that this is…" / "do you think this is…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask or state someone’s opinion about something. After "pensare che" Italian normally uses the subjunctive, so you’ll often see "sia" (from "essere"). It can be adapted for other people: "pensa che questo sia" (he/she thinks…), "pensate che questo sia" (you all think…).
target_language_example: Pensi che questo sia un problema serio?
native_language_example: Do you think this is a serious problem?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion or guess. After "pensi che" Italian typically uses the subjunctive, so you often see "sia" (subjunctive of "essere"). "Sia" can refer to "it," "he," or "she" depending on context. In the past you may also see "pensi che sia stato/a" (do you think it was / has been).
target_language_example: Pensi che sia una buona idea partire domani?
native_language_example: Do you think it’s a good idea to leave tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to question someone’s belief/opinion, often with surprise or skepticism. It’s the 2nd-person singular (tu) form; with "Lei" you’d say "pensa davvero che". After "che" Italian commonly uses the subjunctive (e.g., "sia", "stia", "abbia").
target_language_example: Pensi davvero che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to challenge or express surprise/doubt about what someone believes. Often followed by a clause with "che" + verb (sometimes in the subjunctive, e.g., "che sia"). You may also hear it as "(Tu) pensi veramente che…?"
target_language_example: Pensi veramente che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it's a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief about something. It is commonly followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially when the idea is uncertain or subjective: "Penso che sia…" In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative, particularly when the speaker feels sure: "Penso che è…"
target_language_example: Penso che sia una buona idea.
native_language_example: I think it's a good idea.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to say what you think about something involving an indirect object introduced by **a** (e.g., **piace a…** = “is liked by…”, **serve a…** = “is needed by…”). Very often **penso che** is followed by the **subjunctive** (e.g., *penso che a Maria piaccia…*, *penso che a Tom serva…*). In other tenses you may see the conditional (e.g., *sarebbe piaciuto*).
target_language_example: Penso che a Giulia serva più tempo.
native_language_example: I think Giulia needs more time.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or a suggestion about what someone ought to do. "Dovrebbe" is the conditional of "dovere" (must/should) and often sounds like a polite recommendation. You typically add an infinitive: "penso che dovrebbe + verbo" (e.g., "penso che dovrebbe parlare").
target_language_example: Penso che dovrebbe studiare un po' di più.
native_language_example: I think he should study a bit more.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion or suggestion about what the group (we) ought to do. After "penso che" (“I think that”), Italian typically uses the conditional "dovremmo" (“we should / we ought to”) to sound polite and tentative. You can follow it with an infinitive (e.g., chiamare, dirlo, parlare, uscire).
target_language_example: Penso che dovremmo aspettare ancora cinque minuti.
native_language_example: I think we should wait another five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or suggestion to a group, often politely. "Penso che" introduces your thought/opinion, and "dovreste" is the conditional form of "dovere" (you all should/ought to), which softens the advice compared to "dovete" (you must). In correct Italian, this structure is often followed by the subjunctive ("Penso che dovreste..." is common in speech, but you may also hear "Penso che dobbiate...").
target_language_example: Penso che dovreste chiedere scusa.
native_language_example: I think you should apologize.

meaning: "I think you should" (giving advice or a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to express your opinion and recommend an action to someone. After "penso che" (I think that), Italian normally uses the subjunctive ("penso che tu debba..."). In everyday speech, many people also use the conditional "dovresti" (you should) as in this phrase, especially in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Penso che dovresti riposarti un po'.
native_language_example: I think you should rest a bit.

meaning: "I think that the..." (introduces an opinion about a specific masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to state your opinion or belief: penso che + clause. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), often with "sia" (e.g., "penso che il Giappone sia..."). "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and changes depending on the noun (lo, l’, la, i, gli, le).
target_language_example: Penso che il tempo oggi sia bello.
native_language_example: I think the weather today is nice.

additional_notes: Used to give your opinion about a specific feminine noun (la = “the” for feminine singular). After “penso che…”, Italian often uses the subjunctive, especially with “essere”: e.g., “penso che la paga sia…” (“I think the pay is…”). You’ll change “la” to “il/lo/i/gli/le” depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Penso che la soluzione sia semplice.
native_language_example: I think the solution is simple.

meaning: "I think that she..." / "I think that you (formal)..."
additional_notes: "Penso che" is commonly followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo) in Italian, especially when expressing an opinion/uncertainty: "penso che lei abbia...", "penso che lei possa...", "penso che lei sappia...". "Lei" can mean "she" or the formal "you" (used with people you don’t know well, customers, older people, etc.); the verb form is the same either way, so context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Penso che lei possa venire domani.
native_language_example: I think she (or you, formal) can come tomorrow.

meaning: "I think that this is..." (introduces your opinion/guess).
additional_notes: Used to give an opinion or make a guess about something feminine singular (questa = “this one/this”). After "penso che" Italian commonly uses the subjunctive, so you’ll often see "sia" (subjunctive of "essere", “to be”) instead of "è".
target_language_example: Penso che questa sia la strada giusta.
native_language_example: I think this is the right road.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion/guess about some objects or people (“these”). After penso che, Italian normally uses the subjunctive: siano (subjunctive of essere, “to be”). questi is masculine plural (“these”); for feminine plural you’d use queste (penso che queste siano…). Often followed by a possessive: miei/tuoi/suoi/vostri, etc.
target_language_example: Penso che questi siano i tuoi occhiali.
native_language_example: I think these are your glasses.

additional_notes: Used to give an opinion/guess about what something is. After "penso che" Italian typically uses the subjunctive, so you often see "sia" (from "essere" = to be) instead of "è".
target_language_example: Penso che questo sia il tuo zaino.
native_language_example: I think this is your backpack.

meaning: “I think that (it/he/she) is …” (introduces an opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Used to state what you think, believe, or guess. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive: **sia** (from *essere*, “to be”). Depending on context, it can refer to “it,” “he,” or “she.” It can also introduce another clause: *Penso che sia importante che…* = “I think it’s important that…”.
target_language_example: Penso che sia la scelta migliore.
native_language_example: I think it’s the best choice.

meaning: "I think (that) you..." (introduces your opinion about someone).
additional_notes: Used to express your belief/opinion about what someone does, knows, needs, etc. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): abbia, conosca, debba, possa, sappia. In everyday speech some people use the indicative instead, but the standard form after "penso che" is the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Penso che tu sia molto gentile.
native_language_example: I think you’re very kind.

meaning: "I think (that) I…" / "I think I can…" + infinitive.
additional_notes: Used to express your opinion or guess about yourself/your own actions. It’s followed by an infinitive (often a past infinitive: "penso di aver capito" = "I think I understood / I think I’ve understood"). With ability/possibility, you often add "poter(e)": "penso di poter…" = "I think I can / might be able to…".
target_language_example: Penso di poter venire domani.
native_language_example: I think I can come tomorrow.

meaning: "I think I have" (I believe I've done something).
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion/guess about a past action. It’s formed with: penso di + aver + past participle (e.g., penso di aver capito). With verbs that take "essere" in the passato prossimo, Italian uses "essere" instead: "penso di essere andato/a", not "penso di aver andato".
target_language_example: Penso di aver perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: I think I’ve lost my keys.

meaning: “I think I have …” (I believe I’ve done/have something).
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a personal opinion about something you have (possession) or have done (past action). It’s often followed by a past participle (avere fatto, avere perso, avere messo, avere mangiato) to mean “I think I’ve [done]…”. With a noun, it can mean possession: “Penso di avere le chiavi” = “I think I have the keys.”
target_language_example: Penso di avere lasciato il telefono a casa.
native_language_example: I think I left my phone at home.

additional_notes: Used to say the purpose of a trip or someone’s presence is work/business, not tourism or personal reasons. Common with verbs like andare/venire/essere and with viaggio/viaggio di lavoro (business trip).
target_language_example: Sono a Milano per affari, ma domani ho un po' di tempo libero.
native_language_example: I’m in Milan on business, but tomorrow I have a bit of free time.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (while waiting).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + infinitive to express purpose: doing something just to fill time (often because you’re waiting or bored). Common with activities like reading, playing cards, scrolling, chatting. "Ammazzare" literally means "to kill," so it’s a vivid but normal expression.
target_language_example: Abbiamo fatto una passeggiata per ammazzare il tempo prima del treno.
native_language_example: We went for a walk to kill time before the train.

meaning: "to go to" / "in order to go (and) to" (expresses purpose).
additional_notes: Used to say the purpose of an action: per + infinitive. With andare, it often means “in order to go to (a place)” or “to go and do (something)”, depending on what follows (a place name or another infinitive). In Italian you can often avoid repetition by dropping the second andare: e.g., “Siamo andati a Boston per trovarlo.”
target_language_example: Dove devo scendere per andare a Piazza Duomo?
native_language_example: Where do I have to get off to go to Piazza Duomo?

additional_notes: Used with "per" to express purpose: getting ready/being ready in order to go to bed (go to sleep). Often follows verbs like "prepararsi" (to get ready) or expressions like "essere pronto/a" (to be ready).
target_language_example: Ho messo il pigiama per andare a letto.
native_language_example: I put on my pajamas to go to bed.

meaning: to go to school (in order to go to school).
additional_notes: Uses "per" + infinitive to express purpose (“in order to”). Often follows verbs like "avere bisogno"/"servire" (to need) or describes transport and timing: "un passaggio per andare a scuola" (a ride to get to school), "l'autobus per andare a scuola" (the bus to go to school).
target_language_example: Devo prendere la metro per andare a scuola.
native_language_example: I have to take the subway to go to school.

meaning: 'for having' / 'for + past infinitive' (to explain a reason).
additional_notes: Used to give the reason for a credit, punishment, criticism, etc. It means “for having done” something (past action). Structure: per + avere (conjugated as aver before a past participle) + past participle: per aver mentito = for having lied. With verbs that use essere in the passato prossimo, you can also see “per essere + past participle” (e.g., per essere arrivato/a = for having arrived).
target_language_example: Mi hanno ringraziato per aver aiutato i miei colleghi.
native_language_example: They thanked me for having helped my coworkers.

additional_notes: Uses **per** + **avere** (infinitive) + past participle (**rubato**) to say the reason for an action, emphasizing that the stealing happened **before** the main event (e.g., being arrested/fired). In everyday English it’s often translated simply as **"for stealing"**.
target_language_example: È stato condannato per aver rubato dei soldi.
native_language_example: He was convicted for having stolen money.

meaning: for having written the book; for writing the book (as the reason).
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express the reason why something happened (“because of / for”). Here **aver scritto** is the **past infinitive** (literally “to have written”), often used when the action happened before the main verb: *È stato messo in prigione per aver scritto il libro* = he was imprisoned because he had written the book.
target_language_example: È stato criticato per aver scritto il libro.
native_language_example: He was criticized for having written the book.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like grazie (thank you) or scusa (sorry) to give the reason: per + infinitive past (avere + past participle) + mi. It means “for having + past participle,” often translated as “for + -ing” in English. Example patterns: “Grazie per avermi aiutato/a” (Thanks for helping me) and “Scusa per avermi disturbato/a” (Sorry for bothering me). Agree the past participle with the person being “me” only when the verb uses essere; with avere, the participle often matches the speaker in practice (aiutato/a, avvisato/a).
target_language_example: Scusa per avermi chiamato così tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry for calling me so late.

meaning: for having (done something) to me; for (doing something) for me.
additional_notes: Used after expressions like grazie (thank you), ti sono grato (I’m grateful), voglio ringraziarti/la (I want to thank you), or vergognarsi (to be ashamed), to introduce the reason. It’s formed by per + infinitive past (avere + past participle) + mi (“me”). The past participle can agree with the speaker if the object is female: per avermi salvata / aiutata / trattata.
target_language_example: Grazie per avermi aspettato.
native_language_example: Thanks for waiting for me.

meaning: "By any chance, what time is it?"
additional_notes: "Per caso" is a polite, softening phrase meaning "by chance / by any chance". It’s often used in questions to sound less direct: "Sa(i/te) per caso... ?". You can use it with different forms of "sapere" depending on who you’re speaking to (Lei sa… / tu sai… / voi sapete…).
target_language_example: Scusi, sa per caso che ore sono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you happen to know what time it is?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone will eat at dinner, or to invite/ask someone to stay/go out for dinner. Common with verbs like mangiare (to eat), avere (to have), restare/rimanere (to stay), uscire (to go out), invitare (to invite).
target_language_example: Hai già deciso cosa vuoi mangiare per cena?
native_language_example: Have you decided what you want to eat for dinner?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is punished, blamed, or faces consequences because of their actions. The verb changes with the subject (ha fatto = he/she has done; hanno fatto = they have done).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per ciò che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I did.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone eats/drinks in the morning. It often follows verbs like mangiare/bere (to eat/drink) or preparare (to prepare): “Mangio yogurt per colazione.” You can also ask about someone’s breakfast habits: “Cosa prendi per colazione?”
target_language_example: Di solito bevo un caffè e mangio un cornetto per colazione.
native_language_example: I usually drink a coffee and eat a croissant for breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone or without help/without involving others. It can also imply acting without permission or outside a group plan (e.g., “He acted on his own”). Don’t confuse with “per conto di (qualcuno)”, which means “on behalf of (someone)”.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: lo farà per conto suo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’ll do it on his own.

additional_notes: Used with a time expression after **per** to say how long something lasts (duration). Often used with the present or past to describe an activity or situation continuing for that amount of time (e.g., *Ha nevicato per due giorni*).
target_language_example: Resterò a Roma per due giorni.
native_language_example: I’ll stay in Rome for two days.

meaning: for speeding; due to driving over the speed limit.
additional_notes: Used to say the reason for an arrest or a fine. Common with verbs like "essere multato" (to be fined) and "essere arrestato" (to be arrested), and with "multa" (fine).
target_language_example: Mi hanno fermato per eccesso di velocità sull'autostrada.
native_language_example: They pulled me over for speeding on the highway.

additional_notes: Used with *per* + infinitive to express purpose or a criterion involving "being" something. Common patterns: *troppo + aggettivo + per essere...* (“too … to be …”), and *una ragione/motivo per essere...* (“a reason to be …”). Note: in *sta per essere...* the full expression is *stare per* (“to be about to”), and *essere* is the infinitive that follows it.
target_language_example: È troppo presto per essere sicuri.
native_language_example: It’s too early to be sure.

meaning: for being late; for arriving late.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like scusarsi (to apologize) or inventare una scusa (to make up an excuse) to give the reason. Literally "in order to be late," but in these contexts it means "for being late."
target_language_example: Mi sono scusato per essere in ritardo al lavoro.
native_language_example: I apologized for being late to work.

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (is needed).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives/expressions like "troppo + adjective" (e.g., "troppo spaventato/a") to mean "to do anything". It can also express that something is necessary in order to do anything (e.g., needing money to be able to do things in general). "Qualsiasi cosa" = "anything/whatever" and the subject (spaventato/spaventata) changes to match the speaker.
target_language_example: Mi serve una macchina per fare qualsiasi cosa in questa città.
native_language_example: I need a car to do anything in this city.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like uscire/andare fuori/essere fuori to say you go out (or are out) with the purpose of taking a walk. Literally “in order to do a walk,” but in natural English it’s usually “to go for a walk.” You can add where: per fare una passeggiata al parco / sulla spiaggia.
target_language_example: Sono uscito per fare una passeggiata al parco.
native_language_example: I went out to go for a walk in the park.

additional_notes:
Used to politely ask someone to call you (on the phone) or to address you by a certain name. 
- chiamami = “call me” (imperative + mi = “me”).
- If followed by a name/title ("chiamami Joe"), it means “call me Joe” (how to address you).
- If followed by a time ("più tardi", "questa sera") or a clause ("quando arrivi"), it means “call me later/this evening/when you arrive.”
target_language_example: Per favore, chiamami domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please call me tomorrow morning.

meaning: "please, give me" (asking someone to hand you something).
additional_notes: Used to make a polite request. "Dammi" is the informal (tu) command form of "dare" (to give), so it’s for friends, family, kids, or peers. With strangers or in formal situations, use "Per favore, mi dia..." or "Mi può dare...". Often followed by a noun ("il menù") or by "qualcosa da..." ("qualcosa da bere").
target_language_example: Per favore, dammi una bottiglia d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a bottle of water.

meaning: "please, give me" / "please, give us" (polite request to more than one person, or formal).
additional_notes: "Per favore" means "please." "Datemi" is the imperative of "dare" (to give) with "-mi" = "to me"; it can also mean "to us" in contexts like ordering for a group. It’s used to ask for something in shops/restaurants, or more figuratively (e.g., "datemi la vostra attenzione" = "give me your attention"). Often addressed to multiple people ("you all") or used as a polite/formal "you" (Lei), especially with staff.
target_language_example: Per favore, datemi due caffè e un cornetto.
native_language_example: Please, give me two coffees and a croissant.

meaning: "Please, tell (someone)…" (addressing you plural or a group).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to pass on a message: "Per favore, dite a Maria di…" = “Please tell Maria to…”. "Dite" is the imperative of "dire" for "voi" (you plural), so it’s used when speaking to more than one person (or sometimes as a polite form in some contexts). The person being told is introduced with "a" (or its combined forms: "al", "alla", "allo", etc.).
target_language_example: Per favore, dite al direttore che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Please tell the manager/director that I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: “Please, could you … for me?” (polite request using “mi” = “to me/for me”).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a polite request when the action is directed to you or done for you. “Mi” is an indirect object pronoun (“to me/for me”) and commonly goes with verbs like comprare (buy), consigliare (advise), far sapere (let [someone] know), rispondere (reply), scrivere (write), spiegare (explain). In formal polite requests you often see the subjunctive/imperative forms like “mi compri / mi spieghi / mi faccia sapere”.
target_language_example: Per favore, mi può aiutare con questo esercizio?
native_language_example: Please, can you help me with this exercise?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something politely, especially in shops, restaurants, or when speaking to someone you don’t know well. "Mi dia" is the formal command form of "dare" (Lei form). You can follow it with an item: "mi dia un/una…", "mi dia del/della…", "mi dia due…".
target_language_example: Per favore, mi dia un biglietto per Roma.
native_language_example: Please, give me a ticket to Rome.

meaning: “please, don’t …” (a polite request not to do something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to politely ask someone to avoid an action: “Per favore, non + verb.” The verb is in the imperative (e.g., non aggiungere/non aggiungete) or another form addressed to the person (e.g., non ti dimenticare / non vi dimenticate). In writing, a comma after “per favore” is common but optional.
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare così forte.
native_language_example: Please, don’t speak so loudly.

meaning: "Please, come" (talking to more than one person, or using polite you).
additional_notes: "Per favore" means "please". "Venite" is the "you (plural)" command form of "venire" (to come), and it’s also used as a polite command in formal situations (like speaking to customers). It can be followed by places ("venite nel mio ufficio" = come into my office) or by a phrase describing how to come/dress ("venite vestite bene" = please come dressed well).
target_language_example: Per favore, venite qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used with plural masculine nouns to mean “for its … / for his … / for their …” depending on context. Very common after expressions like “essere famoso per …” (to be famous for …) or “essere rispettato per …” (to be respected for …). If the noun is feminine plural, use “per le sue” (e.g., per le sue idee).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è conosciuto per i suoi piatti di pesce.
native_language_example: This restaurant is known for its seafood dishes.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done for the benefit of someone’s children. "Suoi" agrees with a plural noun (figli). Depending on context, "suoi" can mean either "his" or "her" in English; Italian doesn’t mark gender of the owner here. With "è un peccato per..." it means “it’s a shame for … / for …’s sake.”
target_language_example: Ho accettato questo lavoro per i suoi figli.
native_language_example: I accepted this job for his/her children.

additional_notes: "Per" means "for" (also "to"/"in order to" in some contexts). "Il" is "the" (masculine singular). Together, "per il" is used before a masculine singular noun: per il weekend (for the weekend), per il soggiorno (for the living room), per il festival (for the festival). In polite phrases it can introduce the reason/apology or thanks: "Grazie per il tuo aiuto" / "Mi scusi per il disturbo." Often contracts to "pel" in older/literary Italian, but in modern everyday Italian you normally use "per il."
target_language_example: Grazie per il consiglio!
native_language_example: Thanks for the advice!

additional_notes: Used with per + il + lavoro to say something is for work (the reason/purpose) or for the job (suitable/needed for a particular role). Often appears with adjectives like perfetto/a (perfect for the job) or with being late: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work).
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer affidabile per il lavoro.
native_language_example: I need a reliable computer for work.

meaning: 'for my' (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say the reason, cause, or responsibility: e.g., apologizing or getting credit/blame for something. Grammar note: it must match the noun that follows. Masculine singular: per il mio lavoro. Feminine singular: per la mia idea. Masculine plural: per i miei amici. Feminine plural: per le mie amiche.
target_language_example: Grazie per il mio regalo!
native_language_example: Thanks for my gift!

additional_notes: Used to say something is given, done, or happens in connection with your birthday (often a gift or a phone call). It commonly follows verbs like "regalare" (to give as a gift), "ricevere" (to receive), "portare" (to bring), or "chiamare" (to call).
target_language_example: Mi hai fatto una festa sorpresa per il mio compleanno.
native_language_example: You threw me a surprise party for my birthday.

meaning: 'for the gift' (as in thanking someone for it).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like ringraziare/dir(e) grazie to say what you’re thanking someone for. Often appears in phrases like “Grazie per il regalo” or “Ti ringrazio per il regalo.”
target_language_example: Ti ringrazio per il regalo, è bellissimo!
native_language_example: Thank you for the gift, it’s beautiful!

meaning: about global warming / for global warming (i.e., concerning it).
additional_notes: Most often used after verbs/adjectives like preoccupato/a/e/i (“worried”) to mean “about/concerning global warming.” Literally “for the global warming,” but in this context English uses “about.”
target_language_example: Sono molto preoccupata per il riscaldamento globale.
native_language_example: I’m very worried about global warming.

meaning: "for his/her/its" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a possessive (suo = his/her/its) after a preposition: per il suo + noun. It refers back to the subject or to someone already understood from context. Changes with gender/number: per la sua (fem. sing.), per i suoi (masc. plural), per le sue (fem. plural).
target_language_example: L'ho ringraziato per il suo aiuto.
native_language_example: I thanked him for his help.

additional_notes: Used with gifts or plans made for someone’s birthday. "suo" agrees with the person who has the birthday (his or her), not with the gift. You can change it to match the person: "per il mio compleanno" (for my birthday), "per il tuo compleanno" (for your birthday), "per il loro compleanno" (for their birthday).
target_language_example: Che cosa hai comprato per il suo compleanno?
native_language_example: What did you buy for his/her birthday?

additional_notes: Used to say what something relates to (e.g., an explanation) or what you feel sorry about. "Suo" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Often appears with verbs like "dare una spiegazione" (to give an explanation) and "essere dispiaciuto/a" (to be sorry).
target_language_example: Sono davvero dispiaciuto per il suo errore.
native_language_example: I’m really sorry about his/her mistake.

additional_notes: Used to indicate purpose/recipient ("a gift for your birthday") or cause ("if it hadn’t been for your courage"). It must agree with the noun that follows: masculine singular = "per il tuo" (per il tuo compleanno / per il tuo futuro). Feminine singular: "per la tua"; masculine plural: "per i tuoi"; feminine plural: "per le tue".
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per il tuo fratello.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your brother.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ringraziare (to thank) or essere grato/a (to be grateful) to say what you’re thanking someone for. It agrees with the informal singular "tu" (your). In the examples, "grati" is masculine/mixed plural and "grate" is feminine plural; both mean "grateful."
target_language_example: Grazie per il tuo aiuto!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help!

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (your = "vostro") or when using polite/formal address (e.g., in formal writing). It often introduces what something is intended for (per il vostro esame = for your exam) or indicates benefit/purpose (per il vostro vantaggio = to your advantage). The noun that follows is typically masculine singular (il vostro + noun); for feminine singular you’d use "per la vostra" (e.g., per la vostra famiglia).
target_language_example: Ho preparato un regalo per il vostro bambino.
native_language_example: I prepared a gift for your child.

additional_notes: Used after thanks or expressions of gratitude/appreciation (e.g., "Grazie..." / "Siamo grati...") to specify what you are thanking someone for. "Vostro" is formal (to one person: "per il Suo aiuto") or plural (to multiple people: "per il vostro aiuto").
target_language_example: Grazie per il vostro aiuto, è stato davvero prezioso.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help; it was really valuable.

meaning: to learn Berber / in order to learn Berber.
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). **Imparare** = “to learn.” **Il berbero** refers to the Berber language (Tamazight); you can replace it with another language (e.g., *per imparare l’italiano*).
target_language_example: Sto seguendo un corso online per imparare il berbero.
native_language_example: I’m taking an online course to learn Berber.

additional_notes: Used to express purpose, benefit, reason, or thanks: per la nazione (for the nation), per la pittura (for painting), per la settimana prossima (for next week), grata per la gentilezza (grateful for the kindness). It can also appear in a formal relative phrase: per la quale = "for which" (feminine singular).
target_language_example: Grazie per la tua pazienza.
native_language_example: Thanks for your patience.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for dinner (food, plans) or that someone is ready/late for dinner. With people it often pairs with essere pronto/a (“to be ready”) or essere in ritardo (“to be late”). It refers to dinner in general, or a specific dinner everyone knows about from context.
target_language_example: Ho comprato una bottiglia di vino per la cena.
native_language_example: I bought a bottle of wine for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true during most of a time period or for most of a quantity. It’s often followed by a noun with an article/possessive (e.g., della giornata, della sua vita). You can also see: “per la maggior parte del” (masculine singular) and “per la maggior parte dei/degli/delle” (plural).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa per la maggior parte della settimana.
native_language_example: I stayed home for most of the week.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean “for my …”. Common with things like la mia gente (my people), la mia lezione (my lesson), la mia reazione (my reaction), la mia salute (my health), la mia malinconia (my sadness), la mia vacanza (my vacation). The noun can be explicit or understood from context (e.g., “per la mia” meaning “for mine”/“for my [thing]”).
target_language_example: Grazie per la mia prenotazione.
native_language_example: Thank you for my reservation.

meaning: for music; (having) an ear/talent for music.
additional_notes: Uses "per" to mean "for" in different senses, depending on context. Common with abilities or preferences (e.g., "avere orecchio per la musica" = to have an ear for music), and also with gratitude or appreciation ("grati/e per la musica" = grateful for the music). "La" can be generic, meaning music in general.
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha una vera passione per la musica.
native_language_example: My brother has a real passion for music.

additional_notes: Used to say something is directed toward or intended for something that belongs to “us,” followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la nostra professoressa*, *la nostra casa*). *Nostra* agrees with the noun: feminine singular (*la nostra*), masculine singular (*il nostro*), feminine plural (*le nostre*), masculine plural (*i nostri*).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per la nostra mamma.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for our mom.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens on the first occasion (never before). Often placed at the end of the sentence or near the verb: "venne per la prima volta", "la incontrai per la prima volta".
target_language_example: Oggi guido in autostrada per la prima volta.
native_language_example: Today I’m driving on the highway for the first time.

meaning: for school (e.g., for school-related needs; to go/prepare for school).
additional_notes: Uses per (“for”) + la scuola (“school”). Common with verbs like prepararsi (“to get ready”) and essere pronto/a (“to be ready”) to mean “getting ready to go to school,” and with servire (“to be needed”) to mean something is needed for school. Agreement: pronto (m. sing.), pronta (f. sing.), pronti (m./mixed pl.), pronte (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un quaderno per la scuola.
native_language_example: I bought a notebook for school.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the recipient/beneficiary: *per* = “for”, and *la sua* = “his/her” agreeing with a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la sua bambina*, *la sua amica*). Often, Italian drops possessive articles in some family contexts (e.g., *mia madre*), but with other nouns you commonly use the article: *la sua…*.
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per la sua mamma.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for his/her mom.

meaning: for his/her age; considering his/her age.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s appearance, height, health, etc. with what you would normally expect at that age (often meaning “surprisingly” young/tall/healthy, etc.). It agrees with the person: per la sua età (his/her), per la mia età (my), per la tua età (your), per la loro età (their).
target_language_example: È molto energica per la sua età.
native_language_example: She’s very energetic for her age.

meaning: for his/her health; about his/her health (often: worried/concerned).
additional_notes: Literally “for his/her health.” Used either to say something is good/bad for someone’s health (è dannoso/terribile per la sua salute) or to express concern/worry about someone’s health (essere in ansia per la sua salute). "Sua" agrees with the person’s health (salute), not with the person; it can mean “his” or “her.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando di mangiare meglio per la sua salute.
native_language_example: I’m trying to eat better for his/her health.

meaning: 'for your' (with a feminine singular noun); sometimes 'because of your'.
additional_notes: Made of per (“for / because of”) + la tua (“your”, feminine singular). Use it before a feminine singular noun: per la tua mamma (for your mom), per la tua gentilezza (for your kindness). With per it can express either purpose/support (“be strong for your mom”) or cause/reason (“angry because of your rudeness”).
target_language_example: Sono felice per la tua vittoria.
native_language_example: I'm happy for your victory.

additional_notes: Used to say something affects someone’s health (positively or negatively), or to express concern about someone’s health. Often follows adjectives like "buono" (good) or "dannoso" (harmful): "è buono/dannoso per la tua salute."
target_language_example: È importante dormire abbastanza per la tua salute.
native_language_example: It’s important to sleep enough for your health.

meaning: 'for your' (formal/plural), with a feminine singular noun.
additional_notes: Used with the polite/plural possessive "vostro": "vostra" agrees with a feminine singular noun (e.g., salute, amicizia, maleducazione). Often follows expressions like "grazie" / "ringrazio" (thanks for) or adjectives like "arrabbiato" (angry about/at). The full structure is typically "per la vostra + [noun]".
target_language_example: Grazie per la vostra pazienza.
native_language_example: Thank you for your patience.

meaning: 'for her/its (feminine plural)' (referring to things that belong to someone).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine plural noun: per + le + sue + noun. "Sue" agrees with the noun (feminine plural), not with the owner. Depending on context, "sue" can mean her/its/their/your (formal) + feminine plural noun (e.g., "le sue scarpe" = her shoes; "le sue cascate" = its waterfalls). Common with reasons/causes too: "scusarsi per le sue azioni" (apologize for her actions).
target_language_example: Ha ringraziato tutti per le sue parole gentili.
native_language_example: She thanked everyone for her kind words.

meaning: for her; for you (formal, feminine); about her (with some verbs).
additional_notes: “Lei” is the formal “you” in Italian (used with strangers, customers, officials). So “per lei” can mean “for you, ma’am” as well as “for her,” depending on context and capitalization in writing. Common uses: doing something on someone’s behalf (“Ho lucidato le sue scarpe per lei.”), intended recipient/benefit (“Mary spera che Tom lo farà per lei.”), or with certain expressions meaning “about her”/“concerning her,” e.g. “mi dispiace per lei” = “I feel sorry for her/you (formal).” “Garantire per lei” means “to vouch for her/you (formal).”
target_language_example: Ho prenotato un taxi per lei, signora.
native_language_example: I booked a taxi for you, ma’am.

meaning: 'for them' (for their benefit / directed to them).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + the stressed pronoun "loro" to talk about doing something for someone, working for someone, being worried about someone, or addressing/sending something to someone. It can mean either 'for their benefit' (Ho fatto questo per loro) or 'intended for them' (un messaggio per loro).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei biglietti per loro.
native_language_example: I bought some tickets for them.

meaning: for him; (with verbs like "votare") for him (= in support of him).
additional_notes: "Per" + "lui" (stressed pronoun) is used to say something is intended for, done for the benefit of, or because of a man/boy ("for him"). It can also mean "as far as he is concerned" (e.g., "Per lui è facile" = "For him, it’s easy") and with "votare" it means voting in support of someone ("Ha votato per lui" = "He voted for him").
target_language_example: Ho preparato la cena per lui.
native_language_example: I made dinner for him.

meaning: "for me" / "for my sake"; sometimes "to myself" (with verbs like *tenere*).
additional_notes: Most often used to say something is done for your benefit: *Puoi farlo per me?* (“Can you do it for me?”). With feelings/thoughts/secrets, it can mean “to myself/privately,” especially in set phrases like *tenere per me* (“to keep to myself”). It can also mean “as for me / in my opinion” (*Per me, va bene*), though that meaning isn’t shown in the examples.
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmelo per me, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that something lasts/d lasted a long period. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. As a question ("Per molto tempo?") it means "For a long time?" to confirm or show surprise.
target_language_example: Ho aspettato per molto tempo, ma non è arrivato nessuno.
native_language_example: I waited for a long time, but nobody arrived.

meaning: 'for us' (to our benefit, for our use, or concerning us).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone does something for your group (a favor, buying something, doing a task): "farlo per noi", "comprarlo per noi". It can also mean "for us" in the sense of "for people like us / in our situation" (e.g., something is difficult for us), or "for us" as support in voting/cheering: "Vota per noi!".
target_language_example: Puoi prenotare un tavolo per noi?
native_language_example: Can you book a table for us?

meaning: "to talk/speak with" (in order to talk with).
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose: *per parlare* = “to/in order to talk.” Add **con + person** for “with [someone].” Often used after verbs of coming/being somewhere (*venire*, *essere qui*) or to explain why you did something.
target_language_example: Sono qui per parlare con il dottore.
native_language_example: I'm here to talk with the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or give you something. **Dammi** is the imperative of **dare** (“to give”) + **mi** (“to me”) attached: **da’ + mi = dammi**. Often followed by a noun (e.g., *dammi una penna*) or something abstract (e.g., *dammi la tua attenzione* = “give me your attention”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, dammi il menu.
native_language_example: Please, give me the menu.

meaning: "Please, give me …" (addressing "you" plural or a polite/formal "you").
additional_notes: "Datemi" is the command form of "dare" (to give) for "voi" (you all). It’s used when speaking to more than one person, or as a polite/formal way to address a single person in some contexts (e.g., in customer service). Often followed by what you want: "Per piacere, datemi il menù" / "...due hot dog".
target_language_example: Per piacere, datemi un caffè e un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee and a glass of water.

meaning: 'Please, (to me)…' used to make a polite request (often with 'mi' + a verb).
additional_notes: Common pattern for polite requests: “Per piacere, mi + verb (Lei form)” = “Please + verb (for me).” Here “mi” is an object pronoun meaning “to me/me,” used with verbs like ascoltare (listen), passare (pass), prestare (lend), perdonare (forgive), richiamare (call back). Often paired with formal “Lei” verb forms (e.g., mi ascolti, mi passi) to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi può dire dov’è la stazione?
native_language_example: Please, can you tell me where the station is?

meaning: "Please call me" (on the phone / contact me).
additional_notes: Used as a polite request. "Mi chiami" is the polite (Lei) form, like saying “please call me.” For an informal request to a friend (tu), you’d usually say "Per favore, chiamami". It can also be followed by a name (“Call me Joe”) or a time (“this evening/tonight”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi chiami domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please call me tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request, especially with strangers, in shops, restaurants, or formal situations. “Mi dia” is the formal (Lei) command form of dare (“to give”). For friends/family you’d usually say “Per favore, dammi …” or “Mi dai …?”. You can add what you want after it: “mi dia un caffè”, “mi dia la borsa”, etc.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi dia un caffè.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee.

meaning: 'please, speak' (polite request to more than one person or to someone you address with 'voi').
additional_notes: "Per piacere" means "please." "Parlate" is the present-tense imperative for "you (plural) speak"; it’s used when talking to a group, or as a polite/formal address to one person in some contexts/regions. It’s often followed by "con ..." (with/to someone) or "in ..." (in a language), and can be modified with adverbs like "più forte" (louder) or "più lentamente" (more slowly).
target_language_example: Per piacere, parlate più lentamente: non capisco bene.
native_language_example: Please, speak more slowly: I don’t understand well.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come somewhere, addressing them with Lei (formal “you”). Venga is the formal command form of venire (“to come”). For an informal request to a friend, you’d say: Per favore/piacere, vieni. It can also introduce polite instructions like “come tomorrow” or “come well-dressed” (venga vestito/a bene).
target_language_example: Per piacere, venga qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say what you eat/have at lunchtime, or to invite someone to stay for lunch ("Resta per pranzo" = "Stay for lunch"). Often answers questions like "Cosa mangi per pranzo?" (What do you eat for lunch?).
target_language_example: Oggi mangiamo pasta per pranzo.
native_language_example: Today we’re having pasta for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is happening. It’s a more formal/explicit version of "perché?" and is common in careful speech or writing. Often followed by a full sentence (e.g., "Per quale ragione sei qui...?"), and you can swap "qui" and "qua" with no real change in meaning.
target_language_example: Per quale ragione non vuoi venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why don’t you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (the length of time something lasts), often with verbs like aspettare (wait), rimanere (stay), essere (be), prendere in prestito (borrow). In questions it’s very common at the start: Per quanto tempo...?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Italy?

meaning: "How long were you…?" / "How long have you been…?"
additional_notes:
Used to ask the duration of a stay or a state, usually followed by a past participle: 
- movement/stay: "Per quanto tempo sei stata in Giappone?" (How long were you in Japan?)
- a state/condition: "Per quanto tempo sei stato innamorato di Tom?" (How long were you in love with Tom?)
The past participle agrees with the subject: "sei stato" (male), "sei stata" (female); plural: "siete stati/state". Often you’ll also see it with "rimanere" (to stay): "Per quanto tempo sei rimasto/a…?"
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo sei stato a Roma?
native_language_example: How long were you in Rome?

meaning: "How long were you (all)?" / "For how long did you (all) stay...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration with "voi" (you plural) or the polite "Lei" in formal speech (same verb form: siete). It’s usually followed by a past participle (e.g., "siete rimasti/e", "siete stati/e") and/or a place: "Per quanto tempo siete rimasti a Caracas?" The past participle can agree in gender/number: "stati" (mixed/masculine plural) and "state" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo siete rimasti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long did you stay in Italy?

meaning: 'how long has/was' (asking the duration of something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration. It’s typically followed by a past participle with the auxiliary verb essere (è + stato/a, è rimasto/a, è restato/a, etc.). The past participle often agrees with the subject: è rimasto (he stayed) / è rimasta (she stayed). Often completed with a place or situation: Per quanto tempo è stata via? = How long was she away?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo è stata in Italia?
native_language_example: How long was she in Italy?

additional_notes: Common at the start of a clause. In fixed phrases like "per quanto (ne) so" or "per quanto a mia conoscenza" it means "as far as I know / to my knowledge". In questions with quantities, time, or extent (often with numbers or time expressions), it means "how much / how long" (e.g., "Per quanto tempo...?", "Per quanto (denaro)?").
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo rimarrai in Italia?
native_language_example: How long will you stay in Italy?

meaning: "for what" / "because of what" (for something that happened or was done).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or cause, usually followed by a clause with **che** (e.g., *per quello che hai detto/fatto*). Common after verbs and expressions about feelings or reactions: *arrabbiarsi per...*, *essere triste/furioso per...*, *incolpare qualcuno per...*, *perdonare qualcuno per...*.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che ho detto ieri.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for what I said yesterday.

additional_notes:
Used to refer to a specific action someone did, often with the idea of consequences (e.g., being punished, paying, being blamed). The verb changes with the subject: 
- per quello che ho fatto = for what I did
- per quello che hai fatto = for what you did
- per quello che hanno fatto = for what they did
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che ho fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I did.

meaning: for himself; for his own benefit / for himself alone.
additional_notes: Used to say that a man does something for his own benefit or keeps something for himself (not for others). It changes with the person: per se stessa (for herself), per se stessi / per se stesse (for themselves). Often used after verbs like volere (to want), tenere (to keep), fare (to do).
target_language_example: Ha comprato il biglietto per se stesso, non per gli altri.
native_language_example: He bought the ticket for himself, not for the others.

meaning: 'to study French' / 'in order to study French'.
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). The verb stays in the infinitive (**studiare**). You can replace **il francese** with another subject: *per studiare l’italiano / per studiare la matematica*.
target_language_example: Ho scaricato un’app per studiare il francese.
native_language_example: I downloaded an app to study French.

additional_notes: Used to say something is intended for one person (a gift, an idea, help, etc.). Often appears with verbs like fare (to do/make) or with è (is) to indicate who something is for: "È per te" = "It’s for you." Uses te (informal singular); for formal singular use "per Lei", and for plural use "per voi".
target_language_example: Questo regalo è per te.
native_language_example: This gift is for you.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) in math to mean multiplication ("X per tre" = "X times three"); (2) to express duration/quantity with a time or unit word ("per tre minuti/notti" = "for three minutes/nights"). You’ll often see it as part of a longer phrase like "in fila per tre" (= in rows of three / three abreast).
target_language_example: Rimaniamo qui per tre giorni.
native_language_example: Let’s stay here for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted. It often goes with the passato prossimo (e.g., ho abitato/ho vissuto/ho lavorato/sono stato) to describe a completed period of time in the past. You can swap the number: per due anni, per cinque anni, etc.
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per tre anni.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for three years.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long something lasts (duration). Often follows verbs like stare (to stay), rimanere (to remain), essere (to be) or describes weather/events. Not the same as "in tre giorni" (= in three days, within three days).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a Roma per tre giorni.
native_language_example: We stayed in Rome for three days.

additional_notes: Used with an action or state to say its duration. Often follows the verb: “aspettare per tre ore” (to wait for three hours), “studiare per tre ore” (to study for three hours). You can change the number: “per due ore”, “per mezz’ora”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo camminato per tre ore senza fermarci.
native_language_example: We walked for three hours without stopping.

meaning: for the whole (time period); for the entire.
additional_notes: Used to say something continues during an entire period of time. It’s usually followed by a feminine singular noun (la mattina, la settimana, la sera, la vita). With masculine nouns you use “per tutto il” (per tutto il giorno). With plural nouns: “per tutta/e i/le” (e.g., per tutti i giorni, per tutte le settimane). In “per tutta la famiglia”, it means “for the whole family” (for everyone in the family), not time.
target_language_example: Resterò qui per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here all night.

meaning: for the whole morning / all morning.
additional_notes: Used with a duration (how long something lasts). It often implies continuously or throughout the morning. You can swap in other time periods: per tutto il giorno (all day), per tutta la settimana (all week).
target_language_example: Abbiamo camminato per tutta la mattina.
native_language_example: We walked all morning.

meaning: all night (long); for the whole night.
additional_notes: Used with an action that lasts continuously throughout the night. Often follows a verb (e.g., dormire/studiare/ballare/aspettare per tutta la notte).
target_language_example: Abbiamo studiato per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: We studied all night.

meaning: for his/her whole life; all his/her life.
additional_notes: Used to say something was true during someone’s entire lifetime. It refers to a third person (sua = his/her/its); you can change the possessive: per tutta la mia vita (my), per tutta la tua vita (your), per tutta la nostra vita (our), etc. Often follows a verb (Ha lavorato... / È stato...).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto in questa città per tutta la mia vita.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city my whole life.

meaning: for the whole (time period) / throughout the entire (thing).
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts during an entire period of time (per tutto il weekend, per tutto il tragitto) or extends across an entire place/thing (per tutto il paese). With possessions it can mean “for all the” in thanks/acknowledgment: per tutto il tuo/suo aiuto (“for all your/his/her help”). Agrees with a masculine singular noun (il); for feminine singular you’ll often see per tutta la.
target_language_example: Sono rimasto a casa per tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I stayed home all day.

meaning: all day (long); for the whole day.
additional_notes: Used to express duration: something happens continuously or for most of the day. Often with the passato prossimo/imperfetto (e.g., “ha piovuto…”, “camminava…”). Similar idea: “tutto il giorno” = “all day”; adding “per” emphasizes “for the whole day/for the entire day.”
target_language_example: Ho lavorato per tutto il giorno e ora sono stanco.
native_language_example: I worked all day long and now I'm tired.

additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time period to say something lasts the entire afternoon (duration). Often goes with verbs like essere (to be), restare (to stay), lavorare/cucinare (to work/cook), etc. You can swap in other time words: "per tutta la mattina" (all morning), "per tutta la sera" (all evening).
target_language_example: Resterò a casa per tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I'll stay at home all afternoon.

meaning: for a moment; for a second.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts a very short time, or to ask someone to do/stop something briefly. Common with requests (e.g., watch something, wait, be quiet) and with thoughts/feelings that happened briefly (e.g., 'I thought for a moment that...').
target_language_example: Aspettami per un attimo, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me a moment, I'll be right back.

meaning: for a minute; for a moment (briefly).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time expression to say how long something lasts or to ask for a short amount of time (e.g., to talk, to borrow something, to wait/relax). Often means “just a moment” rather than exactly 60 seconds.
target_language_example: Aspettami per un minuto, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me a minute, I’ll be right back.

meaning: for a moment; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to mean "briefly" or "just for a second," either about needing/borrowing something for a short time (Ho bisogno di..., Posso prendere in prestito...) or about a short pause/temporary feeling (esitò per un momento, per un momento mi sentii...). Often interchangeable with "per un attimo" (very common) and "per un secondo" (more literal).
target_language_example: Aspetta qui per un momento, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait here for a moment; I’ll be right back.

meaning: for a second; for a moment.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly, interrupt briefly, or say something will only take a very short time. Often appears in polite requests ("Posso/Potrei parlarvi/le per un secondo?" = “Can/Could I talk to you for a second?”) and also in commands ("Aspetta/Taccia per un secondo" = “Wait/Be quiet for a second”). Can be extended: "per un secondo o due" (“for a second or two”).
target_language_example: Aspetta per un secondo, arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker doesn’t know (or doesn’t want to say) the exact reason. Often implies the reason is unclear or unexplained. Common in everyday speech; you can also hear "per qualche ragione" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Per una qualche ragione, oggi il computer non si accende.
native_language_example: For some reason, the computer won’t turn on today.

meaning: for a week (for the duration of one week).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time period to say how long something lasts (stay, rent, be sick, etc.). Very common with verbs like restare/rimanere (to stay), noleggiare (to rent), andare (to go), and essere (to be). You can change the time period: per due settimane (for two weeks), per una settimana o due (for a week or two).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a Firenze per una settimana.
native_language_example: We stayed in Florence for a week.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason or cause, often with a negative or explanatory tone. It’s normally followed by **di** + a noun: **per via di** + noun, which becomes **per via del/della/dei/degli/delle** (e.g., *per via del caldo*, *per via dello sciopero*). Similar to *a causa di*.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati tardi per via del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason, followed by a noun or noun phrase. It’s common in speech and writing. The article changes with the noun: per via del (masc. sing.), della (fem. sing.), dei/degli (masc. plural), delle (fem. plural). Similar to "a causa di"; if you want to emphasize blame, you can use "per colpa di".
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in ritardo per via del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause/reason for something, usually followed by a noun: per via della malattia = “because of the illness.” With masculine singular nouns use “per via del” (e.g., per via del traffico). It’s fairly common in speech and writing; “a causa di” is a close synonym.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati tardi per via del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("you all") or to one person with the formal "voi" (common in some regions or older style). It can mean something is intended for someone (a gift, information) or addressed to someone: "Ho un regalo per voi" = "I have a gift for you."
target_language_example: Questo messaggio è per voi.
native_language_example: This message is for you.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. "Perché" means "why" here, and "avete" is "you (plural) have" (present tense of avere). It’s followed by a past participle to make the passato prossimo (e.g., "Perché avete venduto...?" = "Why did you sell...?"), or it can introduce a clause in the present (less common in these examples).
target_language_example: Perché avete chiamato la polizia?
native_language_example: Why did you call the police?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a purchase. "Perché" = why; "avete comprato" is passato prossimo of "comprare" with "voi" (you all) or formal "you" when addressing more than one person. Often followed by an object ("questo…") or by "così tanto" (so much).
target_language_example: Perché avete comprato due biglietti invece di uno?
native_language_example: Why did you buy two tickets instead of one?

meaning: "why do you need (to)…?" (you = plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a need/requirement. Structure: perché + avete bisogno di + noun ("...of two bikes") or + infinitive ("...to do this"). "Avete" is 2nd person plural (voi) and can also be used as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Perché avete bisogno di parlare con il direttore?
native_language_example: Why do you need to speak with the manager?

additional_notes: "Perché" means “why” (or “because,” depending on context). Here it’s used in questions: “Why…?” "Ci" is a very common pronoun meaning “us / to us” (e.g., "Perché ci dici questo?" = “Why are you telling us this?”). With some verbs it can also be part of a fixed expression, like "metterci" (“to take [time]”): "Perché ci mette così tanto?" = “Why is it taking so long?”
target_language_example: Perché ci chiami così tardi?
native_language_example: Why are you calling us so late?

meaning: "Why should I…?" (questioning the reason/need to do something).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or ask for a justification for an action, often implying skepticism or reluctance. It’s followed by an infinitive (perché dovrei andare?) or by a verb in the subjunctive (perché dovrei che… is not used; instead: perché dovrei pensare che… / perché dovrei credere che…).
target_language_example: Perché dovrei accettare questa offerta?
native_language_example: Why should I accept this offer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s past state or behavior. "Era" is the imperfect tense of "essere" (was), and "così" means "so" and is usually followed by an adjective: "Perché era così stanco?" (Why was he so tired?). The subject (he/she/it) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Perché era così arrabbiata ieri?
native_language_example: Why was she so angry yesterday?

additional_notes:
Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior or state in the past. 
- perché = “why”
- eri = “you were” (past, informal singular “tu”)
- così = “so” (intensifier before an adjective)
It’s typically followed by an adjective that agrees with the person (e.g., scortese works for all genders; sgarbato/sgarbata, sorpreso/sorpresa change).
target_language_example: Perché eri così nervoso ieri?
native_language_example: Why were you so nervous yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason behind a decision. "Ha deciso di" is the passato prossimo of "decidere" and can refer to **he** (lui), **she** (lei), or the polite **you** (Lei), depending on context. It is followed by an infinitive verb: "ha deciso di + [infinitive]" (e.g., "ha deciso di partire").
target_language_example: Perché ha deciso di cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why did he/she decide to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s need. "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" (he/she/you-formal has). "Bisogno di" means "need (of)" and is followed by a noun ("di due biciclette") or by an infinitive ("di farlo"). You can change the subject: "perché ho bisogno di…" (why do I need…), "perché hai bisogno di…" (why do you need…), "perché abbiamo bisogno di…" (why do we need…).
target_language_example: Perché ha bisogno di chiamare un taxi?
native_language_example: Why does he/she/you (formal) need to call a taxi?

meaning: 'why did you...?' / 'why have you...?' (asking the reason for something you did).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind an action done by 'you' (singular, informal): perché = why, hai = you have (present tense of avere, used as an auxiliary for many past actions: hai comprato = you bought / have bought). In questions it often refers to the recent past (passato prossimo), but can translate as either simple past or present perfect in English depending on context.
target_language_example: Perché hai detto così?
native_language_example: Why did you say that?

meaning: "why did you buy" / "why have you bought".
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a purchase. It’s a question in the passato prossimo: "hai comprato" = "you bought / you have bought" (literally "you have bought"). Usually followed by the thing bought (e.g., "Perché hai comprato questo...?"), and it can imply surprise or criticism depending on tone.
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato due biglietti se non possiamo andare?
native_language_example: Why did you buy two tickets if we can’t go?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for the reason behind a past decision. Follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., andare, diventare, restare). You can also use it more generally as a polite question about motivation: Perché hai deciso di + [infinitive] ?
target_language_example: Perché hai deciso di cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why did you decide to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone needs to do something or needs something. Follow it with an infinitive (perché hai bisogno di andare/fare/leggere…) or a noun (perché hai bisogno di una motosega?). Often implies surprise or curiosity about the necessity.
target_language_example: Perché hai bisogno di parlare con il manager?
native_language_example: Why do you need to talk to the manager?

additional_notes: Used inside a question after verbs like sapere (“to know”) to ask if someone knows the reason for something. Note the difference between perché (why/because) and che (“that”): Tu sai perché il cielo è blu? = “Do you know why the sky is blue?”
target_language_example: Non so perché il cielo è blu, ma posso cercarlo su internet.
native_language_example: I don’t know why the sky is blue, but I can look it up online.

additional_notes: Used to ask a general question about people in general (not specific individuals). Often followed by a verb phrase: "Perché la gente + verbo...?" (e.g., fa, ha, pensa, spreca). In Italian, "perché" can mean both "why" (question) and "because" (answer), but here it’s the question form.
target_language_example: Perché la gente parla così in metro?
native_language_example: Why do people talk like that on the subway?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to ask for the reason behind what people do or what happens. In Italian, perché can mean both “why” (in questions) and “because” (in answers), so punctuation and context matter.
target_language_example: Perché le persone sono sempre di fretta?
native_language_example: Why are people always in a hurry?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. "Perché" means "why" in questions. "Le" is a clitic pronoun placed before the verb: most often an indirect object meaning "to her" (e.g., Perché le ha detto…? = Why did you tell her…?). In some sentences it can be a direct object meaning "them" (feminine plural), and then the past participle often agrees in the feminine plural (e.g., Perché le ha portate qua? = Why did you bring them here?).
target_language_example: Perché le hai parlato così?
native_language_example: Why did you talk to her like that?

additional_notes: Used when a verb has the direct-object pronoun lo (“it” or “him”) and you’re asking “why” about that action. Lo goes before the verb: Perché lo stiamo ascoltando? (“Why are we listening to him/it?”). Often, English will add a preposition (“listen to”), but Italian keeps lo as a direct-object pronoun.
target_language_example: Perché lo hai comprato?
native_language_example: Why did you buy it?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for an action done by “you” plural (voi). "Perché" means “why/because.” "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “him” (depending on context).
