"Avete" is the "you (plural)" form of *avere* and is often used with a past participle (e.g., *detto, colpito, gettato via, licenziato, ucciso*) to form the past tense (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Perché lo avete comprato se non vi serve?
native_language_example: Why did you buy it if you don’t need it?

meaning: "why (are you) ... to me? / why do you ... me?"
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question: perché = “why” and mi is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “me” (often “to me” or “me” depending on the verb). It’s followed by a verb phrase: “Perché mi ami?”, “Perché mi stai chiamando?”, “Perché mi chiedi dei soldi?”.
target_language_example: Perché mi guardi così?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason about something a group of people (“voi”) did that affects the speaker (“mi” = to me). It’s followed by a past participle to form the passato prossimo: perché mi avete + lasciato/scelto/abbandonata, etc. The past participle may agree with the speaker when a direct-object pronoun is used (e.g., abbandonata if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Perché mi avete chiamato così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

meaning: “why did you … to me?” / “why have you … to me?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason when someone did something that affects you. It’s typically followed by a past participle (passato prossimo): “Perché mi hai invitato?” (Why did you invite me?). “mi” means “to me” (object pronoun), and “hai” is “you have” (tu) used to form the past tense.
target_language_example: Perché mi hai chiamato così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question explaining the reason someone isn’t trusted. The verb is "fidarsi di" (reflexive) = "to trust" and it takes "di" before a person/thing: "si fida di Tom" (he/she trusts Tom). You can change "nessuno" (nobody) to "tutti" (everyone) or swap in a pronoun: "di lui/lei" (him/her), "di me" (me).
target_language_example: Mi spieghi perché nessuno si fida di lui?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me why nobody trusts him?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason something didn’t happen ("Why didn’t you…?") or to make a suggestion ("Why not…?"). It’s typically followed by a verb (e.g., "Perché non vieni?" = "Why don’t you come?") or by an option/idea (e.g., "Perché non qui?" = "Why not here?").
target_language_example: Perché non andiamo al cinema stasera?
native_language_example: Why don’t we go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason or explanation for an opinion/belief. It’s followed by a clause introduced by che, typically with the subjunctive (e.g., sia, stia, abbia, stesse). Often used when asking about someone’s assumptions: Perché pensi che…?
target_language_example: Perché pensi che sia successo questo?
native_language_example: Why do you think this happened?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. With an adjective it means “Why are you…?” (Perché sei arrabbiato/a?). With a past participle it often forms the passato prossimo with essere, meaning “Why did you…?/Why have you…?” (Perché sei entrato/a…?).
target_language_example: Perché sei in ritardo?
native_language_example: Why are you late?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior, mood, or personality trait. Follow it with an adjective (e.g., stanco, arrabbiato, felice). Can sound accusatory or rude depending on tone and the adjective; to soften, you can say “Come mai sei così…?” or add “oggi” (today).
target_language_example: Perché sei così nervoso oggi?
native_language_example: Why are you so nervous today?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with frustration or surprise) why someone consistently behaves in a certain way. It’s typically followed by an adjective or description (e.g., geloso = jealous, lenta = slow, stanco = tired). You can change the subject: perché siete sempre così… (you plural/formal), perché è sempre così… (he/she/it).
target_language_example: Perché sei sempre così pessimista?
native_language_example: Why are you always so pessimistic?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s coming/arriving. Literally “why are you come,” but in Italian this present tense form (“sei venuta”) is the normal way to express the past (“you came/you have come”). Venuta is feminine, so you say it to a woman; to a man: “perché sei venuto?”. You can add a place/time: “Perché sei venuta qui/qua stamattina?” In a blaming tone it can mean “why did you even come?”
target_language_example: Perché sei venuta qui oggi?
native_language_example: Why did you come here today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something about a group of people, using the present tense of essere (siete = you all are). It’s followed by an adjective (Perché siete felici?), a preposition phrase (Perché siete in ritardo?), or a past participle as an adjective (Perché siete arrabbiati?). For mixed or all-male groups use siete venuti/tornati/arrabbiati; for all-female groups use siete venute/tornate/arrabbiate.
target_language_example: Perché siete qui così presto?
native_language_example: Why are you here so early?

meaning: "why are you so …?" (asking the reason for a quality or reaction).
additional_notes: Used to ask why a group of people ("voi") has a certain characteristic or feels/reacts a certain way. "Siete" is the "you" plural/formal form of "essere" (to be). "Così" means "so" and is usually followed by an adjective: "così generose/popolari/sorpresi".
target_language_example: Perché siete così stanchi oggi?
native_language_example: Why are you so tired today?

meaning: "why are you (plural, feminine) so good at …?"
additional_notes:
Used to ask why a group of women/girls are very skilled at something. 
- perché = why
- siete = you are (plural)
- così = so
- brave = good/capable (feminine plural; masculine would be bravi)
- a = at (used before many activities; also before nouns like baseball/scacchi)
Often followed by a noun (a scacchi, a baseball) or an infinitive verb (a nuotare, a cucinare, a farlo).
target_language_example: Perché siete così brave a parlare italiano?
native_language_example: Why are you (all, women/girls) so good at speaking Italian?

meaning: "Why are you always like this?" / "Why are you always so…?" (to a group).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people ("voi") why they repeatedly behave in a certain way. Often followed by an adjective: "Perché siete sempre così felici/gelosi/irritabili/tranquilli?". Can sound accusing or teasing depending on tone; for one person you’d say "Perché sei sempre così…?".
target_language_example: Perché siete sempre così in ritardo?
native_language_example: Why are you always so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what someone is doing right now. It’s typically followed by a gerund (sta + -ando/-endo): e.g., “Perché sta piangendo?” = “Why is he/she crying?” The subject (lui/lei/Lei/it) is often implied from context.
target_language_example: Perché sta parlando così piano?
native_language_example: Why is he/she speaking so quietly?

meaning: "why are you...?" / "why do you...?" (introduces a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what someone is doing or how they are acting. Very often followed by the gerund (stai + -ando/-endo): "Perché stai piangendo?" = "Why are you crying?" It can also be followed by an adjective: "Perché stai zitto?" = "Why are you quiet?" In more formal Italian you may also hear "Perché sei..." or "Perché fai...", but "perché stai..." is common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Perché stai aspettando qui?
native_language_example: Why are you waiting here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what a group of people (or “you” plural) are doing. Often followed by the present continuous with a gerund: “Perché state + verb-ando/-endo …?” (e.g., “Perché state aspettando?” = “Why are you waiting?”).
target_language_example: Perché state parlando così forte?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking so loudly?

meaning: "why do you…?" / "why are you…?" (starting a question addressed to 'you').
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question. "Perché" = "why" and "ti" is the object/reflexive pronoun for "you" (informal singular), placed before the verb (e.g., "Perché ti serve…?" = "Why do you need…?", "Perché ti arrabbi?" = "Why are you getting angry?").
target_language_example: Perché ti preoccupi tanto?
native_language_example: Why are you worrying so much?

meaning: 'why you…' (addressing more than one person, or formal 'you').
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. "Perché" means "why" and "vi" is the object/reflexive pronoun for "you" plural (or formal "you"), placed before the verb (e.g., "Perché vi importa…?" = "Why do you care…?"; "Perché vi state comportando…?" = "Why are you behaving…?").
target_language_example: Perché vi siete arrabbiati con me?
native_language_example: Why did you get angry with me?

meaning: “Why are you hiding?” (talking to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior. "Vi" = to/you (plural). "Stare" + gerund ("state nascondendo") expresses an action happening right now: "you are hiding". Often followed by "da" + person ("da lui/da me/da Tom") meaning "from" someone.
target_language_example: Perché vi state nascondendo qui?
native_language_example: Why are you hiding here?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s reason for wanting to do something. Typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., essere, imparare, incontrare) or by a noun phrase (e.g., perché vuoi questo?). Often introduces a direct question.
target_language_example: Perché vuoi andare in Italia quest'estate?
native_language_example: Why do you want to go to Italy this summer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is the case. It’s formed with perché (“why/because”) + è (third-person singular of essere, “is”). In Italian you don’t invert word order like in English; you typically say “Perché è …?” + subject/place/adjective.
target_language_example: Perché è così difficile?
native_language_example: Why is it so difficult?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone or something has a certain quality/state. You typically add an adjective after it (e.g., assonnato/a, divertito/a, egoista). The verb agrees with the subject (è = 'is'), and the adjective often changes for gender/number (assonnato/assonnata; divertito/divertita).
target_language_example: Perché è così arrabbiata oggi?
native_language_example: Why is she so angry today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone is consistently a certain way. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., burbero, felice, geloso/a). You can change the subject pronoun: Perché sono sempre così...? (Why am I always like this?), Perché sei sempre così...? (Why are you always like that?).
target_language_example: Perché è sempre così nervoso?
native_language_example: Why is he always so nervous?

additional_notes: Commonly used when giving advice about health or dieting. It’s built from perdere (“to lose”) + peso (“weight”). You can also say: Devo perdere peso. / Vorrei perdere peso.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di perdere peso prima dell’estate.
native_language_example: I’m trying to lose weight before summer.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring results or value. Often appears with intensifiers like una pura/una totale/una tale perdita di tempo (“a pure/total/such a waste of time”). Can be exclaimed: Che perdita di tempo! (“What a waste of time!”).
target_language_example: Fare la fila per due ore è stata una perdita di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting in line for two hours was a waste of time.

additional_notes: “Perse” is the passato remoto (simple past) of *perdere* (“to lose”). In everyday spoken Italian you’ll more often hear *ha perso i suoi occhiali* (passato prossimo). *I suoi occhiali* means “his/her glasses” (owned by the subject).
target_language_example: Ieri perse i suoi occhiali e non riuscì più a leggere.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she lost his/her glasses and couldn’t read anymore.

additional_notes: Past simple (passato remoto) of *perdere* = “to lose.” *Il suo* means “his/her/its” and usually refers to something owned by a previously mentioned person. In everyday speech you’ll often hear the present perfect instead: *ha perso il suo…* (“has lost his/her …”). This phrase is typically followed by the noun of the thing lost (e.g., *il suo telefono*).
target_language_example: Ieri perse il suo telefono in treno.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she lost his/her phone on the train.

additional_notes: “Perse” is the passato remoto (remote past) of perdere (“to lose”). It’s common in writing and storytelling; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear “ha perso il suo lavoro.” The possessive and article can change: “persi il mio lavoro” (I lost my job), “perse il suo lavoro” (he/she lost his/her job), “persero il loro lavoro” (they lost their job). Often used without naming the person when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente, perse il suo lavoro.
native_language_example: After the accident, he lost his job.

meaning: “(he/she) lost his/her …” (past simple of perdere, used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone lost something they possessed or something abstract (like credibility). The verb is in the passato remoto (common in storytelling, history, and in some regions; in everyday speech many people use passato prossimo: “ha perso”). “La sua” agrees with the thing owned (feminine singular): la sua borsetta, la sua fede, la sua terra, la sua credibilità. With a masculine singular noun you would use “perse il suo …”.
target_language_example: Durante il viaggio, perse la sua valigia.
native_language_example: During the trip, he/she lost his/her suitcase.

meaning: "he/she/it lost all of his/her/its" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: "Perse" is the passato remoto (past historic) of "perdere" (to lose), used mainly in narratives, books, news reports, and in some regions in everyday speech instead of "ha perso". "tutti" agrees with the noun that follows: "tutti i suoi" + masculine plural noun (soldi, risparmi, libri), but "tutte le sue" + feminine plural noun (chiavi, cose). You’ll usually add the thing lost right after: "perse tutti i suoi soldi".
target_language_example: Durante la crisi, perse tutti i suoi risparmi.
native_language_example: During the crisis, he lost all his savings.

additional_notes: Past tense of the expression “perdere di vista” = “to lose sight of.” Used when you can’t see someone anymore (e.g., because of a crowd, distance, turning a corner). Often used with direct object pronouns: lo/la/li/le + persi di vista (e.g., “Lo persi di vista”).
target_language_example: Ti ho cercato, ma ti ho perso di vista per un attimo.
native_language_example: I looked for you, but I lost sight of you for a moment.

additional_notes: From the verb *perdere* (“to lose; to miss”). *Perso* is the masculine singular past participle, used with *avere*: *ho perso il...* (“I lost/missed the ...”). It can mean physically losing something (*Ho perso il quaderno*) or missing an event/opportunity (*Mi sarei perso il compleanno* = “I would have missed the birthday”). Use *perso il* before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *il lavoro, il cane, il quaderno*).
target_language_example: Ho perso il treno perché ero in ritardo.
native_language_example: I missed the train because I was late.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "perdere il controllo". Used both literally (losing physical control) and figuratively (losing self-control or temper). You can add "di" to specify what you lost control of: "ho perso il controllo di/delle..."
target_language_example: Ho perso il controllo e ho detto cose che non pensavo.
native_language_example: I lost control and said things I didn’t mean.

additional_notes: Used with the verb perdere (to lose) in the passato prossimo: ha perso il suo + noun. "Il suo" agrees with the thing that is lost (masculine singular). Variations: ha perso la sua borsa (his/her bag), ha perso i suoi documenti (his documents), ha perso le sue chiavi (his keys).
target_language_example: Ha perso il suo telefono e non riesce più a chiamare nessuno.
native_language_example: He lost his phone and he can’t call anyone anymore.

additional_notes: From the verb "perdere" (to miss/lose) + "il suo treno" (his/her train). In Italian you commonly use "perdere" to mean "to miss" a train, bus, flight, appointment, etc. The literal translation is "lost his/her train," but the natural meaning is "missed his/her train."
target_language_example: Ho perso il mio treno e ora devo aspettare il prossimo.
native_language_example: I missed my train and now I have to wait for the next one.

meaning: "missed the train" (arrived too late to catch it).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "perdere" (to miss/lose). In the past it’s usually in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha perso il treno" = "I/you/he/she missed the train." It can also be used more generally to mean “missed the chance/opportunity” ("Hai perso il treno" = “You missed your chance”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho perso il treno e arrivo più tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I missed the train and I’ll arrive later.

additional_notes: *Perso* is the past participle of **perdere** (“to lose / to miss”), used with **avere** in the passato prossimo: **ho/ha perso la + noun**. With things like **la chiamata** or **la parte migliore**, it often means “missed” rather than “lost.” The *la* changes with the noun (il/lo/i/gli/le).
target_language_example: Ho perso la chiave di casa e ho perso la prima parte del film.
native_language_example: I lost my house key and I missed the first part of the movie.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *perdere* (to lose): *Hai/Abbiamo/Avete perso la partita* = “You/We/You all lost the match.” In the reflexive form (*perdersi*), it often means “to miss” an event: *Ti sei perso la partita?* = “Did you miss the match?” (auxiliary *essere*: *mi/ti/si/ci/vi sono perso/a*).
target_language_example: Ho perso la partita, ma mi sono divertito lo stesso.
native_language_example: I lost the match, but I still had fun.

additional_notes: "Perso" is the past participle of "perdere" (to lose). With "avere" (e.g., "ha perso", "di aver perso", "sembra aver perso"), it expresses a completed action: "(someone) has lost...". "La sua" means "his/her" and usually refers back to the subject (e.g., Mary → her key).
target_language_example: Credo che abbia perso la sua chiave.
native_language_example: I think he/she has lost his/her key.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing which person you mean. Often preceded by an article or demonstrative (la/una/questa/quella persona che...). With 'persona' (feminine), the relative pronoun is still 'che' for both genders: "la persona che...", "la sola persona che...".
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli inglese.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a person who speaks English.

meaning: “the person (that/who) …” (used to introduce a clause with di cui = “about whom/that”).
additional_notes: Used when you refer to a specific person and then add information in a relative clause introduced by **di cui**. Most often it means **“the person (that) you’re talking about”** or **“a person you can trust.”** The verb after **di cui** often takes **parlare (di)** (“talk about”) or **fidarsi (di)** (“trust”). With **fidarsi**, you’ll see forms like **di cui mi posso fidare / di cui posso fidarmi** (same meaning).
target_language_example: Non è una persona di cui mi posso fidare.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t a person I can trust.

meaning: "people who" (introduces a relative clause about people).
additional_notes: Used when you’re describing a group of people and then adding information about them with a clause starting with che (= who/that). Often appears after "(ci) sono" or "delle/le" (e.g., "Ci sono persone che...", "le persone che...").
target_language_example: Conosco persone che parlano tre lingue.
native_language_example: I know people who speak three languages.

meaning: "but ... not" / "however, ... not" (introduces a contrast with a negative).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what you expect with what actually happens, followed by a verb in the negative. Often comes after a comma: "..., però non ...". Similar to "ma non", but "però" can sound a bit more like "however".
target_language_example: Volevo uscire, però non ho tempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go out, but I don't have time.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a portion or chunk of something, often food: "un pezzo di pizza/pane". It’s usually preceded by an article ("un/uno/una", "questo") and followed by a noun. With amounts you’ll often hear "un altro pezzo di..." = "another piece of...".
target_language_example: Mi dai un pezzo di torta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of cake, please?

additional_notes: Used when offering, asking for, or giving someone a portion of cake. Often follows articles/quantities like "un/altro" (a/another): "un pezzo di torta", "un altro pezzo di torta". "Torta" can mean cake (and sometimes pie depending on context), but this phrase is straightforward in food situations.
target_language_example: Posso avere un pezzo di torta al cioccolato?
native_language_example: Can I have a piece of chocolate cake?

meaning: "(Do/does) … like the …?" / "… like(s) the …" (with plural masculine nouns starting with a vowel, s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, y).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say that someone likes something; the thing liked is the grammatical subject (piacciono = plural). The person who likes it is introduced with an indirect pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with a + name (A Tom…). “Gli” is the plural masculine article used before certain sounds (e.g., gli sport, gli orologi, gli asiatici, gli ananas, gli involtini). Word order often starts with the person: “Mi piacciono gli …” = “I like the …”.
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono gli involtini primavera.
native_language_example: Marco likes spring rolls.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to express likes. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Tom..."); the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you often use a pronoun like "gli/le" (to him/to her). Because "gli animali" is plural, you use the plural verb form "piacciono" (vs. singular "piace").
target_language_example: A me piacciono gli animali, soprattutto i cani.
native_language_example: I like animals, especially dogs.

meaning: "(They) like the ..." (plural masculine) / "the ... are pleasing to (someone)".
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to talk about liking things. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you often add an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: mi piacciono i... (I like...), ti piacciono i... (you like...), gli/le piacciono i... (he/she likes...), ci piacciono i... (we like...), vi piacciono i... (you all like...), gli piacciono i... (they like...). Use piacciono (plural) because i + noun is plural; for singular use piace: mi piace il.... With feminine plural use piacciono le....
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i film italiani.
native_language_example: I like Italian movies.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (indirect object): "A Tom piacciono i cani" = "Tom likes dogs." The thing that is liked ("i cani") is grammatically the subject, so the verb is plural: "piacciono" (because dogs = plural). With a singular thing you use "piace" (e.g., "A Tom piace il cane").
target_language_example: A mia sorella piacciono i cani, ma non le piacciono i gatti.
native_language_example: My sister likes dogs, but she doesn't like cats.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”). The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so it often appears after the verb: piacciono (plural) i cani piccoli. The person who likes them is shown with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or with “a + person”: Mi piacciono… / A te piacciono… / Le piacciono…
target_language_example: A me piacciono i cani piccoli, ma a mio fratello piacciono i cani grandi.
native_language_example: I like small dogs, but my brother likes big dogs.

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the thing liked (i film) is the grammatical subject, so you use the 3rd-person plural verb form piacciono. The person who likes is introduced with a + indirect object pronoun/name: A me/te/lui/lei/Lei/noi/voi/loro piacciono i film. If the thing liked is singular, use piace (e.g., Mi piace questo film).
target_language_example: A me piacciono i film d’azione.
native_language_example: I like action movies.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). Grammatically, "i fiori" is the subject, and the person who likes them is introduced with "a" (e.g., "a lui", "a Layla") or an indirect object pronoun ("mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi"). Because "i fiori" is plural, it takes the plural verb form "piacciono" (singular would be "piace").
target_language_example: A mia madre piacciono i fiori, soprattutto le rose.
native_language_example: My mother likes flowers, especially roses.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing liked (i frutti di mare) is the grammatical subject, so you use piacciono (plural). The person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (a lui/a noi/a loro) or with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): e.g., Ci piacciono i frutti di mare = We like seafood.
target_language_example: Ti piacciono i frutti di mare?
native_language_example: Do you like seafood?

meaning: (they) like cats / cats are pleasing (to someone).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The thing liked (“i gatti”) is the grammatical subject, so you often add the person with a + pronoun/name: “A me/A Susan…”. With plural things (like i gatti), use piacciono; with a singular thing, use piace.
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono i gatti, ma a sua sorella piacciono i cani.
native_language_example: Marco likes cats, but his sister likes dogs.

additional_notes: Uses piacere (to be pleasing) with an indirect object: Mi/Ci/Gli/Le piacciono i giochi = “I/We/He/She like games.” The person who likes something is introduced with a (A Tom piacciono i giochi). With plural things (i giochi), use piacciono; with a singular thing (il gioco), use piace.
target_language_example: A mia sorella piacciono i giochi da tavolo.
native_language_example: My sister likes board games.

meaning: 'they are liked' / 'they please' (used to say someone likes things—plural feminine).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing to”: the person who likes is an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) and the thing liked is the subject. "Piacciono" is 3rd-person plural to match a plural thing, and "le" is the feminine plural article (le auto, le acciughe). Structure: A + person + piacciono le + plural noun. Example: "A me piacciono le..." = "I like...".
target_language_example: A me piacciono le fragole.
native_language_example: I like strawberries.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say someone likes something. The thing liked ("le mele") is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: "piacciono" for plural, "piace" for singular. The person who likes it is introduced with "a" (e.g., "a me", "a te", "a lei", "a noi"). In questions, intonation often changes or you can add a question mark in writing: "A te piacciono le mele?" For negation: "non piacciono".
target_language_example: A Marco non piacciono le mele, ma gli piacciono le pere.
native_language_example: Marco doesn’t like apples, but he likes pears.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”). The person who likes is usually introduced with an indirect object: a me/a te/a lui/a lei/a noi/a loro, or pronouns like gli/le/mi/ti/ci/gli. Because ragazze is plural, you use piacciono (plural) rather than piace (singular). Word order can vary: Le ragazze gli piacciono = “He likes girls.”
target_language_example: A te piacciono le ragazze?
native_language_example: Do you like girls?

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with “a + name/pronoun.” The thing liked (here: “cantare”) is the subject, so you say “Mi piace cantare” = “Singing is pleasing to me” → “I like to sing.” You can add what you like to sing: “Mi piace cantare canzoni italiane.”
target_language_example: Mi piace cantare quando sono da solo in macchina.
native_language_example: I like to sing when I’m alone in the car.

additional_notes: Used with piacere, where the thing liked is the grammatical subject and the person who likes it is introduced by an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): e.g., «Perché ti piace così tanto Boston?» = “Why do you like Boston so much?” Often appears in questions with «Perché…?» and can refer to a specific thing («ti piace così tanto il basket») or just “it” («ti piace così tanto?»).
target_language_example: Mi piace così tanto questa città che vorrei viverci.
native_language_example: I like this city so much that I’d like to live here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to emphasize that someone genuinely likes something/someone. Remember piacere works “backwards” in English: the thing/person liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced by a + indirect object pronoun/noun (Mi piace…, A Tom piace…). You can use it with people, things, or activities (verbs in the infinitive). Word order is flexible: A Tom piace davvero Mary / Mary piace davvero a Tom.
target_language_example: Mi piace davvero questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I really like this restaurant.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing), so the person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Mary...") or with an indirect object pronoun ("gli" = to him, "le" = to her). "Il suo impiego" means “his/her job/employment,” and "davvero" adds emphasis (“really”).
target_language_example: A Marco piace davvero il suo impiego, anche se è stancante.
native_language_example: Marco really likes his job, even if it's tiring.

additional_notes: Used with piacere to compare preferences (more than something else) or to say what you like the most. Often appears in questions with a choice (Cosa ti piace di più, X o Y?) and in relative clauses: Il/La ... che mi piace di più = “my favorite ...”. Remember the grammar: the thing you like is the subject (Mi piace...), and the person is an indirect object (mi/ti/le/gli/ci/vi/gli).
target_language_example: Tra questi due ristoranti, quale ti piace di più?
native_language_example: Between these two restaurants, which one do you like more?

meaning: “to like doing / to like to do”.
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive to say someone likes an activity. The person who likes it is marked with an indirect object pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with “a + name”: “Mi piace fare…”, “A Maria piace fare…”. Often used in questions about hobbies: “Cosa ti piace fare…?”
target_language_example: Mi piace fare una passeggiata dopo cena.
native_language_example: I like to go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive. The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (a me, a te, a Mary, a loro). With an infinitive like giocare, you normally use piace (singular). Note: piace looks like English “please,” but here it means “(to) like,” so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: A mio fratello piace giocare a calcio dopo scuola.
native_language_example: My brother likes to play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing being watched is the grammatical subject. Common patterns: “Mi piace guardare…” = “I like to watch…”, “Ti piace guardare…?” = “Do you like to watch…?”, “A Tom piace guardare…” = “Tom likes to watch…”. You can also use “piace guardare + noun” (e.g., “piace guardare le serie TV”).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare film in italiano con i sottotitoli.
native_language_example: I like watching movies in Italian with subtitles.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked is the subject (guardare la TV), and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (a me, a lui, a Felicja). Example patterns: A me piace guardare la TV. / A loro piace guardare la TV mentre mangiano. With a plural thing liked, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i film).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare la TV la sera.
native_language_example: I like to watch TV in the evening.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + name/pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli). With il, it refers to a masculine singular noun (piace il gelato). For a plural thing: piacciono i/le; for feminine singular: piace la; with an infinitive: piace + verb (Mi piace nuotare).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato, ma non mi piace il caffè.
native_language_example: I like ice cream, but I don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked (il basket) is the subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli + a Tom). So it’s literally “basketball is pleasing to (someone),” even though in English we say “(someone) likes basketball.” Questions are often formed just with intonation: A Tom piace il basket?
target_language_example: Ti piace il basket o preferisci il calcio?
native_language_example: Do you like basketball, or do you prefer soccer?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom…, A loro…). With singular thing: piace; with plural things: piacciono. Common forms: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace il caffè.
target_language_example: Mi piace il caffè, ma non mi piace il tè.
native_language_example: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object (a me, a te, a Tom, a tutte le mie amiche). Because calcio is singular, you use piace (not piacciono). Word order is flexible: A Tom piace il calcio / Il calcio piace a Tom.
target_language_example: A me piace il calcio, ma a mio fratello piace il basket.
native_language_example: I like soccer, but my brother likes basketball.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom, A me, A tutti), and the thing liked is the grammatical subject: A Tom piace il cibo = “Tom likes food” (literally: “Food is pleasing to Tom”). With plural things, use piacciono: A Tom piacciono i dolci (“Tom likes sweets”).
target_language_example: A me piace il cibo italiano.
native_language_example: I like Italian food.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (often with a + pronoun/noun): a me/mi (I), a te/ti (you), a lui/gli (he), a lei/le (she), a noi/ci (we), a voi/vi (you all), a loro/gli. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so with a singular noun you use piace; with plural nouns you use piacciono.
target_language_example: Mi piace il cibo cinese, ma oggi preferisco la pizza.
native_language_example: I like Chinese food, but today I prefer pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The thing liked (il gelato) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi piace il gelato (I like ice cream), ti piace...? (do you like...?), le piace...? (formal you), a chi piace...? (who likes...?). With plural things, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i gelati).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato al cioccolato, ma non mi piace quello alla vaniglia.
native_language_example: I like chocolate ice cream, but I don’t like vanilla one.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (A me/ a te/ a lui/ a lei/ a Tom...), and the verb agrees with what is liked: "piace" + singular thing (il jazz), "piacciono" + plural things (i film).
target_language_example: A me piace il jazz, ma a mio fratello no.
native_language_example: I like jazz, but my brother doesn't.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing), so the thing liked is the grammatical subject: il latte al cioccolato piace a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro. The person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or with a + pronoun/noun (a noi, a Maria). With a singular thing: piace; with plural things: piacciono.
target_language_example: Mi piace il latte al cioccolato, ma oggi preferisco il tè.
native_language_example: I like chocolate milk, but today I prefer tea.

additional_notes: Used to say you like (or don’t like) someone’s behavior/style of doing something. Italian often uses the structure "A + person + piace" (e.g., "A Maria piace...") or "Mi piace / Non mi piace...". "il modo" = “the way/manner,” and "in cui" = “in which/that.” You can also use the plural: "Mi piacciono i modi in cui..." (“I like the ways (that) ...”).
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui parli italiano.
native_language_example: I like the way you speak Italian.

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the thing liked (il riso) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace...). Common pattern: (A me/Marco) piace il riso; (A noi) piace il riso.
target_language_example: A me piace il riso, ma non mi piace la pasta.
native_language_example: I like rice, but I don’t like pasta.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing): the thing liked (il tè) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object (a/ad + pronoun/name), e.g., Mi piace il tè = I like tea; A lui piace il tè = He likes tea; Ti piace il tè? = Do you like tea?
target_language_example: Mi piace il tè, ma preferisco il caffè.
native_language_example: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to express liking. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (or a pronoun like "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli"). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use "piace" for singular ("la ...") and "piacciono" for plural. Example: "A Maria piace la macchina" = "Maria likes the car" (literally: "To Maria, the car is pleasing").
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza.
native_language_example: I like pizza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”) where the thing liked is the grammatical subject: la carne di coniglio piace. The person who likes it is introduced with a + name (A Tochtli…) or with an indirect object pronoun: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace… For questions: Ti piace la carne di coniglio? (“Do you like rabbit meat?”).
target_language_example: A Marco piace la carne di coniglio, ma a me no.
native_language_example: Marco likes rabbit meat, but I don’t.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally “to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (indirect object): "A Nancy piace la musica" = “Nancy likes music.” The thing liked (“la musica”) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is singular (piace). With pronouns you’ll often hear: "Mi piace la musica" (I like music), "Ti piace la musica" (Do you like music?).
target_language_example: A Marco piace la musica classica.
native_language_example: Marco likes classical music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object: A Tom piace la musica classica = “Tom likes classical music” (literally, “Classical music is pleasing to Tom”). Question form: A te piace la musica classica? (“Do you like classical music?”).
target_language_example: A mia sorella piace la musica classica, ma a me piace il rock.
native_language_example: My sister likes classical music, but I like rock.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere": the thing liked ("la pasta") is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with "a" (often combined with an article: "a + il = al"). So "A Tom piace la pasta" is literally “To Tom, pasta is pleasing.” For more than one person, use "piacciono" (e.g., "A Tom e Maria piacciono i film").
target_language_example: A me piace la pasta, ma a mia sorella piace il riso.
native_language_example: I like pasta, but my sister likes rice.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works differently from English “to like.” The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (or an indirect object pronoun: mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli). The thing that is liked is the grammatical subject: piace with singular nouns (la pizza), and piacciono with plural nouns (Le pizze mi piacciono). Common pattern: A Marco piace la pizza / A loro piace la pizza.
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza, ma a mia sorella piacciono gli hamburger.
native_language_example: I like pizza, but my sister likes hamburgers.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A Tom piace leggere libri = “Tom likes reading books” (literally: “Reading books is pleasing to Tom”). The thing liked is the subject (here: leggere libri). Question form is the same word order, with rising intonation or a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Ti piace leggere libri in italiano?
native_language_example: Do you like reading books in Italian?

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: literally “to be pleasing.” The person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or with a + name (A Tom piace...). The thing liked is the subject: with an infinitive you get “Mi piace mangiare...” = “I like to eat...”. For plural subjects, use piacciono (e.g., “Mi piacciono le mele”).
target_language_example: A me piace mangiare la pizza il sabato sera.
native_language_example: I like to eat pizza on Saturday night.

meaning: "really likes" (talking about a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to express liking/enjoying something. The person who likes is introduced with a + pronoun/name (A me..., A Tom...), and the thing liked is the grammatical subject (il + noun). Word order can vary: "Mi piace molto il..." is also common.
target_language_example: A Marco piace molto il caffè italiano.
native_language_example: Marco really likes Italian coffee.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to ask/say that someone likes something. The person who likes it is expressed with an indirect object pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with 'a + name/pronoun' (A me, A Tom). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use 'piace' with singular nouns (questo colore) and 'piacciono' with plural nouns (queste scarpe). Often used in questions: 'Ti piace questo...?' = 'Do you like this...?'
target_language_example: Ti piace questo ristorante?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to emphasize a strong liking. Remember the structure: A + person + piace + thing/activity (literally “To [someone], [thing] is pleasing”). With pronouns: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi piace veramente… (e.g., Gli piace veramente = He really likes it).
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente questa pizza.
native_language_example: I really like this pizza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing you like (here, viaggiare = “to travel”) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A me piace viaggiare (I like traveling), A Tom piace viaggiare (Tom likes traveling). With an infinitive like viaggiare, you typically use piace (singular).
target_language_example: Ti piace viaggiare in treno?
native_language_example: Do you like traveling by train?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Fadil..."), and the thing liked is grammatically the subject. "Piaceva" is for singular things; for plural things use "piacevano". It agrees with the noun after it (here "la" + a feminine singular noun). Often translates to English as "liked" in the past.
target_language_example: Da bambino, a me piaceva la pizza.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense (piaceva) to talk about liking in the past, often in reported speech after che (e.g., Ha detto che...). Remember the structure: the thing liked is the subject (la mia idea), and the person who likes it is an indirect object pronoun (gli/le/mi) or a + pronoun (a lui/a loro).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che le piaceva la mia idea.
native_language_example: He/She told me that she liked my idea.

meaning: "(Someone) liked the snow" (in the past / used to like the snow).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing”: a lei piaceva la neve = “she liked the snow” (literally, “the snow was pleasing to her”). Piaceva is the imperfect tense, common in reported speech after ha detto che… and for describing past preferences/habits. The person who likes something is shown with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with a + pronoun (a me, a lei, a loro).
target_language_example: Da bambino, mi piaceva la neve, ma ora preferisco il sole.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked the snow, but now I prefer the sun.

meaning: “(he/she) liked the rain” / “(he/she) used to like the rain.”
additional_notes: Imperfect of piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli (to him), le (to her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). So “A lui piaceva la pioggia” literally means “To him, the rain was pleasing,” i.e., “He liked the rain,” often describing a past habit or ongoing feeling.
target_language_example: Da bambino, gli piaceva la pioggia perché poteva saltare nelle pozzanghere.
native_language_example: As a child, he liked the rain because he could jump in puddles.

meaning: “(someone) liked pizza” / “pizza was pleasing to (someone)” (past, imperfect).
additional_notes: With piacere, the thing liked is the grammatical subject (la pizza), and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object: a Ziri, a lei, mi, gli, le, etc. Piaceva is the imperfect tense, used for a past state or habitual liking (“used to like,” “liked (back then)”). Word order can vary: A lei piaceva la pizza / La pizza le piaceva.
target_language_example: Quando era bambina, a Marta piaceva la pizza margherita.
native_language_example: When she was a child, Marta liked margherita pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the past: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject, so you say Mi è piaciuta la cena (“The dinner pleased me” = “I liked the dinner”). Piaciuta agrees with a feminine singular noun (la cena, la scuola, la minestra). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli, or a + person (A me, a te).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la mostra?
native_language_example: Did you like the exhibition?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **piacere** (“to be pleasing/liked”), which works differently from English: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject (**il mio libro**), and the person who likes it is introduced with **a + person** (e.g., **a lei**, **a loro**). In the past tense (**è piaciuto**), the verb agrees with what is liked: **è piaciuto** (masc. singular, for **il libro**), **è piaciuta** (fem. singular), **sono piaciuti/piaciute** (plural).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto il mio libro?
native_language_example: Did you like my book?

additional_notes: Used to indicate the position of a planet when you count outward starting from a reference point (usually the Sun): “il quarto pianeta a partire dal Sole” = “the fourth planet from the Sun.” The pattern is: [number + pianeta] a partire da/dal + [starting point]. Use “dal” before masculine singular nouns like “il Sole” (a partire dal Sole) and “dalla” before feminine singular nouns (a partire dalla Terra).
target_language_example: Giove è il quinto pianeta a partire dal Sole.
native_language_example: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly whenever a certain situation occurs. “Ogni volta che” (“every time that/whenever”) is followed by a verb (often in the present tense for a general habit): e.g., “piango ogni volta che lo vedo” = “I cry every time I see it/him.”
target_language_example: Piango ogni volta che penso a quei giorni.
native_language_example: I cry every time I think about those days.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (piani per un picnic = plans for a picnic) or with an infinitive (piani per andare = plans to go). Common with "avere": "Ho dei piani per..." = "I have plans to/for...".
target_language_example: Hai già dei piani per il weekend?
native_language_example: Do you already have plans for the weekend?

meaning: the upstairs floor; the floor above.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an upper level in a building (often in a house). Common with verbs of movement like andare/salire (to go up) or with sounds coming from above (sentire qualcuno al piano di sopra).
target_language_example: Il bagno è al piano di sopra, a destra.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs, on the right.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive verb form "sia" (from "essere" = to be), typically after expressions like "penso che..." (I think that...) to give an opinion. "Piuttosto" often means "rather/pretty" (a bit, fairly). Note: "piano" here means "plan" (not the musical instrument).
target_language_example: Penso che questo piano sia piuttosto stupido, ma possiamo discuterne.
native_language_example: I think this plan is rather stupid, but we can discuss it.

additional_notes: Used to describe a village that is small in size/population. Often follows a preposition like "in" ("in the small village"). "Piccolo" agrees with the noun: "piccolo villaggio" (masc. sing.), "piccoli villaggi" (masc. plural).
target_language_example: In quel piccolo villaggio tutti si conoscono.
native_language_example: In that small village everyone knows each other.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns/adjectives (e.g., una scatola/stanza/persona è piena di...). With masculine nouns use "pieno di"; plural: "pieni di" (masc.) / "piene di" (fem.). Can describe something literally filled ("una scatola piena di mele") or figuratively ("piena di energia/curiosità").
target_language_example: Sono piena di impegni questa settimana.
native_language_example: I'm full of commitments this week.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something (physical or abstract): "pieno di sale" (filled with salt), "pieno di rabbia" (full of anger). With people it can describe an attitude: "pieno di sé" means "full of oneself" → conceited/very self-important.
target_language_example: La stanza è piena di gente.
native_language_example: The room is full of people.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like riuscire a (manage to), sapere (know how to), and potere (can) to talk about having the ability to operate and fly a helicopter. In everyday English you’d usually say “fly a helicopter,” while Italian commonly uses pilotare (“to pilot/operate”) for aircraft and other vehicles.
target_language_example: Non so pilotare un elicottero, ma so pilotare un aereo.
native_language_example: I can’t fly a helicopter, but I can fly a plane.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the auxiliary verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno pitturato" + "le pareti" (the walls). You can add a color with "di" + color: "pitturare le pareti di bianco" = "to paint the walls white".
target_language_example: Abbiamo pitturato le pareti di grigio chiaro.
native_language_example: We painted the walls light gray.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something fairly well (often better than expected, but not necessarily perfectly). It can sound a bit modest/understated. Position: usually after the verb (e.g., parlare piuttosto bene).
target_language_example: Me la cavo piuttosto bene in italiano.
native_language_example: I get by pretty well in Italian.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about a specific pizza topping. "Salame piccante" is spicy salami (often like pepperoni), and "con" means "with." In questions like "Le piace...?" and "Vi piace...?" it means "Do you like...?" (formal singular / plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una pizza con il salame piccante, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a spicy salami pizza, please.

additional_notes: Used to compare duration ("more long"), often with verbs like vivere, restare/rimanere, parlare, aspettare. It can be followed by "di/che" to compare two durations: "più a lungo di/che...".
target_language_example: Possiamo restare qui più a lungo?
native_language_example: Can we stay here longer?

meaning: “taller than his/her …” (comparative, with a feminine subject).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with the pattern **più + adjective + di + possessive + noun**. **Alta** agrees with a feminine subject (Lei/Mary). **Sua** means “his/her” and must be followed by the noun it refers to (e.g., *sua sorella*, *sua madre*). For a masculine subject, you’d say **più alto di suo …**.
target_language_example: Giulia è più alta di sua cugina.
native_language_example: Giulia is taller than her cousin.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with di: più alto di me = taller than me. With il/la/i/le + più alto it forms the superlative: il ragazzo più alto = the tallest boy. You can strengthen it with molto (much) or ancora (even): molto più alto, ancora più alto. "Alto" can describe people (tall) and things/positions (high).
target_language_example: Questa sedia è più alta di quella.
native_language_example: This chair is higher than that one.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective + di. Use it to compare height (people) or level/height (objects). Often intensified with molto (much) or only slightly with soltanto leggermente. After di you can use a noun or pronoun (e.g., di Mary, di lui). Superlative pattern: il più alto di tutti = “the tallest of all”.
target_language_example: Questo edificio è più alto di quello.
native_language_example: This building is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages or how old someone looks. It agrees in gender/number with the person described: più anziano di (male singular), più anziana di (female singular), più anziani di / più anziane di (plural). You can use it with a person or with “quel che/di quanto” to mean “than (what/how much)”: più anziano di quel che sembra = older than he seems.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è più anziana di me di tre anni.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons and quantities: "più di + number/amount" = "more than/over" (Più di 30 miglia). You can also use it to compare actions or amounts with someone/something: "più di suo padre" = "more than her father." Often followed by a number, a noun, or a pronoun (me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro).
target_language_example: Ho lavorato qui per più di cinque anni.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for more than five years.

più di cinque fette di pizza al mese

target_language_multi_word_term: più di cinque fette di pizza al mese
meaning: more than five slices of pizza per month.
additional_notes: A quantity phrase used to talk about frequency/amount over a month. Structure: "più di" (more than) + number + noun ("fette di pizza") + time period ("al mese" = per month). Often used in questions with "Di solito" or "Solitamente" (usually).
target_language_example: Non mangio più di cinque fette di pizza al mese.
native_language_example: I don't eat more than five slices of pizza per month.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "più" (more) + "di" (than) + the stressed pronoun "me" (me). It can refer to quantity, frequency, or degree: "lavora più di me" (works more than me), "ama più di me" (loves more than me). After "di" you use "me" (not "io").
target_language_example: Parli italiano meglio di me.
native_language_example: You speak Italian better than me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone should increase their effort or intensity (e.g., cercare/guardare più duramente = look/search more thoroughly; lavorare/provare più duramente = work/try harder). Common in advice or commands. In everyday Italian you may also hear "più forte" (especially for physical effort) or "di più" (more in general).
target_language_example: Se vuoi passare l’esame, devi studiare più duramente.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to study harder.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective (facile) = “more …”. Used to compare things (più facile di … = “easier than …”) or to say something becomes easier (diventare più facile). With object pronouns: lo/la rende più facile = “it makes it easier.”
target_language_example: Con questo metodo, è più facile imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: With this method, it’s easier to learn Italian.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective/adverb = “more …”. With forte it can mean physical strength (“stronger”) or volume/intensity (“louder,” “harder”). Often used in requests like “Più forte!” (“Louder!” / “Hit/press harder!”) and in slogans like “più veloce, più alto, più forte” (“faster, higher, stronger”).
target_language_example: Puoi parlare più forte, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you speak louder, please?

additional_notes: Used as a comparative with più (“more”) + forte (“strong”). Most commonly means “louder” when talking about speaking, shouting, or sound (Parla più forte! = Speak louder!). With wind, blows, or force/effort it means “harder/more strongly” (Il vento soffiava più forte = The wind was blowing harder). It can also be used with ancora/sempre to mean “even/always” louder or stronger (ancora più forte, sempre più forte).
target_language_example: Scusi, può parlare più forte? Non la sento bene.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you speak louder? I can’t hear you well.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages, often with "di" (più giovane di lui = younger than him) and can add the difference: "di due anni". With "il/la ... più giovane" it means "the youngest" (e.g., il figlio più giovane). "Non è più giovane" usually means "He/She isn’t young anymore" (no longer young).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è più giovane di me di cinque anni.
native_language_example: My sister is five years younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages (or how old someone looks). It follows the common comparative pattern "più + adjective + di" (= "more + adjective + than"). It can also be followed by a clause: "più giovane di quel che pensi" = "younger than you think."
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più giovane di me, ma sembra più grande.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me, but he looks older.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: "più grande di" = "bigger/larger/older than." With a noun phrase, it can mean "the biggest/largest": "il/la + noun + più grande" (often with "della/del" = "in the/of the"). For age, Italians commonly say "più grande" rather than "più vecchio" in neutral contexts.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più grande di me.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons: più + adjective + di/che. With grande you usually use di, which combines with the definite article: di + la = della, di + il = del, di + lo = dello, di + i = dei, di + gli = degli, di + le = delle. You can also use di + pronoun: più grande di te/lui/lei. Often the noun is omitted when it’s clear: La mia (casa) è più grande della tua.
target_language_example: Questo zaino è più grande del tuo.
native_language_example: This backpack is bigger than yours.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: X è più grande di Y. With people, it often refers to age (older). You can intensify with numbers/expressions (e.g., tre volte più grande di = three times bigger than) or make it negative: non più grande di = no bigger than.
target_language_example: Questo appartamento è più grande di quello, ma è più caro.
native_language_example: This apartment is bigger than that one, but it's more expensive.

additional_notes: Comparative/superlative of "grande" (big/great). Use it to compare size: "più grandi di ..." = "bigger than ...". With family members, it commonly means older: "sorelle più grandi" = "older sisters". It can also be part of a superlative: "una delle più grandi" = "one of the biggest".
target_language_example: Questo zaino è più grande del mio.
native_language_example: This backpack is bigger than mine.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons and superlatives. With "più" + adjective you get a comparison: "A è più importante di B" (A is more important than B). With an article + "più" you often get a superlative: "la cosa più importante" (the most important thing). In phrases like "cosa ancora più importante" it means "something even more important".
target_language_example: Per me, la cosa più importante è stare bene.
native_language_example: For me, the most important thing is to be well.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to slow down (walking, talking, driving, etc.). Often appears in polite requests with "Per favore/Per piacere". With commands you may see either informal "Parla/Cammina" (to a friend) or formal "Parli/Camini" (to a stranger). You can also compare speeds with "più lentamente di ..." (more slowly than ...).
target_language_example: Mi puoi spiegare più lentamente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after a certain time. Often with a time expression: qualche minuto/giorno più tardi (“a few minutes/days later”). Common in everyday plans: Lo faccio più tardi (“I’ll do it later”).
target_language_example: Ci sentiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: We’ll talk later.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: "più + adjective + di" = "more + adjective + than". With age, Italians often also say "più grande di". It agrees with the person described: "più vecchio" (masc.), "più vecchia" (fem.). "Di" is used before a noun or pronoun (di Maria, di noi).
target_language_example: Lei è più vecchia di me.
native_language_example: She is older than me.

additional_notes: Comparative: più veloce = faster (often followed by “di …” for “than …”). Superlative: il/la più veloce = the fastest (e.g., Tu sei la più veloce). Common in commands and encouragement: “Più veloce!” = “Faster!” With “possibile/che puoi” it means “as fast as possible / as fast as you can.”
target_language_example: Possiamo andare più veloce, ma non troppo.
native_language_example: We can go faster, but not too fast.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: più + adjective/adverb (veloce) + di + person/thing. With verbs, it often appears as "correre più veloce di..." (to run faster than...). You can also use it with nouns: "un corridore più veloce di..." (a faster runner than...).
target_language_example: Questo treno è più veloce di quello.
native_language_example: This train is faster than that one.

additional_notes: Comparative adverb used to say someone does something at a higher speed than before or than someone else. Often followed by a comparison: "più velocemente di..." (faster than...).
target_language_example: Puoi parlare più velocemente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you speak faster, please?

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts of money or to say someone wants/has/earns a larger amount. Often followed by a comparison: “più soldi di me/dei suoi genitori” (more money than me/his parents). With verbs like “fare” it commonly means “to earn”: “fare più soldi” = “to make/earn more money.”
target_language_example: Vorrei più soldi per comprare un computer nuovo.
native_language_example: I’d like more money to buy a new computer.

additional_notes: Used to say you need additional time to finish something or to ask someone to wait longer. Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "dare" (to give), "servire" (to need), and "bisognare" (to be needed): "Mi serve più tempo" = "I need more time."
target_language_example: Possiamo parlarne domani? Ho bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: Can we talk about it tomorrow? I need more time.

più tempo a casa o al lavoro

target_language_multi_word_term: più tempo a casa o al lavoro
meaning: more time at home or at work.
additional_notes: Used to compare where someone spends the larger share of their time (often with verbs like passare/trascorrere = “to spend (time)”). You can change the places: “più tempo in ufficio o in viaggio?”
target_language_example: In questo periodo passo più tempo a casa che al lavoro.
native_language_example: These days I spend more time at home than at work.

additional_notes: Means a small number of days. Often used with time expressions like "entro pochi giorni" (within a few days) or "pochi giorni più tardi" (a few days later).
target_language_example: Ritorno tra pochi giorni.
native_language_example: I'll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "portare" to talk about wearing items like glasses, contact lenses, clothes, etc. It describes a usual or current characteristic (often with "solitamente" = usually). In questions, subject pronouns are often omitted: "Porta gli occhiali?" = "Do you wear glasses?"
target_language_example: Mio padre porta gli occhiali da lettura.
native_language_example: My father wears reading glasses.

additional_notes: Common household chore meaning to bring the garbage outside (often to the bins/curb). You may also hear: "buttare la spazzatura" (throw away the trash) or "portare giù la spazzatura" (take the trash down, e.g., to the building’s dumpster).
target_language_example: Puoi portare fuori la spazzatura prima di uscire?
native_language_example: Can you take out the trash before you go out?

additional_notes: Formed by possiamo (we can) + fare (to do/make). Used to say what is possible/feasible (“we can do this”) or to ask about options (“Possiamo fare qualcosa?”). Often followed by an object (qualcosa, questo) or an activity (un passo, una pausa). In contexts like “non possiamo fare più niente”, it means “there’s nothing more we can do.”
target_language_example: Possiamo fare una pausa adesso?
native_language_example: Can we take a break now?

meaning: "can we do to ...?" / "what can we do to ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible in order to achieve a goal. It’s often followed by an infinitive (per aiutare, per fermare, per risolvere) or a noun (per te, per il problema). In questions, it commonly appears as: Che cosa possiamo fare per...? / Come possiamo fare per...?
target_language_example: Che cosa possiamo fare per risolvere questo problema?
native_language_example: What can we do to solve this problem?

additional_notes: From the verb "fidarsi" = "to trust." It’s used with "di" before a person/pronoun/thing you trust: "fidarsi di qualcuno/qualcosa". "Possiamo" means "we can" (also "can we" in questions). With a pronoun, use: "possiamo fidarci di lui/lei/loro"; often "di" + name: "possiamo fidarci di Maria".
target_language_example: Possiamo fidarci di questo sito?
native_language_example: Can we trust this website?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for something (information or an item). Very common in cafés, shops, and service situations. Often followed by a noun: “Posso avere un caffè?” You can add “per favore/per piacere” to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: “Can I have a …?” (polite way to ask for something).
additional_notes: Used to request an item or a serving (often in cafés, restaurants, shops, or at an event). It’s a polite, common formula; you can also use it with feminine nouns: “Posso avere una…?” (e.g., una bottiglia). Often preceded by “Scusi/Scusami/Scusatemi” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: “Can I have a…?” / “May I have a…?” (polite request).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you want to receive (a drink, an item, a document, an opinion). It’s often followed by a noun: “Posso avere una birra…?”, “Posso avere una lista…?”, “Posso avere una seconda opinione?”. Add “per favore” or “per piacere” to be extra polite. The “una” changes with gender/number: “un” (masc. singular), “una” (fem. singular), “due” + plural (e.g., “Posso avere due biglietti?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una bottiglia d’acqua?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is reliable or willing to help. It’s the verb phrase “contare su” (to count on / rely on) with “posso” (can I). Often followed by a person (su Tom, su di lei) or by an action: “Posso contare su di te per…” (Can I count on you to…). “su di lei” is formal (“you” = Lei).
target_language_example: Posso contare su di te domani mattina?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used when you’ll see someone and want to relay a message to them for another person. Very common with an indirect object pronoun: gli posso dare un messaggio? (to him), le posso dare un messaggio? (to her). You can also name the person: Posso dare un messaggio a Tom?
target_language_example: Certo, posso dargli un messaggio quando lo vedo.
native_language_example: Sure, I can pass him a message when I see him.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "potere" (posso = I can) + "fare" (to do/make). Used to talk about ability or possibility ("Lo posso fare più tardi" = I can do it later) and also to ask permission/offers ("Posso fare una doccia?" = Can I take a shower?; "Posso fare qualsiasi cosa per te?" = Can I do anything for you?). Often followed by a noun (fare una doccia) or by a direct object pronoun (lo/la) in front of "posso" ("Lo posso fare"). In "Ce la posso fare", it means "I can manage / I can make it."
target_language_example: Posso fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Can I ask a question?

additional_notes: Used to offer instruction: posso = “I can”, insegnare = “to teach”, come = “how”. It’s normally followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., come guidare = “how to drive”). Often includes an object pronoun before posso (e.g., Le posso… = “I can teach you…” formal; vi posso… = “I can teach you all…”).
target_language_example: Ti posso insegnare come cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to cook pasta.

additional_notes: Used to offer or say you have the ability to teach someone how to do an action. It’s made of: posso (I can) + insegnarti (teach you) + a (to), and it’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., cantare, nuotare). You can also drop "io" because it’s implied: "Posso insegnarti a…"
target_language_example: Posso insegnarti a cucinare un piatto italiano.
native_language_example: I can teach you to cook an Italian dish.

additional_notes: Used to offer to teach a skill. "posso" = I can; "insegnarvi" = teach you (to you all / to you in formal "voi"); followed by "a" + an infinitive verb (e.g., scrivere, tradurre, cantare). In everyday modern Italian, for one person you’ll more often hear "posso insegnarti a…" (informal "tu") or "posso insegnarle a…" (formal "Lei").
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso insegnarvi a cucinare piatti semplici.
native_language_example: If you want, I can teach you to cook simple dishes.

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to speak with someone, especially on the phone or in a polite request. Follow with a name or a person: "Posso parlare con Mike?" / "Posso parlare con il direttore?". With pronouns it changes: "con lei" (formal you/her), "con te" (informal you), "con voi" (you all or formal you in some regions). Often paired with "per favore".
target_language_example: Buongiorno, posso parlare con la responsabile, per favore?
native_language_example: Good morning, can I speak to the manager, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission or possibility to take/get something. In cafés/restaurants it often means “May I have…?” (ordering). With extra words it can form common expressions like “prendere cura di” = “take care of.”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere un caffè e un cornetto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I have a coffee and a croissant?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to borrow something temporarily. Very common in polite requests; you can make it more formal by using Lei forms (e.g., i suoi / il suo). Often followed by an object and a time expression (per un minuto, per un momento, per oggi).
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito la tua penna per un attimo?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your pen for a moment?

posso prendere in prestito il vostro

target_language_multi_word_term: posso prendere in prestito il vostro
additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow something from the person you’re addressing. “Prendere in prestito” = “to borrow.” “Il vostro” agrees with a masculine singular noun (il coltello, il computer, il laptop); for feminine singular use “la vostra” (la penna), masculine plural “i vostri,” feminine plural “le vostre.” You can add the item after it: “Posso prendere in prestito il vostro coltello?”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il vostro caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow your charger?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow an object. Literally “can I take it on loan.” Often followed by a time limit: “per un secondo/un minuto/per quanto tempo…”. Use “Scusa” (informal) or “Scusi” (formal) to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Posso prenderlo in prestito per un attimo?
native_language_example: Can I borrow it for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something that belongs to you to be returned. You normally add the noun after it (e.g., “Posso riavere il mio telefono?”). If the item is feminine, change it to “la mia” (e.g., “Posso riavere la mia borsa?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso riavere il mio passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have my passport back?

additional_notes: "Posso" is the 1st-person singular of "potere" (to be able to / can). It’s followed by an infinitive like "usare" (to use). Use it to ask permission (especially with a question mark and rising intonation): "Posso usare…?" or to say you’re allowed/able to use something: "Posso usare…".
target_language_example: Scusa, posso usare il tuo telefono per un minuto?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I use your phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to look at something or to meet/see someone. Common in shops (asking to see an item) and in official contexts (asking to see a document). Often followed by a noun (Posso vedere la tua licenza?) or a person (Posso vedere i miei nipoti?). Adding "per favore" makes it more polite.
target_language_example: Posso vedere il menu, per favore?
native_language_example: May I see the menu, please?

additional_notes: 3rd-person plural of "potere" + infinitive "essere". Used to say something is possible, allowed, or generally true about multiple things/people (loro). Often followed by an adjective or noun ("possono essere diversi", "possono essere un dolore") or a past participle in the passive ("possono essere visti" = "can be seen").
target_language_example: Questi problemi possono essere risolti facilmente.
native_language_example: These problems can be solved easily.

meaning: a place where (…); a place in which (…).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes what happens/exists in that place: “un posto in cui + verb” (e.g., abitare, dormire, lavorare, nascondersi). It’s similar to “dove” (“where”), but a bit more explicit because it names the place (posto). You can also see it after a comma as an apposition: “Laramie, posto in cui…”.
target_language_example: Cerco un posto in cui studiare in pace.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place where I can study in peace.

meaning: a place to go (often: ‘nowhere to go’).
additional_notes: Literally “a place where to go.” Very common after negatives like non… nessun/alcun (“no/any”), especially to express having no options or no home/safe place: Non ho nessun posto in cui andare = “I have nowhere to go.” You can also add altro (“other”) to mean “no other place to go.”
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, non avevo nessun posto in cui andare.
native_language_example: After the argument, I had nowhere to go.

additional_notes: Used to describe a location as suitable for living there, or to say you have accommodation. Often follows adjectives like bello/buon (nice/good): “un bel/buon posto in cui vivere.” In everyday speech you may also hear “un posto dove vivere” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cerco un posto in cui vivere vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place to live near work.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "potere" + infinitive "aiutare". Often used in reported speech (after verbs like "disse", "chiese", "pensava") to talk about ability or possibility to help in the past. Depending on context it can mean a general past ability (“could”) or a specific possibility (“might be able to”).
target_language_example: Non sapevo se poteva aiutare, ma ho chiesto lo stesso.
native_language_example: I didn't know if he/she could help, but I asked anyway.

additional_notes: Conditional of essere (“to be”), used to express possibility or uncertainty. Often followed by a noun or name (Potrebbe essere Tom. = It might be Tom) or an adjective (potrebbe essere imbarazzato = might be embarrassed). You can also negate it: non potrebbe essere… = it/he/she couldn’t be…
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere una buona idea.
native_language_example: It might be a good idea.

meaning: might be able to / could be able to.
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty about someone’s ability to do something. It combines the conditional of "potere" (potrebbe = could/might) with "essere in grado di" (= to be able/capable of) + an infinitive (e.g., aiutare, venire).
