target_language_example: È uscito con le sue figlie questo pomeriggio.
native_language_example: He/She went out with his/her daughters this afternoon.

additional_notes: “Sue” is the feminine plural possessive adjective (agreeing with “mani,” which is feminine plural). It can refer to “his,” “her,” “their,” or “your” (formal) depending on context. Common patterns: “nelle sue mani” = “in his/her hands” (often figurative: someone has control/responsibility); “con le sue mani” = “with his/her hands” (e.g., without tools); “sulle sue mani” = “on his/her hands.”
target_language_example: Non voglio lasciare il progetto nelle sue mani.
native_language_example: I don’t want to leave the project in his/her hands.

additional_notes: “Sue” is the feminine plural possessive meaning “his/her” (referring to a feminine plural noun like “parole”). It’s used when talking about someone’s statements or the impact of what they said. Often appears with verbs like credere a (“believe”), dubitare di (“doubt”), and expressions like sentirsi ferito/a da (“feel hurt by”).
target_language_example: Non dimenticherò mai le sue parole.
native_language_example: I will never forget his/her words.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. It’s formed with the verb "suggerire" (to suggest) + "di" + infinitive: "Suggerisco di parlare" = “I suggest talking / I suggest that you talk.” You can replace "suggerisco" with other forms (e.g., "ti suggerisco di..." = “I suggest you…”).
target_language_example: Ti suggerisco di prendere un taxi.
native_language_example: I suggest you take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used to say something is placed or happens on top of a table. It’s the combination of "su" (on) + "il" (the) → "sul"; often followed by more detail like "sul tavolo della cucina" (on the kitchen table).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the table.

additional_notes: Literally “su” (on) + “il” (the) → “sul”. “Banco” is a flat surface like a counter, bench, or (in a classroom) a student’s desk. Used to say where something is placed: “Il libro è sul banco.”
target_language_example: Lascia la borsa sul banco, per favore.
native_language_example: Leave the bag on the counter/desk, please.

additional_notes: “Sul” = “su” (on) + “il” (the). Used with actions like sitting, lying down, or taking a nap on the sofa. With verbs of movement (e.g., mettersi, sedersi), it can mean ending up onto/onto the sofa (“sit down on the sofa”).
target_language_example: Ci siamo addormentati sul divano dopo cena.
native_language_example: We fell asleep on the couch after dinner.

additional_notes: Formed from "su" + "il" = "sul" + "mio". Used for location (something is on top of/over something you own: "sul mio tavolo") and for movement to a position on something ("salire sul mio cavallo" = to get onto my horse). It can also be figurative with "mettere (qualcosa) sul mio conto" = "put it on my bill/tab/account". Use with masculine singular nouns; with feminine singular: "sulla mia".
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare la giacca sul mio letto?
native_language_example: Can you leave the jacket on my bed?

additional_notes: Means being physically on the stage where performers or speakers are (e.g., at a concert, theater, or event). It’s the contraction of “su” + “il” (“on the”). You’ll often see it with verbs like essere/andare/salire (to be/go/get up) and with feelings like essere nervoso/a (to be nervous) when performing.
target_language_example: Tra cinque minuti saliamo sul palco.
native_language_example: In five minutes we’re going on stage.

additional_notes: “Sul” is the contraction of “su” + “il” (= “on the”). “Pavimento” means “floor” (the surface you walk on). Used to describe something located, lying, or happening on the floor (e.g., objects, blood, sleeping/sitting on the floor).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi sul pavimento vicino alla porta.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the floor near the door.

meaning: in the back; at the back (behind).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location behind something (e.g., behind a house/building: “in the backyard / out back”) or on the back side of an object (e.g., “on the back”). In directions, it can mean “take the path in the back/behind.”
target_language_example: Il parcheggio è sul retro dell’edificio.
native_language_example: The parking lot is behind the building (at the back of the building).

additional_notes: Contraction of "su" + "il" ("on the") + "suo" (his/her/your—formal). It’s used before a masculine singular noun: e.g., "sul suo conto" (about his/her account), "sul suo divano" (on his/her sofa). With feminine singular you typically use "sulla sua"; with masculine plural "sui suoi"; with feminine plural "sulle sue".
target_language_example: Non so niente sul suo passato.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about his/her past.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is located on top of a table. It’s the contraction of "su" + "il" → "sul" ("on the"). Similar contractions: "sulla" (su + la), "sui" (su + i), "sugli" (su + gli), "sulle" (su + le).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the table.

additional_notes: “Sul” is the contraction of “su + il” (“on + the”). Used to say something/someone is located on top of a building’s roof: “sul tetto di casa” = “on the roof of the house.” In titles you may also see it literally, e.g. “Il pazzo sul tetto” (“Fiddler on the Roof”).
target_language_example: Il gatto è sul tetto.
native_language_example: The cat is on the roof.

meaning: on the train; onto the train.
additional_notes: Contraction of "su" + "il" = "sul". With verbs like "essere/stare" or to describe where something is, it usually means "on the train" (location): "Sono sul treno". With verbs of movement like "salire" (to get on), it often means "onto the train" (direction): "Salgo sul treno".
target_language_example: Sono sul treno, arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: I'm on the train; I'll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: "on his/her" or "about his/her" (depending on the noun that follows).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "su" + "la" + "sua". Used (1) for location: "sulla sua scrivania" = "on his desk"; and (2) for topic/subject: "tutto sulla sua infanzia" = "everything about his childhood". The gender/number changes with the noun: "sul suo" (masc.), "sulla sua" (fem.), "sui suoi" (masc. pl.), "sulle sue" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ho letto un articolo sulla sua carriera.
native_language_example: I read an article about his/her career.

additional_notes: A common wordplay because **costa** can mean both **(the) coast** (noun) and **it costs** (verb, from *costare*). Pattern: **[thing] sulla costa costa + (meno/più/caro/il doppio/troppo)**. Example: *Vivere sulla costa costa caro* = living on the coast is expensive.
target_language_example: Un appartamento sulla costa costa molto di più.
native_language_example: An apartment on the coast costs much more.

meaning: on the bench in the park.
additional_notes: A location phrase: "su + la" becomes "sulla" (on the), "panchina" = bench, "nel" = "in + il" (in the), "parco" = park. Used to say where someone is/was sitting or staying.
target_language_example: Aspettiamoci sulla panchina nel parco.
native_language_example: Let’s wait for each other on the bench in the park.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like andare/arrivare/essere to say someone went to, arrived at, or is at the place where a crime happened. Literally it’s “on the scene of the crime,” but in English you normally say “at the crime scene.” A common synonym is "sul luogo del delitto".
target_language_example: La polizia è già sulla scena del crimine.
native_language_example: The police are already at the crime scene.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located or where you should put it. It’s the preposition "su" (on) + the definite article "la" (the), contracted to "sulla", plus "scrivania" (desk). Often follows verbs like "lasciare" (to leave), "mettere" (to put), or "essere" (to be).
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare le chiavi sulla scrivania?
native_language_example: Can you leave the keys on the desk?

additional_notes: Used to say you are located or doing an activity on the beach. It’s the contraction of "su" + "la" = "sulla" (feminine singular), and it commonly follows verbs like camminare/passeggiare (to walk), costruire (to build), stare (to be/stay).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a leggere un libro sulla spiaggia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to read a book on the beach.

additional_notes: "Su" + "la" → "sulla" (= "on the"). "Sua" means "his" or "her" (it agrees with the thing owned: "scrivania" is feminine, so "sua"). Used to say where something is located, or where you’re putting something (often with verbs like "è" or "mettere": "La metto sulla sua scrivania").
target_language_example: Ho lasciato i documenti sulla sua scrivania.
native_language_example: I left the documents on his/her desk.

additional_notes: "Suo" is the possessive for the 3rd person singular (his/her/its) and also for the polite form "Lei" (your, formal). It agrees with the thing owned: "aiuto" is masculine singular, so "suo aiuto". Common in polite or formal thanks: "La ringrazio per il suo aiuto" (Thank you for your help).
target_language_example: Grazie per il suo aiuto, signora.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, ma’am.

additional_notes: “Suo” is the possessive for “his/her/its” and also “your” in the formal “Lei” form. It agrees with the thing owned (amico = masculine singular), not with the owner. Often you’ll also hear “un suo amico” = “a friend of his/hers/yours (formal)”.
target_language_example: Scusi, sono suo amico: posso entrare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’m your friend: can I come in?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective suo (“his/her/its”) before caffè. In Italian, suo can refer to either “his” or “her” (the owner is understood from context). Very common when talking about adding sugar/milk to someone’s coffee: nel suo caffè / al suo caffè (“in/into his/her coffee”).
target_language_example: Ha messo un po' di cannella nel suo caffè.
native_language_example: He/She put a little cinnamon in his/her coffee.

additional_notes: `suo` is a possessive adjective meaning “his/her/its/your (formal)”. It agrees with the thing owned: **suo** (masculine singular) + **cane** (dog). In context, it can refer to a man’s dog (his), a woman’s dog (her), a pet belonging to an animal (its), or to someone you address formally (your).
target_language_example: Dov'è il suo cane?
native_language_example: Where is his/her/your (formal) dog?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suo" (masculine singular) with "cavallo". In Italian, "suo" can mean "his", "her", or "its"—the context tells you whose. (For a woman’s horse, you still say "il suo cavallo" because "cavallo" is masculine.)
target_language_example: Il cowboy è tornato al suo cavallo.
native_language_example: The cowboy went back to his horse.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone else’s birthday. "Suo" is a formal/neutral possessive meaning "his" or "her" (it agrees with the thing owned: compleanno is masculine singular, so suo). In conversation you often use "il suo compleanno" with "è": "Oggi è il suo compleanno?"
target_language_example: Domani è il suo compleanno, non dimenticarlo!
native_language_example: Tomorrow is his/her birthday—don’t forget!

additional_notes: “Suo” is a possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (and sometimes “its” or polite “your”). It agrees with the noun: computer is masculine singular, so you use “suo” (not “sua/suoi/sue”). In everyday speech, “their computer” is more often “il loro computer” rather than “il suo computer.”
target_language_example: Ho salvato il file sul suo computer.
native_language_example: I saved the file on his/her computer.

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his/her/its" (formal "your" is also possible in other contexts). With "corpo" it refers to someone’s physical body. Often used with prepositions: "sul suo corpo" (on his/her body), "tutto il suo corpo" (his/her whole body). Context usually makes the gender clear; if you need to specify, you can say "il corpo di lui" (his) / "il corpo di lei" (hers).
target_language_example: Ha delle cicatrici sul suo corpo.
native_language_example: He/She has scars on his/her body.

additional_notes: Means “his money” or “her money,” depending on who “suo” refers to. Italian possessives agree with the noun (denaro = masculine singular → suo), not with the owner. Often used with “con” (generous with his/her money) or in phrases like “la migliore offerta per il suo denaro” (“best value for his/her money”).
target_language_example: Non spendere tutto il suo denaro in un giorno.
native_language_example: Don't spend all his/her money in one day.

meaning: his speech; his talk (what he said).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a speech/talk given by a man: suo = “his”, discorso = “speech/talk/discourse.” Often appears with verbs like parlare (“to speak”), cominciare (“to begin”), or when describing the content (il contenuto del suo discorso). For a woman speaker: il suo discorso can still mean “her speech” (because suo agrees with discorso, not with the person), but in many contexts you’ll see "il suo discorso" without clarifying gender, and the meaning comes from context.
target_language_example: Dopo il suo discorso, tutti hanno applaudito.
native_language_example: After his speech, everyone applauded.

additional_notes: "Suo" is the possessive adjective meaning "his/her/its" and agrees with the noun: errore (masculine singular). It can refer to a person or sometimes an organization/thing, so you choose "his" or "her" from context. Often used with prepositions like "di" (ridere del suo errore = to laugh at his/her mistake) or in phrases like "essere dovuto a" (è dovuto al suo errore = it’s due to his/her mistake).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è stato un suo errore.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it was his/her mistake.

additional_notes: Suo means “his/her/its” (not “your”); it agrees with the noun: suo fidanzato (male partner), sua fidanzata (female partner). Fidanzato can mean “boyfriend” or “fiancé”; use context (or add “futuro” / talk about marriage) to make “fiancé” clear. Often used with a preposition: con il suo fidanzato (with her/his boyfriend), al suo fidanzato (to her/his boyfriend).
target_language_example: Stasera esce con il suo fidanzato.
native_language_example: Tonight she’s going out with her boyfriend.

meaning: his son / her son / your (formal) son.
additional_notes: “Suo” is the formal possessive (used with Lei), and it can also mean “his” or “her” depending on context. In speech and writing, the meaning is usually clear from who is being talked about. With family members in the singular, Italian normally drops the article: “suo figlio” (not *il suo figlio*). Plural takes the article: “i suoi figli” = his/her/your (formal) children.
target_language_example: Dov'è suo figlio?
native_language_example: Where is your son? (formal)

suo figlio in un incidente stradale

target_language_multi_word_term: suo figlio in un incidente stradale
meaning: his/her son in a traffic (road) accident.
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s son was involved in (and often died in) a road accident, especially after the verb "perdere" ("to lose"), as in "Ha perso suo figlio in un incidente stradale". "Suo" can mean both "his" and "her" depending on context. "Incidente stradale" is a common way to say "road/traffic accident".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace molto: ha perso suo figlio in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry: he/she lost his/her son in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive that can mean both "his" and "her"; the context tells you whose brother it is. With family members in the singular (fratello, sorella, madre, padre, etc.), Italian often drops the article: "suo fratello" (not usually "il suo fratello").
target_language_example: Non conosco suo fratello, ma conosco sua sorella.
native_language_example: I don’t know his/her brother, but I know his/her sister.

additional_notes: Suo/sua means “his”, “her”, or “your” (polite/formal) depending on context. It agrees with the noun: giardino is masculine singular, so you use suo (not sua). Often used with the article: il suo giardino = “his/her/your (formal) garden.”
target_language_example: Non entrare nel suo giardino senza permesso.
native_language_example: Don’t go into his/her garden without permission.

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive that can mean "his", "her", "its", or "your" (formal) depending on context. It agrees with the noun: "impiego" (masculine singular) → "suo impiego". "Impiego" is a fairly neutral word for a job/employment (similar to "lavoro").
target_language_example: Non è felice del suo impiego attuale.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t happy with his/her current job.

additional_notes: “Suo/sua” means “his/her/its,” but with the polite form Lei it also means “your.” In many real sentences, “al suo insegnante” can mean either “to his teacher” or “to your teacher (Lei).” The gender of the teacher is shown by the noun: “insegnante” can be male or female; articles/adjectives show it (il suo insegnante / la sua insegnante).
target_language_example: Parli con il suo insegnante dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: Speak with your teacher after the lesson.

additional_notes: "Suo" means "his" or "her" (and also "your" in the formal "Lei" form). It agrees with the noun: "lavoro" is masculine singular, so it’s "suo lavoro". Often used with prepositions like "con/col" (busy with) or "per" (enthusiasm for): "occupato col suo lavoro" = busy with his/her work.
target_language_example: È molto orgogliosa del suo lavoro.
native_language_example: She is very proud of her job.

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive adjective meaning "his," "her," "its," or "your" (formal: addressing someone as Lei). It agrees with the thing owned: "libro" is masculine singular, so you use "suo" (not "sua"). Often used with an article: "il suo libro" = "his/her/your book." The context tells you whose book it is.
target_language_example: Scusi, questo è il suo libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your book?

meaning: her husband / his husband (also: your husband, formal).
additional_notes: “Suo” is a possessive adjective that agrees with the thing owned (here, marito = husband), not with the owner. So “suo marito” can mean “her husband” or “his husband”; in formal Italian it can also mean “your husband” (Lei/Loro). Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Ho parlato con suo marito ieri sera.
native_language_example: I spoke with her/his husband last night.

additional_notes: “Suo” is the possessive adjective meaning “his” or “her” (it agrees with the noun, not the owner). “Nonno” means “grandfather” (also used like “grandpa”). Often appears with a preposition: “di suo nonno” (of his/her grandfather), “con suo nonno” (with his/her grandfather). You can also use the definite article: “il suo nonno” (especially for clarity or emphasis).
target_language_example: Oggi vado a trovare suo nonno in ospedale.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to visit his/her grandfather in the hospital.

additional_notes: Made of the possessive adjective "suo" (his/her/its; also "your" in the formal polite form) + "nuovo" (new). Both words change to match the noun in gender/number: suo nuovo libro (his new book), sua nuova macchina (her new car), suoi nuovi amici (his new friends), sue nuove scarpe (her new shoes). Often used after prepositions like "di/del/della": "del suo nuovo romanzo" = "about his new novel".
target_language_example: Sono felice del suo nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m happy about his/her new job.

meaning: "his/her new job" (also "your new job" in formal address).
additional_notes: "Suo" is the polite/formal possessive (Lei) and can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. "Impiego" means a job/employment (often more formal than "lavoro"). Common with "piacere" (to like) and with congratulations: "Congratulazioni per il suo nuovo impiego".
target_language_example: Sono felice per il suo nuovo impiego.
native_language_example: I'm happy about his/her new job.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "suo" (= his/her/its/your formal) with "padre" (= father). In Italian, "suo" refers to the owner, but it can be ambiguous without context (it might mean his father or her father). Unlike English, possessives agree with the thing owned (padre), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto suo padre ieri.
native_language_example: I met his/her father yesterday.

additional_notes: "Suo" is the possessive for "lui/lei" (his/her) and also for "Lei" (your, formal). It agrees with the noun: suo (masc. sing.) + piano. In context, "piano" means "plan" (not the musical instrument). Often used after prepositions: "del suo piano" = "about his/her/your plan", "al suo piano" = "to his/her/your plan".
target_language_example: Non conosco ancora il suo piano, ma mi interessa ascoltarlo.
native_language_example: I still don't know his/her/your plan, but I'm interested in hearing it.

additional_notes: "Suo" is a possessive adjective that agrees with the noun (here, "successo" is masculine singular). It usually means "his" or "her" (or "its") depending on context; Italian often relies on context to show whose it is. You can also say "sul suo successo" (= "about his/her success") or "riguardo al suo successo" (= "regarding his/her success").
target_language_example: Sono felice per il suo successo.
native_language_example: I’m happy about his/her success.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "suo/sua" with a noun: it agrees with the noun (telefono = masculine singular → suo). In context it can mean his phone, her phone, or your phone when speaking formally (Lei). Often used after prepositions like "al" (to/on the phone: rispondere al suo telefono) or "sul" (on the phone: un messaggio sul suo telefono).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, posso chiamare dal suo telefono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I make a call from your phone?

meaning: 'his/her/its own time' (the time that belongs to that person/thing).
additional_notes: Used with a possessive (il suo tempo, il mio tempo, il tuo tempo, etc.) to mean the time someone has available or spends on something. Common with verbs like dedicare (to devote), passare (to spend), and phrases like essere generoso/a con il suo tempo (to be generous with one’s time) and grazie per il suo tempo (thank you for your time).
target_language_example: Grazie per il suo tempo, le risponderò presto.
native_language_example: Thank you for your time; I’ll reply soon.

additional_notes: Suo is a possessive that agrees with the noun: suo (masc. sing.) + ufficio (masc. sing.). It can mean “his,” “her,” “its,” or (formal) “your,” depending on context. Often used with prepositions like in/nel suo ufficio (in his/her office) and a/al suo ufficio (to his/her office).
target_language_example: Il direttore è nel suo ufficio.
native_language_example: The director is in his/her office.

additional_notes: Suo is the possessive adjective used with Lei (formal "you") and with "he" or "she". The exact meaning (his, her, or your-formal) depends on context. Often used after prepositions like "di/del": parlare del suo viaggio = to talk about his/her/your (formal) trip. With family members, Italian usually uses the article (il mio fratello → mio fratello), but with most other nouns like viaggio the article stays (il suo viaggio / del suo viaggio).
target_language_example: Mi può raccontare del suo viaggio?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about your trip? (formal)

additional_notes: Used to talk about a trip that belongs to “him” (someone male). With the masculine singular noun *viaggio*, you typically say **il suo viaggio** (“his trip”). It’s followed by **in** + a country/region (e.g., *in India, in Russia*) and sometimes also for some cities (e.g., *in Italia*; but many cities use *a* instead: *a Roma*).
target_language_example: Mi ha mostrato le foto del suo viaggio in Giappone.
native_language_example: He showed me photos from his trip to Japan.

additional_notes: “Suo” is the possessive used with the polite form (Lei) and with “he/she/it” depending on context. “Volto” means “face,” often in a slightly more literary/formal way than “faccia.” Common in expressions like “sul suo volto” (“on his/her face”) or “È scritto sul suo volto” (“It’s written all over his/her face.”).
target_language_example: Aveva un sorriso sul suo volto.
native_language_example: He/She had a smile on his/her face.

additional_notes: "Suo" is the possessive adjective for "his/her/its" and also the formal "your" (to one person: Lei). It agrees with the noun: suo zio (uncle, masculine singular), sua zia (aunt). In Italian you often use the definite article with possessives (il suo zio), but it’s usually dropped with family members in the singular (suo zio).
target_language_example: Domani pranzerò con suo zio.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll have lunch with his/her uncle.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like conoscere/incontrare/vedere to say you met or saw someone there (e.g., “Ho conosciuto suo zio al negozio” = “I met his/her uncle at the shop”). Note: “suo” can mean “his” or “her” and agrees with the thing owned (“zio”), not with the owner, so it’s ambiguous without context.
target_language_example: Ho visto suo zio al negozio ieri.
native_language_example: I saw his/her uncle at the shop yesterday.

additional_notes: “Suoi” is the plural form of the possessive “suo” and agrees with the noun it describes: amico (sing.) → suo amico; amici (pl.) → suoi amici. It can mean either “his friends” or “her friends” depending on context (who the owner is). Often used with “i” (the): “i suoi amici” = “his/her friends.”
target_language_example: Domani esce con i suoi amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow he/she is going out with his/her friends.

additional_notes: Possessives in Italian usually take the definite article: **i suoi cani** = “his/her/their dogs.” **Suoi** agrees with the thing owned (**cani** = masculine plural), not with the owner’s gender—so **i suoi cani** can mean “her dogs” (Mary) or “his dogs” (Tom) depending on context.
target_language_example: Sta portando a spasso i suoi cani ogni mattina.
native_language_example: He/She takes his/her dogs for a walk every morning.

additional_notes: "Suoi" means "his" (also "their" in formal/older usage), agreeing with the masculine plural noun "compiti". Used to talk about the tasks/homework that belong to a male person (or a masculine subject). You’ll often see it as part of a larger phrase like "fare i suoi compiti" (to do his homework).
target_language_example: Ha già finito i suoi compiti.
native_language_example: He has already finished his homework.

meaning: his children / her children (depending on context).
additional_notes: “Suoi” is the possessive adjective (plural) used with “figli” (children/sons). It agrees with the noun owned (figli = masculine plural), not with the owner. In context, it can mean “his” or “her.” You’ll also see it as “i suoi figli” = “his/her children.”
target_language_example: È molto orgogliosa dei suoi figli.
native_language_example: She is very proud of her children.

additional_notes: "Suoi" is the possessive adjective for "loro" (their), but it’s also used for "his/her" when the owner is expressed as a third-person subject (lui/lei). The exact meaning (his, her, or their) comes from context. It agrees with the noun: "genitori" is masculine plural, so you use "suoi". Often used after a preposition: "dai suoi genitori" = "from his/her parents".
target_language_example: Non parla spesso con i suoi genitori.
native_language_example: He/She doesn’t talk often with his/her parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you can see in someone’s eyes (e.g., tears, anger, fear). It’s the possessive form: suoi = “his” (masc. plural) or “her” (plural), used with occhi (plural). Often appears with the preposition in: nei suoi occhi = “in his/her eyes.”
target_language_example: C'era una luce strana nei suoi occhi.
native_language_example: There was a strange light in his/her eyes.

additional_notes: “Suoi” is the plural masculine possessive (matching “piani”). It can refer to “his,” “her,” or “their” depending on context. Often used with prepositions like “di” (dei suoi piani = about his/her plans) or “in/nei” (nei suoi piani = in his/her plans, i.e., part of what he/she intended). Note: “piani” means “plans,” not musical “pianos.”
target_language_example: Non voglio rovinare i suoi piani.
native_language_example: I don’t want to ruin his/her plans.

additional_notes: "Suoi" is the plural form of the possessive (suoi/sue) and agrees with the noun (ristoranti, masculine plural), not with the owner. It can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context. Often used in the pattern "uno dei suoi ristoranti preferiti" = "one of her/his favorite restaurants."
target_language_example: Andiamo a cenare in uno dei suoi ristoranti preferiti.
native_language_example: Let’s go have dinner at one of her/his favorite restaurants.

meaning: his money / her money / their money (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Suoi" is the plural possessive adjective (masculine plural) used with plural nouns like "soldi" (money). It agrees with the noun (soldi), not with the owner. So it can mean "his/her/their money" based on who you’re talking about. Often used with "con" to describe how someone uses/spends their money (e.g., "generoso con i suoi soldi").
target_language_example: Non vuole spendere i suoi soldi per cose inutili.
native_language_example: He/She/They doesn’t want to spend their money on useless things.

additional_notes: "Suonare" means "to play" a musical instrument. "Suona il piano" is the 3rd person singular present tense ("he/she plays the piano"). It can also be used as a yes/no question with rising intonation: "Suona il piano?" = "Do you play the piano?"
target_language_example: Mia sorella suona il piano da quando aveva sei anni.
native_language_example: My sister has played the piano since she was six years old.

additional_notes: From the verb "suonare" (to play an instrument). "Suona" is the 3rd-person singular present tense (he/she/it plays). In questions, Italian often uses the same word order and relies on intonation: "Suona il pianoforte?" = "Does he/she play the piano?"
target_language_example: Mia sorella suona il pianoforte ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano every day.

additional_notes: From the verb "suonare" = "to play" (a musical instrument). "Suona" is the present tense for "lui/lei" (he/she) and also the command form for "tu" (you): "Suona la chitarra!" = "Play the guitar!" You can swap the instrument: "suona il piano", "suona il violino".
target_language_example: Mio padre suona la chitarra ogni sera.
native_language_example: My dad plays the guitar every evening.

additional_notes: "Suonando" is the gerund of "suonare" (to play an instrument). It’s very commonly used with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno suonando la chitarra" = "I am/you are/he is/we are/you all are/they are playing the guitar (right now)". You can add time words like "adesso" or "ora" to emphasize 'right now'.
target_language_example: Stiamo suonando la chitarra in salotto.
native_language_example: We’re playing the guitar in the living room.

meaning: 'to play' (a musical instrument); also 'to ring/sound' (a bell/doorbell).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular instruments or sound-makers: suonare il banjo / il flauto / il campanello. For feminine nouns you use "suonare la" (e.g., suonare la chitarra). With bells/doorbells it means to ring/sound, not to play music.
target_language_example: Sai suonare il pianoforte?
native_language_example: Can you play the piano?

additional_notes: "Suonare" means “to play” (a musical instrument). You can swap in other instruments: suonare la chitarra (guitar), suonare il violino (violin). Often used after verbs like piacere (mi piace suonare il piano) or sapere to talk about ability (sai suonare il piano?).
target_language_example: Vorrei imparare a suonare il piano.
native_language_example: I’d like to learn to play the piano.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "suonare" (to play an instrument) + "il pianoforte" (the piano). You can swap in other instruments: "suonare la chitarra" (to play the guitar).
target_language_example: Mia sorella suona il pianoforte ogni sera.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano every evening.

additional_notes: Used with "suonare" to talk about playing a musical instrument. Common with verbs like "sapere" (to know how to), "potere" (can), and "piacere" (to like): "So/Può/Mi piace suonare la chitarra". You can swap the instrument: "suonare il piano", "suonare il violino".
target_language_example: Sai suonare la chitarra?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the guitar?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "suonare" (to play, for instruments) + "uno strumento musicale" (a musical instrument). Often appears in questions with "sapere" (to know how to): "Sai/Sa/Sapete suonare uno strumento musicale?" (Do you know how to play a musical instrument?).
target_language_example: Non so suonare uno strumento musicale, ma mi piacerebbe imparare.
native_language_example: I can’t play a musical instrument, but I’d like to learn.

additional_notes: Used to say you play the guitar (as an ability or as something you do regularly). From the verb "suonare" (to play an instrument); "suono" is the 1st-person singular present tense (“I play”). You can add time expressions like "nel mio tempo libero" (in my free time) or "quasi ogni giorno" (almost every day).
target_language_example: Suono la chitarra da tre anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been playing the guitar for three years.

additional_notes: Used for getting through problems or hard times (emotional, practical, financial, etc.). Often appears after verbs like aiutare (to help) or dovere (must): “aiutare qualcuno a superare le difficoltà” = “to help someone overcome difficulties.”
target_language_example: Con il tuo sostegno, ho potuto superare le difficoltà.
native_language_example: With your support, I was able to overcome the difficulties.

meaning: awake all night (stayed up all night).
additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t sleep during the night. Often with verbs like "restare/rimanere/essere" (to stay/be) or "tenere" in the sense of "keep": "Mi terrà sveglio tutta la notte" = "It will keep me awake all night."
target_language_example: Sono rimasto sveglio tutta la notte perché avevo troppo lavoro.
native_language_example: I stayed up all night because I had too much work.

meaning: “Yes, but …” (agreeing at first, then adding an objection/condition).
additional_notes: Used to partially agree or acknowledge what someone said and then introduce a contrast, doubt, limitation, or counterpoint. In speech it often signals “I see, however…”.
target_language_example: Sì, ma non ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: Yes, but I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something about yourself, typically as an answer to a question (e.g., “Are you ready?” → “Sì, sono pronto.”). “Sono” is the 1st-person singular (“I am”) of the verb *essere* (to be), and it’s often followed by an adjective or a phrase (assicurato, pronto, in ritardo, ecc.).
target_language_example: — Sei stanco? — Sì, sono un po' stanco.
native_language_example: — Are you tired? — Yes, I’m a little tired.

additional_notes: Used to confirm what someone just asked or said, often followed by a noun/adjective or an explanation: "Sì, è con me" (Yes, he/she is with me), "Sì, è così" (Yes, that’s how it is). It can refer to people or things depending on context. For different subjects you change the verb: "Sì, sono…" (I/they am/are), "Sì, sei…" (you are), etc.
target_language_example: —È questa la tua valigia? —Sì, è quella.
native_language_example: —Is this your suitcase? —Yes, that one is.

additional_notes: Polite request/instruction using the formal "Lei" form of the verb: "tagli" (from "tagliare", to cut). Often followed by what you want it divided into, e.g., "in tre fette" (into three slices) or "in tre parti" (into three parts). Used when ordering food or asking someone (e.g., a waiter) to divide something.
target_language_example: Per favore, tagli la pizza in tre fette uguali.
native_language_example: Please, cut the pizza into three equal slices.

meaning: to cut hair; to get a haircut.
additional_notes: Often used with "farsi" (reflexive + infinitive) to mean having someone cut your hair: "(andare a) farsi tagliare i capelli" = "(to go to) get a haircut." In the examples, "mi/si sono/si fece" shows who is getting their hair cut.
target_language_example: Sabato mattina vado a farmi tagliare i capelli.
native_language_example: On Saturday morning I'm going to get a haircut.

additional_notes: Past participle of "tagliare" used with "avere" (ho/hai/ha/hanno tagliato). With hair, Italian uses an indirect object pronoun to show whose hair it is: "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi hanno tagliato i capelli" = "they cut my/your/his/her/our/your (pl.) hair." Often used to talk about a haircut, usually done by a hairdresser ("il parrucchiere/la parrucchiera").
target_language_example: Ho tagliato i capelli ieri dal parrucchiere.
native_language_example: I got my hair cut yesterday at the hairdresser’s.

additional_notes: Tagliò is the passato remoto (a simple past tense), common in narratives and in some regions; in everyday speech you’ll often hear the passato prossimo instead: ha tagliato con il suo coltello. The direct object is often a pronoun before the verb (lo = him/it, la = her/it). Suo agrees with the thing owned (coltello), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Il panettiere tagliò il pane con il suo coltello.
native_language_example: The baker cut the bread with his knife.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the insult/criticism: “un/una tale idiota” = “such an idiot.” It’s rude/insulting, though you can also use it about yourself to mean “I feel so stupid.” Agree "tale" with the noun: un tale idiota (male), una tale idiota (female). Often used in questions like “Come puoi essere un tale idiota?” (“How can you be such an idiot?”).
target_language_example: Non fare il tale idiota, ascoltami un attimo.
native_language_example: Don’t be such an idiot, listen to me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many activities, tasks, events, or topics. Common with "fare" (to do): "fare tante cose" (do lots of things), and with "avere ... da" to express things you have to do/say: "Ho tante cose da fare/dirti" (I have lots of things to do/to tell you). "Tante" agrees with the feminine plural noun "cose".
target_language_example: Oggi ho tante cose da fare, quindi esco più tardi.
native_language_example: Today I have lots of things to do, so I’m going out later.

meaning: 'as much as I hate' (used to compare how strongly two people hate).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons with **tanto quanto** = “as much as / just as much as.” The subject **io** can change (e.g., *tanto quanto lui odia...*), and the verb can change too (e.g., *tanto quanto io amo...*). Often appears in sentences like *X mi odia tanto quanto io odio X* (“X hates me as much as I hate X”).
target_language_example: Lui mi detesta tanto quanto io odio lui.
native_language_example: He hates me as much as I hate him.

additional_notes: Used to say two people feel/do/want something to the same degree. It’s built from "tanto quanto" (“as much as / just as”) + "te" ("you" after a comparison). You can swap "te" for another person: "tanto quanto me" (as much as me), "tanto quanto lui/lei" (as much as him/her), "tanto quanto noi" (as much as us).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato tanto quanto te.
native_language_example: I like ice cream as much as you.

meaning: a long time; so long (of time).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration, often with verbs like essere passato (“it’s been…”) and non vedere/non fare… da (“not … for…”). It can refer to the past (“È passato tanto tempo”) or a duration (“Per tanto tempo…”).
target_language_example: Non ci vediamo da tanto tempo.
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a serving of coffee in a cup (often at home or in a café). In Italy, in a bar you more commonly order “un caffè” (usually an espresso); “una tazza di caffè” is more explicit and can suggest a larger cup/mug of coffee.
target_language_example: Prendo una tazza di caffè e torno subito.
native_language_example: I’ll have a cup of coffee and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: "Tazza" = cup; "da" here means "for" (used to say what something is used for), as in "tazze da tè" (teacups). In shops or at home you might also hear "tazzina da caffè" for a small espresso cup.
target_language_example: Hai delle tazze da caffè pulite?
native_language_example: Do you have any clean coffee cups?

additional_notes: Combination of object pronouns: te = “to you” (indirect object) and lo = “it” (direct object, masculine; can also stand for “that”). It usually comes before the verb: Te lo porto. With infinitives it can attach to the end: portartelo (“to bring it to you”). Often used in promises/threats/reminders: Te lo prometto / Te lo ricordi.
target_language_example: Te lo dico domani.
native_language_example: I'll tell it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Made of pronouns + verb: te = “to you”, lo = “it”, dico = “I say/tell”. Used when you’re about to say something or to add emphasis (“I’m telling you!”). With io (“te lo dico io”) it can sound like “trust me / I’ll tell you myself” and can add insistence.
target_language_example: Te lo dico: domani pioverà di sicuro.
native_language_example: I’m telling you: it will definitely rain tomorrow.

additional_notes:
Used when a verb needs both an indirect object pronoun (te = to you) and ne (= of it/them; about it; from it). Very common in fixed patterns like: 
- Che te ne pare...? = What do you think of it?
- Non te ne frega niente... = You don’t care at all about it.
- Te ne ricordi? = Do you remember it? (lit. “Do you remember about it/of it?”)
It usually comes before the verb: te ne pare, te ne frega, te ne ricordi.
target_language_example: Se te ne ricordi, dimmelo domani.
native_language_example: If you remember it, tell me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Second-person singular of **andarsene** (“to go away/leave”). **Te** and **ne** are pronouns that go with the verb; in English they usually don’t translate word-for-word. Common in orders or strong statements: **Te ne vai!** = “Get out!/Leave!”; **Te ne vai già?** = “Are you leaving already?”. Can sound rude depending on tone; adding insults (e.g., *cazzo*) makes it vulgar.
target_language_example: Se hai finito, prendi le tue cose e te ne vai.
native_language_example: If you’re done, take your things and leave.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weather in a more explicit or formal way than just tempo (which can also mean “time”). Common with verbs like essere (“Il tempo atmosferico è bello/brutto”) and phrases like che tempo fa? (“What’s the weather like?”).
target_language_example: Oggi il tempo atmosferico è brutto, quindi restiamo a casa.
native_language_example: Today the weather is bad, so we’re staying home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about spending time in someone’s company, often with verbs like passare (to spend) or trascorrere (to spend). You can add amounts like molto tempo con (a lot of time with) or poco tempo con (little time with).
target_language_example: Vorrei passare più tempo con te questo weekend.
native_language_example: I’d like to spend more time with you this weekend.

meaning: “some time ago” / “a while back” (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the past, without giving an exact time. Often appears with words like poco (not long ago), un po’ (a little while ago), molto (a long time ago), or un sacco di (a long time ago, informal).
target_language_example: Ci siamo visti tempo fa, ma non ricordo dove.
native_language_example: We saw each other some time ago, but I don’t remember where.

meaning: "time for" / "time to" (time available or the right moment).
additional_notes: Used to talk about having enough time to do something (often with avere + tempo per + noun/infinitive: "Ho tempo per leggere"), or about the right/necessary moment ("È tempo per..." = "It’s time for/to..."). In expressions like "in tempo per", it means "in time to/for" (arrive before it’s too late).
target_language_example: Non ho tempo per fare la spesa oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to do the grocery shopping today.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb *avere*: *avere (il) tempo per...* = “to have time for...”. The article *il* is sometimes included (*il tempo*) but is often omitted in everyday speech (*tempo*). Used frequently with *mai* to complain or emphasize that someone “never” has time.
target_language_example: Oggi ho finalmente tempo per le cose importanti: la famiglia e la salute.
native_language_example: Today I finally have time for the important things: family and health.

meaning: to keep your mouth shut; to not say anything.
additional_notes: Used to say someone should stay silent (often because speaking would cause trouble, reveal a secret, or be inappropriate). In the examples it’s used with "avrei/avresti/avrebbe dovuto" (= “should have”), expressing regret about having spoken.
target_language_example: È meglio tenere la bocca chiusa se non sai la verità.
native_language_example: It’s better to keep your mouth shut if you don’t know the truth.

additional_notes: "Lo" means “it” (referring to something already known in the conversation). You can change it to match what you’re talking about: "tenerla segreta" (keep it secret, feminine), "tenerli segreti" (keep them secret), "tenerle segrete" (keep them secret, feminine). Common with "dovere" (to have to/should) and "promettere" (to promise).
target_language_example: Per favore, tienilo segreto fino a domani.
native_language_example: Please keep it secret until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a lab test that analyzes someone’s DNA (for example, for identity, paternity, or forensic evidence). It’s often used in the plural: i test del DNA (DNA tests). You may also see: test del DNA / esame del DNA.
target_language_example: Hanno fatto un test del DNA per confermare l’identità.
native_language_example: They did a DNA test to confirm the identity.

meaning: “you have/you are” (used with reflexive or “essere” auxiliaries).
additional_notes: Combination of the pronoun ti (“yourself/you”) + sei (“you are”) used in common conversational patterns like: ti sei + past participle. Often forms the passato prossimo of reflexive verbs (e.g., registrarsi → Ti sei registrato? “Did you register?”) or verbs that take essere (e.g., dimenticarsi → Ti sei dimenticato di…? “Did you forget about…?”). The participle usually agrees in gender/number (Ti sei registrato/registrata).
target_language_example: Ti sei svegliato presto stamattina?
native_language_example: Did you wake up early this morning?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission or check if something is okay with someone. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present tense) describing what you want to do: "Ti dispiace se + [verb]?" You can also use the more formal version "Le dispiace se…?" with someone you don’t know well.
target_language_example: Ti dispiace se apro la finestra?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: '(he/she/it) has [done something] to you' / '(he/she/it) [did] to you' (with a past participle).
additional_notes: Made of the indirect-object pronoun "ti" (to you) + the auxiliary verb "ha" (has). It’s used in the passato prossimo (present perfect) with a past participle: "ti ha detto" = "he/she told you". With some verbs it means "to you" (e.g., "ti ha detto"), and with others it can mean "you" as a direct object (e.g., "ti ha visto" = "he/she saw you").
target_language_example: Perché ti ha chiamato ieri?
native_language_example: Why did he/she call you yesterday?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire" (to say/tell). "Ti" means "to you". Used when the subject (he/she/Name) told you something: "Lui ti ha detto..." / "Tom ti ha detto...". For "I told you," say: "Ti ho detto...".
target_language_example: Marco ti ha detto quando arriva?
native_language_example: Did Marco tell you when he’s arriving?

meaning: "I (have) ..." to you (used before a past participle).
additional_notes: Very common in the passato prossimo (present perfect) when speaking to one person informally (tu). It combines the direct/indirect object pronoun ti (“you”) + the auxiliary ho (“I have”). It’s usually followed by a past participle: ti ho visto (I saw you / I’ve seen you), ti ho detto (I told you), ti ho chiesto (I asked you). Word order: pronoun + auxiliary + past participle.
target_language_example: Ti ho chiamato ieri sera, ma non hai risposto.
native_language_example: I called you last night, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of dire: ho detto = “I said/told,” with ti = “to you.” Used to report what you previously told someone, often to remind them or stress that you already said it. Common patterns: “Ti ho detto di + infinitive” (I told you to do…), “Ti ho detto che + clause” (I told you that…), and “Ti ho detto di non + infinitive” (I told you not to…).
target_language_example: Ti ho detto di chiamarmi quando arrivi.
native_language_example: I told you to call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you already told the other person, often to remind them or emphasize that it was said before. Very common in conversation; you can stress it if the other person didn’t listen or forgot. (ti = to you, ho detto = I said/told, che = that).
target_language_example: Ti ho detto che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: I told you that I can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone you already gave them an instruction/order. Very common with an infinitive verb after di: “Ti ho detto di partire” (I told you to leave). Tone can range from neutral to annoyed, depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Ti ho detto di non toccare quella cosa!
native_language_example: I told you not to touch that thing!

additional_notes: Used to remind or scold someone because they’re doing (or about to do) something you already told them not to do. Structure: "Ti ho detto di non" + infinitive verb (chiamare, svegliare, toccare, venire, ecc.). Often said with emphasis in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Ti ho detto di non aprire la finestra!
native_language_example: I told you not to open the window!

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "portare" with a direct object pronoun: "ti" = "to you" (or "you" as the person taken somewhere). Commonly used when you deliver/bring something to someone: "Ti ho portato + [something]". If you’re talking to more than one person or being formal, use "vi ho portato" or "Le ho portato".
target_language_example: Ti ho portato un caffè.
native_language_example: I brought you a coffee.

meaning: "I saw you" / "I’ve seen you" (to a female).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of vedere (“to see”) with the direct object pronoun ti (“you”). The past participle vista ends in -a because it agrees with a female person being seen; for a male you’d say ti ho visto. Often used for spotting someone somewhere (Ti ho vista al parco) or seeing someone do something (Ti ho vista sorridere = “I saw you smile”).
target_language_example: Ti ho vista davanti al cinema ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw you in front of the cinema last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of vedere: ho visto = "I saw / I have seen"; ti = "you" (direct object). Often followed by a time/place (Ti ho visto ieri) or by an infinitive to mean "I saw you + doing" something: Ti ho visto piangere = "I saw you cry/crying."
target_language_example: Ti ho visto uscire di casa stamattina.
native_language_example: I saw you leave the house this morning.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. Literally “(they) please you,” so the thing liked is the grammatical subject: Ti piacciono i film? = “Do you like movies?” Use singular for one thing: Ti piace questo film? (not *ti piacciono*). You can answer with: Sì, mi piacciono / No, non mi piacciono.
target_language_example: Ti piacciono i ristoranti italiani?
native_language_example: Do you like Italian restaurants?

meaning: “do you like the …?” (asking if someone likes plural masculine things).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion/taste about something. It’s the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”) in the 2nd person singular: literally “are the … pleasing to you?”. Use with plural masculine nouns: Ti piacciono i tortellini? For plural feminine nouns, use: Ti piacciono le …? For singular, use: Ti piace il/la …?
target_language_example: Ti piacciono i film italiani?
native_language_example: Do you like Italian movies?

meaning: "Do you like the ...?" (for feminine plural things).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (literally "to be pleasing"): the thing you like is the grammatical subject. So "Ti piacciono le fragole?" is literally "Are strawberries pleasing to you?" Use it with feminine plural nouns that take "le" (e.g., le fragole, le cozze). For masculine plural, use "ti piacciono i / gli ...?"
target_language_example: Ti piacciono le pizze?
native_language_example: Do you like pizzas?

meaning: "do you like?" / "you like" (talking to one person).
additional_notes: From piacere: literally “it pleases you.” Used to ask or say what someone likes (music, food, people, activities). Often appears in questions like “Ti piace…?” (Do you like…?) and with question words: “Che musica ti piace?” (What music do you like?), “Quando ti piace farlo?” (When do you like to do it?).
target_language_example: Ti piace questo ristorante?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s preference between two or more options, very often with a question word like "quale" (which/what): "Quale ti piace di più?" You can compare two items directly: "Ti piace di più A o B?" It literally means “it pleases you more,” but in English you usually translate it as “you like … more / you prefer ….”
target_language_example: Quale gelato ti piace di più, cioccolato o fragola?
native_language_example: Which ice cream do you like more, chocolate or strawberry?

meaning: "do you like the" (asking if someone likes a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to ask about preferences. "Ti" = to you, "piace" = is pleasing, "il" = the (masculine singular). If the noun takes a different article, it changes: "ti piace lo...", "ti piace l'...". For feminine: "ti piace la...", "ti piace l'...". Plural: "ti piacciono i/le...".
target_language_example: Ti piace il caffè?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

meaning: 'Do you like the...?' (asking if someone likes something feminine singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone if they like a specific thing. "Ti" = to you, "piace" = is pleasing, "la" = the (feminine singular). For masculine nouns, use "ti piace il"; for plural nouns, use "ti piacciono i/le".
target_language_example: Ti piace la pizza?
native_language_example: Do you like pizza?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of "piacere" to make a polite invitation or suggestion. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "Ti piacerebbe venire?" = Would you like to come?). Literally it’s closer to “would it please you?”.
target_language_example: Ti piacerebbe venire al cinema con me stasera?
native_language_example: Would you like to come to the cinema with me tonight?

additional_notes: Used to make a strong request or to plead, often with emotion (e.g., asking someone to stop, to help, or to agree). It’s stronger than “per favore” and can sound dramatic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ti prego, aiutami un attimo.
native_language_example: Please, help me for a moment.

additional_notes: From the verb ricordarsi (“to remember”). It can be a question (Ti ricordi…?) or a statement (Ti ricordi, vero?). Often followed by: di + noun (Ti ricordi del secondo gruppo?); a direct object (Ti ricordi il numero?); or quando/dove/come + clause (Ti ricordi quando…?). In many contexts English uses “remember” without a preposition, but Italian may use ricordarsi di.
target_language_example: Ti ricordi di chiamare tua madre stasera?
native_language_example: Do you remember to call your mother tonight?

meaning: “you have” / “you are” (used to form the past tense with reflexive or “essere” verbs).
additional_notes: “Ti” is “yourself/you” (reflexive pronoun) and “sei” is “you are” (2nd person singular of essere). Together they introduce the passato prossimo for reflexive verbs and many movement/change-of-state verbs: ti sei lavato/a (you washed yourself), ti sei laureato/a (you graduated), ti sei messo/a (you put yourself / you got), ti sei chiuso/a fuori (you locked yourself out). The past participle often agrees in gender/number with the subject: -o (male), -a (female), -i/-e (plural).
target_language_example: Ti sei ricordato di chiamarmi?
native_language_example: Did you remember to call me?

meaning: "do you feel" / "you feel" (asking about how someone feels).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "sentirsi" (to feel, to be feeling). Used with adjectives to ask about someone’s physical or emotional state: "Ti senti bene?" (Do you feel well?), "Ti senti felice/stanca?" (Do you feel happy/tired?). The adjective usually agrees with the person (e.g., "stanco" for a man, "stanca" for a woman). You can also use it with comparatives like "meglio" (better): "Ti senti meglio?"
target_language_example: Ti senti pronto per uscire?
native_language_example: Do you feel ready to go out?

meaning: “Did you like the …?” (to you it was pleasing).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone liked something feminine singular (la + noun). It’s the passato prossimo of piacere: the thing is the subject (la canzone è piaciuta) and “ti” = “to you.” For masculine singular use “ti è piaciuto il…”, and for plural “ti sono piaciuti/e i/le…”.
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la cena di ieri?
native_language_example: Did you like yesterday’s dinner?

meaning: “did you like it?” / “did you enjoy it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone liked or enjoyed something in the past. With piacere, the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so Italian literally says “it pleased you.” Common pattern: “Ti è piaciuto/a + noun?” (piaciuto for masculine nouns like il film; piaciuta for feminine nouns like la cena). For plural nouns: “Ti sono piaciuti/e”.
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la cena?
native_language_example: Did you like the dinner?

additional_notes: From the verb "succedere" (to happen) in the passato prossimo: "è successo" = "(it) happened". With "ti" it means something happened to you. Very common in questions like "Che cosa ti è successo?" (What happened to you?), often expressing concern or surprise. You can also add a place/body part: "ti è successo a Boston" (happened to you in Boston), "ti è successo al braccio" (happened to your arm).
target_language_example: Tutto bene? Che cosa ti è successo?
native_language_example: Everything ok? What happened to you?

additional_notes: Used to say someone regularly keeps something clean. It’s usually followed by a feminine noun like "camera" or "stanza" (room): "tiene sempre pulita la sua camera/stanza". Italian often drops the subject, so "tiene" can mean "he/she keeps" from context. "La sua" means "her/his" and agrees with a feminine singular noun; with "il" nouns you’d use "il suo".
target_language_example: Tiene sempre pulita la sua camera.
native_language_example: She always keeps her room clean.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb *tingersi*: *tingersi i capelli di + colore*. It agrees with the subject: *mi sono tinto/tinta i capelli di...*, *si è tinto/tinta...*, *ti sei tinto/tinta...*. You can also hear the shorter version *tingersi i capelli* (without saying the color).
target_language_example: Mi sono tinta i capelli di biondo.
native_language_example: I dyed my hair blonde.

additional_notes: From the verb *tingersi* (to dye, to color oneself). It’s usually used with a reflexive pronoun and the auxiliary *essere*: *mi sono tinto/a i capelli di...*, *si è tinto/a i capelli di...*. The color comes after *di* (e.g., *di blu*, *di nero*, *di rosso*). Past participle agrees with the person: *tinto* (male) / *tinta* (female).
target_language_example: Mi sono tinta i capelli di castano.
native_language_example: I dyed my hair brown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about categories or varieties of something; followed by a noun (usually plural), e.g. "tipi di film" (types of movies). Often used in questions with "che" or "quali" to ask what someone likes or what is available.
target_language_example: Che tipi di musica ascolti di solito?
native_language_example: What kinds of music do you usually listen to?

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe what category something belongs to. Very common after indefinite words like “un/una” (“a kind of…”) or “nessun” (“no kind of…”). Not the same as “tipo” meaning “like/sort of” as a filler in casual speech.
target_language_example: Che tipo di musica ti piace?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like?

additional_notes: Used to talk about musical categories or styles you like or listen to. Often appears with adjectives (un tipo di musica rilassante) or in the pattern "il tipo di musica che..." (“the kind of music that...”).
target_language_example: Che tipo di musica ti piace?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like?

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "tirare fuori". Used in narratives to say someone took something out of a pocket, bag, drawer, etc. In everyday speech you’ll more often hear: "ha tirato fuori" (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Quando arrivò, tirò fuori le chiavi dalla tasca.
native_language_example: When he arrived, he pulled the keys out of his pocket.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "togliersi" (= to remove from oneself), so the subject and the person taking the shoes off are the same. You can also say "togliti le scarpe" (informal singular command: take off your shoes) or "si è tolto/a le scarpe" (he/she took off their shoes).
target_language_example: Per favore, puoi toglierti le scarpe all’ingresso?
native_language_example: Please, can you take off your shoes at the entrance?

meaning: 'to go back/return to' (a place), or 'to go back to' doing something.
additional_notes: Used with a destination (often a city/place): tornare a Boston = return to Boston. With an infinitive, it means resuming a previous action: tornare a studiare = go back to studying. In the past, you often see it with essere: è tornato/a a casa (he/she went back home).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo devo tornare a lavorare.
native_language_example: After lunch I have to go back to work.

meaning: to go back home; to return home.
additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to your home/house from somewhere else. You can conjugate it for time: deve tornare (has to return), doveva tornare (had to return). Often used with an indirect object to say whose home: Tornare a casa mia/tuA/suA (go back to my/your/his/her home).
target_language_example: Devo tornare a casa presto.
native_language_example: I have to go back home early.

meaning: to go back; to return (to a previous place).
additional_notes: Used when you need to turn around or return to where you were before (e.g., because you forgot something or to get someone). It can also be used in a more abstract sense to mean that you can’t undo the past (“Non si può tornare indietro” = “You can’t go back / there’s no going back”).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato le chiavi: devo tornare indietro.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys: I have to go back.

additional_notes: Used for talking about time travel or, more commonly, imagining going back to a past moment to change something (often introduced by "se" = "if"). It’s built from tornare (to return) + indietro (back) + nel tempo (in time).
target_language_example: Se potessi tornare indietro nel tempo, cambierei quella scelta.
native_language_example: If I could go back in time, I would change that choice.

additional_notes: Past participle feminine singular of "tornare a casa" (to go/come back home). Used with the auxiliary "essere": "sono tornata a casa" (I came back home, said by a woman) / "è tornata a casa" (she came back home). For a man: "tornato a casa".
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro sono tornata a casa e ho cenato.
native_language_example: After work I came back home and had dinner.

additional_notes: Past participle of "tornare" used with "essere" (e.g., "sono tornato/a a casa" = "I came back home"). Change the ending for gender/number: tornato (male singular), tornata (female singular), tornati (male/mixed plural), tornate (female plural). Often used with time words like "appena" (just) or to emphasize being safely home.
target_language_example: Siamo tornati a casa tardi dopo il concerto.
native_language_example: We got back home late after the concert.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something shared or happening within a group that includes the speaker (noi). With two people it often means “between us”; with a larger group it can mean “among us.” Common with verbs like dividere (to split/share), and in phrases like Non ci sono segreti tra di noi (“There are no secrets between us”). It can also refer to a relationship: tra di noi = “between us (as a couple/friends).”
target_language_example: Teniamolo tra di noi, per favore.
native_language_example: Let’s keep it between us, please.

meaning: "among the" / "between the" (before a plural masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate being in the middle of people/things (physical or figurative), or to express choice/comparison within a group. It’s the preposition "tra" + the plural masculine article "i". Typical uses: "tra i migliori/peggiori" (among the best/worst), "tra i pasti" (between meals), "scegli tra i due" (choose between the two).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è tra i più economici del quartiere.
native_language_example: This restaurant is among the cheapest in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns after "tra" (same meaning as "fra"). Common for: position between two things (Tra le due città), space separating things (tra le righe), being in a group/among (tra le migliori; tra le varie cose), and ranges/repetition (tra le cinque e le sei volte = between five and six times).
target_language_example: Il mio posto è tra le due finestre.
native_language_example: My seat is between the two windows.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically in your embrace. Common with verbs like "addormentarsi" (to fall asleep) or "morire" (to die), often in emotional contexts. "Tra" here means "between/among," but the natural English translation is usually "in my arms."
target_language_example: È rimasta tra le mie braccia per un po'.
native_language_example: She stayed in my arms for a while.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone being physically held by another person (often romantic or comforting). With "morire" it can mean someone died while being held by the other person. The possessive "sue" agrees with "braccia" (feminine plural) and can refer to either "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi sento al sicuro tra le sue braccia.
native_language_example: I feel safe in his/her arms.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to translate a specific sentence. Often followed by a target language with "in" (e.g., "in inglese", "in esperanto"). In requests you may see it with "puoi... ?" (informal), "può... ?" (formal), or "mi potrebbe... ?" (very polite).
target_language_example: Mi puoi tradurre questa frase in inglese, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you translate this sentence into English for me, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone spends a lot of time doing something (often followed by “a” + infinitive, e.g., “a studiare”) or with someone/at a place (often with “con” or “a/in”). The subject can be omitted in Italian when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Trascorro molto tempo a studiare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I spend a lot of time studying Italian.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’d like to be with someone more often/for longer. Very common with verbs like "vorrei" (I’d like) and "voglio" (I want). In the present tense: (io) trascorro, (tu) trascorri, (lui/lei) trascorre, (noi) trascorriamo, (voi) trascorrete, (loro) trascorrono.
target_language_example: Dovremmo trascorrere più tempo con i nostri amici.
native_language_example: We should spend more time with our friends.

trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro

target_language_multi_word_term: trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro
meaning: to spend more time outside and less time inside.
additional_notes: Used as advice or a recommendation, often with "dovresti/dovrebbe/dovreste" (you should / he-she should / you all should). "Trascorrere" means "to spend" (time). "Fuori" = outside; "dentro" = inside.
target_language_example: Per stare meglio, dovresti trascorrere più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro.
native_language_example: To feel better, you should spend more time outside and less time inside.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *trascorrere* (“to spend” time), usually in the *passato prossimo*: *ho/ha/abbiamo/avete trascorso...*. It’s commonly followed by **con** + people (*con loro* = with them) or **a/in** + place, and can also be followed by **a** + infinitive to say what you spent time doing (*ha trascorso molto tempo a studiare* = she spent a lot of time studying).
target_language_example: Ho trascorso molto tempo a studiare per l’esame.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of time studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **trascorrere** (“to spend” time) in the **passato prossimo**: *ho/abbiamo trascorso tutta la giornata…* It’s commonly followed by **in + place** (*in spiaggia, in biblioteca*) or **con + person** (*con lei, con loro*) to say where/with whom you spent the entire day.
target_language_example: Ieri abbiamo trascorso tutta la giornata a Roma.
native_language_example: Yesterday we spent the whole day in Rome.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "trascorrere" (to spend/pass time). It usually takes "avere" as the helping verb: "ho/ha/hai trascorso". The past participle "trascorso" agrees only in gender/number when used with a direct object pronoun (e.g., "l’ho trascorsa"), but in this phrase it typically stays "trascorso". Often followed by a person: "con Tom", "con Maria".
target_language_example: Ho trascorso tutta la mattinata con mia sorella.
native_language_example: I spent the whole morning with my sister.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something lasts) or a point in the past. Common patterns: "da tre anni" = "for three years" (continuing up to now), "tre anni fa" = "three years ago", "per tre anni" = "for three years" (duration, not necessarily continuing), "in tre anni" = "in/within three years".
target_language_example: Studio italiano da tre anni.
native_language_example: I've been studying Italian for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It usually comes at the end of the sentence (or right after the time expression). You can replace the number: "due anni fa" (two years ago), "dieci anni fa" (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Ho cambiato lavoro tre anni fa.
native_language_example: I changed jobs three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state the length of time someone was incarcerated, often with verbs like "passare" or "trascorrere" (to spend): "Ha passato/trascorso tre anni in prigione".
target_language_example: Mio cugino ha passato tre anni in prigione.
native_language_example: My cousin spent three years in prison.

additional_notes: Used to talk about amounts of money in dollars, often with verbs like costare (to cost), venire (to come to/cost), spendere (to spend), and dovere (to owe). You can also say it on its own to state how much money you have: Ho solo tre dollari.
target_language_example: Quanto costa? Tre dollari.
native_language_example: How much does it cost? Three dollars.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or had) three children. In Italian, "figli" is the plural of "figlio" and can mean “children” in general (not only “sons”), especially when talking about a parent’s kids. Common with verbs like "avere" (to have), "crescere" (to raise), and "perdere" (to lose).
target_language_example: Hanno tre figli e vivono a Milano.
native_language_example: They have three children and live in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for three days: "per tre giorni"), or about time relative to another moment (three days before/after: "tre giorni prima/dopo"). It can also describe something that lasts three days ("un viaggio di tre giorni").
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per tre giorni.
native_language_example: I'm staying in Rome for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three days before now. It typically comes after the verb or at the end of the sentence (e.g., “È successo tre giorni fa”). With other numbers you can swap out “tre” (e.g., “due giorni fa” = two days ago).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato questo corso tre giorni fa.
native_language_example: I started this course three days ago.

additional_notes: Used to indicate an exact quantity: the number 3 + the plural noun "libri" (books). "Tre" stays the same regardless of gender; "libro" → "libri" is the plural. Often appears after a verb (e.g., "Ho portato tre libri" = "I brought three books").
target_language_example: Devo comprare tre libri per la scuola.
native_language_example: I have to buy three books for school.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time or a period, often with verbs like "trascorrere" (to spend): "Ho trascorso tre mesi..." = "I spent three months...". "Tre" agrees with "mesi" (plural of "mese").
target_language_example: Resterò in Italia per tre mesi.
native_language_example: I will stay in Italy for three months.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happened in the past. The time expression usually comes at the end of the sentence (as in the examples), but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis: “Tre mesi fa, …”. “Fa” means “ago” in these expressions (e.g., due giorni fa = two days ago).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a studiare italiano tre mesi fa.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian three months ago.

meaning: three or four; about three or four.
additional_notes: Used to give an approximate number (not exact). Often followed by a plural noun (tre o quattro libri) or by a time expression like “volte” (tre o quattro volte al mese = three or four times a month).
target_language_example: Restiamo qui tre o quattro giorni.
native_language_example: We’ll stay here for three or four days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time needed. Common patterns: **in tre ore** = “in three hours” (time it takes to finish something); **a tre ore (e mezzo) da qui** / **a tre ore di macchina** = “three hours (and a half) from here” / “three hours away by car” (travel time).
target_language_example: Ci vogliono tre ore per arrivare a Firenze in treno.
native_language_example: It takes three hours to get to Florence by train.

additional_notes: A quantity of time (3 weeks). Use it with time expressions like "per tre settimane" (for three weeks) and with recurring events like "ogni tre settimane" (every three weeks). With "passare/trascorrere", it means spending three weeks somewhere or doing something.
target_language_example: Rimango a Roma per tre settimane.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three weeks before now. "Fa" comes after the time expression (e.g., "due giorni fa", "un mese fa"). You can place it at the end of the sentence or after the verb for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ci siamo trasferiti qui tre settimane fa.
native_language_example: We moved here three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on three occasions. Often with frequency expressions like "tre volte la settimana" (three times a week). You can also hear it in requests like "ripetilo tre volte" (repeat it three times).
target_language_example: L'ho controllato tre volte, ma non ho trovato errori.
native_language_example: I checked it three times, but I didn’t find any mistakes.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day (meals, medicine, routines). Common in instructions, especially medical ones: "Prenda/Devi prendere ... tre volte al giorno".
target_language_example: Devo prendere queste gocce tre volte al giorno.
native_language_example: I have to take these drops three times a day.

additional_notes: A specific amount of money (300 USD). Used after verbs like guadagnare (to earn), vendere (to sell), vincere (to win), prendere una multa (to get a fine), and dovere (to owe). The number comes before the currency name: trecento dollari.
target_language_example: Il biglietto costa trecento dollari.
native_language_example: The ticket costs three hundred dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age. In Italian you say someone "has" an age with avere: "Ho tredici anni" = "I’m thirteen." Often used with "solo/soltanto" to mean "only" (emphasizing how young someone is).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha tredici anni.
native_language_example: My sister is thirteen years old.

additional_notes: Used to say a train arrived or departed later than scheduled. Often appears with an article or possessive: “Il treno era in ritardo” (The train was late), “Il mio/tuo/suo treno era in ritardo” (My/your/his-her train was late). Note: “in ritardo” means “late/delayed,” not the English insult “retarded.”
target_language_example: Il treno era in ritardo di venti minuti.
native_language_example: The train was twenty minutes late.

additional_notes: A quantity of money. Used with verbs like dare (to give), prestare (to lend), dovere (to owe), rimanere (to have left). Word order is number + currency; in Italian the currency name stays plural here (dollari).
target_language_example: Non ho che trenta dollari con me.
native_language_example: I only have thirty dollars on me.
