additional_notes: Used for animals kept at home for companionship (e.g., a dog or cat). Often in the plural: “animali domestici.” Related: “cane/gatto domestico” = domestic dog/cat.
target_language_example: Nel mio appartamento non posso avere un animale domestico.
native_language_example: In my apartment I can’t have a pet.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of one year or to count years. The article changes with gender/number: un anno (one year), due anni (two years), l’anno (the year). Note the elision: un anno (not *uno anno*). Common patterns: per un anno (“for a year”), da un anno (“for a year/for one year, up to now”), un anno di + noun (“a year of …”).
target_language_example: Studio italiano da un anno.
native_language_example: I’ve been studying Italian for a year.

un anno da quando mi sono

target_language_multi_word_term: un anno da quando mi sono
meaning: “a year since I …” (it’s been a year since I …).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions like "È passato un anno" (“A year has passed”) to say how much time has passed since a past event involving yourself. "da quando" = “since/ever since (the time when)”, and "mi sono" starts a past tense with "essere" (passato prossimo) for reflexive verbs (e.g., mi sono sposato/a = “I got married”). You normally continue the sentence with a past participle (e.g., "mi sono trasferito/a", "mi sono laureato/a").
target_language_example: È passato un anno da quando mi sono trasferito a Milano.
native_language_example: It’s been a year since I moved to Milan.

additional_notes: Used for a self-contained home unit in a building. The indefinite article changes depending on gender/number: un appartamento (masc. sing.), un appartamento di tre camere = a three-bedroom apartment; vivo in un appartamento sopra un negozio = I live in an apartment above a shop.
target_language_example: Stiamo affittando un appartamento vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: We are renting an apartment near the station.

additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings (e.g., with a doctor, at an office) and also for a romantic date. Common patterns: "Ho un appuntamento dal dentista" (appointment with the dentist), "prenotare/fissare un appuntamento" (to book/set an appointment), "chiedere un appuntamento" (to ask someone out / request a meeting), "andare a un appuntamento" (to go to an appointment/date).
target_language_example: Domani ho un appuntamento con il medico alle 10.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an appointment with the doctor at 10.

additional_notes: A very common noun in travel/hotel situations (bathroom, beach, gym). Plural: asciugamani. In Italian the indefinite article changes with gender/starting sound; here it’s masculine so you say un asciugamano.
target_language_example: Mi può portare un asciugamano, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you bring me a towel, please?

additional_notes: Used mainly to describe someone’s physical appearance or the impression they give: “avere un aspetto + adjective” (to look + adjective), e.g. un aspetto splendido/terribile. It can also mean “an aspect” (a part of something), but in these examples it’s about how someone looks.
target_language_example: Oggi hai un aspetto stanco: hai dormito poco?
native_language_example: Today you look tired: did you sleep little?

additional_notes: Used to compare how someone looks (often health/tiredness/condition). It follows the pattern: avere + un aspetto + adjective + di + person/thing. The adjective changes for gender/number: peggiore stays the same for masculine/feminine and singular/plural.
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, ho un aspetto peggiore di ieri.
native_language_example: After the trip, I look worse than yesterday.

meaning: a moment; for a moment; just a second.
additional_notes: Common in everyday Italian to ask someone to wait briefly (Aspetta un attimo), to excuse yourself briefly (Scusami un attimo), or to say something happened very recently (un attimo fa = a moment ago). Often used with solo/giusto/proprio to mean “just”.
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo, arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used for a male actor; the feminine form is "un’attrice". Plural: "attori" (male or mixed group), "attrici" (all female). Often used with adjectives like "famoso" (famous) or to describe someone’s job: "Lui è un attore".
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un attore e lavora a teatro.
native_language_example: My brother is an actor and works in the theater.

additional_notes: Indefinite form: use when talking about one bus (not a specific one). Plural: "degli autobus" or "alcuni autobus". Often used with "prendere" (to take/catch): "prendere un autobus".
target_language_example: Scusi, dove posso prendere un autobus per il centro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I catch a bus to the city center?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s profession or to say you need legal help. The article changes with gender/number: un avvocato (male), un’avvocata / un avvocato (female, depending on preference), un avvocato e una avvocata; plural: degli avvocati (mixed or all male), delle avvocate (all female). Common phrases: parlare con un avvocato (to talk to a lawyer), mi serve un avvocato (I need a lawyer).
target_language_example: Mi serve un avvocato per questo contratto.
native_language_example: I need a lawyer for this contract.

additional_notes: Used for a single kiss. Common in romantic contexts, but also for a quick affectionate kiss with family (often on the cheek). With verbs like dare (to give) and volere (to want): “Dategli un bacio” = “Give him a kiss.”
target_language_example: Mi dai un bacio prima di andare via?
native_language_example: Will you give me a kiss before you leave?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like fare (to take/give): fare un bagno = to take a bath; fare un bagno a qualcuno/qualcosa = to give someone/something a bath (e.g., a dog). Note: bagno can also mean “bathroom” (more often il bagno), but in these examples it means “bath.”
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra, faccio un bagno caldo.
native_language_example: After the gym, I take a hot bath.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a child (usually male) in general or a specific boy: Un bambino = “a child/a boy.” For a female child, say una bambina. With essere (“to be”), it often means “just a kid” (e.g., Lui è solo un bambino). In comparisons like Anche un bambino..., it means “even a child could…” to show something is very easy.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è solo un bambino.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s just a kid.

additional_notes: It’s the shortened form of **un bello**. In Italian, **bello** often changes form depending on the next word: **un bel** comes before a masculine singular noun that starts with most consonants (e.g., *un bel viaggio, un bel parco, un bel cane*). It means something like “a nice,” “a lovely,” or “a beautiful.” (Before *s + consonant*, *z*, *gn*, etc., you typically use **uno bello** → **uno bello/uno** pattern, e.g., *uno bello spettacolo* / *uno spettacolo*.)
target_language_example: Abbiamo passato un bel pomeriggio al mare.
native_language_example: We spent a nice afternoon at the beach.

meaning: a nice gift; a lovely present.
additional_notes: Means “a nice/lovely gift,” with bel as the shortened form of bello used before a masculine singular noun starting with most consonants (bel regalo). Often used when giving something to someone: fare/dare un bel regalo (to give someone a nice gift) or comprare un bel regalo per qualcuno (to buy a nice gift for someone).
target_language_example: Ti ho comprato un bel regalo per il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought you a nice gift for your birthday.

additional_notes: A common compliment about someone’s smile. "Bel" is the shortened form of "bello" used before a masculine singular noun ("un bel sorriso"). Often used with "avere" ("ha un bel sorriso" = "he/she has a nice smile").
target_language_example: Hai proprio un bel sorriso!
native_language_example: You have a really nice smile!

additional_notes: Common when ordering a drink or asking someone to pour you beer. In Italy you might also hear/see specific sizes or containers (es. una birra piccola/media/grande, una birra alla spina, una bottiglia di birra), but this phrase is always understood as “a glass of beer.”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un bicchiere di birra, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a glass of beer, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single serving of milk. Often appears with verbs like bere (to drink) and versare (to pour). “Che ne dice/dite di…?” means “How about…?” when making a suggestion.
target_language_example: Vuoi un bicchiere di latte prima di andare a letto?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of milk before going to bed?

additional_notes: Common when ordering in a bar/restaurant or describing what someone drank. Use it with polite requests like "Posso avere..." or "Vorrei...". "Un bicchiere" = "a glass" (quantity/container), "di vino" = "of wine".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Common in cafés/restaurants when ordering a drink. “Un bicchiere di…” = “a glass of…”. You may also hear “Vorrebbe…?” as a polite way to ask what someone would like.
target_language_example: Dopo cena prendo un bicchiere di vino rosso.
native_language_example: After dinner I have a glass of red wine.

meaning: a ticket (e.g., for a train, bus, concert).
additional_notes: Used for a pass you buy to travel or enter an event/place. Often followed by “del/della + [thing]”: “un biglietto del treno” (a train ticket), “un biglietto dell’autobus” (a bus ticket). You can also specify one-way/round-trip: “un biglietto di sola andata” / “un biglietto di andata e ritorno”.
target_language_example: Vorrei un biglietto del treno per Firenze, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a train ticket to Florence, please.

un biglietto andata e ritorno per

target_language_multi_word_term: un biglietto andata e ritorno per
additional_notes: Used when buying travel tickets (train, bus, plane). Follow it with the destination: “...per Roma / per Chicago”. “Andata e ritorno” literally means “outbound and return.” You can also hear “biglietto di andata e ritorno” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vorrei un biglietto andata e ritorno per Roma, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a round-trip ticket to Rome, please.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying, getting, reserving, or asking for a concert ticket. "Un biglietto" = "a ticket"; "per" indicates what the ticket is for (the concert). Often used with verbs like prendere (to get/buy), comprare (to buy), ottenere (to obtain), and with questions like "Mi prendi...?" (Can you get me...?).
target_language_example: Devo comprare un biglietto per il concerto di stasera.
native_language_example: I have to buy a ticket for tonight’s concert.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (often a job/role) to praise someone’s ability or how well they do something: "un bravo avvocato" = "a good lawyer", "un bravo insegnante" = "a good teacher". Often implies competence/skill, not just being “nice.” Can agree in gender/number: "una brava", "un bravo", "dei bravi", "delle brave".
target_language_example: Cerco un bravo medico.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a good doctor.

meaning: a good boy / a good guy.
additional_notes: Used to describe a male (often a young man) as kind, well-behaved, and generally trustworthy. With "essere" or "sembrare": "È un bravo ragazzo" (He’s a good guy), "Sembra un bravo ragazzo" (He seems like a good guy). "Bravo" can also mean “skilled,” but in this phrase it usually means “good/nice” as a person.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: è un bravo ragazzo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a good guy.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a strong cold. Very common with: "avere" (to have) → "Ho un brutto raffreddore"; "prendere" (to catch) → "Ho preso un brutto raffreddore"; and "soffrire di" (to suffer from) → "Ha sofferto di un brutto raffreddore". "Brutto" here means "bad" in the sense of "severe," not "ugly."
target_language_example: Non vengo a lavoro oggi: ho un brutto raffreddore.
native_language_example: I’m not coming to work today: I have a bad cold.

additional_notes: Noun used to accuse or describe someone who lies. It’s masculine; for a woman you say "una bugiarda". Often used with "sei" (you are): "Sei un bugiardo".
target_language_example: Non fidarti di lui: è un bugiardo.
native_language_example: Don’t trust him: he’s a liar.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns: **un buon + noun**. It’s the shortened form of **un buono** before most consonants (e.g., *un buon libro*). Before **s + consonant**, **z**, **ps**, **gn**, etc., use **un buon** with the article **uno**: *uno buon* is not used; instead say **un buon**? Actually you say **un buon** only with **un**; with those nouns you use **uno** and **buon**: **uno buon** is still not standard—use **un buon** only where **un** is correct, and use **uno** + **buon**? In standard Italian you say **uno** + **buon** is uncommon; instead you typically keep **buon** but choose the correct article: **uno** + adjective usually: *uno **buon**?* better: **un buon** is for nouns that take **un** (e.g., *libro, ristorante, padre*). For nouns that take **uno**, say **un buon** is not correct; use **uno** + **buon** only if you hear it in speech, but in careful Italian prefer **un buon** with **un**-nouns and **uno** + **buono** (e.g., *uno buono* is possible but sounds unusual) or rephrase (e.g., *un ottimo...*). Before a vowel, you still use **un buon**: *un buon amico*. Feminine is **una buona** (or **un’ottima** etc.).
target_language_example: Cerco un buon albergo vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a good hotel near the station.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "avere" (to have) to describe how someone looks (health, style, general appearance): "avere un buon aspetto" = "to look good" / "to look well." In the plural it becomes "un buon aspetto" → "un buon aspetto" stays the same if referring to one person; for multiple people you typically still say "hanno un buon aspetto" (the thing they “have” is the singular "aspetto").
target_language_example: Dopo le vacanze hai un buon aspetto!
native_language_example: You look good after the vacation!

additional_notes: Used to talk about having or needing a competent lawyer, often in legal trouble or court contexts. It’s masculine singular: un avvocato; with the adjective buon before a noun starting with a vowel: buon avvocato (instead of buono avvocato). Feminine: una buona avvocata / una buona avvocatessa (less common).
target_language_example: Se vai in tribunale, ti serve un buon avvocato.
native_language_example: If you go to court, you need a good lawyer.

additional_notes: Used when recommending or asking for a reliable dictionary. Often followed by a language with "di" (un buon dizionario di esperanto = a good Esperanto dictionary). "A portata di mano" means "within reach/handy" (keep a good dictionary handy).
target_language_example: Per iniziare a studiare italiano, ti consiglio un buon dizionario.
native_language_example: To start studying Italian, I recommend a good dictionary.

additional_notes: Uses the noun "impiego" (employment/job) with the adjective "buon" (= "buono" before a noun). Common in statements about having/looking for stable or desirable work (often implying good conditions, pay, or security). Typically used with "avere": "Ho un buon impiego" = "I have a good job."
target_language_example: Dopo la laurea, ha trovato un buon impiego in banca.
native_language_example: After graduating, he found a good job at a bank.

meaning: a good job (good work; or a good job/employment).
additional_notes: Most often means “good work” in phrases like “fare un buon lavoro” (to do a good job). With verbs like “trovare/avere/cercare un buon lavoro,” it usually means “a good job” as in good employment/position. Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Hai fatto un buon lavoro con questa presentazione.
native_language_example: You did a good job with this presentation.

additional_notes: Used when asking for a recommendation nearby. Often appears in questions with conoscere (“to know”) or consigliare (“to recommend”), especially when speaking to staff or locals. You can swap in other places: un buon hotel/un buon ristorante/un buon bar nella zona.
target_language_example: Scusi, conosce un buon motel nella zona?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know a good motel in the area?

meaning: a good seat/spot; a good place.
additional_notes: Used for a seat (e.g., at a concert, on a train) or a physical spot/location. Often with verbs like avere/trovare (“to have/find”) and with a clause like “un buon posto dove…” (“a good place to…”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo trovato un buon posto vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: We found a good spot near the window.

additional_notes: Indefinite form: "un" = "a" (masculine singular). Used when talking about one dog in general or when the listener doesn’t know which dog. Plural: "dei cani" (some dogs) / "i cani" (the dogs).
target_language_example: In casa abbiamo un cane molto tranquillo.
native_language_example: At home we have a very calm dog.

additional_notes: "Cappello" is a masculine singular noun; "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Plural: "dei cappelli" (some hats) or simply "cappelli" (hats). Used when shopping or describing clothing.
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare un cappello nero.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a black hat.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "un/una + noun + da + role/use" to describe what something is for or associated with. Here, "cappello" = hat and "da cowboy" = cowboy-style/for a cowboy. Common verbs with it: "comprare" (to buy) and "indossare" (to wear).
target_language_example: Ho visto un uomo con un cappello da cowboy.
native_language_example: I saw a man with a cowboy hat.

additional_notes: Used when a vehicle has broken down or needs to be towed away. Often with the verb chiamare (“to call”): chiamare un carro attrezzi = to call a tow truck.
target_language_example: La macchina non parte: chiamo un carro attrezzi.
native_language_example: The car won’t start: I’m calling a tow truck.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine indefinite article "un" to mean "a/one" with the singular noun "cavallo" (horse). In questions it often means "Do you have a horse?"; with numbers it can be the subject (e.g., "How many teeth does a horse have?").
target_language_example: Vorrei un cavallo, ma non ho spazio.
native_language_example: I'd like a horse, but I don't have space.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person, thing, time, or quantity that isn’t named or isn’t important to specify. Common patterns: "un certo periodo (di tempo)" = "a certain period (of time)"; "un certo numero di..." = "a certain number of... / some ...".
target_language_example: Ci vuole un certo tempo per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: It takes a certain amount of time to learn Italian.

meaning: “a certain Mr. …” (a man named …, usually not well-known to the speaker).
additional_notes: Used when introducing someone by name but implying the person is unknown, only vaguely known, or being referred to with some distance (e.g., in phone messages: “There’s a Mr. Brown on the line”). It can sound neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone/context. Often followed by a surname: “un certo signor Rossi”.
target_language_example: C'è un certo signor Rossi che chiede di parlarle.
native_language_example: There’s a certain Mr. Rossi asking to speak to you.

additional_notes: Used for a meeting where you talk with an employer about a job. Common verbs: avere un colloquio di lavoro (to have a job interview), andare a un colloquio di lavoro (to go to a job interview). Often followed by a time expression: domani, stamattina, domani pomeriggio, etc.
target_language_example: Oggi ho un colloquio di lavoro alle tre, quindi devo vestirmi bene.
native_language_example: Today I have a job interview at three, so I need to dress well.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean one sudden act or impact: a gunshot (un colpo di pistola), a warning shot (un colpo di avvertimento), or more generally a blow/strike. It also appears in fixed expressions like "un colpo di Stato" = "a coup d’état" (a sudden takeover of government).
target_language_example: Abbiamo sentito un colpo di pistola in lontananza.
native_language_example: We heard a gunshot in the distance.

additional_notes: Common in requests with dare (“to give”): Dai/Dammi/Dacci/Date… un colpo di telefono = “Give me/us… a quick call.” Often implies “just call briefly / to let someone know,” not a long conversation.
target_language_example: Quando arrivi, fammi un colpo di telefono.
native_language_example: When you arrive, give me a quick call.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single knife. With masculine singular nouns like coltello, you use the indefinite article un (not una). Plural: dei coltelli (“some knives”).
target_language_example: Hai un coltello per tagliare il pane?
native_language_example: Do you have a knife to cut the bread?

additional_notes: "Computer" is a masculine noun in Italian, so it uses the article "un" (indefinite) or "il" (definite). The plural is often "i computer" (invariable), though you may also see "i computers". Used for desktops or laptops depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer per lavorare da casa.
native_language_example: I need a computer to work from home.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase with the indefinite article (un) + noun (computer, masculine) + adjective (nuovo). The adjective usually comes after the noun: un computer nuovo. With plural: dei computer nuovi (some new computers).
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer nuovo per lavorare da casa.
native_language_example: I need a new computer to work from home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a laptop. Gender: masculine (un/il). Plural: (dei/i) computer portatili. You can also just say "un portatile" in context. "Computer" is invariable in Italian (same in singular/plural), while "portatile" changes to "portatili" in the plural.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un computer portatile per studiare.
native_language_example: I need a laptop to study.

additional_notes: Used to name the animal (common as a pet) or to describe something that looks like a rabbit (e.g., a cloud). Masculine noun: il coniglio; plural: i conigli.
target_language_example: Abbiamo visto un coniglio nel parco.
native_language_example: We saw a rabbit in the park.

meaning: a farmer; a peasant (rural farm worker).
additional_notes: Refers to a male farmer or country person who works the land. Feminine: "una contadina". Plural: "contadini/contadine". It can be neutral (job) but in some contexts can sound old-fashioned or slightly insulting if used to mean "peasant" (e.g., "Sembri un contadino").
target_language_example: Mio nonno era un contadino e lavorava nei campi.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a farmer and worked in the fields.

additional_notes: Used to say what event/occasion the pirate costume is intended for. Structure: "un costume" (a costume) + "da pirata" (pirate-style / pirate) + "per" (for) + occasion (e.g., Halloween, una festa, carnevale).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un costume da pirata per la festa di domani.
native_language_example: I bought a pirate costume for tomorrow’s party.

additional_notes: Used for a book (or app) that lists words and their meanings/translations. With "avere" (to have), "comprare" (to buy), or "prendere in prestito" (to borrow). In the phrase "un dizionario ambulante," it means "a walking dictionary"—a person who knows a lot of words/facts.
target_language_example: Hai un dizionario italiano-inglese?
native_language_example: Do you have an Italian-English dictionary?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about a dictionary in French. Often extended as “un dizionario francese-inglese” (a French–English dictionary). In questions, it’s common with “avere” (to have) or “servire” (to need): “Avete…?” / “Lei ha…?” / “Mi serve…”.
target_language_example: Mi serve un dizionario francese-inglese, per favore.
native_language_example: I need a French–English dictionary, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe physical pain in your side/upper hip area (the “flank”), often with body verbs like avere (“to have”), sentire (“to feel”), or svegliarsi con (“to wake up with”). The usual pattern is: avere un dolore + in/nel + body part (e.g., un dolore nel fianco).
target_language_example: Da ieri ho un dolore nel fianco destro.
native_language_example: Since yesterday I’ve had a pain in my right side.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used when you mean “a/some doctor” (not a specific one). In everyday Italian, dottore can mean a medical doctor; it can also be used as a title for someone with a university degree, but in contexts like “Chiama un dottore” it clearly means a medical doctor.
target_language_example: C'è un dottore in sala?
native_language_example: Is there a doctor in the room?

additional_notes: Used for both everyday mistakes (wrong choice, wrong action) and more formal/technical errors (in a text, on a computer, in math). Often with verbs like fare (to make), correggere (to correct), and trovare/imbattersi in (to find/run into).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho fatto un errore.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to refer to a person as a member of the human species (often used in comparisons with animals, aliens/robots, or in general statements). Plural: "esseri umani". You can also say "un umano", but "un essere umano" is more common/formal-sounding.
target_language_example: Non sono un robot: sono un essere umano.
native_language_example: I'm not a robot: I'm a human being.

meaning: a ghost; (figuratively) someone who looks very pale/ghost-like.
additional_notes: Means a ghost in the literal sense (a spirit). It can also be used jokingly/figuratively when someone looks very pale or blurry in a photo: "Sembri un fantasma" / "Pare un fantasma".
target_language_example: In quella foto sembro un fantasma!
native_language_example: In that photo I look like a ghost!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like fare (to do): fare un favore a qualcuno = to do someone a favor. Often used when asking politely: (Vorrei) chiedere un favore = (I’d like) to ask a favor. You can also use it to point out you’re helping someone: Ti sto facendo un favore = I’m doing you a favor.
target_language_example: Mi fai un favore e mi mandi questo file?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and send me this file?

additional_notes: "Figlio" usually means "son". It can also mean "child" in the sense of someone’s offspring, especially when the gender is known or when contrasting with "figlia" (daughter). Plural: "figli" = children/sons (mixed group can be "figli").
target_language_example: Mio padre ha un figlio e una figlia.
native_language_example: My father has a son and a daughter.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Film" is commonly used in Italian (often invariable: un film, due film). You’ll hear it with verbs like "fare" (to make) and "girare" (to shoot/film) when talking about making or shooting a movie.
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo un film a casa?
native_language_example: Shall we watch a movie at home tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to one single flower. Often used with verbs like dare (to give) or mettere (to put/wear), e.g., giving someone a flower or wearing one in your hair. Plural: i fiori (the flowers), dei fiori (some flowers).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un fiore per la mia amica.
native_language_example: I bought a flower for my friend.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a single piece/sheet of paper (e.g., to write something down). In requests you’ll often see it with polite forms like per favore/per piacere, or formal commands like Prenda… / Portatemi….
target_language_example: Mi serve un foglio di carta per prendere appunti.
native_language_example: I need a sheet of paper to take notes.

additional_notes: Refers to the kitchen appliance used to heat food quickly. Often used with the verb "usare" (to use) or "utilizzare" (more formal: to use). You may also hear the shorter form "un microonde" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Scusa, puoi scaldare la zuppa nel forno a microonde?
native_language_example: Sorry, can you heat up the soup in the microwave?

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Gatto" is masculine; plural: "gatti". The feminine form is "una gatta" (“a female cat”). Often used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho un gatto" = “I have a cat.”
target_language_example: Vorrei un gatto, ma il mio appartamento è piccolo.
native_language_example: I’d like a cat, but my apartment is small.

un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato

target_language_multi_word_term: un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato
meaning: a lost cat that was being searched for.
additional_notes: "Gatto smarrito" means “lost cat.” "Che stava venendo cercato" is a passive form meaning “that was being looked for / searched for,” often followed by "da" + the person searching (e.g., "dalla sua padrona" = “by its owner,” female). You may also hear the simpler active form: "un gatto smarrito che cercavano" (“a lost cat they were looking for”).
target_language_example: Ho visto un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato dai vicini.
native_language_example: I saw a lost cat that the neighbors were searching for.

additional_notes: With a noun sense, it means a 24-hour period or a specific day (e.g., "un giorno speciale"). With a time/hope sense, it means "one day" in the future (= someday), often with the idea of a plan or possibility ("farlo un giorno"). For "in one day" you often use "in un giorno"; for "one day or two" you can say "fra un giorno o due".
target_language_example: Un giorno andrò in Italia.
native_language_example: One day I'll go to Italy.

meaning: "a big/major" (before a noun); also "a great one" (compliment about a person).
additional_notes: Before a noun, it means something important or serious: "un grande errore" = "a big/major mistake". Said about a person without a noun (often "Sei un grande"), it’s a common compliment meaning “You’re great / You’re the best.” It agrees in gender and number: "una grande" (f.), "un grande" (m.), "dei grandi" (m. pl.), "delle grandi" (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Grazie per l’aiuto: sei un grande!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help: you’re great!

additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or difficult to deal with. Often appears with verbs like essere (Questo è un grande problema) and causare (ha causato un grande problema). You can change the adjective for emphasis: un enorme problema (a huge problem), un grosso problema (a big problem).
target_language_example: Se perdi il passaporto, è un grande problema.
native_language_example: If you lose your passport, it’s a big problem.

additional_notes: "Grosso" is an adjective meaning "big/large". With "un" it often works like "a big one" or "a big [noun]" (e.g., un grosso pesce = a big fish). It can also mean "major/serious" with abstract nouns like "errore" (mistake) or "favore" (favor). Agreement: un grosso (masc. sing.); una grossa (fem. sing.); dei grossi / delle grosse (plural).
target_language_example: Mi serve un grosso aiuto per traslocare domani.
native_language_example: I need a big help to move tomorrow.

meaning: "a group of" (a number of people or things together).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate multiple people/things seen or considered as one set: un gruppo di studenti/bambini/soldati. Very common in everyday descriptions. It agrees in number/gender with the verb as a singular unit (e.g., Un gruppo di bambini stava giocando).
target_language_example: C'era un gruppo di turisti davanti al museo.
native_language_example: There was a group of tourists in front of the museum.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Hamburger" is a common loanword in Italian; the plural is usually "hamburger" (invariable): "due hamburger".
target_language_example: Vorrei un hamburger, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hamburger, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or ask for a hot dog (the food). In Italian it’s a masculine noun, so you’ll often see it with articles like un (a) or il (the): un hot dog, il hot dog. Plural is usually hot dog (unchanged) or sometimes hot dogs.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un hot dog, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a hot dog, please?

additional_notes: An insult meaning a very stupid or annoying person, or a self-criticism meaning “I feel like such a fool.” Uses the masculine article un; for a woman you often hear una idiota (many speakers keep idiota the same form).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato le chiavi: sono proprio un idiota.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys: I’m such an idiot.

additional_notes: Used for a job or work position, often in a fairly general or formal way. You’ll also hear it in phrases like “trovare un impiego” (to find a job) and “un impiego migliore” (a better job). Similar in meaning to “un lavoro,” but “impiego” can sound a bit more like “employment/position.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando un impiego a tempo pieno.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a full-time job.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for car/road accidents: “Fare un incidente” = “to have/get into an accident.” The plural is “incidenti.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo fatto un incidente sulla strada per Roma.
native_language_example: We got into an accident on the way to Rome.

additional_notes: Used for an accident involving vehicles on the road (from minor crashes to serious accidents). Often used with verbs like "avere" (to have) or "fare" (to have/get into): "Ho avuto un incidente stradale". You may also hear the shorter "un incidente" when the context is clearly about the road.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, sono in ritardo perché c’è stato un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late because there was a traffic accident.

additional_notes: "Insegnante" means "teacher". With "un" it refers to a male teacher (or a teacher referred to with masculine grammar). For a female teacher you usually say "un'insegnante" (often written with an apostrophe). Used to talk about someone’s job or role: "È un insegnante" = "He is a teacher."
target_language_example: Mio zio è un insegnante di matematica.
native_language_example: My uncle is a math teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject someone teaches. The noun is insegnante (“teacher”), and di introduces the subject: un insegnante di scienze (a science teacher), un insegnante di storia (a history teacher). Feminine form: un’insegnante di … can refer to a woman teacher (often written the same, but pronounced with the apostrophe).
target_language_example: Lei è un'insegnante di matematica.
native_language_example: She is a math teacher.

meaning: a job; a piece of work (task).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “a job” (employment), especially with verbs like trovare (to find), cercare (to look for), fare domanda per (to apply for). It can also mean “work” in the sense of a task or project, depending on context.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un lavoro a Milano.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a job in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to say you have, found, or are looking for a job that is not full-time. "Part-time" is often written with a hyphen and is commonly used in Italian (alongside "a tempo parziale"). With verbs like "cercare" (to look for) and "trovare" (to find): "cercare/trovare un lavoro part-time".
target_language_example: Sto cercando un lavoro part-time per pagare l’affitto.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a part-time job to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the animal (common in contexts like the zoo). "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”); plural: "dei leoni" (“some lions”).
target_language_example: C'è un leone nel recinto?
native_language_example: Is there a lion in the enclosure?

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Libro" is masculine (il libro / i libri). Use it to talk about an unspecified book: Ha un libro (“He/She has a book”). With indirect-object pronouns you can say: Le sto dando un libro (“I’m giving her a book”).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un libro in italiano.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a book in Italian.

meaning: "a book in" (a language) / "a book in" (a place).
additional_notes: Use **un libro in + language** to say what language the book is written in: *un libro in italiano / in olandese*. You can also use **in + place** to say where it was written or located: *Ha scritto un libro in Cina* = he wrote a book in China.
target_language_example: Cerco un libro in inglese.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a book in English.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one wolf as an animal. "Un" is the indefinite article "a/an" (masculine singular), and "lupo" is the noun "wolf". Plural: "dei lupi" (some wolves) / "i lupi" (the wolves).
target_language_example: Ho visto un lupo nel bosco.
native_language_example: I saw a wolf in the woods.

additional_notes: Medico is a masculine noun meaning “doctor/physician.” Use un medico for “a (male) doctor” or when gender is unknown in general statements; for a female doctor you often hear una medica or una dottoressa (common in everyday speech). To ask someone’s profession: “È un medico?” / “Sua moglie è un medico?”
target_language_example: Cerco un medico: mi fa male la gola.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a doctor: my throat hurts.

additional_notes: Used for someone who belongs to an organization, club, team, etc. It’s often followed by a preposition to say which group: "un membro di questo club" (a member of this club), "un membro della squadra" (a member of the team).
target_language_example: Sono un membro del club da due anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been a member of the club for two years.

additional_notes: Used for any kind of message (spoken, written, voicemail, text). Very common with verbs like lasciare (to leave), mandare (to send), and avere (to have/for someone). You can specify the type: un messaggio di testo = a text message.
target_language_example: Puoi lasciarmi un messaggio dopo la riunione?
native_language_example: Can you leave me a message after the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to say who the sender is. The name usually follows: “un messaggio da Tom”. You can also hear “un messaggio da parte di …” (“a message from/on behalf of …”).
target_language_example: C'è un messaggio da Maria per te.
native_language_example: There’s a message from Maria for you.

additional_notes: Used both literally (60 seconds) and very commonly to politely ask someone to wait briefly: "Aspetta un minuto" = "Wait a minute." Also used in requests like "Mi dai un minuto?" (Can you give me a minute?) and in time expressions like "Tra un minuto" (In a minute).
target_language_example: Puoi aspettare un minuto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you wait a minute, please?

meaning: "One moment/minute, please." (a polite way to ask someone to wait briefly).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a short pause or to buy time. Common in shops, on the phone, or when you need a moment to think. Often said alone as “Un minuto, per favore.” You can make it more formal with the Lei form: “Aspetti un minuto, per favore.”
target_language_example: Un minuto, per favore: devo controllare l’orario.
native_language_example: One moment, please: I need to check the schedule.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "un/una mio/mia + noun" to mean “one of my …” (someone/something belonging to your group). It’s common when introducing someone or mentioning a person you know. Contrast: "il mio amico" = “my (specific) friend.”
target_language_example: Domani esco con un mio amico che vive qui vicino.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going out with a friend of mine who lives nearby.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pause briefly (“Un momento!” = “One moment!”). It can mean a short time, often vaguely: “aspettare un momento” (wait a moment), “tra un momento” (in a moment). In formal situations you can also hear “Un attimo” (more casual) or “Un momento, per favore.”
target_language_example: Un momento, per favore: arrivo subito.
native_language_example: One moment, please: I’ll be right there.

meaning: a lot of; a pile of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun. Often means “a lot of” in everyday speech (quantity, sometimes a bit vague): un mucchio di lettere = lots of letters. It can also mean a literal “pile/heap of” physical things: un mucchio di vecchie scatole = a pile of old boxes. With “un mucchio di roba” it can sound a bit informal and dismissive (“a bunch of stuff”).
target_language_example: Ho un mucchio di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something new: un nuovo ufficio (a new office), un nuovo presidente (a new president). Before a noun starting with most consonants. Agreement changes with gender/number (e.g., una nuova…, un nuovo…, dei nuovi…, delle nuove…). Note that some masculine nouns take a different form: uno nuovo + noun with s+consonant / z / gn / ps / pn / x / y (e.g., uno nuovo studente).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un nuovo telefono.
native_language_example: I bought a new phone.

meaning: an eye; (idiomatic) a quick look / watch.
additional_notes: Often used in common expressions: "dare un occhio (a...)" = to take a look at / check; "tenere un occhio su (qualcuno/qualcosa)" = to keep an eye on / watch (someone/something). It can also be literal (e.g., "perdere un occhio" = to lose an eye).
target_language_example: Puoi dare un occhio al forno mentre preparo la pasta?
native_language_example: Can you keep an eye on the oven while I make the pasta?

additional_notes: A masculine noun: (un) ombrello. Used with verbs like prendere (to take), comprare (to buy), prestare (to lend), and in polite requests: Mi potresti prestare un ombrello? (informal) / Potrebbe prestarmi un ombrello? (formal).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato un ombrello sul treno.
native_language_example: I forgot an umbrella on the train.

additional_notes: "Orologio" can mean either a watch (worn on the wrist) or a clock (on a wall/table). Use "un" because it’s a masculine singular noun: un orologio. Common clarifications: "un orologio da polso" (a wristwatch), "un orologio da parete" (a wall clock).
target_language_example: Mi serve un orologio da polso nuovo.
native_language_example: I need a new wristwatch.

additional_notes: Literally “a watch for (the) wrist.” Used for a watch worn on your wrist (not a wall clock or pocket watch). Often used with adjectives like costoso (expensive) or prezioso (valuable).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato a casa il mio orologio da polso.
native_language_example: I forgot my wristwatch at home.

meaning: a bear (one male bear; also used generically for “a bear”).
additional_notes: “Orso” is the noun for “bear.” With “un” it means “a/one bear.” In Italian, the indefinite article changes with gender: un orso (male), un’orsa (female). You’ll often see it after verbs like vedere (to see) or in questions like “È un orso quello laggiù?” (“Is that a bear over there?”).
target_language_example: Ho visto un orso vicino al sentiero.
native_language_example: I saw a bear near the trail.

additional_notes: "Ottimo" means "excellent/very good." With "un" it often describes a person or thing: "un ottimo capo" (a great boss), "un ottimo chitarrista" (an excellent guitarist), "un ottimo sugo" (an excellent sauce). It can also be used more generally like "a great one" (e.g., "farà un ottimo lavoro" = he’ll do an excellent job). Match gender/number: un ottimo (m. sing.), un’ottima (f. sing.), dei/degli ottimi (m. pl.), delle ottime (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è un ottimo posto per cenare.
native_language_example: This restaurant is a great place for dinner.

additional_notes: Used either (1) literally for two matching items (e.g., gloves, jeans, boots), or (2) more loosely to mean “a couple of” (= about two) with time and countable things like questions/steps/years. Often followed by a plural noun: un paio di guanti, un paio di domande, un paio di anni.
target_language_example: Dammi un paio di minuti, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me a couple of minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to scissors as a set of two blades (Italian treats it as a singular item: “un paio di…” = “a pair of…”). Often used with verbs like comprare (to buy) and tagliare (to cut): “Taglio la carta con un paio di forbici.”
target_language_example: Mi serve un paio di forbici per aprire questo pacco.
native_language_example: I need a pair of scissors to open this package.

meaning: a couple of days; two-ish days.
additional_notes: Used to mean roughly two days, often without being exact (like “a couple of days” in English). Common after time expressions with per (“for”) and with verbs like aspettare (“to wait”) or dare (“to give”): Aspetta un paio di giorni / Dammi un paio di giorni.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra un paio di giorni.
native_language_example: See you in a couple of days.

meaning: a couple of messages (two or a few).
additional_notes: Used when you left/sent two messages, or roughly “a few” messages. Common with the verb lasciare (“to leave” a message): Ho lasciato un paio di messaggi. You can add the person with a (“to”): Ho lasciato a Tom un paio di messaggi. With indirect object pronouns: gli (to him), le (to her).
target_language_example: Ti ho lasciato un paio di messaggi ieri sera.
native_language_example: I left you a couple of messages last night.

additional_notes: Used when talking about earrings as a set of two. Italian commonly uses “un paio di …” (“a pair of …”) with plural nouns like orecchini. You can add a material with “di” (e.g., “orecchini di diamante” = “diamond earrings”).
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare un paio di orecchini per mia sorella.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a pair of earrings for my sister.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes as a set (left + right). "Un paio di" means "a pair of" and is commonly used with things that come in twos (e.g., un paio di pantaloni = a pair of pants).
target_language_example: Vorrei un paio di scarpe comode per camminare.
native_language_example: I’d like a comfortable pair of shoes for walking.

meaning: a couple of weeks; about two weeks.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate length of time, often roughly two weeks (not necessarily exactly 14 days). You can use it with expressions like “tra/fra un paio di settimane” (in a couple of weeks) or “per un paio di settimane” (for a couple of weeks).
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per un paio di settimane, poi torno a casa.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a couple of weeks, then I’m going home.

additional_notes: Used as a set phrase before an activity or purpose: "stivali da + noun" = boots meant for that use (e.g., stivali da passeggio = walking boots, stivali da neve = snow boots). "Un paio di" means "a pair of" and is used for things that come in twos (shoes, boots, socks).
target_language_example: Mi serve un paio di stivali da pioggia.
native_language_example: I need a pair of rain boots.

meaning: a ride (a lift) in someone’s car; also a passage/way through.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like dare/avere/accettare un passaggio = to give/get/accept a ride. Often implies a favor (someone drives you somewhere). In other contexts it can mean a (secret) passage or corridor (e.g., un passaggio segreto).
target_language_example: Puoi darmi un passaggio fino alla stazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me a ride to the station, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dare (to give) or servire (to need): dare un passaggio a casa = to give someone a ride home; mi serve un passaggio a casa = I need a ride home. You can add the person with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or with a + name (un passaggio a casa a Mary).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti do un passaggio a casa dopo cena.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll give you a ride home after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about a portion of something (usually food or a material). It’s followed by a noun: un pezzo di pane (a piece of bread), un pezzo di formaggio (a piece of cheese). For countable objects you’ll often use “un pezzo di” when you mean a part/chunk rather than a whole item.
target_language_example: Vorrei un pezzo di torta, grazie.
native_language_example: I’d like a piece of cake, please.

additional_notes: Literally “a piece of meat.” Used for a portion/chunk/slice of meat, often in everyday contexts (feeding an animal, eating). Note: “carne” can also mean “flesh” in some contexts, but in these examples it’s simply meat as food.
target_language_example: Per cena ho comprato un pezzo di carne.
native_language_example: For dinner I bought a piece of meat.

additional_notes: Used for a small sheet/bit of paper, often when you need something to write on or to hand to someone. In everyday speech it can also mean “just a piece of paper” (something not very important), depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi serve un pezzo di carta per scrivere il tuo numero.
native_language_example: I need a piece of paper to write your number.

additional_notes: Used when asking for, offering, or talking about cake. It’s common in cafés or at home. With polite requests you’ll often hear: “Mi dia un pezzo di torta, per piacere.” The noun “torta” is feminine, so you might also see agreement with a feminine adjective (e.g., “era deliziosa”).
target_language_example: Posso avere un pezzo di torta al cioccolato?
native_language_example: Can I have a piece of chocolate cake?

additional_notes: Used to talk about an idea or strategy for what you’re going to do (often for the future). Common with verbs like avere (“to have”) and bisogno di (“to need”): avere un piano, avere bisogno di un piano.
target_language_example: Se vogliamo partire domani, ci serve un piano.
native_language_example: If we want to leave tomorrow, we need a plan.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe something small: un piccolo libro (a small book), un piccolo incidente (a minor/small accident). The adjective agrees in gender/number: una piccola (feminine), piccoli/piccole (plural). As a noun, un piccolo can also mean “a little one/child,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vorrei un piccolo caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like a small coffee, please.

meaning: a little/small secret (a minor personal secret).
additional_notes: Used when someone is about to share a secret that’s not too serious or important. Common with verbs like dire/raccontare (to tell) and with the intro phrase: “Ti/Vi dico un piccolo segreto” (“I’ll tell you a little secret”). Often followed by details with prepositions like su (about) or riguardo a (regarding).
target_language_example: Ti dico un piccolo segreto: mi piace l'Italia più di quanto pensi.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you a little secret: I like Italy more than you think.

additional_notes: A common, slightly softer way to say “a little” than "un po'". Often used to tone down an adjective ("un pochino arrabbiato" = "a bit angry") or to describe doing something in a small amount ("Un pochino" = "A little", e.g., "just a bit").
target_language_example: Puoi aspettare un pochino, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little, please?

additional_notes: "Poeta" is a noun for someone who writes poetry. With "un" it’s singular and usually refers to a man, though it can also be used generically. For a woman you often hear "una poetessa" (though "una poeta" is also used by some). It commonly appears after verbs like "essere" (to be) or "diventare" (to become).
target_language_example: Da bambino sognavo di diventare un poeta.
native_language_example: As a child I dreamed of becoming a poet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one (male) police officer. With professions in Italian, the article changes for gender and number: una poliziotta (female), i poliziotti (male or mixed group), le poliziotte (female group).
target_language_example: C'è un poliziotto davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: There’s a police officer in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used like the English word “pony” for a small horse. It’s a regular masculine noun: un pony (a pony), il pony (the pony), due pony (two ponies; plural is often unchanged). Common with verbs like cavalcare (to ride) and avere/comprare (to have/buy).
target_language_example: Da piccola volevo un pony per andare a cavallo ogni weekend.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted a pony to go riding every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a physical location in general (a place, a spot). With verbs like prendere/trovare can mean getting/finding a place/seat (depending on context): e.g. "Ha preso un posto" often means "He/She took a seat". "Un posto migliore" means "a better place" (to live, to work, etc.).
target_language_example: C'è un posto libero qui?
native_language_example: Is there a free seat/place here?

additional_notes: Used when you need or have accommodation (often temporary), like for a night. It can refer to anywhere you can sleep or live for a short time (a home, a room, a friend’s place, etc.). The structure is: "un posto" (a place) + "in cui" (where) + "stare" (to stay).
target_language_example: Se arrivi tardi, puoi dormire da me: hai un posto in cui stare.
native_language_example: If you arrive late, you can sleep at my place: you have a place to stay.

additional_notes: Used to say you need or found housing/accommodation. Literally “a place in which to live”; often comes after verbs like avere bisogno di / servire / trovare.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un posto in cui vivere vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place to live near work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male priest (often Christian). You can specify the type with an adjective, e.g. "un prete cattolico" (a Catholic priest), "un prete ortodosso" (an Orthodox priest). Feminine form: "una prete" is sometimes used, but many speakers prefer "una sacerdotessa" depending on the context/denomination.
target_language_example: In paese c’è un prete molto gentile.
native_language_example: In the town there’s a very kind priest.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a difficulty, concern, or situation that needs a solution. Very common in everyday speech. In questions like "Sarà un problema?" it can mean "Will that be an issue?"
target_language_example: Se c’è un problema, chiamami subito.
native_language_example: If there’s a problem, call me right away.

additional_notes: Used with avere (“to have”): avere un problema con + person/thing. It can mean a practical difficulty (“a problem with the computer”) or a negative feeling/objection toward someone or something (“an issue with Tom / with what was suggested”).
target_language_example: Ho un problema con questa app: non si apre.
native_language_example: I have a problem with this app: it won’t open.

additional_notes: Used for the figure made of snow (typically built by children). Often used with verbs like fare/costruire (“to make/build”) and can be described with adjectives like grande/gigante (“big/giant”).
target_language_example: Dopo la scuola, facciamo un pupazzo di neve nel giardino.
native_language_example: After school, let's make a snowman in the yard.

additional_notes: Used when you’re not sure exactly what something is, or when you speak vaguely (sometimes with surprise or suspicion in questions: "Is this some kind of…?"). It agrees with the noun: un qualche tipo di (masc. sing.), una qualche tipo di (fem. sing.), though "un qualche tipo di" is most common.
target_language_example: Mi serve un qualche tipo di documento d’identità.
native_language_example: I need some kind of ID.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" (a) + "ragazzo" (boy/guy). Used to introduce an unknown or not-yet-specified male person. Often means “boy” in the sense of a male child or teenager, but in everyday speech it can also mean “guy/young man.”
target_language_example: C'è un ragazzo fuori che ti sta cercando.
native_language_example: There's a guy outside looking for you.

additional_notes: Used for something you give to someone (for a birthday, holiday, or to show appreciation). It’s masculine: un regalo (a gift), il regalo (the gift). Plural: regali.
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for your birthday.

meaning: “a gift/present for …” (e.g., for a birthday) or “a gift from …”.
additional_notes: In Italian, “un regalo di + noun” is often used like “a … gift”: *un regalo di compleanno* (“a birthday present”). But with a person after **di**, it can mean “a gift from …”: *un regalo di mia zia* (“a gift from my aunt”). If you want to be extra clear, you can also say **un regalo per** (for) vs **un regalo da parte di** (from).
target_language_example: Ti ho preso un regalo di compleanno.
native_language_example: I got you a birthday present.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a present given for Christmas. "Regalo" = gift/present; "natalizio" = Christmas-related (from "Natale" = Christmas). You can also say "un regalo di Natale" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ti ho comprato un regalo natalizio, ma non posso dirti cos'è!
native_language_example: I bought you a Christmas present, but I can't tell you what it is!

un rigido coprifuoco a casa mia

target_language_multi_word_term: un rigido coprifuoco a casa mia
meaning: a strict curfew at my house (at home).
additional_notes: Used to say that your family/parents set a strict time by which you had to be home. "Coprifuoco" means "curfew"; "rigido" adds the idea of "very strict." "A casa mia" means "at my place/at my home" (often implying your family home).
target_language_example: Da adolescente avevo un rigido coprifuoco a casa mia: dovevo rientrare entro le dieci.
native_language_example: As a teenager I had a strict curfew at home: I had to be back by ten.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article un (“a/an”) to talk about a restaurant in general or one that isn’t specified yet. Common with verbs like andare/mangiare a/in un ristorante (to go/eat at a restaurant) and with adjectives/nationalities to describe the type: un ristorante cinese, un ristorante algerino. Opposite: il ristorante (“the restaurant”).
target_language_example: Stasera andiamo a mangiare in un ristorante vicino a casa.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to eat at a restaurant near home.

additional_notes: A noun phrase with the indefinite article "un" ("a"). Used to say you met/encountered/got to know a person who is both a novelist and a poet, or two people: one a novelist and one a poet (context usually makes it clear).
target_language_example: Ieri ho conosciuto un romanziere e un poeta a una presentazione di libri.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met a novelist and a poet at a book presentation.

meaning: a lot of; lots of; a bunch of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean “many/much” in an informal, everyday way: un sacco di frasi/telefonate/pesci. You can also use it with uncountable nouns (e.g., un sacco di tempo = a lot of time). Often interchangeable with molto/molti, but “un sacco di” sounds more casual.
target_language_example: Ho un sacco di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

meaning: a lot of things; lots of things.
additional_notes: Very common, informal way to say you have/make/do/know “a lot of things.” It works like “molte cose,” but sounds more casual. You can also use “un sacco di + noun” with other nouns (e.g., un sacco di lavoro = a lot of work).
target_language_example: Ho ancora un sacco di cose da fare stasera.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of things to do tonight.

meaning: a lot of money; a ton of money.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to emphasize a large amount of money. Often used with verbs like spendere (to spend), dare (to give), avere (to have), trovare (to find). Literally means “a sack/bag of money,” but it usually just means “a lot of money,” not an actual bag.
target_language_example: Non voglio spendere un sacco di denaro per questo regalo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend a lot of money on this gift.

meaning: a lot of money; tons of money.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say “a lot of” (un sacco di + noun). You can also say “un sacco” by itself: “Ho speso un sacco.” Less formal than “molti soldi.”
target_language_example: Per quel telefono ho speso un sacco di soldi.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of money on that phone.

meaning: a lot of time; loads of time.
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you have (or save) a lot of time. Literally “a sack of time,” but it just means “a lot of.” Often used with verbs like avere (to have) or risparmiare (to save): “Mi hai risparmiato un sacco di tempo” = “You just saved me a lot of time.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, abbiamo un sacco di tempo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we have plenty of time.

additional_notes: A very common noun for a sandwich (masculine). Plural: "dei sandwich" / "i sandwich" (often invariable). You can add ingredients with "con": "un sandwich con prosciutto e formaggio". Used with "prepararsi" (make for yourself) and "passare" (hand/pass to someone).
target_language_example: Mi preparo un sandwich con tonno.
native_language_example: I'm making myself a tuna sandwich.

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about food. In Italian, "al" means "with/with the flavor of" here, so it’s a sandwich made with turkey (tacchino). You may also see the spelling "sandwich" unchanged, or "panino al tacchino" for a turkey sandwich on a roll.
target_language_example: Per pranzo prendo un sandwich al tacchino.
native_language_example: For lunch I’m having a turkey sandwich.

un sandwich con burro di arachidi e gelatina

target_language_multi_word_term: un sandwich con burro di arachidi e gelatina
meaning: a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.
additional_notes: Common food phrase. In Italian, food ingredients are often linked with con (“with”): sandwich con X. The literal meaning is “a sandwich with peanut butter and jelly.”
target_language_example: Per pranzo mi sono fatto un sandwich con burro di arachidi e gelatina.
native_language_example: For lunch I made myself a peanut butter and jelly sandwich.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere (“to have”) to describe what something tastes like: "avere un sapore + adjective" (un sapore dolce/acido/salato/strano). It can also be followed by "di" to specify the flavor: "un sapore di limone" (“a lemon flavor”).
target_language_example: Questo tè ha un sapore amaro.
native_language_example: This tea has a bitter taste.

meaning: a second; a moment (briefly, used to ask someone to wait).
additional_notes: Common in polite requests to pause or wait: "Aspetta un secondo" (informal) / "Aspetti un secondo" (formal). With pronouns it means “give me a moment”: "Dammi/mi dia un secondo". Often used with "solo" or "un attimo" as a similar alternative. Not always a literal time measurement—more like “just a moment.”
target_language_example: Aspetta un secondo, arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article (un) to mean “a secret.” Common with verbs like avere (to have), dire (to tell), sapere (to know), and tenere (to keep): “tenere un segreto” = “to keep a secret.”
target_language_example: Posso dirti un segreto, ma non lo dire a nessuno.
native_language_example: Can I tell you a secret? But don’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: Noun phrase with the indefinite article: "un" (a) + "serpente" (snake). Used for any kind of snake; you can add an adjective like "velenoso" (venomous).
target_language_example: Attento! C'è un serpente nel giardino.
native_language_example: Watch out! There's a snake in the garden.

additional_notes: Common way to say “a website” in Italian. The noun is masculine: un/il sito web. Often used with verbs like creare (to create), avere (to have), visitare (to visit). Plural: i siti web.
target_language_example: Hai un sito web dove posso vedere i tuoi lavori?
native_language_example: Do you have a website where I can see your work?

meaning: “a website for” (used to say the purpose or intended user).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what the website is meant for: followed by an infinitive (per + verb) to express purpose (e.g., per imparare = to learn), or by a noun to express what it’s about (per le traduzioni = for translations), or by a person (per Mary = for Mary).
target_language_example: Ho trovato un sito web per prenotare hotel economici.
native_language_example: I found a website to book cheap hotels.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a dream you have while sleeping. It can also mean an ideal/wish (“a dream” in the figurative sense), but in these examples it’s about dreaming at night. Often used with the verb phrase “fare un sogno” (to have a dream).
target_language_example: Stanotte ho fatto un sogno strano.
native_language_example: Last night I had a strange dream.

additional_notes: Used to describe a dream that felt unusual, confusing, or unsettling. Common with the verb "fare" (to have a dream): "fare un sogno" → "to have a dream" (often in the past: "ho fatto...", "feci...").
target_language_example: Stanotte ho fatto un sogno strano.
native_language_example: Last night I had a strange dream.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to emphasize degree or type: *un tale lavoro/comportamento/desiderio* = “such a job/behavior/desire.” Often expresses surprise, criticism, or intensity. Don’t confuse **tale** with English “tale” (story).
target_language_example: Non avrei mai accettato un tale accordo.
native_language_example: I would never have accepted such a deal.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). You’ll often hear it with verbs like "chiamare" (to call): "Chiama un taxi" = “Call a taxi.” In some sentences you may see "su un taxi" meaning “in/by taxi” (literally “on a taxi”), especially when describing arriving or being on the way.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso chiamare un taxi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I call a taxi?

meaning: “a taxi or an Uber?” (offering a choice for a ride).
additional_notes: Used when asking someone which kind of ride they’d prefer. The article changes with number: un taxi o un Uber (singular). Often appears with the verb preferire (“to prefer”) in polite questions (preferirebbe/preferiresti/preferireste).
target_language_example: Dopo cena, vuoi un taxi o un Uber?
native_language_example: After dinner, do you want a taxi or an Uber?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a genetic test (often in police/legal contexts to prove identity or innocence, or in medical/paternity contexts). In Italian you’ll also see: “un test del DNA” / “un test del Dna” / “un test del DNA”.
target_language_example: Per confermare la paternità, hanno fatto un test del DNA.
native_language_example: To confirm paternity, they did a DNA test.

additional_notes: Usually means the animal “mouse” (plural: *topi*). In some contexts it can be used as an insult like “rat” (someone unpleasant or sneaky), depending on tone and situation.
target_language_example: C'è un topo in cucina!
native_language_example: There’s a mouse in the kitchen!

additional_notes: Common noun phrase with the indefinite article ("un" = "a/an"). Used to identify or talk about a bird in general. For a specific bird you’d use "l’uccello" (the bird). In questions it’s used for identification: "È un uccello?"
target_language_example: In giardino c’è un uccello piccolo.
native_language_example: There’s a small bird in the garden.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article "un" (= "a/an") + "uomo" (= "man"). The plural is "degli uomini" (some men) or "uomini" (men). In phrases like "comportarti come un uomo" it can mean "act like a man" in the sense of behaving bravely/responsibly (depending on context).
target_language_example: C'è un uomo alla porta che ti cerca.
native_language_example: There’s a man at the door looking for you.

meaning: “a man who …” (introduces a description of a man).
additional_notes: Used before a relative clause with che (“who/that”) to add information about the man. Very common in descriptions: un uomo che + verb (e.g., può aiutare, parla francese, farà…).
target_language_example: Cerco un uomo che sappia riparare le biciclette.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a man who knows how to fix bicycles.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone by name: “un uomo” (a man) + “che” (who/that) + “si chiama” (is called/is named). You normally add the person’s name right after it (e.g., “... che si chiama Tom”). It’s neutral and common in both formal and informal situations.
target_language_example: Sto cercando un uomo che si chiama Marco Rossi.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a man named Marco Rossi.

meaning: “a very … man” (a man who is very …).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective: **un uomo molto + adjective** (e.g., *un uomo molto affidabile/modesto/ricco*). *Molto* means “very” here and usually comes right before the adjective; the adjective agrees with *uomo* (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Cerco un uomo molto paziente.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a very patient man.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man’s character (honest, trustworthy). Often comes after verbs like essere (to be) or sembrare (to seem), or in phrases like considerare qualcuno (to consider someone). In Italian, adjectives usually agree with the noun: un uomo onesto (male), una donna onesta (female).
target_language_example: Penso che sia un uomo onesto e affidabile.
native_language_example: I think he’s an honest and reliable man.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: "un" (a) + "uomo" (man) + "ricco" (rich). With a specific rich man, you may see "l'uomo ricco" (the rich man). Adjective agreement: ricco (masc. sing.); ricca (fem. sing.), ricchi (masc. pl.), ricche (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Ha incontrato un uomo ricco a una festa.
native_language_example: She met a rich man at a party.

additional_notes: A very common everyday noun. "Uovo" is masculine singular (un uovo); plural: "due uova" (feminine). Often used with cooking verbs like "bollire" (to boil) and "fare bollire" (to boil/bring to a boil).
target_language_example: Mi fai un uovo sodo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you make me a hard-boiled egg, please?

meaning: an old (one); an old + masculine noun.
additional_notes: From the adjective vecchio (“old”) used with the masculine singular indefinite article un. It’s commonly used before a masculine noun to mean “an old …” (un vecchio libro = “an old book”). As a standalone noun, un vecchio can mean “an old man” depending on context, but in these examples it’s used as an adjective meaning “old.”
target_language_example: Ho trovato un vecchio telefono in soffitta.
native_language_example: I found an old phone in the attic.

meaning: an old friend (usually someone you’ve known for a long time, often not seen recently).
additional_notes: Often refers to a long-time friend, or someone from the past you run into again (like a school friend). In Italian it can mean “old” in the sense of “long-standing,” not necessarily elderly. Feminine: "una vecchia amica".
target_language_example: Oggi ho rivisto un vecchio amico del liceo.
native_language_example: Today I saw an old friend from high school again.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to emphasize that something is genuine or truly deserves that description: un vero amico, un vero capolavoro. It agrees with the noun: una vera (feminine singular), dei veri / delle vere (plural). Often translated as “a real” or “a true,” depending on what sounds natural in English.
target_language_example: È stato un vero successo.
native_language_example: It was a real success.

meaning: a dress; an outfit/a piece of clothing.
additional_notes: Often means “a dress” (especially a one-piece garment), but in many contexts it can also mean “an outfit” or “a garment/piece of clothing.” Used with colors and when talking about making/choosing/wearing clothes: un vestito blu, fare/selezionare/indossare un vestito.
target_language_example: Cerco un vestito elegante per la festa.
native_language_example: I’m looking for an elegant dress/outfit for the party.

meaning: a (little) girl; a young female child.
additional_notes: “Bambina” is the feminine form of “bambino” (boy/child). It’s used for a young girl, or to emphasize that someone is “just a child” (e.g., “È solo una bambina”). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone is being treated like a child (“mi tratta come una bambina”).
target_language_example: Scusi, ho una bambina con me: dov'è il bagno?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a little girl with me: where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article meaning "a/one." Use it when talking about one banana, especially when ordering, buying, or eating. Plural: "delle banane" (some bananas) or "due/tre banane" (two/three bananas).
target_language_example: Puoi darmi una banana, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me a banana, please?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a financial bank (where you keep money). In phrases like "banca del cibo" it means a food bank (a place/organization that collects and distributes food to people in need). Feminine noun: una banca, la banca.
target_language_example: Dov'è la banca più vicina?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest bank?

additional_notes: Refers to a single snack bar made of granola (often oats, nuts, honey, etc.). "Barretta" means a (small) bar, and "di" means "of"—so it’s used for counting: una/due barrette di granola (one/two granola bars).
target_language_example: Prima di allenarmi, prendo una barretta di granola.
native_language_example: Before working out, I grab a granola bar.

meaning: “a nice / beautiful / good (one)” (often used to emphasize the noun that follows).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (feminine singular) to add emphasis. Depending on the noun, it can mean literally “beautiful” (una bella principessa = a beautiful princess) or more generally “nice/big/good” (una bella risata = a good/big laugh). Masculine: un bel / un bello; plural: una bella → delle belle.
target_language_example: Dopo la notizia, ci siamo fatti una bella risata.
native_language_example: After the news, we had a good laugh.

meaning: a pretty girl; a beautiful girl.
additional_notes: Literally “a beautiful/pretty girl.” Used to describe a girl’s appearance. “Bella” agrees with the feminine singular noun “ragazza.” You may also hear “una ragazza bella” (less common; can sound more descriptive/contrastive, like “a girl who is pretty”).
target_language_example: C'è una bella ragazza alla festa.
native_language_example: There’s a pretty girl at the party.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s voice (often their speaking or singing voice). Usually said with the verb "avere" (to have): "Hai una bella voce" = "You have a nice voice." "Davvero/veramente" add emphasis: "really."
target_language_example: Complimenti, hai una bella voce!
native_language_example: Compliments, you have a beautiful voice!

additional_notes: Common everyday word for a pen, especially a ballpoint pen. It comes from the brand name “Biro” and is used like a normal noun (una biro / le biro). Often contrasted with “una matita” (a pencil).
target_language_example: Mi presti una biro? Devo firmare questo modulo.
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen? I have to sign this form.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or saying you need a red pen. In Italian, "biro" commonly means a ballpoint pen (penna a sfera). "Una" is the feminine form of “a/an” because "biro" is feminine in Italian.
target_language_example: Mi presti una biro rossa, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a red ballpoint pen, please?

additional_notes: Used to order or offer a single beer. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Often used with verbs like "volere" (to want), "prendere" (to get/have), "comprare" (to buy), and in questions like "Vuoi una birra?".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una birra, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a beer, please?

additional_notes: Commonly used for a shopping bag (e.g., “una borsa di plastica”) or a handbag you carry. In shops you may hear/ask: “Le serve una borsa?” / “Posso avere una borsa?”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una borsa per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a bag, please?

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about one bottle of something, especially drinks. The noun after di often doesn’t need an article in Italian (e.g., una bottiglia di vino, una bottiglia di latte). In shops/bars you can also use it as a request: Mi dia / Vorrei una bottiglia di…
target_language_example: Vorrei una bottiglia di acqua naturale, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of still water, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about a single bottle (not a can or a glass). You’ll often hear it in shops, bars, or restaurants. The structure is very common: "una bottiglia di + [drink]" (e.g., una bottiglia d’acqua).
target_language_example: Vorrei una bottiglia di birra, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of beer, please.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one full bottle of champagne. Common after verbs like portare (to bring), comprare (to buy), bere (to drink), or aprire (to open). Note the structure: una bottiglia di + drink (e.g., una bottiglia di vino, una bottiglia d’acqua).
target_language_example: Per festeggiare, abbiamo aperto una bottiglia di champagne.
native_language_example: To celebrate, we opened a bottle of champagne.
