additional_notes: Used to talk about buying, bringing, giving, or drinking a single bottle of wine. "Una" = "a/one" (feminine), "bottiglia" = "bottle" (feminine), "di" = "of", "vino" = "wine".
target_language_example: Per cena porto una bottiglia di vino.
native_language_example: For dinner I’m bringing a bottle of wine.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (e.g., una brava madre, una brava insegnante, una brava chitarrista) to say someone is good at something or a good person in that role. It agrees in gender/number: un bravo (male), una brava (female), dei bravi / delle brave (plural). Note: it can look like English “brave,” but it usually means “good/capable,” not “brave” (coraggiosa).
target_language_example: Giulia è una brava cuoca.
native_language_example: Giulia is a good cook.

additional_notes: A compliment about a woman’s cooking ability. Feminine singular: **una brava cuoca**. For a man, say **un bravo cuoco**. Note: **brava** usually means “good/skillful” (not “brave” in the English sense).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è una brava cuoca e cucina spesso per tutta la famiglia.
native_language_example: My sister is a good cook and often cooks for the whole family.

meaning: a good person; a decent/nice person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character or morals in a general way. "Bravo/brava" agrees with the person (una brava persona, un bravo ragazzo). You can negate it (Non è una brava persona) or use it with verbs like essere (to be) and fingere (to pretend).
target_language_example: Secondo me, è una brava persona e ti vuole aiutare.
native_language_example: In my opinion, he’s a good person and he wants to help you.

additional_notes: Feminine noun: una bugia (sing.), le bugie (pl.). Common with verbs like dire una bugia (to tell a lie) and raccontare una bugia (to tell/make up a lie). You can also use it after "è" to say something is a lie: È una bugia.
target_language_example: Non dire una bugia: dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Don’t tell a lie: tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine and understood from context or already mentioned. Common with implied items like an answer, idea, portion, deal, etc. It can also appear before a feminine noun: "una buona domanda" = "a good question". With "dare" it can mean "to give (someone) a good one" depending on the missing noun (e.g., "una buona occhiata" = "a good look").
target_language_example: Ne voglio una buona, non una qualsiasi.
native_language_example: I want a good one, not just any one.

additional_notes: Used to describe that the day went well, or as a wish/goodbye meaning “Have a good day.” Often with verbs like "passare" (to spend) or "avere" (to have): "passare/avere una buona giornata". It can be made plural: "Passate una buona giornata" (to more than one person), or adjusted for different levels of formality with "Lei": "Passi una buona giornata".
target_language_example: Spero che tu abbia una buona giornata!
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day!

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a sensible or smart plan/suggestion. Often appears with verbs like "essere" (È/è stata una buona idea), "sembrare" (sembra una buona idea), and in opinions like "Non credo che sia una buona idea". It can also describe a general choice: "I fiori sono sempre una buona idea" (Flowers are always a good idea).
target_language_example: Portare un ombrello oggi è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Bringing an umbrella today is a good idea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere una buona memoria" = to be good at remembering things (names, facts, dates, etc.). It can also be used more figuratively, e.g., "è la sua arma" (“it’s his/her weapon/strength”).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha una buona memoria per i nomi.
native_language_example: My sister has a good memory for names.

meaning: a good opinion of; to think well of.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere una buona opinione di qualcuno" = to have a positive view of someone / to respect them. The "di" is followed by a person or thing (di lui/lei/me/te, di Marco, di questo ristorante).
target_language_example: Ho una buona opinione di questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I have a good opinion of this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one (unspecified) song. You’ll often see it after verbs like scrivere (to write), cantare (to sing), and suonare (to play an instrument): scrivere/cantare/suonare una canzone. For a specific song, use la canzone (“the song”).
target_language_example: Puoi cantarmi una canzone?
native_language_example: Can you sing me a song?

additional_notes: Used when talking about paying in shops, restaurants, hotels, or online. Often used with verbs like usare (to use), avere (to have), and pagare (to pay). In questions, you’ll often hear: “Posso usare una carta di credito?” (Can I use a credit card?).
target_language_example: Accettate una carta di credito?
native_language_example: Do you accept a credit card?

additional_notes: “Casa” can mean the physical building (“house”) or the place where someone lives/feels they belong (“home”), depending on context. In requests like “Potete darmi una casa?”, it can mean “a home/place to live” (housing/shelter).
target_language_example: Vorrei affittare una casa vicino al centro.
native_language_example: I’d like to rent a house near the city center.

meaning: "a big house and two …" (often: “a big house and two cars”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a quantity/list pattern: “una/uno + noun + adjective + e + number + (plural noun)”. In normal Italian you usually include what “due” refers to (e.g., “due auto / due macchine”). The examples show it as “una casa grande e due auto/macchine” = “a big house and two cars.”
target_language_example: Ha una casa grande e due auto.
native_language_example: He has a big house and two cars.

additional_notes: Used when buying or carrying beer in a packaged quantity (a box/crate containing multiple bottles or cans). In shops you might also hear "una cassa di bottiglie" (a crate of bottles).
target_language_example: Per la festa prendiamo una cassa di birra e del ghiaccio.
native_language_example: For the party, let's get a case of beer and some ice.

meaning: "a call from" (a phone call received from someone).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ricevere (to receive) to say who the caller was. Follow it with a person/pronoun: una chiamata da lui/lei, una chiamata da Tom, una chiamata da mia madre.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una chiamata da mia madre ieri sera.
native_language_example: I got a call from my mother last night.

additional_notes: Used for a physical key (house, room, car). Common with verbs like: avere/bisognare di (to have/need), prendere (to take), dare (to give), servire (to be needed). Example: "Le servirà una chiave" = "You will need a key" (formal "you").
target_language_example: Mi serve una chiave per questa porta.
native_language_example: I need a key for this door.

additional_notes: Used when talking about an extra key kept for emergencies (at home, for a car, etc.). Often asked as a yes/no question: "Hai/Avete una chiave di riserva?" You can add where it is: "Ho una chiave di riserva sotto lo zerbino" (under the doormat).
target_language_example: Scusa, hai una chiave di riserva per l'appartamento?
native_language_example: Sorry, do you have a spare key for the apartment?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "una" = "a/an" for feminine singular nouns, and "città" (city) is feminine. Used when talking about any (not specific) city: "vivere in una città" = "to live in a city." For a specific city, you’ll often use "la città" (the city) or the city name (e.g., "Roma").
target_language_example: Mi piacerebbe vivere in una città vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I’d like to live in a city near the sea.

additional_notes: Used for a duplicate of a document, photo, file, etc. Common with verbs like fare (to make) or avere (to have): fare una copia = to make a copy.
target_language_example: Puoi fare una copia di questo documento, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you make a copy of this document, please?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a single copy of something masculine singular: una copia del documento (= a copy of the document). It’s the contraction of “di + il” → “del.” For feminine singular, use “una copia della …”; for plural, “una copia dei/delle …”.
target_language_example: Potrei avere una copia del biglietto, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a copy of the ticket, please?

meaning: a thing; something (also used like “one thing”).
additional_notes: Very common, general word used when you don’t name the specific object/idea. In conversation it often introduces what you’re about to say: “Voglio dire una cosa” (I want to say something / one thing). In questions it can mean “something” (“Sai una cosa?” / “Posso chiederti una cosa?”).
target_language_example: Posso chiederti una cosa?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or event of that kind, often with surprise, disbelief, or disapproval. Common in questions and negative statements: Hai mai visto una cosa del genere? (Have you ever seen something like that?), Non ho una cosa del genere (I don’t have anything like that).
target_language_example: Non dire una cosa del genere!
native_language_example: Don’t say something like that!

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere": "avere una cotta per qualcuno" = to have a crush on someone (often a light, sometimes short-term romantic interest). You can also say "Mi sono preso/a una cotta per..." (I got a crush on...).
target_language_example: Ho una cotta per una ragazza della mia classe.
native_language_example: I have a crush on a girl in my class.

additional_notes: “Avere una cotta per (qualcuno)” means to have a romantic crush (often secret or not serious yet). “Lei” can mean “her” or the formal “you” (to a woman), depending on context. You can swap the person: “una cotta per lui / per te / per Maria”.
target_language_example: Credo che Marco abbia una cotta per lei.
native_language_example: I think Marco has a crush on her.

additional_notes: A feminine noun: (una) cravatta. Used with clothing verbs like indossare (“to wear”) and with colors/adjectives: una cravatta gialla, una cravatta nuova. Often refers to a necktie worn with a shirt, especially for work or formal situations.
target_language_example: Devo mettere una cravatta per la riunione.
native_language_example: I have to wear a tie for the meeting.

additional_notes: Means a choice you make after thinking about options. Often used with the verb "prendere" (to make/take): "prendere una decisione" = "to make a decision". You may also see it in passive form: "Deve essere presa una decisione" = "A decision must be made."
target_language_example: È una decisione difficile, ma dobbiamo prenderla oggi.
native_language_example: It’s a difficult decision, but we have to make it today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to do/take”): fare una doccia = “to take a shower.” With reflexive forms (farsi una doccia), it means the same and emphasizes that the subject takes the shower themself: Mi faccio una doccia / Si è fatto una doccia. Often used with time expressions like ogni giorno (“every day”).
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra, faccio una doccia veloce.
native_language_example: After the gym, I take a quick shower.

additional_notes: Used when you mean a single question. Common in situations like class, meetings, customer service, or interviews: “Ho una domanda” (“I have a question”). With verbs like fare/porre/chiedere: “fare una domanda” = to ask a question; “porre una domanda” = to pose a question (more formal).
target_language_example: Scusi, ho una domanda: a che ora chiudete?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: what time do you close?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "una" = "a/an" (feminine singular) and "donna" = "woman". Used to talk about any (unspecified) woman. Contrast: "la donna" = "the woman"; plural "delle donne" = "some women" / "women" (in general, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con una donna molto simpatica al mercato.
native_language_example: I spoke with a very nice woman at the market.

additional_notes: Used when shopping or talking about quantities. "Una dozzina" means "a dozen" (12) and is followed by "di" + the item (often plural): "una dozzina di uova", "una dozzina di biscotti". You can also say "una dozzina d’uova" (di + uova).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi dà una dozzina di uova, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a dozen eggs, please?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to talk about “a/one family” in general or an unspecified family. For a specific one, you’d typically use “la famiglia” (“the family”).
target_language_example: Ha una famiglia numerosa.
native_language_example: He/She has a big family.

meaning: a family to take care of; family responsibilities.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has responsibilities toward their family (supporting them, providing for them, looking after them). The structure “a cui + verb” means “to whom/which + verb,” so literally it’s “a family to think about,” but the natural sense is “a family to look after.” Often used to remind someone to be careful or responsible.
target_language_example: Non posso trasferirmi all'estero: ho una famiglia a cui pensare.
native_language_example: I can’t move abroad: I have a family to take care of.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has many people in their family, often implying many children or siblings. You can change the article depending on context (e.g., "ho una famiglia numerosa" = I have a big family; "vengo da una famiglia numerosa" = I come from a big family).
target_language_example: Vengo da una famiglia numerosa: siamo in sette.
native_language_example: I come from a big family: there are seven of us.

additional_notes: Used for a social event or celebration. Often followed by “di …” to say what kind of party/celebration it is (una festa di Halloween = a Halloween party) or “a casa di …” / “a casa sua” to say where it is (una festa a casa sua = a party at his place). You can also use it for holidays/feast days (es. una festa nazionale = a national holiday).
target_language_example: Stasera c’è una festa: vuoi venire con me?
native_language_example: There’s a party tonight: do you want to come with me?

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun to talk about one slice/portion of something, especially cake, bread, pizza, etc. The noun after di usually has no article: una fetta di torta, una fetta di pane. Plural: due fette di…
target_language_example: Prendo una fetta di pizza, grazie.
native_language_example: I’ll have a slice of pizza, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one single slice of bread (often from a loaf). With amounts, you may also see: "due fette di pane" (two slices). Often appears with food verbs like mangiare (to eat), tagliare (to cut), and spalmare ... su (to spread ... on).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo una fetta di pane con marmellata.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have a slice of bread with jam.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering pizza by the slice. "Una fetta" means "a slice" (a portion cut from a larger pizza). Common with verbs like "mangiare" (to eat), "passare" (to pass/hand), and "servirsi" (to serve oneself/take).
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere una fetta di pizza ciascuno?
native_language_example: Can we each get a slice of pizza?

additional_notes: "Figlia" means "daughter"; "una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Used when saying someone has a daughter: "Ho una figlia" = “I have a daughter.” To specify her name, you’ll often see "che si chiama..." or "chiamata..." (feminine to match "figlia").
target_language_example: Abbiamo una figlia di cinque anni.
native_language_example: We have a five-year-old daughter.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often used with verbs like fare una foto (take a photo), scattare una foto (snap/take a photo), and farsi fare una foto (have someone take a photo of you). You can specify the subject with di (una foto di Roma = a photo of Rome) or the person/thing being photographed with a (ha scattato una foto alla mia casa = he took a photo of my house).
target_language_example: Mi fai una foto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject of a photo (the person/thing shown). Often followed by a noun or a possessive phrase: “una foto di mia nonna”, “una foto di sua madre”.
target_language_example: Hai una foto di tuo fratello sul telefono?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your brother on your phone?

additional_notes: Use "una" because "fotografia" is feminine. "di" means "of" here, showing who is in the photo. "mia nonna" means "my grandmother/grandma" ("mia" agrees with the feminine noun "nonna"). Often used with "solo/solamente/soltanto" to mean you have only one photo.
target_language_example: Vorrei incorniciare una fotografia di mia nonna.
native_language_example: I'd like to frame a photo of my grandma.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a sentence” in everyday Italian (a complete unit with a subject/verb), especially in learning contexts: *capire una frase*, *leggere una frase*. It can also mean “a phrase/wording” (how something is expressed), often with qualifiers like *una frase del genere* (“a phrase/sentence like that”).
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere l’ultima frase, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat the last sentence, please?

meaning: a day (often emphasizing what the day was like or how it was spent).
additional_notes: Common with adjectives to describe the day (una giornata bella/calda/fredda/orribile/speciale). Also used in phrases like “prendere una giornata libera” = to take a day off. Can refer to a specific day (e.g., Monday) or a day in general.
target_language_example: Domani sarà una giornata lunga, quindi vado a dormire presto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow will be a long day, so I’m going to bed early.

meaning: 'a big' / 'a great' (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Una" is the feminine singular form of "a" and must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., "una grande famiglia", "una grande sorpresa"). "Grande" can mean physical size ("big") or importance/quality ("great"), depending on context. The masculine form is "un grande".
target_language_example: È stata una grande idea.
native_language_example: It was a great idea.

meaning: a letter (a written message, usually on paper).
additional_notes: Used for a physical letter you write, send (spedire/inviare), receive (ricevere), and read (leggere). It often takes an indirect object: scrivere una lettera a qualcuno (to write a letter to someone) / scrivere a qualcuno una lettera. Distinguish from "una mail/un'email" (an email).
target_language_example: Ti mando una lettera domani.
native_language_example: I'll send you a letter tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” + a person’s name to indicate the recipient of the letter: “una lettera a Judy” = “a letter to Judy.” Often appears with verbs like scrivere (to write), consegnare (to deliver), and spedire (to send).
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera a mia nonna ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my grandma last night.

additional_notes: Used when saying who a letter is from. With places, it can mean a letter sent from that place (e.g., “una lettera da Boston”). Often follows verbs like ricevere (to receive), leggere (to read), arrivare con (to arrive with).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una lettera da mia nonna ieri.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my grandmother yesterday.

additional_notes: Use it for (1) a teaching session (a lesson/class/lecture): “una lezione di storia”, “tenere una lezione su…”; and (2) a life lesson or a harsh experience that teaches you something: “La vita mi ha dato una lezione.” Also in the expression “insegnare una lezione (a qualcuno)”, meaning “to teach someone a lesson” (often in a negative/punishing sense).
target_language_example: Domani ho una lezione di italiano alle nove.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an Italian class at nine.

additional_notes: Used for a line that doesn’t curve, especially in math, geometry, maps, or drawing instructions. Often follows verbs like "disegnare" (to draw) or "tracciare" (to trace). In questions like "La chiami una linea retta?" it can be sarcastic: “You call that a straight line?”
target_language_example: Per arrivare più velocemente, vai in una linea retta verso la piazza.
native_language_example: To get there faster, go in a straight line toward the square.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken language in general. After "una lingua" you can add an adjective: "una lingua difficile" (a difficult language), "una lingua nuova" (a new language). Also common in menus or settings: "Scelga una lingua" = "Choose a language."
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language.

additional_notes: Used for any language that is not your native language. Often appears with verbs like imparare (to learn), studiare (to study), parlare (to speak). With a specific language you’d usually say: una lingua + adjective (e.g., una lingua italiana/inglese) or simply the language name (l’italiano, l’inglese).
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera per lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to say something lasted a long time or covered a lot (e.g., una lunga discussione, una lunga passeggiata, una lunga assenza, una lunga storia). It agrees with the noun: masculine is “un lungo …” (un lungo viaggio), feminine plural “delle lunghe …” (delle lunghe giornate). In “È una lunga storia,” it can imply “it’s a long story” (often meaning the explanation is complicated).
target_language_example: Scusa se sono in ritardo: ho avuto una lunga riunione.
native_language_example: Sorry I’m late: I had a long meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone wrote/sent a letter that is long (often implying detailed or lengthy). The adjective *lunga* agrees with *lettera* (feminine singular), so it’s *una lunga lettera*.
target_language_example: Ti ho scritto una lunga lettera ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote you a long letter last night.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a (usually passenger) car/automobile. In other contexts, macchina can also mean “machine” (e.g., una macchina da caffè = a coffee machine), but in these examples it clearly means a car.
target_language_example: Scusa, dov’è parcheggiata una macchina qui vicino?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is a car parked nearby?

additional_notes: Used for a device that takes photographs. Often just "macchina fotografica" without the article. In everyday speech you may also hear "fotocamera". Plural: "macchine fotografiche".
target_language_example: Hai una macchina fotografica? Vorrei fare qualche foto.
native_language_example: Do you have a camera? I’d like to take a few photos.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hand.” Very commonly used to mean “help,” especially in the expression dare una mano (to give a hand/help): Dammi/Dagli una mano (Help me/him), Mi dai una mano? (Can you help me?). It can also be literal, meaning using one hand (con una mano). In games, una mano can mean a “hand” (of cards), depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano a spostare il tavolo?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand moving the table?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical or digital map. Often followed by "di/del/della" to specify what kind of map it is (e.g., "una mappa della città" = a city map; "una mappa del tesoro" = a treasure map).
target_language_example: Hai una mappa della città?
native_language_example: Do you have a map of the city?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single pencil. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an"; plural: "delle matite" (some pencils) or "matite" (pencils). Often paired with "una penna" (a pen).
target_language_example: Mi serve una matita per scrivere.
native_language_example: I need a pencil to write.

additional_notes: Refers to the piece of sports equipment used to hit the ball in baseball. With an indefinite article (una) it means “a baseball bat”; without the article (mazza da baseball) it can mean “baseball bat” in general.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato una mazza da baseball in macchina.
native_language_example: I left a baseball bat in the car.

additional_notes: Basic noun phrase: the indefinite article “una” + the feminine noun “mela”. Used when asking for or referring to one (unspecified) apple. Plural: “delle mele” (some apples) or “due/tre mele” (two/three apples).
target_language_example: Posso avere una mela, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have an apple, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who remembers things well (names, facts, dates, details). It often follows the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho una memoria molto buona". You can change the intensity: "una memoria buona" (a good memory), "una memoria eccellente" (an excellent memory), "una memoria pessima" (a terrible memory).
target_language_example: Ho una memoria molto buona per i nomi.
native_language_example: I have a very good memory for names.

additional_notes: Used for a single coin (loose change). It can also mean “a currency” in general when talking about money systems, but with “una” it usually means one physical coin.
target_language_example: Hai una moneta da un euro?
native_language_example: Do you have a one-euro coin?

meaning: a mosque (a Muslim place of worship).
additional_notes: Feminine noun: la moschea / una moschea. Plural: le moschee. Used with common verbs like andare in (to go to), pregare in (to pray in), visitare (to visit), vivere accanto a (to live next to).
target_language_example: C'è una moschea vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There is a mosque near the station.

additional_notes: Indefinite phrase: "una" = "a/one" (feminine singular) + "mucca" = "cow". Used to talk about an unspecified cow. For a male, use "un toro" (a bull).
target_language_example: C'è una mucca nel campo.
native_language_example: There’s a cow in the field.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form of “nuovo” used before a feminine noun (e.g., una nuova scuola). It can also stand alone as “a new one” when the noun is implied. If the feminine noun starts with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, or y, you usually use “una nuova” (not “un’ nuova”).
target_language_example: Domani apro una nuova attività.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m starting a new business.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying, needing, or choosing a new car. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), "nuova" means “new,” and "auto" means “car” (feminine in Italian).
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova auto per la famiglia.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new car for the family.

meaning: a new house; a new home.
additional_notes: Used when talking about building, buying, or moving into a different house/home. "Casa" can mean both the physical house and the idea of a home; "una" is feminine singular (“a”), and "nuova" agrees with "casa".
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova casa vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new home near work.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. "Macchina" often means "car" in Italian (short for "macchina (automobile)"). "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), and "nuova" agrees with the feminine noun "macchina". You can swap the adjective: "una macchina nuova" also means “a new car.”
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una nuova macchina quest'anno.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a new car this year.

meaning: a ball (a round object used for playing; also used for spherical shapes).
additional_notes: Literally “a ball.” Used for a physical ball you throw/kick (e.g., in sports). It can also describe something that is round/spherical: “La Terra è una palla blu” = “The Earth is a blue ball.”
target_language_example: Mi presti una palla per giocare in spiaggia?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a ball to play with at the beach?

additional_notes: Used to name a type of ball by adding the sport after da: una palla da basket (a basketball), una palla da golf (a golf ball). In Italian you can also say palla da + sport, or use a more specific sport name (e.g., palla da pallacanestro).
target_language_example: Hai una palla da tennis?
native_language_example: Do you have a tennis ball?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single word in general or in a text. In negative expressions it often means “a word” = “anything”: "non dire una parola" / "non mi ha detto una parola" = “don’t say a word / he didn’t say a word.”
target_language_example: Non dire una parola, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word, please.

additional_notes: Used with sports to mean a single game/match. With "fare" or "giocare" it means to play a game; with "guardare" it means to watch a game. In plural: "due/tre partite di baseball".
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo una partita di baseball al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing a baseball game at the park.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to take/go for”): fare una passeggiata = to go for a walk. It can be a short, relaxed walk (often in a park or around town). In the idiom La vita non è una passeggiata, it means “Life isn’t easy” (literally, “Life isn’t a walk in the park”).
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo una passeggiata in centro.
native_language_example: After dinner we go for a walk downtown.

meaning: a break; a pause (a short rest).
additional_notes: Used for a short rest from an activity (work, walking, cooking, etc.). Common with verbs like fare una pausa (to take a break), prendersi una pausa (to take a break for yourself), and dare una pausa (to give someone a break / let them rest). It can also mean a pause in speaking or action.
target_language_example: Facciamo una pausa di dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Let’s take a ten-minute break.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a pen. With the indefinite article "una" (feminine singular), it means “a pen”; the plural is "delle penne". Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "prendere" (to take), and "prendere in prestito" (to borrow).
target_language_example: Mi presti una penna, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, meeting, lesson, etc. wasn’t useful or worth doing. Often follows “è stata” (it was) or “è” (it is): “È/È stata una perdita di tempo.”
target_language_example: Aspettare qui senza informazioni è una perdita di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting here with no information is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified individual (“someone”), or to describe someone’s character with an adjective (e.g., "una persona gentile" = a kind person). With "frequentare una persona" it often means “to date/see someone.” You may also see it in structures like "una persona chiamata ..." (“a person named ...”).
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who speaks English.

meaning: “a person who …” (used to describe someone by what they do/are).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that defines or describes someone: una persona che + verb (e.g., fuma, disegna, è…). It’s singular; plural is “delle persone che” / “persone che.” Often used for general statements and definitions.
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli bene inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a person who speaks English well.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character (honest, trustworthy). Often with verbs like essere (to be), considerarsi (to consider oneself), or conoscere qualcuno come… (to know someone as…).
target_language_example: Mi fido di lei: è una persona onesta.
native_language_example: I trust her: she’s an honest person.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una + feminine adjective piccola) to describe something small in size, amount, or importance (e.g., una piccola sorpresa, una piccola somma, una piccola busta). With some nouns it can imply “just a little” in a polite or minimizing way (e.g., asking for a tip: Una piccola mancia?). The masculine form is "un piccolo".
target_language_example: Posso avere una piccola informazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a little bit of information, please?

additional_notes: Means a pistol/handgun (a small gun). The article changes with gender/number: un/una (a), la (the), delle pistole (some pistols). Often used with verbs like comprare (to buy), possedere (to own), dare (to give).
target_language_example: Non voglio avere una pistola in casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a gun at home.

additional_notes: Used to order or choose food. With "andare" (e.g., "A me va una pizza"), it means "A pizza works for me / I'd like a pizza."
target_language_example: Per me, una pizza margherita, grazie.
native_language_example: For me, a margherita pizza, please.

additional_notes: Literally “a girl.” In everyday speech, especially with verbs like avere (“to have”), it often means “a girlfriend” (a romantic partner): Ho una ragazza = “I have a girlfriend.” In other contexts (vedo/conobbe/una ragazza), it usually just means “a girl/young woman.”
target_language_example: Ho una ragazza, si chiama Chiara.
native_language_example: I have a girlfriend; her name is Chiara.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase on its own: it normally needs an adjective after molto (e.g., una ragazza molto timida/giovane/simpatica). Ragazza means “girl/young woman.” Molto is an intensifier meaning “very.”
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto una ragazza molto simpatica alla festa.
native_language_example: I met a very nice girl at the party.

additional_notes: Used for social networks/messaging apps when someone asks to add you as a friend/connection. Common verbs: mandare/inviare una richiesta di amicizia (to send a friend request), accettare/rifiutare una richiesta di amicizia (to accept/decline).
target_language_example: Ti ho mandato una richiesta di amicizia su Facebook.
native_language_example: I sent you a friend request on Facebook.

meaning: an answer; a reply (to a message/request).
additional_notes: Used for both answering a question and replying to an email/message or giving an official response. Common with verbs like avere (to have): “Hai una risposta?”, dare (to give): “Mi dia una risposta”, mandare (to send): “mandare una risposta”. You can add adjectives to specify the type: “una risposta definitiva” (a final/definitive answer).
target_language_example: Mi può dare una risposta entro domani?
native_language_example: Can you give me an answer by tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used for a container, usually made of cardboard, wood, or plastic. Often followed by “di” to say what’s inside or what it contains: “una scatola di mele” = “a box of apples.” You can also describe it with adjectives like “piena di …” (full of …): “una scatola piena di mele.”
target_language_example: Puoi mettere questi biscotti in una scatola?
native_language_example: Can you put these cookies in a box?

additional_notes: Used literally for the animal. It can also be used as an insult or to say someone looks/behaves like a monkey (often childish and can be offensive). Common patterns: "sembra una scimmia" (he/she looks like a monkey), "si comporta come una scimmia" (he/she behaves like a monkey), "imitare una scimmia" (to imitate a monkey).
target_language_example: Non fare la scimmia: smettila di imitarmi!
native_language_example: Don’t act like a monkey: stop imitating me!

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to forgive a mistake or allow someone to try again. Often appears with verbs like dare (“to give”) and meritarsi (“to deserve”). It changes with the indirect object pronoun: dagli/dalle/gli dia una seconda occasione = “give him/her a second chance.”
target_language_example: So che ho sbagliato, ma ti chiedo una seconda occasione.
native_language_example: I know I made a mistake, but I’m asking you for a second chance.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or refer to a single chair. Often appears with verbs like "dare" (to give), "portare" (to bring), and "sedere/siedere" (to sit).
target_language_example: C'è una sedia libera vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: There’s a free chair near the window.

meaning: a series of; a number of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a sequence/collection of things,” often translating naturally as “a number of.” Very common with “tutta una serie di” = “a whole series of / all sorts of.”
target_language_example: Devo fare una serie di telefonate prima di partire.
native_language_example: I have to make a series of phone calls before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (“for a week”) or a point in time in the future (“in a week”). Often appears with prepositions like “in una settimana” (in/over the course of a week) and “fra/tra una settimana” (in a week, from now).
target_language_example: Resto qui per una settimana.
native_language_example: I'm staying here for a week.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single cigarette. With verbs like "fumare" (to smoke), "accendere" (to light), and with items like "un accendino" (a lighter). In requests you’ll often hear: "Posso avere una sigaretta?" (Can I have a cigarette?).
target_language_example: Scusa, hai una sigaretta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a cigarette?

meaning: a solution; a way to solve a problem.
additional_notes: Used for an answer or practical way to fix/resolve a problem (“trovare una soluzione” = to find a solution). Also used for a possible option/approach (“una soluzione migliore” = a better solution). Feminine noun: la soluzione / una soluzione; plural: le soluzioni.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo una soluzione insieme.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a solution together.

additional_notes: Used to say something is surprising to a specific person or group: “una sorpresa per noi/lui/lei”. It can also mean you have a surprise intended for someone: “Ho una sorpresa per te”.
target_language_example: Ho una sorpresa per te: domani partiamo presto!
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you: tomorrow we’re leaving early!

additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately or loosely: it’s similar to X, but not exactly X. Very common in spoken Italian. It can also soften what you’re saying (making it less direct). Usually followed by a noun: "una specie di test", "una specie di crisi".
target_language_example: È una specie di scusa, ma non mi convince.
native_language_example: It’s kind of an excuse, but it doesn’t convince me.

additional_notes: Used when you want a reason or clarification for something. Often followed by "per" (for) to explain what it’s about: "una spiegazione per ciò" / "una spiegazione per il suo errore". "Hai una spiegazione?" is a common way to ask "Do you have an explanation?"
target_language_example: Puoi darmi una spiegazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me an explanation, please?

additional_notes: Used when talking about seeing a streak of light in the night sky (a meteor). Often said as an exclamation when you spot one: “Guarda, una stella cadente!” You can use it with “vedere” (to see) and “mai” (ever): “Hai mai visto…?”
target_language_example: Ieri notte abbiamo visto una stella cadente.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a shooting star.

additional_notes: Means "a story" when talking about something told or read (a tale, an anecdote). It can also mean "a history" when referring to the past of a person, place, or country. Plural: "storie".
target_language_example: Mi racconti una storia?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a story?

additional_notes: Used to describe a story (spoken or written) that is engaging or catches your attention. Common with verbs like raccontare (to tell) and leggere (to read). Agreement: una storia (feminine singular) + interessante (same form for masculine/feminine singular).
target_language_example: Vuoi sentire una storia interessante?
native_language_example: Do you want to hear an interesting story?

additional_notes: "Studentessa" is the feminine form of "studente". Use "una" before a singular feminine noun starting with a consonant sound (e.g., una studentessa). To talk to someone directly: "Sei una studentessa?" = "Are you a student?"
target_language_example: Una studentessa cerca il professore.
native_language_example: A (female) student is looking for the professor.

meaning: “a cup of” (a cupful of a drink or ingredient).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a quantity measured in cups, especially in recipes (“una tazza di riso”) and when ordering drinks (“una tazza di caffè”). With ingredients you can often also say “una tazza *d’*…” before a vowel (e.g., “una tazza d’acqua”).
target_language_example: Vorrei una tazza di tè, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Common in everyday requests and orders. Use it with verbs like voglio (I want), mi piacerebbe (I’d like), ordinare (to order), and versare (to pour). You can change the article: una tazza di caffè (a cup), due tazze di caffè (two cups), la tazza di caffè (the cup). In many cafés you might also hear just un caffè for an espresso.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una tazza di caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a cup of coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering a drink. Common with polite requests like (Mi) dia / Datemi… per favore (“Please give me…”) and with offers/questions like Vuoi/Volete…? or Vorresti/Vorreste…? (“Would you like…?”).
target_language_example: Potrei avere una tazza di latte caldo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a cup of warm milk, please?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for offering or talking about a drink. Often used with verbs like preparare (to prepare), portare (to bring), versarsi (to pour oneself), and with offers/questions like Vuoi una tazza di tè? (Do you want a cup of tea?).
target_language_example: Dopo cena, prendo sempre una tazza di tè.
native_language_example: After dinner, I always have a cup of tea.

additional_notes: Used to say who the caller is. "Da" means “from” (the source/origin of the call). Often used with pronouns: "una telefonata da lui/lei" (“a call from him/her”). In speech you may also hear "ho ricevuto una telefonata da…" (“I got a call from…”).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una telefonata da mia madre ieri sera.
native_language_example: I got a call from my mother last night.

additional_notes: Noun phrase: the indefinite article "una" (a/an) + feminine singular noun "tigre". Used when talking about a tiger in general or an unknown tiger. In questions like "Ha mai visto..." it often means "Have you ever seen...".
target_language_example: Ho visto una tigre allo zoo.
native_language_example: I saw a tiger at the zoo.

additional_notes: Used for a sweet cake (e.g., banana cake, Christmas cake). Common patterns: "una torta alla ..." (a ...-flavored cake, like banana), "una torta di ..." (a ... cake, often for an occasion or style, like Christmas), and "tagliare una torta in due" (to cut a cake in half).
target_language_example: Per il suo compleanno ho comprato una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For her birthday I bought a chocolate cake.

additional_notes: Medical term. Often used with: “fare una trasfusione di sangue (a qualcuno)” = “to give someone a blood transfusion” (passive is very common: “A Tom è stata fatta…”), and “servire/essere necessaria una trasfusione di sangue” = “to need a blood transfusion.”
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente, gli hanno fatto una trasfusione di sangue.
native_language_example: After the accident, they gave him a blood transfusion.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for time off from work/school for rest or travel. Often used with verbs like fare (to take/go on) and avere bisogno di (to need): fare una vacanza, avere bisogno di una vacanza. Plural: vacanze.
target_language_example: Quest’estate voglio fare una vacanza al mare.
native_language_example: This summer I want to take a vacation at the seaside.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something is genuine or truly has a quality: una vera amica (a true friend), una vera festa (a real party). It’s the feminine form of the adjective vero; compare: un vero amico (masculine), una vera amica (feminine), dei veri amici / delle vere amiche (plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una vera pizza napoletana.
native_language_example: I’d like a real Neapolitan pizza.

meaning: a life; a lifetime; (figuratively) ages/a long time.
additional_notes: Often used literally to talk about someone’s life ("una vita lunga", "una vita difficile"). It can also mean “a whole lifetime” in phrases like "i risparmi di una vita" (“a lifetime’s savings”). In a figurative sense, it can mean “a very long time,” especially with time expressions: "sembra passata una vita" (“it feels like ages since…”).
target_language_example: Non ci vediamo da una vita!
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in ages!

additional_notes: Common phrase meaning a life that is generally happy and satisfying. Used with verbs like vivere (to live), aver(e) avuto (to have had), and condurre (to lead): vivere/condurre una vita felice. In questions, it can ask whether someone’s life overall has been happy.
target_language_example: Spero che tu possa vivere una vita felice.
native_language_example: I hope you can live a happy life.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens (frequency). It commonly goes after the verb: "Ci vediamo una volta al mese". Related patterns: "una volta alla settimana" (once a week), "due volte al mese" (twice a month).
target_language_example: Faccio la spesa una volta al mese.
native_language_example: I do the grocery shopping once a month.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with weekly frequency. It often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier for emphasis. You can change the time unit: una volta al giorno (once a day), una volta al mese (once a month), una volta all’anno (once a year).
target_language_example: Vado in piscina una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the pool once a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (often after the verb): “Ci vediamo una volta alla settimana.” Similar patterns: “una volta al giorno” (once a day), “due volte alla settimana” (twice a week).
target_language_example: Vado in palestra una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym once a week.

meaning: once in a while; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally, not regularly. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also go after the verb (e.g., "Gioco a tennis una volta ogni tanto").
target_language_example: Una volta ogni tanto prendo un caffè al bar.
native_language_example: Once in a while I have a coffee at the café.

additional_notes: Used when asking for coffee or tea to specify one cube of sugar. Often said on its own as a polite request (e.g., at a bar/café). Plural: "due zollette di zucchero" (two sugar cubes).
target_language_example: Nel tè vorrei una zolletta di zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: In my tea I’d like a sugar cube, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group: “una di + plural noun/pronoun.” Common with demonstratives (una di queste/quelle…), numbers (una di queste due…), or pronouns (una di loro/voi). For masculine you usually say “uno di” (one of).
target_language_example: Vorrei una di queste magliette, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like one of these T-shirts, please.

meaning: “one of us” (referring to a female person).
additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl belongs to your group (“one of us”). With a male person or a mixed group, you typically use **uno di noi**. You can also specify a smaller group: **una di noi due** = “one of the two of us.”
target_language_example: Giulia è una di noi, quindi può venire alla riunione.
native_language_example: Giulia is one of us, so she can come to the meeting.

meaning: “one of those” (referring to a feminine singular thing).
additional_notes: Used to point to or refer back to a specific type of item already known from context (something you can see, or that was mentioned). It’s the feminine singular form; for masculine you’ll hear “uno di quelli”.
target_language_example: Posso provare una di quelle scarpe?
native_language_example: Can I try on one of those shoes?

meaning: "one of these" (referring to a feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to pick one item from a group indicated by "queste" (“these”, feminine plural). It agrees with the noun: for masculine you say "uno di questi"; for plural “some of these” you can say "alcune di queste" (fem.) / "alcuni di questi" (masc.). Often used in questions like "Hai mai usato una di queste?" (“Have you ever used one of these?”).
target_language_example: Posso provarne una di queste?
native_language_example: Can I try one of these?

meaning: "one of these before" / "one of these earlier".
additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether someone has previously seen/received one item from a group you’re pointing to or talking about (often with "Hai/Ha mai visto...?"). It agrees with the noun: "una di queste" (feminine singular), but you may also hear "uno di questi" (masculine singular) or plural versions ("alcune di queste", etc.). "Prima" here means "before/earlier" (not "first").
target_language_example: Ho già comprato una di queste prima, ma questa è più grande.
native_language_example: I’ve already bought one of these before, but this one is bigger.

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask someone to become part of your group or activity. "Unirsi" is a reflexive verb (unirsi = to join), and it’s often followed by "a" + a person/group: unirsi a noi/voi/loro. Common in requests with verbs like chiedere/convincere/invitare or in offers like "Può unirsi a noi".
target_language_example: Vuoi unirti a noi per cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to join us for dinner?

additional_notes: Used to say something is meant as humor or not serious: "È/era solo uno scherzo" (“It’s/it was just a joke”). Often appears in the negative to stress seriousness: "Non è uno scherzo!" / "Questo non è uno scherzo" (“This is no joke”).
target_language_example: Scusa, era solo uno scherzo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was just a joke.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying/getting a gift for someone’s mother. Note that "sua" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the thing owned: "madre"), so the context tells you whose mother. "Uno" is used because "scialle" starts with s + consonant (sc-).
target_language_example: Ho comprato uno scialle per sua madre.
native_language_example: I bought a shawl for his/her mother.

additional_notes: Used for a male person; for a female scientist, say “una scienziata”. “Uno” is used (instead of “un”) because “scienziato” starts with “s” + consonant (sc-). Often used with “diventare” (to become) or “essere” (to be).
target_language_example: Da grande, vuole diventare uno scienziato.
native_language_example: When he grows up, he wants to become a scientist.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s job or identity is “a writer,” often with adjectives (e.g., uno scrittore famoso) or with “di…” to add details (e.g., uno scrittore di grande talento). For a female writer, say “una scrittrice.”
target_language_example: Mio fratello è uno scrittore e lavora da casa.
native_language_example: My brother is a writer and works from home.

additional_notes: Used for looking briefly at something (dare uno sguardo = to take/have a look) or for an exchanged look between people (scambiarsi uno sguardo). It can also mean a meaningful look (a look can “say” something).
target_language_example: Puoi dare uno sguardo a questo documento?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this document?

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity isn’t useful or worth doing. Often appears with extra details like “prezioso” (precious) or “e sforzi” (and effort). You can use it after “è/era/è stato” (it is/was/it was) to judge a situation: “È uno spreco di tempo.”
target_language_example: Aspettare senza informazioni è uno spreco di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting with no information is a waste of time.

meaning: a lifestyle; a way of living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s habits and daily choices (diet, exercise, work-life balance, etc.). Often followed by an adjective like sano/salutare (healthy), sedentario (sedentary), frenetico (hectic), semplice (simple), oppure “di + noun” (e.g., uno stile di vita da atleta = an athlete’s lifestyle).
target_language_example: Da quando lavoro da casa, ho cambiato il mio stile di vita.
native_language_example: Since I started working from home, I’ve changed my lifestyle.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a foreigner” (a person from another country): *Tom è uno straniero.* It can also be used more figuratively as “a stranger/someone unfamiliar” to a situation or idea: *La morte resterà per lui sempre uno straniero* (“death will always remain something unfamiliar to him”). Masculine singular; the feminine is *una straniera*.
target_language_example: Per uno straniero è facile perdersi in questa città.
native_language_example: For a foreigner, it’s easy to get lost in this city.

meaning: a tool; an instrument (especially a musical instrument).
additional_notes: Used for something you use to do a task (a tool) or to achieve a goal (“a powerful tool”, “a tool for improving…”). With music verbs like "suonare" it usually means a musical instrument: "suonare uno strumento" = "to play an instrument". It can also be used figuratively to mean someone is being used as a means to an end (and can sound insulting, e.g. "uno strumento inutile").
target_language_example: Questo sito è uno strumento utile per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: This website is a useful tool for learning Italian.

meaning: "a tool with which" / "a tool to (do something) with".
additional_notes: Used to introduce the tool or instrument needed to perform an action. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aprire, tagliare, riparare). "Con cui" literally means "with which" and refers back to the tool (strumento).
target_language_example: Mi serve uno strumento con cui tagliare questa corda.
native_language_example: I need a tool to cut this rope with.

additional_notes: "Uno" is the masculine singular indefinite article used before words starting with s + consonant (st-, sp-, sc-, etc.), z, ps, pn, or gn (e.g., "uno studente"). With "a" (to) you often see the combined form "a uno" → "ad uno" in more formal/written Italian, though in everyday speech "a uno studente" is also common.
target_language_example: In casa con me vive uno studente di medicina.
native_language_example: A medical student lives in my house with me.

additional_notes: Used when you mention an uncle and then add extra information about him with a relative clause starting with che (= who/that), e.g. where he lives or where he works. It can also be plural: due zii che…
target_language_example: Ho uno zio che parla tre lingue.
native_language_example: I have an uncle who speaks three languages.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate a single item/person from a group: "uno dei piaceri" = "one of the pleasures". It agrees with the gender/number: feminine "una delle"; plural "alcuni/e dei/delle". Often followed by a plural noun, sometimes with "che" + verb (e.g., "uno dei miei amici che vive a Roma").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei migliori ristoranti della città.
native_language_example: This is one of the best restaurants in the city.

additional_notes: Used to single out one animal/person/thing from a known group: uno/una dei/delle + plural noun (e.g., uno dei cani, una delle ragazze). Often followed by a verb describing what that one did.
target_language_example: Uno dei cani è scappato dal giardino.
native_language_example: One of the dogs escaped from the yard.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or plural idea to mean a single member of a set: uno dei ristoranti (one of the restaurants), uno dei guanti (one of the gloves). It often takes a possessive: uno dei miei/tuoi/suoi (one of mine/yours/his/hers/theirs). With feminine singular: una delle; plural: alcuni/e dei/delle.
target_language_example: Vorrei uno dei tuoi consigli.
native_language_example: I’d like one of your pieces of advice.

meaning: “one of (the) …” (one person/thing out of a group).
additional_notes: Used to single out one element from a plural group: uno dei ragazzi (one of the boys), uno dei nostri (one of ours/one of our people), uno dei ristoranti (one of the restaurants). It’s often followed by a superlative: uno dei migliori / più popolari (one of the best / most popular). The verb that follows typically agrees with “uno” (singular): Uno dei nostri è morto.
target_language_example: Luca è uno dei miei amici più cari.
native_language_example: Luca is one of my closest friends.

meaning: "one of my" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say a single person/thing from your group: uno dei miei + plural noun (libri, cani, denti, amici, zii). It agrees with what “one” is: uno (masc. singular); una delle mie (fem. singular). You can also use plural: due dei miei = “two of my.”
target_language_example: Uno dei miei vicini parla inglese.
native_language_example: One of my neighbors speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group that belongs to someone. The possessive "suoi" agrees with what is owned (masculine plural): "uno dei suoi libri" = one of his/her books. For feminine plural, use "una delle sue" (e.g., "una delle sue amiche"). For masculine singular, "uno dei suoi" often appears as part of a longer phrase (e.g., "uno dei suoi studenti").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei suoi film preferiti.
native_language_example: This is one of his/her favorite movies.

additional_notes: Used to pick a single person or thing from a plural group: uno di voi (one of you), uno di questi libri (one of these books), uno di quei cani (one of those dogs). It agrees in gender/number with what you mean: uno di (masc. singular), una di (fem. singular); also: alcuni/e di (some of).
target_language_example: Posso prendere uno di questi dolci?
native_language_example: Can I take one of these desserts?

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to a group (often to show solidarity, protection, or shared identity). It can also be used with suspicion/accusation depending on context (e.g., pointing out a traitor or someone who’s secretly part of the group). You can specify the group: "uno di noi due" = "one of the two of us."
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è uno di noi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s one of us.

meaning: "one of those" (one item/person from a group already understood).
additional_notes: Used to point to or refer back to a specific thing (or person) among several, usually something visible or already mentioned. Agree it with what you mean: uno di quelli (masc. sg.), una di quelle (fem. sg.), uno di quelle (mixed/unspecified group; often for people), una di quelli (rare).
target_language_example: Non so quale scegliere: prendo uno di quelli in vetrina.
native_language_example: I don’t know which one to choose: I’ll take one of those in the window.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single item within a group of things that are present, shown, or understood from context. It often appears with questions like Avete mai…? (“Have you ever…?”) and with Ti serve… (“You need…”). You can change gender/number depending on what you’re referring to: una di queste (feminine), uno di quelli / una di quelle (“one of those”).
target_language_example: Vuoi provare uno di questi?
native_language_example: Do you want to try one of these?

additional_notes: Used to say that eggs are what you eat at breakfast time. Very common with verbs like mangiare (to eat) and adverbs like di solito/sempre/spesso (usually/always/often). You can also add other foods: pancetta e uova per colazione (“bacon and eggs for breakfast”).
target_language_example: Oggi voglio uova per colazione.
native_language_example: Today I want eggs for breakfast.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun starting with most consonants: usare il dizionario, usare il computer, usare il microonde. With nouns starting with s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y (and some others), Italian usually uses "lo" instead: usare lo smartphone, usare lo zaino. In questions you may also see the pronoun added: usarlo = to use it (masc.).
target_language_example: Posso usare il tuo telefono per un minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use your phone for a minute?

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for talking about being careful and responsible with spending. Often used with dovere (devo/devi/deve/dobbiamo/dovete/devono) to express advice or obligation.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo usare il denaro con saggezza se vogliamo risparmiare.
native_language_example: We have to use money wisely if we want to save.

additional_notes: Means using someone else’s computer (suo/sua = “his/her” depending on who owns it). Often appears after verbs like lasciare (“to let/allow”) or permettere (“to permit/allow”), e.g., “Mi ha lasciato usare il suo computer” = “He/She let me use his/her computer.” You can swap in other possessives: usare il mio computer (my), usare il tuo computer (your), usare il loro computer (their).
target_language_example: Posso usare il suo computer per cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Can I use his/her computer for five minutes?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (la macchina = the car, la ragione = reason). In real speech you’ll often change the article depending on the noun: usare il (masc. sing.), usare i/le (plural), or use a possessive: usare la sua… (“use his/her…”).
target_language_example: Posso usare la tua penna?
native_language_example: Can I use your pen?

meaning: to get out of here / to leave this place.
additional_notes: Used to say you want (or need) to leave the current place. Often expresses urgency or frustration, especially with adesso (“now”) or with an exclamation. It can be used literally (leaving a room/building) or more generally (leaving a situation).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo uscire da qui prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here before it’s too late.

additional_notes: "Utilizzare" means "to use" (a bit more formal than "usare"). "Il suo" is a polite/formal way to say "your" (to one person, Lei), and it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Often used with verbs like "permettere" or "lasciare" to ask/allow someone to use a computer.
target_language_example: Potrei utilizzare il suo computer per un minuto?
native_language_example: Could I use your computer for a minute?

additional_notes: Form of the verb andare (“to go”): va = “he/she goes” or “you (formal) go.” Use va a + place/destination (va a Boston, va a casa) or va a + activity/event (va a un picnic, va a caccia). Often answers “Where is he/she going?” (Dove va?). In questions, Italian may omit the subject: Va a Londra? = “Is he/she going to London?”
target_language_example: Va a scuola in bici.
native_language_example: He/She goes to school by bike.

meaning: “(He/she) goes to work on foot” / “(He/she) walks to work.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone commutes to their workplace by walking. You can change the subject: io vado…, tu vai…, lui/lei va…, noi andiamo…, voi andate…, loro vanno…. "A piedi" means "on foot" (by walking).
target_language_example: Io vado a lavorare a piedi quando fa bel tempo.
native_language_example: I walk to work when the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Formed from andare (to go): va = 'he/she goes' + a scuola = 'to school'. Used to talk about someone attending school or going there regularly (often as part of a routine). You can add how someone goes (in autobus, in bicicletta) or when (il sabato). For 'I go to school' you say: vado a scuola.
target_language_example: Mia sorella va a scuola ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My sister goes to school every day.

meaning: (He/she) goes to school on foot (walks to school).
additional_notes: A common way to say someone goes somewhere walking. Structure: andare + a + place (a scuola) + a piedi (“on foot”). Change the verb for the subject: vado/va/andiamo/vanno a scuola a piedi.
target_language_example: Io vado a scuola a piedi quando fa bel tempo.
native_language_example: I walk to school when the weather is nice.

meaning: “goes to work by/in (a means of transport)”.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone commutes to work. After "in" you usually add the transport: "in treno" (by train), "in auto / in macchina / in automobile" (by car). With a specific vehicle you often use "con" instead (e.g., "va al lavoro con la mia macchina").
target_language_example: Lei va al lavoro in autobus ogni mattina.
native_language_example: She goes to work by bus every morning.

meaning: “Is it okay if…?” / “Is it alright if…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or check if something is acceptable. Often followed by a verb phrase (usually in the present tense): “Va bene se entro adesso?” = “Is it okay if I come in now?” You can also use it without “se”: “Va bene se…?” is a very common spoken pattern.
target_language_example: Va bene se pago con la carta?
native_language_example: Is it okay if I pay by card?

meaning: "Do you feel like going to the theater?" / "Would you like to go to the theater?"
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to ask if someone is in the mood for doing something: "Ti va di…?" (to you), "Le va di…?" (formal to you), "Vi va di…?" (to you all). Literally it contains "va" (goes), but the meaning is "feel like" rather than physical going.
target_language_example: Ti va di andare a teatro domani sera?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going to the theater tomorrow evening?

meaning: "(he/she/it) goes to" (a place/country) or "goes by" (a means of transport).
additional_notes: “Va” is the 3rd person singular of *andare* (to go). With **in** it’s used for destinations like **countries** (*va in Croazia, va in Francia*) and some **places/buildings** (*va in una moschea*). It’s also used for **how someone goes somewhere** with certain transport words: *va in bicicletta* = “goes by bike.” (For many specific places like cities you often use *a*: *va a Roma*.)
target_language_example: Marta va in Italia a luglio.
native_language_example: Marta goes to Italy in July.

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go). "Va" is the present tense for lui/lei/Lei (he/she/you-formal). Often followed by a purpose: "per + infinitive" (per leggere = to read) or "a + infinitive" (a studiare = to study). You can swap the subject: "Io vado in biblioteca", "Noi andiamo in biblioteca".
target_language_example: Oggi va in biblioteca per studiare.
native_language_example: Today he/she goes to the library to study.

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go): va = “goes” (also used for “you go” in the formal Lei form). In everyday use it often means attending church services (e.g., on Sundays, at Christmas), not just physically entering the building. For “I go,” say vado in chiesa; for “we go,” andiamo in chiesa.
target_language_example: Mio padre va in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My dad goes to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to ask if everything is going well in a situation or relationship (often with a rising tone), or to reassure someone that things are fine. Very common in everyday conversation; can be followed by a context like “a casa” (at home) or “tra noi” (between us).
target_language_example: Ehi, va tutto bene? Ti vedo un po’ preoccupato.
native_language_example: Hey, is everything okay? You look a bit worried.

additional_notes: Refers to holidays taken in the summer. Often used with possessives: le mie/le tue/le nostre vacanze estive. Common verbs: passare/trascorrere le vacanze estive (to spend your summer vacation).
target_language_example: Quest'anno le nostre vacanze estive saranno in Sicilia.
native_language_example: This year our summer vacation will be in Sicily.

additional_notes: "Vada" is the polite/formal command (Lei form) of andare (“to go”). With "a" it introduces the destination or purpose: vada a casa (“go home”), vada a parlare (“go and speak”). It can also appear after "Lasci che..." meaning “Let (him/her) go to…”.
target_language_example: Scusi, vada a parlare con il direttore, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please go speak with the manager/director.

meaning: "I'm going to" (to go to a place, or to do something).
additional_notes: Form of "andare" (to go): "io vado" = "I go / I'm going" + "a". Use it with a destination: "vado a casa" (I'm going home), "vado a Roma" (I'm going to Rome). Also used before an infinitive to say you’re going to do something soon or as an intention: "vado a spegnere la radio" (I’m going to turn off the radio). With activities, Italian often uses "andare a" + noun: "andare a pesca" (go fishing).
target_language_example: Scusa, vado a prendere un caffè e torno subito.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm going to get a coffee and I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to bed / going to sleep, often with a time (alle dieci = at 10). It’s the 1st-person singular of andare a letto (to go to bed).
target_language_example: Sono stanco: vado a letto.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Used to say you go to school (often as part of your daily routine, or today specifically). Italian often drops the subject, so you can simply say “Vado a scuola.” You can add details like time/frequency (oggi, quasi sempre) or transportation (in macchina, in bici).
target_language_example: Domani vado a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I go to school on foot.

meaning: “I go to school on foot” / “I walk to school.”
additional_notes: Common way to say how you get to school. Uses the present tense of andare (vado = I go). Italians often omit the subject pronoun (Io) because it’s already clear from the verb. You can swap scuola for other places (es. vado al lavoro a piedi = I walk to work).
target_language_example: Quando fa bel tempo, vado a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: When the weather is nice, I walk to school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb andare in the 2nd-person singular (tu). It can be a command ("Vai a casa!" = Go home!) or a question ("Vai a scuola...?" = Do you go to school...?). After "vai a" you often see: (1) a place (vai a casa, vai a scuola) or (2) an infinitive to mean "go and + verb" (vai a vedere, vai a parlare).
target_language_example: Vai a prendere un caffè e poi torniamo.
native_language_example: Go get a coffee and then we’ll come back.

additional_notes: Imperative form addressed to one person (tu): a common way to tell someone to go to bed (often a child). Related questions use the same phrase: “A che ora vai a letto?” = “What time do you go to bed?” You can add time words like adesso/ora (now) or in orario (on time).
target_language_example: Dai, è tardi: vai a letto!
native_language_example: Come on, it’s late: go to bed!

additional_notes: Used to tell someone ("tu") to go and talk to a person. Common in suggestions/questions (Perché non vai a parlare con...?) and in direct instructions (Vai a parlare con...). You can also say "vai a parlare con" + a title/role (il mio collega, la mia collega).
target_language_example: Se hai un problema, vai a parlare con la responsabile.
native_language_example: If you have a problem, go talk to the manager.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action or experience is worth the effort, time, or cost. Often followed by an infinitive: "Vale la pena + verb" (e.g., "Vale la pena vedere..."). In the negative: "non vale la pena" = "it’s not worth it".
target_language_example: Non vale la pena discutere adesso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth arguing right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth doing, especially in passive forms like “vale la pena di essere visitato/tradotto/considerato” = “it’s worth visiting/translating/considering.” The subject is the thing that’s worth it. You’ll often see it with a past participle that agrees in gender/number: visitato/visitata/visitati/visitate.
target_language_example: Quel film vale la pena di essere visto al cinema.
native_language_example: That movie is worth seeing at the cinema.

additional_notes: Used to recommend a place or attraction, meaning the visit is worth the time/effort. Very common pattern: “Vale la pena + infinitive” (e.g., visitare, vedere, provare). You can also use it with a noun: “Vale la pena la visita?” = “Is the visit worth it?”
target_language_example: Se sei in città, vale la pena visitare il centro storico.
native_language_example: If you’re in town, it’s worth visiting the old town.

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions like “Come vanno le cose?” to ask how a situation is progressing or how someone is doing in general. Pronouns can be added depending on who you’re asking: “Come ti vanno le cose?” (to you), “Come vi vanno le cose?” (to you all / formal you), “Come le vanno le cose?” (formal you).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come ti vanno le cose ultimamente?
native_language_example: Hi! How have things been going lately?

additional_notes: Combination of pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you” (to you all, or formal to one person), **lo** = “it” (masculine singular; often stands for a whole idea). Common with verbs like **dire** (to tell), **chiedere** (to ask), **assicurare** (to assure): *Ve lo dico* = “I’m telling you (it).” If the "it" is feminine, you’ll hear **ve la** instead.
target_language_example: Ve lo spiego domani.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you tomorrow.

meaning: "to you" + "of it/them" or "from there" (a common pronoun combo).
additional_notes: It’s a combination of two pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you (plural)” (also used as the polite **you** in some regions), and **ne** = “of it/of them/some” or “from there/away.” Very common with **andarsene** (“to go away/leave”): *Ve ne state andando?* = “Are you leaving?” It’s also used with quantities: *Ve ne posso prendere di più* = “I can take more (of them/it),” and with *una* meaning “one (thing)” in *Ve ne dobbiamo una* = “We owe you one.”
target_language_example: Ve ne posso dare due, se volete.
native_language_example: I can give you two of them, if you want.

meaning: an old friend; a long-time friend.
additional_notes: Used for someone you’ve known for a long time (often from the past, e.g., school/childhood). Here vecchio means “long-standing/previous,” not necessarily “elderly.” Often appears with possessives: il mio/un vecchio amico.
target_language_example: Ho incontrato un vecchio amico al bar dopo tanti anni.
native_language_example: I ran into an old friend at the café after many years.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: vedere + il ("the"). It’s the infinitive “to see” plus the definite article. With other articles: vedere lo (before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y), vedere l’ (before vowel), vedere i/gli (plural). After a conjugated form of vedere, you may still use the article: “vedo il mare” = “I see the sea.”
target_language_example: Da qui puoi vedere il Duomo.
native_language_example: From here you can see the cathedral.

meaning: “to see the” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used when the direct object is feminine singular (la + noun), e.g., la foto, la luna, la mia famiglia. The verb “vedere” changes with the subject (vedo, vedi, vede, vediamo, vedete, vedono). For “to see her/it” as a pronoun, Italian uses “vederla” (one word) instead of “vedere la”.
target_language_example: Da qui possiamo vedere la città.
native_language_example: From here we can see the city.

additional_notes: Used when asking if someone can make out/spot anything inside a place or container. "lì dentro" means "in there/inside (that place)" and often points to something at a distance or not easily visible. Often used with "puoi/potete" (can you) or "riuscire a" (manage to).
target_language_example: Riesci a vedere qualcosa lì dentro, con tutta questa oscurità?
native_language_example: Can you see anything in there, with all this darkness?

additional_notes: Used when pointing out a specific light source (often at a distance) that is visibly unsteady or blinking. You’ll often hear it in questions with "può/puoi" (can you) or "riesce/riuscite" (are you able to), e.g., asking if someone can make it out or spot it.
target_language_example: Riesci a vedere quella luce tremolante in fondo alla strada?
native_language_example: Can you see that flickering light at the end of the street?

additional_notes: Common everyday way to talk about watching a movie, whether at home (TV/streaming) or at the cinema. Uses the verb "vedere" (to see/watch) + "un film" (a movie). You can change the article and add adjectives: "vedere il film" (watch the movie), "vedere un film francese" (watch a French movie).
target_language_example: Stasera voglio vedere un film con te.
native_language_example: Tonight I want to watch a movie with you.

additional_notes: Used when the object is understood from context and is feminine singular (la): usually "la sua casa" (his/her/your house), "la sua macchina" (his/her/your car), etc. It’s a shortened form of "vendere la sua + noun" or "vendere la sua" = "sell theirs" (feminine singular thing). If the noun is masculine, you’d use "vendere il suo" (e.g., "vendere il suo appartamento").
target_language_example: Non voglio vendere la sua casa senza parlarne prima con lei.
native_language_example: I don’t want to sell her house without talking to her first.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "vendere" (to sell) + the possessive "la sua" (his/her/its, feminine singular) + "auto" (car).
